#32. Sutton's predictions v Waffle the Wonder Dog and his owner, Simon

Manchester City have won their first seven Premier League games of the season but will their 100% record survive Saturday's trip to an improving Aston Villa side?

"Villa have beaten City in this fixture in each of the past three years under Unai Emery," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"They will fancy it this time too - they are seven unbeaten in all competitions, and flying at the moment."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week eight, he takes on Waffle the Wonder Dog and his owner Simon, who is played by actor James Merry.

Waffle's After School Club, featuring James and Waffle, is available on CBeebies and BBC iPlayer right now, with lots of fun after-school adventures for families to enjoy together.

Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

Waffle's After School Club often ends in mayhem and mess despite the best efforts of Simon. How will the pair get on at predictions?

Waffle is a talking dog whose adventures on his show often end in chaos for Simon and the rest of his family.

Like most dogs, he loves football - or at least loves chasing one.

"I am an enthusiastic baller," Waffle told BBC Sport. "But technically my best position is right-back... on the sofa.

"My favourite player is the England captain, Harry Kane-9, and I'm a Liverpool fan so my all-time hero is Kenny Dog-leash.

"My fur is red and I am a poodle so of course I support the Reds, or Liverpoodle as I like to call them - they never walkies alone."

Waffle loves watching Liverpool on Match of the Day. "It's past my bedtime on a Saturday night, so instead I like to watch them on iPlayer after an early Sunday morning garden wee."

In real life, actor James Merry is an Aston Villa fan, who has a long connection with the club.

"I grew up in Sutton Coldfield, north Birmingham, and just about everyone is Villa there," he told BBC Sport.

"My mum's side of the family are all fans - my great-aunt was a season-ticket holder for about 40 years and my nan lived most of her life on Witton Road, which is just round the corner from Villa Park.

"My first job was there too - when I was 16 I worked in the catering department serving burgers on matchdays.

"Then, during the summer I had to clean every executive box and polish all the cutlery and make sure everywhere was properly stocked.

"We had the run of Villa Park and I was like a kid in a candy shop."

Chris Sutton, Waffle the Wonder Dog and James Merry were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

So, I am up against a talking dog this week? I'm not sure that improves my chances of winning - I've been barking up the wrong tree with my predictions all season anyway.

One of us has got to beat AI though - I've been reading about it in the news and it is not just with football scores where it seems to be taking over.

This game is a tough one to call, though. It is going to be very tight.

Nottingham Forest can't score. That's their issue, and they have only managed five goals in their first seven league games.

It did make me laugh when I read that Forest boss Oliver Glasner had got Chris Wood to give advice to the other strikers about finishing - why not just play Wood then?

Ipswich are still bottom of the league table based on my predictions (see bottom of page) but they ran Manchester City close in the end last week and are doing better than everyone expected, myself included.

I like what Tractor Boys boss Gary O'Neil is doing there, and they already have three league wins from seven games - the last time they were in the Premier League, in 2024-25, they only managed four all season.

Forest are second bottom and could really do with getting something here, and Ipswich haven't drawn a game yet - so that's what I am going for.

James' prediction: The director of Waffle, Tim Hopewell, is a Forest fan and I have gone for them here. I like the way they play. 1-2

Villa have hit a bit of form and seem to be getting back to the level they were at last season.

They had another good win in the Champions League this week, but then you'd expect them to beat Viking pretty comfortably.

Emery's side played well against Newcastle last week too but I thought Newcastle were a bit too gung-ho, and paid the price. City are a lot more streetwise.

City are going to slip up eventually this season but the fact they have lost on their past three visits to Villa Park actually makes me think it will be different this time.

Erling Haaland is fit too, which will obviously help. With all the heat on the club at the moment it could just turn out to be one of those seasons where they continue on this incredible run.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: Ross BARKley gets two for Villa, but Erling HOWLand to score a hat-trick. Sorry, dad! 2-3

James' favourite Villa players: The early to mid-'90s was the time when I was getting into football so Dean Saunders and Dalian Atkinson were my heroes, and Paul McGrath as well. That was certainly a golden era - I need to mention Shaun Teale too, because he was always a favourite. I think I had his name on the back of a shirt.

Now? I think most people of my generation would pick John McGinn. He is an absolute club legend for what he has done for us down the years and my shirt now has got McGinn on the back.

James on Villa's season: We seem to be picking up some form after another slow start. It looks like Johan Manzambi is going to be pivotal for us this season and Nicolas Jackson has started well, he has stuck a few away.

This might sound a bit bonkers but, with Emery's record in Europe, I am more excited about that than what we might do domestically, because I think we might go deep in the Champions League.

James' prediction: Because we are weak at the back at the moment I think City will score two or three, but we are looking lively up front and could do the same. I've got to be partisan - and I am also going to go for a barnstormer. 3-2

Arsenal were so ugly in the way they beat Nottingham Forest last weekend, but were a lot easier on the eye in the midweek draw with Bayern Munich.

They are going to be without the injured Bukayo Saka for this game, but they are at home and they should still have too much for Everton.

Everton will make it tough for them, of course, but I am not sure how they will hurt the Gunners.

James' prediction: Arsenal are just a machine at home. 3-1

Sometimes these kind of games can be quite cagey, with both teams afraid of being beaten, but here I feel like Coventry and Fulham will have a go and there could be a few goals flying in.

Coventry have a bit about them going forward, especially when they use their pace on the counter-attack, but they are also a bit vulnerable defensively.

Because of that, I am going to go with Fulham. They got their first win of the season against Hull last week and they are definitely capable of getting another one here.

James' prediction: My old man is a Coventry fan - he was born and bred in Cov but then married a Brummie and moved to Birmingham so he was always on a hiding to nothing trying to get me to support Coventry. He won't be happy because I've gone for a draw here. 1-1

Tottenham are not in Europe either, of course, but they don't look like they are going to be challenging at the top of the table the way Xabi Alonso's side are.

People keep saying how Chelsea's attack is so good, but their 2-0 win over Everton last time out was their first clean sheet of their campaign in the league, and that side of thing still needs to improve.

Spurs, meanwhile, do seem to be getting better, albeit slowly.

It was a big result for them to beat Coventry on Monday but they have an awful record at Stamford Bridge, with only one win there in the Premier League era.

I don't see them getting anything this time, either.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: Archie GrayHOUND will score a couple for Spurs, but I'm backing Chelsea because I was a fan of Didier DOGba back in the day. 4-2

James' prediction: Chelsea carry so much attacking threat. 3-1

Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage's future appears to be in some doubt but his critics seem to have forgotten that they are 14th in the table, when the Eagles finished 15th last season under Oliver Glasner.

Yes, Palace had a heavy defeat at Brighton last week and it doesn't help it was at the hands of their big rivals, but it is not like Sage has got one point from his first seven games. They are leaking a few goals, but there are reasons for that.

There has been huge change at Selhurst Park in recent months, with some key players leaving, especially at the back. Others have stayed but are still unhappy, and Sage has had a lot to contend with.

Palace play in Turkey on Thursday night which won't help their preparation for this game, but I still feel like they will get something against Newcastle.

There has been a lot of change at the Magpies too, but the thing that worries me most about Matthias Jaissle's side is that they are so open.

'Chaotic' was the word I used to describe them against Aston Villa last week.

Villa are always very well structured in the way they play but they got chances against Newcastle just by persevering with their build-up play.

If Newcastle don't get their press quite right again here, then Palace will cause them problems too - I definitely don't see this game as being one where defences are on top.

James' prediction: Both teams will be happy just to get a point on the board. 1-1

Although Hull have made a great start I still think they will get relegated.

We know they will have a go at Brentford, but the Bees will be too smart for them.

Brentford would have beaten Liverpool last week without Yehor Yarmoliuk's stupid red card. If they can keep 11 men on the pitch, they will win this one.

James' prediction: Brentford are such an amazingly well-run club with what they have achieved. They are going to be too strong for Hull. 1-2

Liverpool have an extra 48 hours to prepare for this game - they played Villarreal at home on Tuesday, while Brighton are away in the Czech Republic on Thursday.

I don't think it will make any difference, though, because the way that the Seagulls play, I am expecting them to go to Anfield and win.

This has the makings of a great game but, while Liverpool have had a couple of good results, I am still not convinced by them.

Andoni Iraola's side are a work in progress with a tendency to empty their midfield and that means Brighton can hurt them.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: A win for the Liverpoodles! 2-1

James' prediction: This is going to be close. Brighton are playing really well but I am still going to back Liverpool at Anfield. 2-1

After all the stick I got from Manchester United fans for saying they would get thumped by Leeds last weekend, it turns out I was only a few days out - it happened against Como instead.

United have been poor all season, though. That's why I went for them to be despatched like that - the 5-0 scoreline was a little bit tongue in cheek, but the point I was making has been proven this week.

The Bruno Fernandes criticism of Michael Carrick just adds to the problems United have at the moment - it is as if they are at the stage now where you have to pick who you want to back.

I don't know where United go from here but I am going for a Bournemouth win - the Cherries will attack them, and their great recent record at Old Trafford will give them confidence too.

If United do lose, I think it will be the end for Carrick because I just don't see how he survives this.

Even if United get something from this game, it is still just a matter of time before he goes.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: BARKus Rashford to win this for United. 2-1

James' prediction: Carrick really needs a win and they are at home so I think he will get it. 2-0

Sunderland have killed me this season because I just don't seem to be able to predict them at all.

The Black Cats are bottom of the table after losing four league games in a row and their boss Regis le Bris has a few problems to solve.

One of them is having European football that stretches their squad - they are away in Poland on Thursday - but at least they will have striker Brian Brobbey back from injury at the weekend.

After last weekend's loss at Bournemouth, Sunderland defender Nordi Mukiele suggested the Black Cats may have become "arrogant", but I don't see that outburst being as damaging as the ones by Manchester United players recently.

Still, things like that are better kept inside the dressing room because some of Mukiele's team-mates will be asking him if he was calling them arrogant.

I was never arrogant as a player, by the way, but people used to call me far worse than that in my day.

Maybe we will see a reaction from Sunderland here, but I still don't see them winning this because Leeds are battle-hardened and are a good team too.

They weren't at their best against Manchester United but still picked up a point, and they won't be leaving the Stadium of Light empty-handed.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: I like the sound of LEADS United and I love playing with George the cat (who lives next door) but 11 Black Cats means it's hide-behind-the-sofa time! 0-2

James' prediction: I had a look at all the fixtures and I thought one of them has got to finish 0-0, hasn't it? I have gone for this one. 0-0

#33. Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope

Raye is the 35th winner of the Mercury Prize, which was established to recognise albums that push the boundaries of music

Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.

A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the Â£25,000 prize.

"I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."

It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.

Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband?

"Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist."

Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient.

Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians.

Released in March, the album went straight to the top of the UK charts and won glowing reviews from critics.

Rolling Stone magazine praised its "old-school show-tune razzle-dazzle [and] big-band swing frills", while the NME raved that, "Raye's agile voice has never sounded so good, and her pen has never been so strong".

In the BBC's own review, it was described as an "eccentric, kitsch and dramatic" record where Raye "unapologetically goes for broke".

Raye comes out swinging on her new album, This Music May Contain Hope

But the album almost never happened. Two years ago this week, the singer's car was stolen, along with all of her songwriting notebooks and demos.

Although they were eventually recovered, it delayed work on This Music May Contain Hope by almost a year.

Looking back, she was philosophical about the delay.

"I was distraught. I was very worried, but you know, it all turned out great.

"Every little slip, every little accident, every little thing, it creates the path that you take.

"And it's easy to spend time wishing things were the other way. But right now, I certainly do not."

The star performed the big band number I Hate The Way I Look Today during the Mercury Prize ceremony

Established in 1992, the Mercury Prize was envisaged as an antidote to the commercially-focused Brit Awards, recognising albums that moved music forwards, without recourse to fashion or trends.

Of the last 35 winners, 20 have been debut albums - from artists including Arctic Monkeys, Suede and Franz Ferdinand.

Many people have mistakenly assumed it is a prize for first albums - but this year's shortlist included only two: Dove Ellis's heartfelt and delicate Blizzard, and Jade's That's Showbiz, Baby.

'I'm speechless': Olivia Dean on making UK chart history

In the run-up to this year's ceremony, Olivia Dean had been the bookmakers' favourite for her second album, The Art of Loving.

An easy-going, soulful collection of love songs, it had already been named album of the year at the Brit Awards and the Mobos, and is widely expected to earn the singer a Grammy nomination in the same category next month.

Speaking backstage, the singer said she was overwhelmed by the success.

"I don't think I've processed it yet, to be honest," she said. "I feel like I'm still in this crazy whirlwind of it all.

"And maybe, when I take a break over Christmas, I'll reflect on the sofa."

Other nominees included the rapper Kojey Radical, Geordie jazz act Knats, and former Little Mix star Jade - who was the first ever X Factor winner to receive a Mercury nomination.

The shortlist also included the charity compilation album Help (2), recorded in aid of Warchild, which featured new music and cover versions by artists such as Olivia Rodrigo, Damon Albarn, Depeche Mode and The Last Dinner Party.

The tracklist also included nine former Mercury Prize winners: Arctic Monkeys, Young Fathers, Wolf Alice, Pulp, Sampha, Portishead's Beth Gibbons, Arlo Parks, English Teacher and Ezra Collective.

Last year, the prize was won by Newcastle singer-songwriter Sam Fender, who donated his Â£25,000 winnings to grassroots music venues, helping to support up-and-coming songwriters around the UK.

Man United were humiliated in the league phase of the Champions League and the Como boss says it could have been even worse

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Joshua Zirkzee's stoppage-time consolation goal did nothing for Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick's hopes of holding on to his job, but it was suitably irritating for his opposite number in Italy on Wednesday.

Cesc Fabregas saw his Como team race into a 4-0 lead over Man United in the third game of the league phase of the Champions League, and admitted that he was responsible for his team stepping back with a comfortable lead and allowing the visitors to get a futile goal back.

The 4-1 defeat in Lombardy means that United have won just two of their 11 matches in all competitions since Carrick was appointed on a permanent basis, against Sabah in the Champions League and against promoted Ipswich Town in the Premier League.

United conceded three times in the Ipswich match and were earned three points by a Bruno Fernandes hat-trick. The captain made his view on Carrick's tactics clear after the match. While Carrick moved to shift some of the blame back on his players, Fabregas assumed the blame for Como's change of attitude with the game already won.

Speaking after the match, Fabregas said: "I regret the last ten minutes because I was the one who told the team to slow down the tempo because there's another match and at 4-0 we could manage things a little.

"I told the players to stop running and stay in the middle and that is something I regret because I'm the first to always push them to fight until the end.

"Their goal hurt me because we dropped our intensity and dropped our defensive block, but it was my fault."

Sign up for our free live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest matches, their kick-off times, channels and streams

Como were in total control thanks to a Nico Paz double and goals from Anastasios Douvikas and Jacobo Ramon, but Zirkzee's goal in the first minute of time added on was exactly the kind of thing managers hate.

Another of those things is being informed that players are openly questioning their tactics in post-match interviews, which delivered Carrick's final insult of a difficult night in the Champions League.

United captain Bruno Fernandes told TNT Sports that Man United weren't brave enough on the ball, and that it was a decision made by Carrick and his staff to play in that way.

Fernandes has been criticised for making his grumbles public and his candid answers helped add to the mounting pressure on his head coach.

Carrick's sacking is regarded by some pundits as a matter of time, with Eddie Howe, Julian Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte among the favourites to be the next Manchester United manager.

Fabregas himself is also listed at surprisingly short odds.

Chris is a Warwickshire-based freelance football writer specialising in West Midlands football, the Premier League, the EFL and the J.League. He is the author of the High Protein Beef Paste football newsletter and owner of Aston Villa Review. He supports Coventry Sphinx.

#37. JOSEPH DINNAGE: How our national debt of £3TRILLION could pay for ten million new homes or 67 million nurses - if only Labour would get a grip

Published: 23:00 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 02:53 BST, 23 October 2026

This week, it was confirmed that our national debt has now surpassed the dismal milestone of £3trillion. Such an enormous number is hard to comprehend, so let me put it in context.

With £3trillion, we could build ten million new homes, 30 HS2 rail networks or 2,000 Shard skyscrapers.

In terms of public services, we could fund the NHS for 12 years – which you might think is remarkably brief – and pay for all English state schools, universities and colleges for two generations.

If the entire £3trillion was spent in just one year, it could pay for the salaries of 60 million teachers, 67 million nurses or 33 million doctors.

As the economist Liam Halligan pointed out yesterday, between April and September this year, we spent £61billion on servicing our national debt. That is an unconscionable waste. That figure – frittered away in just six months – is equivalent to our annual defence budget, nearly all the education budget or the annual GDP of Slovenia.

We must get to a point where we are able to spend sensibly on defence, schooling and healthcare without further indebting ourselves.

But this is not a priority for the Government, apparently, which seems intent on making the cost of the British state even more expensive.

In his lachrymose 'keynote address' to the Labour Party's annual conference last month, the Prime Minister announced a slew of policies that will cost a fortune.

If the entire £3trillion was spent in just one year, it could pay for the salaries of 60 million teachers, 67 million nurses or 33 million doctors

Joseph Dinnage, senior press officer at the Prosperity Institute, puts the mind-boggling sum of £3trillion into context

Take his flagship 'National Care Service'. This is going to be modelled almost exactly on the ruinously expensive and inefficient National Health Service, which is projected to cost almost £300billion this financial year.

The Chancellor, John Healey, is expected to announce tax rises on banks and online retailers in next week's Budget. But targeting our few remaining profitable industries with pernicious tax hikes is kryptonite for economic prosperity. It is naked short-termism that will harm future growth. Why is the Government implementing such damaging policies when our economy is on the brink of catastrophe? Of course, the answer is political.

As we saw with Keir Starmer's ill-fated Welfare Bill – which failed to cut benefits spending by only £5billion due to rebellion from socialist backbenchers and ultimately torpedoed his premiership – the Labour Party is ideologically incapable of promoting economic growth. It exists to spend other people's money.

But the time for playing politics with our economy is over. One more major economic shock could push us into defaulting on our debt.

Imagine, God forbid, another pandemic was to strike us next month. The virus hits, but the state has no money to pay workers to sit at home, let alone subsidise their lunches.

Businesses go under left, right and centre, causing an unemployment crisis. But there's no money to spend on out-of-work benefits, and there is nothing for a slew of Nightingale hospitals, leaving people to die at home. Britain would be bust. Just as we did under another Labour Chancellor named Healey in 1976, we would have to go cap in hand to the International Monetary Fund for a loan.

Which is why Labour must face down its most toxic elements and start saving money. And, let's be clear, this is easy. All that's needed is political will.

A good place to start is the NHS. Right now, we have a healthcare system that is one of the worst performing among developed nations.

Life expectancy has flatlined and healthy life expectancy has fallen by two years in the past decade, yet NHS spending keeps rising.

With the right reforms we can keep healthcare 'free at the point of use', as socialists demand, and save money in the long run by freeing up the private healthcare sector and keeping Britons healthy.

The Chancellor, John Healey, is expected to announce tax rises on banks and online retailers in next week's Budget

Specifically, we at the Prosperity Institute recommend the reintroduction of tax relief on private medical insurance – lowering the cost of private healthcare for individuals and employers.

This would ease the burden on the NHS while also boosting growth in the wider healthcare industry. Polling commissioned by the Prosperity Institute also found that the public, who have seen for themselves the chaos and filth of state-run hospitals, is on board. Almost 60 per cent of participants preferred systematic healthcare reform to continuing to throw billions at a broken system.

The soaring cost of the welfare state must also be addressed. In the current financial year, Britain is projected to spend almost £335billion on social security and welfare benefits – roughly 10.6 per cent of GDP.

As Mail readers will know, over four million adults in England and Wales claim personal independence payments (PIP), £37.3 billion is spent annually on social housing, and according to the Office for National Statistics over half the population of the UK (53.3 per cent) are net recipients of the state, rather than net contributors.

Fixing this requires root-and-branch reform. The Timms Review, launched last year to assess the system, found that PIP is unfit for purpose and requires reform.

As my colleague, economist Emmanuel Igwe, has argued, PIP does not need reform, it needs to be scrapped and replaced with a properly means-tested, robustly assessed alternative.

It is controversial, yes, but the state pension should also be re-examined. While Andy Burnham has announced that he will 'reform' the triple lock in 2030, he is only doing so to fund other extortionate schemes.

The Centre for Policy Studies think tank calculates that since its introduction in 2010, this shameless bribe to pensioners has cost £78billion and will continue to rise with inflation.

Similarly, unfunded, gold-plated public sector pensions in the NHS and education sector carry liabilities in the hundreds of billions.

The Government is making promises to public servants it will never be able to fulfil. A brave government would do well to switch the remaining public sector pensions to defined contribution schemes, like millions of working taxpayers in the private sector.

Of course, to get working-age people off benefits and into jobs, those jobs need to exist in the first place. Increased red tape, business taxes and a minimum wage soaring far ahead of other earnings have shuttered businesses and made it uneconomic to hire.

We have worked out that by freezing the National Living Wage for five years – it is already hugely generous by global standards – Britain could create up to 600,000 new jobs for young people and contribute £2.4billion to the Exchequer.

This must also be accompanied by giving businesses the freedom to hire talented staff by repealing Angela Rayner's catastrophic Employment Rights Act.

Another great issue of our time is energy. Net Zero has cost us dearly, and though it has come far too late, it is welcome that Burnham has decided to amend some of the worst excesses of Ed Miliband's green madness by approving production at the Jackdaw gas field.

He must go further. We have found that Net Zero will add the equivalent of £1,400 a year to every British household's energy bills by 2030. By reversing this and making the most of the resources we have in the North Sea, Britain could generate an extra £13.4billion in investment. This is a no-brainer for any government serious about repairing the balance sheet.

The answers are staring Burnham and Healey in the face. If the Chancellor stands before the House on Wednesday and delivers yet more expensive tax rises and dodges tricky decisions, know this: he will be doing so out of political expediency – not because it's the right thing.

Joseph Dinnage is senior press officer at the Prosperity Institute.

#40. Bruno Guimarães had sleepless nights before Newcastle exit but hopes for same ‘love’ at Arsenal

Midfielder says there were a lot of tears as he said goodbye at St James’ Park but he is enjoying the remorselessness at his new club

For Bruno Guimarães, it was a time to show his steeliness, to fix his eyes on the prize – even if he knew it would surely mean them welling up. And then some. It was a tumultuous summer for the Brazil midfielder. A fine World Cup on a personal level was marred by a crucial penalty miss in the last-16 loss against Norway. Now he had the dream move lined up to Arsenal but it could not happen without breaking some hearts at Newcastle.

Guimarães admits he lay awake at night as the emotions swirled. How could he leave Newcastle, the club where he made so many connections and enjoyed so many highs after joining from Lyon in January 2022? There were the Champions League qualifications and, above all, the Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 that ended a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. On the other hand, how could he resist Arsenal and the prospect of competing regularly for the game’s top honours?

Sometimes, you simply have to take a deep breath and the plunge. Nobody wants to die wondering. Guimarães knew the Newcastle team was breaking up. Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali had gone to Barcelona and Tottenham. The manager, Eddie Howe, was at the end of the line and would also leave. Guimarães went through with the £75m transfer and nobody can say it has not worked out so far.

Arsenal felt he would provide a different element for them, different ways of unlocking defences, plus his trademark work rate and snarl. Guimarães has brought all of that. Already he has made a difference. He even gave a little back to Newcastle when he scored his first Arsenal goal at Sunderland in September, paving the way for a 2-0 victory. Two Premier League games later, he scored the winner at home against Leeds.

Guimarães almost got another vital goal on Wednesday in the Champions League tie at Bayern Munich only for Manuel Neuer to deny him with an outrageous save. That would have put Arsenal 2-1 up. The game finished 2-2, Arsenal fighting until the end and equalising through Declan Rice in the 82nd minute. Still, it has not been easy for Guimarães and he surely has Arsenal’s visit to Newcastle on 21 November circled in his diary. His greatest hope is that he can build the same relationships at his new club.

“It was not just hard to tell Eddie but to tell the owners and my teammates [about deciding to leave Newcastle],” Guimarães says. “But I think the club went to a new rotation; a lot of players left, as well. The gaffer left. It was tough because my connection with the club was unbelievable. I never felt so loved like the way I was at Newcastle. I hope I can have the same love here at Arsenal.

“It was hard for me to say bye. I remember when I said bye to the lads, I was crying. They were crying as well because we were a family there. I lost many, many nights of sleep because it was difficult for me, for my family. But sometimes in your life you have to make decisions and in my mind, I needed a new challenge. I wish Newcastle all the best because they were so nice to me. It is just time to move on and I’ve been enjoying my time here at Arsenal, as well.”

Guimarães is enjoying his burgeoning midfield partnership with Rice, not to mention Martin Ødegaard, who tends to be the most advanced of the trio. That said, there is plenty of fluidity between the positions. There is the sense that the manager, Mikel Arteta, is searching for the perfect balance.

“Declan can play – like me – as a No 6, No 8 or No 10,” Guimarães says. “The manager is still trying to get the best version of ourselves. Against Bayern, I played more as a No 6, Declan played more as a No 8. I enjoy playing with him a lot; with Martin, as well. We have been on a good run so far.”

Guimarães’ battles when he was at Newcastle against Rice have been well documented. He said Rice had messaged him as he prepared to sign for Arsenal, saying: “No more fights, now we’re friends.” Guimarães is the player you loathe when he is against you but love when he is in your ranks.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

What was the worst thing Guimarães said to Rice when they were in opposition? “It is difficult to say,” he replies with a smile. “I am like this when I play against teams. When we were playing against each other, I was not nice to him, he was not nice to me! Now we try to help each other on the pitch.”

Guimarães cannot believe how Neuer kept out his close-range header; the 40-year-old goalkeeper clawed the ball up against the crossbar and away. “He pulled off a miracle,” Guimarães says. “I asked him after the game: ‘How did you manage to save that?’ He said: ‘I don’t know. I just saved it!’ He’s unbelievable, one of the best keepers in the world. No matter how old he is, he is top.”

What Guimarães has seen with clarity is the remorselessness of the collective attitude at Arsenal; the insatiable will to win, which comes from Arteta. Next up for them is Everton at home on Saturday. Guimarães knows he is in the right place.

“The mentality of the club has changed a lot and Arteta shows this perfectly,” Guimarães says. “We don’t accept a draw at Bayern. We always want to win. That is the mentality that we go to the training ground with every day. Arteta is always a little bit addicted to videos and the way that he can make us feel better on the pitch. We have a top manager with a top mentality. We want to win everything possible.”

#41. Amber warning in place as Storm Austen hits parts of UK

An amber weather warning has come into force in parts of the UK as Storm Austen brings a swathe of powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday.

South West England is forecast to be worst hit by the storm which the Met Office warns could bring travel disruption, power cuts and a possible danger to life.

Wind gusts of 60-70mph, with 80mph in exposed locations, are forecast across Cornwall and parts of Devon, where the Met Office warning is in force until 10:00 BST.

Wind gust of 45-60mph are forecast more widely across most of England and Wales, where two less severe yellow warnings will be in force throughout Friday. A separate yellow warning will also cover part of Scotland, including Glasgow and Edinburgh, from 06:00 BST.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over while buildings could also potentially be damaged, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.

A number of schools are closed in the impacted areas with many others opening later than usual to avoid the strongest winds.

Train cancellations and speed restrictions are possible because of the increased danger of branches and trees blocking railways.

A number of ferry sailings have also been cancelled, including crossings between Pembrokeshire and Ireland.

Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.

As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.

That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.

The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph.

All schools in Jersey have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen.

Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.

Wind warnings have been issued ahead of Storm Austen's arrival on Friday

Closely following Storm Austen will be Storm Boelo, named by the Met Office on Thursday and set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend.

Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways.

The Met Office has issued yellow wind warnings for Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, valid on Saturday and lasting most of Sunday.

Gusts are forecast to reach 50-65mph widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations.

There could be some localised disruption with strong winds funnelling through the Central Lowlands for a time.

Transport disruption is expected and there may be some power cuts. Following recent spells of wet weather, there is an additional risk of some localised flooding.

Yellow wind warnings have been issued ahead of Storm Boelo's arrival over the weekend

It is not unusual to get storms one after another - in fact they quite often arrive in clusters.

A strong jet stream is needed to rapidly develop powerful wind storms. The process involved in creating such storms involves shifting warmer air northwards and cooler air southwards across vast areas of the Atlantic.

These temperature contrasts can provide a fertile environment for new low pressure systems to develop and if these subsequently get steered beneath a developmental area of a powerful jet stream, they can rapidly develop to create a new named storm with damaging winds.

The winter months of December, January and February typically produce the highest number of UK storms

Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer.

May is the only month with no named storms in the 11 years that storms have been named in the UK.

The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months.

This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.

In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

#71. Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds

Medics at el-Fasher's Saudi Hospital performed a Caesarean by phone light on the day it was bombed

A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.

UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.

The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.

Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.

Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.

The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.

"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.

"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."

The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.

Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.

In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.

But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.

UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.

The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.

A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan

Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past

Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.

Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.

Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.

The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.

In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.

The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.

The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.

On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.

The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.

But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.

They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.

"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.

Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.

"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."

That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.

The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.

Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.

According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".

In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.

He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.

Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.

The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.

After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.

Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) sounded the alarm.

"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, butâ¦ the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.

However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.

They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.

Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.

Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.

The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.

Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.

By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.

The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.

Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.

They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.

Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.

In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.

In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.

"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.

Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.

On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.

It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.

On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.

It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.

The burnt-out ruins of a building in a compound that housed a medical warehouse and dialysis centre in el-Fasher pictured after it was hit by a missile

The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.

"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.

Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.

The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.

The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.

The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.

"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," TÃ¼rk said.

Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.

Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.

"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.

The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.

"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."

He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.

They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.

"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.

A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.

The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

Maps and graphics by Miguel Roca-Terry, Jake Friend and Matt Mitchell-Camp

#72. Shola Ameobi: ‘I thought: how can I be most useful to Newcastle? Then the cog started turning’

From experiencing racism growing up in Newcastle to becoming a derby hero and now a member of the executive team, the former striker has been on a remarkable journey

“There were times where I feared for my life as a kid, being harassed and chased by different groups of people,” Shola Ameobi says. “There were situations where I had to sprint to get away from groups of lads who didn’t like me because of what I looked like.”

Ameobi is recalling growing up in Newcastle during the late 1980s and 1990s, having moved from Nigeria aged six. There were lots of moments like that.

“It was almost as if I had to hide myself to be able to do what I love to do,” he says. “It wasn’t a very nice feeling, having to worry about getting from A to B. It was just part of my world. I had to be more aware of my surroundings and what I was doing.”

Ameobi’s “A” was often the family home, situated within a few pitch lengths of Newcastle’s St James’ Park, and “B” was frequently the club’s base at the time in Benwell, where he would head for academy training.

“It built incredible resilience in me,” he says. “That really helped me in a sporting context in my career, but also as a person, understanding that, irrespective of what people thought of me, what really mattered was the value I put on myself.”

That young boy running in fear became the scorer of 79 goals in 397 appearances for Newcastle including seven against their local rivals, Sunderland. The likelihood is that some of those he fled from while wearing a club tracksuit subsequently cheered him.

Since July, Ameobi has been Newcastle’s head of corporate affairs, after seven years as the loans coordinator. His role is to ensure “we’re doing things that are valuable not only to us as a football club but to the region”.

He adds: “We want to make this club the heartbeat of this city. But by being the heartbeat of the city, it’s making sure we integrate well into everything the city is about, whether that’s civically, whether that’s through our sport or through our community engagement.”

Ameobi’s job switch followed the 100-day review conducted by the CEO, David Hopkinson. At the end of a preliminary discussion, Hopkinson told Ameobi to take the weekend to consider things. But Ameobi, while grateful for the “level of trust and commitment”, pushed back, wanting to consider what the role would look like in practice. Six months and plentiful discussions later, he accepted.

For Ameobi, the leap to an executive position was not as huge as it might appear. He started his previous role in the Mike Ashley days and built that department “from nothing”, he says. “That’s really helped me understand how to business-plan and build a team.”

Ameobi has been part of the Premier League’s Black participants advisory group since it formed in 2019. Its successes include implementing the No Room for Racism action plan in 2021 – this weekend marks the second of two match rounds this month dedicated to the initiative – and the pilot launch of the player to executive pathways scheme in 2022. That is designed to help those from underrepresented groups into executive roles and Ameobi was part of the initial seven-strong cohort.

“It gave me a really good framework,” he says. “It took us through, at a very high level, what the different streams of executive work look like, whether that’s finance, brand, the future of working, how organisations work. That gave me a little bit of confidence, if I’m honest, more than anything, to go: ‘Actually, a lot of the things I’m already doing translate into that world.’

“One of the biggest things was working in a pressurised environment, which is what I’ve done for 20 years, and learning how that can really help you in those moments when things get a little squirrelly, when they aren’t going as planned.”

Completing the programme fuelled a fire in Ameobi that had flickered for two decades. In November 2006, having struggled with a hip injury for several years, he had career-saving surgery. The resulting time out was “the start of my thought process beyond the football pitch”. Whether he would return to playing at his previous level, or at all, was uncertain. So, Ameobi’s thoughts turned to: “How can I best be useful to my teammates and this football club? That’s when the cog started turning.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“Football wasn’t always going to be there so who am I outside of the footballer? There were some really hard questions I had to answer during a very, very difficult time. There were some dark moments.”

Ameobi navigated those moments with the help of a psychologist and by leaning on his family. “I’ve always been fascinated with leadership, right from an early age,” he says. “My father was a leader of a church and he’s been the biggest influence of my life when it comes to leadership and how to lead well.”

He cites the late Sir Bobby Robson, who gave him his professional debut aged 18, and Alan Pardew, who managed him at Newcastle and Crystal Palace, as footballing influences. The former “still to this day has such an impact on the way I think about the game, the way I think about the person more than what you’re doing”, while the latter “used me to channel my leadership within the dressing room and wider squad to help him deal with some of the issues we were going through”.

Ameobi holds a master’s in strategic leadership and it is obvious at an event to celebrate the supporters’ group The Black Geordie Club that he is a natural with people. There is a presence to him, a warmth, that puts others at ease.

He is unrelenting in wanting to use his position to improve society. He grew up watching Andy Cole at Newcastle and memories of Tino Asprilla’s 1997 Champions League hat-trick against Barcelona bring the broadest of smiles. “That was the moment where time stood still. It was almost like I said to myself: ‘What’s wrong with you, Shola? You should be giving everything to be there.’

“You need to feel like you belong, you need to see yourself there, and that is so important when it comes to inspiration and people who aspire to be great in whatever sphere.

“It’s so important those who are in those positions give back and share their experience and share what helped them get to where they’re at. Being a young Black kid who has walked the walk throughout the club, from youth team to first team and now into this executive role, I want to show anything’s possible for anybody.

“Part of the reason I want to continue to push myself is because, yes, I want to be successful, but I want to show that anything’s possible if you’ve got the hunger, irrespective of what you look like and where you come from. I want to be an inspiration to the next generation.”

#73. Is Leicester boss Martin turning the Foxes' fortunes?

Russell Martin was appointed Leicester boss on a three-year deal in June

Leicester are at one of the lowest points in their history.

Sitting 10th in League One, it has been a spectacular decline.

A decade ago, they were reigning 5,000-1 Premier League champions and the toast of the world.

Five years ago, the Foxes lifted the FA Cup for the first time and were challenging for Champions League qualification.

Since then they have fallen fast with financial problems, points deductions and the drop to the third tier, leaving the club up for sale.

But back-to-back wins this week - for the first time since last November - have shown the shoots of recovery after a stuttering start.

This summer was a hard reset and, after three relegations in four years, have the Foxes found a way to recover under head coach Russell Martin?

Tuesday's 4-0 thumping of Bromley followed the 2-1 win over Doncaster which dampened the external noise.

Martin - a sometimes polarising personality with fans who have criticised his style and ability following a 17-game spell at Rangers last season - had been the target of anger following two wins in eight which left them 17th in League One and a point above the relegation zone.

Home defeats by Burton, Oxford and Peterborough were a world away from the Champions League quarter-final against Atletico Madrid in 2017.

That has little bearing internally at the club and BBC Sport can reveal the Foxes were working under a transfer embargo for five weeks in the summer.

It related to the EFL's Salary Cost Management Protocol (SCMP) with an independent Club Financial Review Panel agreeing future Premier League distributions within Leicester's SCMP calculation could not be used to increase their spending capacity.

It meant the club could not sign players until they brought money in, although it only disrupted the order of summer business.

Jeremy Monga and Abdul Fatawu were not sold until the middle of July and only after Monga left for Manchester City on 11 July were the Foxes able to bring in Conor Chaplin and Alex McCarthy five days later.

Four of the starting XI on Tuesday signed on deadline day and 66% of the players joined after the season started.

Leicester missed out on targets who were not willing to wait but Chaplin, McCarthy and Wes Burns were just three who were prepared to hold on to join Martin.

It is the relationships the head coach has built and something which has started to turn the tide at Seagrave.

Martin inherited a broken, expensive squad, which had lost the faith and connection with supporters and a dressing room which let egos get in the way and lacked work ethic.

In a different financial reality, it needed to be stripped back and, including loans and academy exits, 34 players left the club in the summer and 16 arrived.

Sources have told BBC Sport the atmosphere at the club has now markedly improved.

The Â£100m training ground is one of the best in the country - with a herb garden and golf course - but has been seen as part of the problem over the decline in standards.

Players have been allowed to become too comfortable but Martin has worked hard to change the culture and behaviours.

There is a blanket ban on mobile phones in the canteen and anyone breaking the rules is not fined, they run.

Players - and staff - have to run the length of the pitch and back in 35 seconds three times, with a 35-second break in between.

The same punishment is handed out for lateness, with Martin and his senior staff also adhering to it to set the standards.

Earlier this season players left tape and drinks at the swimming pool and were shown a picture the next day. The punishment was the same. Run.

King Power bought Leicester in 2010 from Milan Mandaric for Â£35m

There is an acute acceptance the club needs to show and not tell fans about progress.

Yet there is calm and a focus behind the scenes with the appointment of James McCarron as sporting director and Martin viewed as giving the club a strong leadership.

McCarron watches training most days and has a close working relationship with Martin.

Although, despite the positives, it is hard to ignore fan feeling towards the club and chief football officer Jon Rudkin in particular.

The frustration towards Rudkin, who has been at the club since 1998, has been constant for years.

His relationship with former chief executive Susan Whelan had broken down long before her departure a year ago.

Rudkin's policy of also not talking to the media - until this month - has been criticised.

He remained quiet during their plunge to League One and while that has been consistent - having not spoken to the press when Leicester were winning the Premier League - it has left an information vacuum and the club being unable to communicate efficiently to supporters.

That he finally addressed the fans in an interview with BBC Radio Leicester before defeat to Peterborough speaks volumes of the realisation and determination from the club to try to change - and the dire situation.

It was a positive step forward and internally there is a hope it will lead to more appearances, although there needs to be more substance.

"We do have to remember he saw us through the good times as well. He was in when it was all going fantastically," Foxes Trust co-chair Lynn Wyeth told BBC Sport.

"But do we know what he does all day, do we know if it's all his fault? That's a good question.

"It's all very well the fans targeting Russell and Jon but this all goes down to Top (Aiyawatt Srivaddhanaprabha, owner)

"It's pretty clear that Rudkin has had his time and since the end of last season and it being put up for sale we've seen more people coming round to the idea King Power and Top needs to go as well."

Midfielder John Lundstram is seen as a key architect for Leicester's style

Everything has led to a massive fan disconnect with supporters disengaged from the senior leadership.

Even after Rudkin spoke, there was a prevailing feeling from some they did not even want to hear from him, such is the frustration towards him and the club.

Wyeth added: "Against Northampton (a 1-0 Carabao Cup win) I sat next to an old chap who has been going for 56 years and at one point he just sighed really loudly and said: 'I'll always support them, but I don't like them at the moment.'"

Yet the club still sold out their 23,500 season ticket allocation.

Staff are understood not to have been told officially the club is up for sale and BBC Sport has been told Khun Top remains committed to the club.

On deadline day he canvassed the opinion of Martin, Rudkin and McCarron after a Â£15m bid from Manchester United for midfielder Louis Page.

It was rejected after the trio wanted to keep the 18-year-old to help them get promoted.

A pre-season 90 point target remains. Leicester have hit their lowest ebb but are trying to find themselves again.

#80. Trump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham. A reimagined award can still have meaning | Leander Schaerlaeckens

The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer

Poor Fifa peace prize. Unloved, unliked, mocked, tainted by association with its first winner. And now demoted, too, after Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, dumped the thing on the global governing body’s “social responsibility committee” to look after. To redeem it, rather than to ditch it, to spare Infantino the embarrassment of acknowledging that his fake prize was really just a fake prize all along.

Here is where we should probably acknowledge that, as fake prizes go, and in the context of what it was intended to accomplish, the first awarding of the Fifa peace prize was an unqualified success. It achieved exactly what it was meant to, made by Infantino to flatter Donald Trump, the man he needed to keep on his side to safeguard the riches to be extracted from the North American market in order to consolidate his power base within Fifa. Trump, the gullible buffoon, was pleased as punch – handed a big, golden bauble and a medal he placed around his own neck – and briefly forgot about the Nobel peace prize he desperately covets.

The 22-person social responsibility committee is one of the dozens of standing committees Infantino has created to dole out generous per diems to his allies. It has been charged with recasting the prize into a recognition of social harmony and responsibility, as the Guardian has reported, and will probably seek to depoliticize it – or at least stop awarding it to politicians. There are no aspiring autocrats to placate for the foreseeable future, after all, since Saudi Arabia’s de-facto ruler and host of the 2034 World Cup, Mohammed bin Salman, doesn’t seem to go in for that kind of thing.

That first incarnation of the prize will stand as a monument to Infantino’s folly, as the apex of his hubris and his era of genuflecting to strongmen. That is, of course, assuming he survives the fallout of his attempt to privatize a chunk of the World Cup and re-emerges somewhat chastened and cautious, if either of those behaviors are still within his capacity. And if he makes it through another presidential election in March.

But a second version of the Fifa peace prize holds genuine potential to highlight some of the good the sport occasionally does, to platform and recognize those who leverage soccer’s vast cultural influence to improve the lives of others. The magic of soccer is that it transcends the field and reflects cultures and geopolitics; it becomes anthropological ritual, spoken as the world’s common language. Sometimes, it transforms into a vessel for virtue.

You could give the new prize to Afghan Women United for getting recognized as the official representatives of their country all while playing as refugees in exile. In June, they contested a pair of friendlies against the Cook Islands in New Zealand. They lost both matches, yes, but that’s beside the point. Their mere existence doubles as a towering protest against the Taliban, which has resumed its violent oppression of women since storming back into Kabul in 2021.

You could give it to the Ukrainian club Shakhtar Donetsk, for persevering and even thriving in spite of Russia’s invasion – either through proxies or outright – of their Donbas region a dozen years ago, forcing the club to play elsewhere ever since.

Give it to former Spain international Juan Mata, for his work with Common Goal in convincing other players and managers to donate 1% of their earnings to charity; to Marcus Rashford, for shaming the Tory government into feeding children during a pandemic; to Sadio Mané, for bankrolling the construction of a hospital and other infrastructure projects in his native Senegal; to N’Golo Kanté for doing much the same in Mali.

Give it to Scotland’s Tartan Army, for raising money for children’s charities wherever they play. Hell, give it to the England players for donating their match fees to charity causes since 2007, adding up to more than $6.7m (£5m).

How would any of this relate to peace? Fair question. The peace prize could stand to be rebranded, the better to disassociate it from the least peaceful leader of a western nation in generations. It should probably have clearer qualifications and regulations, too, which is to say that it should have qualifications and regulations. And it’s probably best to shy away from the notion of steering entirely clear of politics. You can either have an award that acknowledges social good or you can be apolitical. You cannot do both.

But that needn’t be a bad thing, if this prize is sincere in rewarding one of the sport’s best citizens – and so long as it serves more than the Fifa president’s selfish interests.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

#81. Shazam! star Michael Gray dead at 75... actor starred on popular superhero series in mid 1970s

By ADAM S. LEVY, US SENIOR SHOWBUSINESS REPORTER

Published: 00:59 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 02:36 BST, 23 October 2026

Actor Michael Gray, best known for his work on the superhero series Shazam!, has died of natural causes at the age of 75.

Representatives for Gray told People on Thursday that the performer passed away on October 16.

Gray played the role of Billy Batson across 28 episodes of the series based on the DC comic characters from 1974 to 1976. The premise saw a teen who turned into superhero Captain Marvel (played by Jackson Bostwick then John Davey) by uttering the phrase Shazam!,

'I didn't know the character or the story when I was initially cast, so I had to be a quick study,' he shared in a 2012 Comic-Con panel. 'So it was fun and exhausting, challenging and thrilling, all at once.'

'It didn't matter that it was on Saturday morning or prime time - though the fact that it was one of the first few live-action shows on Saturday morning was exciting.'

The Daily Mail has reached out to representatives for Gray for further comment on the story.

Actor Michael Gray, best known for his work on the superhero series Shazam!, has died of natural causes at the age of 75. PAbove, in 2001

He spoke about his experience on the show during a 2012 appearance at the event Retro-TV Action-Adventure-Thon, Comic Book Resources reported.

Gray said of being cast on the series: 'I don't recall really being in the audition, but I met with the people of the studio. The show was all shot within an hour, hour-and-a half from the studio in the Los Angeles Valley.

'Lots of guys from the crew worked on the Lassie series. It was good, quality stuff for what it was back then. We did an episode in two-and-a-half days, shooting from sunrise to sunset.'

Gray told Comic Book Resources that being a teen idol for a time 'was exhausting and thrilling.'

He added: 'Before I took the role, I was told by a few people in the biz it wasn't a good idea - that I'll be typecast. But a job's a job, so I took it. It truly was a thrilling show to work on and ended way too soon as far as I'm concerned.'

Gray made a cameo appearance in the 2023 film Shazam! Fury of the Gods, which starred Zachary Levi, Asher Angel and Rachel Zegler.

In a statement, John Davey described Gray as 'just a loving, sweet guy with a great sense of humor.'

Gray was raised in Miami Beach prior to landing in Southern California to pursue a career in show business

Gray (R) played the role of Billy Batson across 28 episodes of the series from 1974–1976. Above, with co-star John Davey

He added: 'He loved acting, loved doing the show and, in recent years, loved appearing at Comic-Cons. He really enjoyed meeting and chatting with the fans. Mike was a wonderful man - I don't think he ever stopped smiling.'

The actor was born on September 2, 1951, and raised in Miami Beach prior to landing in Southern California to pursue a career in show business.

Gray honed his craft at the Pasadena Playhouse, and the exposure he received on the cover of teen-oriented magazines at the time such as Tiger Beat paved the way to the role on the show Shazam!

He made a series of appearances on TV shows such as Marcus Welby, MD, The Flying Nun and Room 222 before landing his first recurring role as Ronnie on the NBC series The Little People.

He also appeared in an episode of The Brady Bunch as the boyfriend of Marcia (Maureen McCormick) in 1973.

Gray had worked on films such as Run, Simon, Run; Beyond the Valley of the Dolls; and Myra Breckinridge.

Following Shazam!, Gray took a break from show business and worked in different fields such as theater education, men’s fashion and a flower company he ran with his wife Stacy Benon Gray, according to Variety.

In recent years, Gray appeared on FX's Archer and in the four films in the Surge of Power franchise, with his final role coming in 2024's Surge of Power: Where There's Smoke.

Gray is survived by wife Stacy Benon Gray; stepchildren Ryan Cooper and Laurel Cooper; and son-in-law Lee Barker.

Manchester City uncertainty isn't stopping them from planning for a best case scenario

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester City are waiting to find out how they will be punished for 114 major Premier League rule breaches and have lodged their appeal in the aftermath of the long-awaited verdict.

The extent of the potential punishment is unknown but Man City must prepare for every eventuality regardless of the stack of 'irrefutable' evidence they have at their disposal but elected not to introduce during the lengthy investigation.

That includes the best case scenario as well as the worst. With a January transfer window fast approaching, it's business as usual for City's scouts. According to reports in Portugal, repeat visits to Porto could point to some potential targets.

The possible sanctions facing Man City are significant. Expulsion from the Premier League is on the table along with stripped titles won under Pep Guardiola, points deductions, limits on registering players and even an enforced change of ownership under the powers of the independent football regulator.

A transfer ban of some description is perhaps among the more likely punishments – it has been suggested in some quarters that the club's recent transfer strategy could serve as futureproofing for that – but recruitment will remain a focus until such time as a ban is in place.

According to A Bola via Sport Witness, members of City's scouting team were in attendance for Porto's Champions League loss to PSV at the Estadio do Dragao on Tuesday evening.

Sport Witness reports that City have had scouts at Porto matches twice in a month, both times since the club's own visit to Portugal in the Champions League in September.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The player suggested is Victor Froholdt, who 'impressed' when he was watched against Benfica last time City officials were in town. "Unfortunately, the 20-year-old Danish midfielder wasn’t so good on Tuesday as Porto lost 1-0 to PSV," says Sport Witness.

It was a bad night for Porto and none of their players caught the eye, though 18-year-old Oskar Pietuszewski was given a start on the left and Spanish striker Samu Aghehowa, 22, has long been a player of note for Premier League scouts.

Esmir Bajraktarevic, 21, of PSV produced a more notable performance and is offered up as another possible target of City's interest. Yarek Gasiorowski, also 21, put in a commanding performance at centre-back.

Rumours are rife but it has been reported that a 'multi-year transfer ban' is one of the sanctions under discussion.

That would have a big future impact on City but Guardiola's former player, Philipp Lahm, has highlighted the shadow cast on the club's past achievements by the independent commission ruling.

"From the outside, City fundamentally did not do much differently from the other 10 or so top European clubs," Lahm wrote in his column for The Guardian. "But what are achievements on the pitch worth if they are accompanied by rule-breaking?"
