#84. Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show

The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.

During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.

As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa.

They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".

The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.

William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives Â£1m.

The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.

Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.

The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.

At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".

The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday.

Bruno Fernandes joined Manchester United in January 2020

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes had his home burgled on Wednesday while he was in Italy for his club's Champions League game against Como.

It is understood Fernandes' family were not in the house in Cheshire when it was broken into and that the intruders were inside for less than five minutes before police arrived.

Man United head coach Michael Carrick is already under pressure after consecutive Champions League defeats

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United appointed Michael Carrick as their permanent head coach after he steered them back into the Champions League last season in his second spell in temporary charge.

Man United have lost two of their three matches in the league phase of the Champions League, beating only Sabah in Europe and Ipswich Town in the Premier League so far this season.

After just 153 days, Carrick appears to be heading towards the Old Trafford exit. He was openly criticised by captain Bruno Fernandes after United lost 4-1 to Como on Wednesday, and the escalating problems suggest that Carrick is closer to the end than the beginning of the end.

United being United, there's every chance the club's decision-makers opt for a long-term project option before pulling the trigger again to bring in another former player. What's inevitable is that there will still be serious candidates for one of the biggest jobs in the game.

There are significant names littering the next Manchester United manager odds, with Gary Neville and Wayne Rooney both available at 100/1 along with former Red Devils boss Erik ten Hag.

Eddie Howe is the favourite after leaving Newcastle United in the summer after nearly five full seasons in charge at St James' Park. Howe led the Magpies to their first major trophy for 70 years and took them into the Champions League twice, but would be regarded mostly as a steady hand should he take up the Man United challenge.

Former Germany and Bayern Munich boss Julian Nagelsmann is available at odds of around 4/1, while Brighton & Hove Albion manager Fabian Hurzeler and Premier League alumnus Antonio Conte are both rated around 6/1.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Red Devils' latest conqueror is next on the list at 11/1. Cesc Fabregas has been Como's head coach since 2024 but didn't exactly have to hit the heights to get the better of United on Wednesday.

Kieran McKenna, a familiar face at Old Trafford and once a favourite to be appointed as United manager, is listed at 14/1 along with Aston Villa manager Unai Emery and England boss Thomas Tuchel, both of whom are a little stingily priced by comparison.

Gareth Southgate at 16/1 is next, followed by Mauricio Pochettino, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and Carlo Ancelotti at 25/1.

Carrick's immediate predecessor as caretaker, former United midfielder Darren Fletcher, is the second-favourite among ex-players at 33/1.

It doesn't take much imagination to understand that United's problems run deeper than the manager's office, whatever happens to Carrick this week and beyond. The process of appointing a successor is as likely to be a product of disarray as an answer to it.

For now, Carrick is still in place. United face Bournemouth and Chelsea in their next two Premier League matches. Given the intensity of the situation, one suspects he'll do well to still be in the dugout when they welcome Roma in the Champions League at the start of November.

#93. What are Real's attacking options during Vinicius Jr ban?

Yan Diomande, Carlos Espi and Endrick will give Real Madrid manager Mourinho selection choices over the next three league matches

Real Madrid have never been short of attacking talent, but how best to bring that talent together has long been a subject of debate.

Vinicius Jr's four-match La Liga suspension has forced Jose Mourinho to rethink his forward line and explore alternative combinations.

In their 4-1 victory over Sevilla last weekend Real produced some of their most impressive attacking football of the season, deploying a new-look front three.

Kylian Mbappe led the line, with Endrick on the right, Yan Diomande on the left and Jude Bellingham operating in midfield. It delivered one of Real's most complete attacking performances of the season.

Wednesday's 4â1 Champions League victory over RB Leipzig showcased a different attacking set-up.

Mbappe again led the line, with Vinicius and Arda Guler supporting him, before Mourinho turned to his bench for fresh attacking options.

Diomande replaced Vinicius in the 69th minute and made an immediate impact, scoring Real's fourth with a spectacular volley, while Carlos Espi and Endrick were introduced late on.

Mourinho has made it clear that no player is "untouchable", with performances on the pitch ultimately determining who earns their place in the team.

Real's recent displays have offered an intriguing glimpse on how their attack could evolve without Vinicius, and it has created an opportunity for alternative options to make their case.

So who are the attacking options that could help turn Real's season around?

Diomande is a very exciting prospect in Mourinho's attacking puzzle and he is finally beginning to show why Real invested so heavily in him.

Arriving from RB Leipzig after an impressive 2025â26 campaign when he recorded 12 goals and nine assists, Diomande caught Real's attention with his pace, direct dribbling and ability to beat defenders one-on-one.

However, Mourinho took several weeks to give him opportunities, and the winger did not start any of the club's first five games of the season.

That has changed dramatically, with Diomande starting five of the past six matches, including the most recent three.

He is joint-second for more goal involvements with three goals and four assists, averages the most complete dribbles per 90 minutes, and is third for the most chances created in open play.

Mourinho has praised his attitude, saying: "He works well and hard, he's humble and wants to learn and work. He listens to me and his team-mates. He will grow."

He has also recognised the progress being made, adding: "He has a lot to improve, but he's had a great game. He's developing."

Now, Vinicius' suspension presents Diomande with an even bigger opportunity.

After impressing on the left wing against Sevilla and Leipzig, he is set to have three La Liga matches without direct competition from the Brazilian, beginning with El Clasico against Barcelona on Sunday.

It is arguably his biggest test since arriving at the Bernabeu, giving him the chance to prove he can deliver on the biggest stage and establish himself as more than just a promising prospect and challenge Vinicius for a regular starting spot.

The question for Mourinho will be what happens when Vinicius returns, particularly as he remains available for Champions League action.

If Diomande can turn his recent run of starts into consistent goals, assists and decisive performances, he could become a crucial part of Real's attack and begin to justify the enormous investment the club have made in him.

The 20 year-old Brazilian arrived in Madrid with enormous expectations, but competition for attacking places has made consistent opportunities difficult to secure.

After gaining experience during a loan spell at Lyon in the second half of the 2025-26 campaign, he has returned to a squad packed with established stars.

His performance against Roma offered a reminder of what he can bring. Endrick's acceleration, direct running and willingness to attack defenders gave Real an extra dimension as they fought their way back into the match.

At his best, Endrick is capable of changing the tempo of an attack. He can operate from the right, drive towards goal and threaten as a central striker. That versatility could be especially useful when Real need to change their approach during a game.

His combination of pace and close control also offers a possible solution against opponents who press aggressively.

Rather than relying exclusively on intricate passing, Madrid could use Endrick to carry the ball into dangerous areas and force defenders to retreat.

The priority must be to give Endrick a clearly defined role and enough meaningful minutes to build his confidence.

The Spanish striker is making a name for himself as one of Real's most effective impact players, showing that he could be a real weapon coming off the bench.

The 21-year-old has made the most of his very limited opportunities, scoring three goals in only 37 minutes across La Liga and the Champions League, a brilliant return that has strengthened calls for him to receive more opportunities.

Espi offers Real something different from their more mobile forwards: a natural centre-forward who can occupy central defenders, attack crosses and provide a focal point inside the penalty area.

He is 6ft 4in tall and arrived after an 11-goal league campaign with Levante. He gives Mourinho a different tactical option when Real need to change the game.

Maintaining that scoring rate over a longer period will be difficult, and Mbappe's place as the main striker limits Espi's opportunities to start.

But that may be where his greatest value lies for now. He can enter games against tired defenders, bringing fresh energy into the penalty area and giving Real a different attacking option when they need to chase a result.

If he continues to deliver in those crucial moments, Espi could become far more than a substitute and he could be the reliable game-changer Mourinho turns to when the pressure is highest.

#97. Shoplifters are now so violent their raids are being classed as robberies

Published: 00:49 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 02:30 BST, 23 October 2026

Shoplifting rates have fallen slightly - seemingly to be replaced by more violent crimes against retailers.

A dip in levels of recorded shoplifting was offset by a jump in business robberies, thought to reflect increasingly violent retail thefts in 'Wild West Britain'.

Official data shows recorded robbery surged 10 per cent year-on-year to 88,282 - its highest level since before the pandemic.

Robberies of businesses soared 67 per cent to more than 31,000 - the highest on record. Robbery of personal property dipped 7 per cent to some 57,000 incidents.

The Association of Convenience Stores (ACS) said the rise in robbery may reflect the violence used by shoplifters, leading to a shift in how the crime is recorded by police.

Recorded shoplifting fell 2 per cent to 519,516 from a near-peak the previous year.

The ACS said: 'The reason for the marked increase in robberies is likely due to a change in the way some offences are now recorded as robberies that previously would have been counted as shoplifting.'

Chief executive Ed Woodall added: 'We are extremely concerned about the changing nature of theft against retailers. Offenders are becoming more confident, more brazen and ultimately more violent in their crimes.'

Three armed robbers conducted a daylight raid of a family-run jewellers where they stole gems worth £225,000 in January

It comes after three armed robbers from Essex, who were behind a daylight raid of a family-run jewellers, where they stole gems worth £225,000, were sentenced to 15 years behind bars in July.

Deniz Mehmet, 28, Lee Ramsey, 46, and Robert Clarke, 50, were seen on video smashing the windows of Gregory & Co in Richmond, south-west London, in January.

Footage taken by witnesses that later went viral showed staff bravely trying to fend off the attackers, who escaped on foot.

One of the men, wearing dark clothes and a hood, was seen repeatedly pounding the shop's large glass window, which eventually smashed and was yanked away.

His accomplice, also in dark clothes, stood holding a large blue Ikea bag, which the pair then stuffed full of watches, bracelets and other items.

Staff could be seen trying to stop the thieves, but the trio fled the scene on foot in front of horrified onlookers who feared for their own safety.

Clarke, of Rochford, Ramsey, of Harlow, and Mehmet, of Basildon, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to rob and were each sentenced to five years and three months.

In a separate incident, thieves were caught as they tried to tunnel their way into a jewellery shop after an investigation linked them to a spate of burglaries worth more than £700,000.

Officers caught them at 3.12am on July 17 as they tried to sneak into the shop in Tooting, south London.

Video showed police rumbling the suspects, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit burglary with intent to steal and cause criminal damage, as they retreated back down the tunnel.

Laurentiu-Daniel Nitisoara, 38, was arrested in a nearby alleyway before officers tracked a second man - Ioan Asafeti, 39 - to a hiding place on a rooftop.

The third member of the gang, Sergiu Plastin, 42, was arrested later that day as he attempted to flee to Ireland from Stansted airport.

The group, who mainly targeted jewellers using tunnels to access shops overnight while bypassing security systems between May and July, will be sentenced at Kingston Crown Court today.

Algerian migrant Txomin Huare-Place, 31, who ripped a £65,000 Patek Philippe watch from the wrist of Tim Hortons restaurant chain boss Alex Schwan, was jailed for almost three years.

Txomin Huare-Place, 31, was jailed for two years and nine months for stealing a £60k watch from the wrist of a Canadian tourist in West London

Mr Schwan had been accompanying his wife to an auction at Sotheby's in Mayfair after watching a Wimbledon match when Huare-Place struck on June 30, 2024.

The thief, already serving six years behind bars when he received the sentence, inflicted 'intense pain' on his victim as he yanked at the Aquanaut Travel model.

He is a member of one of the 'Rolex Ripper' gangs that have terrorised wealthy tourists in London's West End.

Huare-Place, who earlier admitted robbery, shut his eyes as he was jailed for two years and nine months, to run consecutively to his six-year term.

He has several previous convictions, including two similar watch robberies in June last year.

Fellow Algerian migrant Ahmed Djidi, 27, was jailed for 22 months in 2025 for his involvement in the theft of Mr Schwan's watch.

An average of £1million worth of watches are snatched from people's wrists every month in London's West End, the Metropolitan Police revealed.

#98. Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow

Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre LÃ©vy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow

"Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.

US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.

But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.

The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.

They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts, and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.

Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.

Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.

"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."

The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.

Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023

Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.

"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.

Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.

The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".

Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.

One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.

Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia

Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back

Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police.

One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear.

One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months.

In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre LÃ©vy.

He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be.

The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible.

And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies.

Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country.

But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning.

Pierre LÃ©vy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024

After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Ðven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers.

One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'."

Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses.

A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase.

"It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour."

A wooden replica of the Great Seal of the US was given to the American ambassador to Russia as a gift in 1945 - it was later found to contain a listening device

Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".

Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.

This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."

Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."

But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow.

"Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."

Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.

But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians.

"Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."

#113. Miatta Fahnbulleh makes U-turn to back immigration plan

Published: 23:08 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 02:28 BST, 23 October 2026

The Energy Secretary has backed the Government's immigration reforms after repeatedly refusing to earlier this week.

Miatta Fahnbulleh apologised on Thursday for saying she would 'never lie' in a reference to an interview in which she refused 16 times to support Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's proposals.

Ms Mahmood has announced plans to extend the time foreign nationals have to wait before being granted Indefinite Leave to Remain. Her proposals to increase this period from five to up to 15 years have prompted a revolt among Labour MPs.

Ms Fahnbulleh became one of the highest-profile detractors after criticising the policy on her constituency website, claiming it threatened 'the process of building cohesion'.

On Thursday, she apologised for the remark about never lying and said she fully supported the migration reforms.

She tweeted: 'I fully support our Home Secretary and the Government's position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it's absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.'

It comes as Ms Fahnbulleh refused seven times on Wednesday to say if she backs a key part of Labour's planned immigration reforms.

She repeatedly dodged questions about proposals by Ms Mahmood to make people wait longer for permanent residency in Britain.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has backed the Government's immigration reforms after repeatedly refusing to earlier this week

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced plans to extend the time foreign nationals have to wait before being granted Indefinite Leave to Remain

Speculation has mounted that Ms Mahmood's proposal to extend the five-year wait by up to 10 years for foreign care workers could be watered down to avoid a Labour rebellion after criticism from senior MPs.

Ms Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner both criticised the plan earlier this year when they were on the backbenches, with the now Energy Secretary attacking any attempt to 'prolong the time people have to wait for settlement' in a now-deleted online post.

Asked on Wednesday on Sky News if she now backed the policy, Ms Fahnbulleh repeatedly said she backed the need for wider reform of the system.

But she would not say she backed the specific policy, eventually snapping at presenter Sophy Ridge: 'Don't put words in my mouth.'

In response to one of the questions she said: 'We have got to reform our immigration system.

'My view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion [and] contribution.

'So there is a package of reforms, the Home Secretary has been consulting on this, she is looking at the range of responses and she will come out with the measures that we take forward.

'The key thing I would say is that no one can look at our immigration system, and I say this as someone that came to this country as a refugee, and not believe it is broken and not believe that we need to fundamentally reform it.'

On Wednesday, Ms Fahnbulleh repeatedly dodged questions about proposals by Ms Mahmood to make people wait longer for permanent residency in Britain

She added: 'I support reforms that say that people have to contribute and make a contribution to this country in order to get citizenship.

'I 100 per cent back Shabana Mahmood and everything she is trying to do.'

On Tuesday, Ms Rayner sought to downplay reports of a Cabinet rift over Ms Mahmood's immigration plans, saying she was sure her colleague would 'land' on a policy that was fair to both taxpayers and migrants following a consultation.

But Downing Street has declined to rule out changes to the proposal, defending Ms Fahnbulleh's decision not to commit to it on TV.

Challenged over their comments, No 10 stressed that Ms Mahmood was 'carefully considering' more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the reforms.

Asked whether tweaks to the Home Secretary's initial revamp – including applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Andy Burnham's press secretary told reporters: 'We set out proposals for consultation. We've consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like (for) people already in the UK who have not received settled status.

'The Home Secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.'

He added: 'The Energy Secretary made clear she backs reforms and the work that Shabana is doing as Home Secretary.

'She was asked about specific elements of the proposals that are subject to the results of the consultation.

'You would not expect ministers to comment on elements subject to the results of the consultation.'

#115. Should Bukayo Saka worry about Rio Ngumoha's emergence?

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This week, Rio Ngumoha took to the pitch for Liverpool in the Champions League and delivered a performance from the right flank that will long be spoken about at Anfield.

Two assists, 9/10 attempted dribbles, 14 progressive carries, and 30 overall, and 10/13 ground duels won. That was the Englishman’s absurd stat-sheet against Villarreal.

Ngumoha was able to have an impact in Europe rivalled only in recent years at Liverpool on the right-hand side by Mohamed Salah, and his performance truly does beg the question: should Bukayo Saka be worried?

Some readers might consider it a stretch, but it’s well-known, as revealed by transfer expert David Ornstein, that Mikel Arteta is an admirer of the 18-year-old.

For England, Ngumoha is already receiving call-ups, despite the last Liverpool starboy, Trent Alexander-Arnold, being oddly absent from international line-ups in his Anfield prime.

At just 18 years of age, the sole thing that is missing from Ngumoha’s locker is goalscoring threat. Additionally, his consistency remains unproven.

But if that’s Ngumoha’s biggest problem(s) at 18, Saka should be worried. Because in his declining form, as the mileage from season upon season of Premier League minutes imprints its mark on his play, Liverpool's starboy could be the future.

Sign up for our free live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest matches, their kick-off times, channels and streams

In comparison to his predecessor on the right, Salah was once a similar talent at Ngumoha’s age, albeit held back by the Egyptian FA’s reluctance to let him leave for Europe.

As a youngster, the Egyptian King was lightning quick, agile, a superb take-on artist, and his goalscoring bag was comparable to the creativity displayed by Ngumoha.

Flash forward to Salah’s mid-20s, and his game was almost perfected. In his early 30s, he became the complete Premier League forward, unlike any other in English history.

The 18-year-old was able to spend a solitary season in the first team under the Egyptian’s wing, who no doubt revealed the blueprint for Premier League success to him, and that should deeply trouble the Arsenal man.

What Saka is facing is a younger, hungrier, and arguably better, in their current forms, player than he is. And that’s a tough winger to beat out, when competing for future places in both the England, and maybe Arsenal, line-up - when Saka was in his prime years, the only ageing winger able to best him was… Salah.

What is working in Saka’s favour, ahead of what promises to be England’s most exciting winger rivalry in the coming years, is that he hasn’t yet achieved it all.

Sure, he’s a Premier League winner with Arsenal, and he has enjoyed standout seasons as the very best fielded by the Gunners. Individually, what does he have to show for it?

He doesn’t have a PFA Players’ Player of the Year title - Salah holds three, the most ever, and even Phil Foden bagged one - nor does he possess a Golden Boot, or a Playmaker Award.

Those individual accolades are still up for grabs as Saka enters the second phase of his career, and this isn’t too dissimilar to what Salah experienced entering his 30s.

Despite that age difference, Saka simply has far more mileage at the top level than his Egyptian rival had in his mid 20s; like Salah, the Englishman must continue to improve.

If he doesn’t, surely the Arsenal icon will come to understand that Ngumoha is breathing down his neck - even if Liverpool never sanction a move, the 18-year-old appears set to become an England mainstay beyond 2030.

If Saka wants to keep Ngumoha at bay, he has a tall task ahead of him. He must unlock the one area of his game that he has, so far, been unable to: become a top goalscorer, and provide both Arsenal and England with a quality that his 18-year-old rival hasn’t yet managed to discover.

Many people have written off the Arsenal winger, but the best players use that as fuel. Ngumoha is going nowhere, but Saka has a lot left to prove before he can roll over.

Kedar Bayley is a trained journalist specialising in culture reporting. As a fan of Liverpool FC, he writes on the Reds often. Knowledgable about all things sports, cinema and television, you can find his words in Screen International, FourFourTwo, Manchester Evening News and more.

#119. AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain a massive flaw in internet technology, after AI discovered issues that could be exploited by hackers.

Developers of the PHP platform - which powers more than 70% of websites, including Wikipedia and digital shopping sites - rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

Cyber-security firm Wiz described the issue as the "most severe" ever detected, while OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

But how did AI discover a massive cyber-security risk in the internet, and what does it mean for you? The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy reports.

#122. Fifa increases preparation money for Women’s World Cup to match men’s teams

Funds for 2027 will match men’s World Cup in 2026

Players given better flights and individual hotel rooms

Teams in the 2027’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil will receive the same preparation money from Fifa as those that played at the 2026 men’s tournament, the world’s governing body has announced.

The preparation money for the 32 teams has been more than doubled to $2.5m (£1.86m) each. In 2023, the total preparation money for the tournament was $31m; it will now be $80m.

Every player will be guaranteed business class or chartered flights, as well as their own hotel room rather than having to share. Fifa says this will bring the provisions for the women’s players in line with the men’s World Cup. That is likely be welcomed after the topic caused controversy at previous tournaments.

A survey conducted by the players’ union Fifpro in 2023, after the most recent Women’s World Cup, co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand, found 80% of players’ return flight had been in business class. Ninety-four per cent flew in business class on their outbound flights.

The total prize fund for the tournament is yet to be decided. Fifa has named the United States as the host of the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028. The Guardian revealed this month the US was lined up to stage the event, with Los Angeles and San Diego among the favoured host cities.

The competition will feature 19 teams, with seven already qualified: Arsenal, Club América Femenil, Barcelona, Gotham FC, Naegohyang from North Korea, Corinthians and Wuhan Jiangda. Six European teams will take part, with the AFC, CAF, Concacaf and Conmebol being represented by three clubs each, plus one team from Oceania.

Fifa’s chief women’s football officer, Sarai Bareman, said: “We undertook a detailed assessment to identify the most suitable host for the inaugural edition of the Women’s Club World Cup. Ultimately, the United States’ recent excellence in staging top Fifa tournaments, combined with the significant interest in women’s football there plus its elite sporting infrastructure, made the country the standout option.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

“Alongside the vibrant and passionate women’s football ecosystem in the United States, the qualified clubs, government, host cities, our commercial and media partners and more, our mission will be to set an impressive standard for global women’s club football and a benchmark for the future.”

Man United lost 4-1 in the Champions League and Carrick's future is already under threat

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned his ire towards head coach Michael Carrick after the Red Devils were beaten 4-1 at Como in the Champions League on Wednesday.

Man United fell behind to goals from Nico Paz, Anastasios Douvikas and Jacobo Ramon before Joshua Zirkzee's stoppage-time consolation goal in Lombardy.

The Red Devils have now lost their last two league phase matches and have beaten only Sabah and promoted Premier League side Ipswich Town in all competitions. Inevitably, the internal disgruntlement is beginning to show on the outside.

Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis after stepping up to take United back into the Champions League after the exit of Ruben Amorim at the beginning of this year, but calls for patience are weakening with each disappointing result.

Fernandes didn't hold back after they lost to Como, telling Champions League broadcaster TNT Sports that the responsibility for getting it right does not belong in the dressing room.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," said the United captain, who was asked directly whether his head coach had opted for the wrong tactical approach.

"That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

Sign up for our free live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest matches, their kick-off times, channels and streams

Carrick was quick to shift the blame to his players' execution of the game plan. The former England midfielder said: "Whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

Dissenting players at Old Trafford are starting to expose the cracks and the public nature of their complaints hasn't gone down well with former professionals. On TNT Sports, former Chelsea and England midfielder Joe Cole condemned Fernandes.

"I've played for managers I've played for where you don't agree with the tactics and you might say that to your mate or your wife," said Cole. You don't come out, as captain of the club, and question the manager.

"He doesn't even do it properly. If you're going to do it, come out and and say it with your chest. He's saying it and he probably thinks he's being clever - 'well I didn't really say it, gaffer'.

"You can think the manager has got the tactics wrong, that's fine. Go into his office tomorrow morning and have a conversation but to come out in front of the nation as club captain and question your manager is simply unacceptable."

Fernandes' thinly veiled criticism of Carrick's tactics followed the furore over comments made by defender Lisandro Martinez.

The Argentina defender apologised after targeting United technical director Jason Wilcox in the aftermath of their previous Champions League loss.

"We don't have the best squad at the moment compared to other top teams," he said after United's game at Atletico Madrid. "I'm not going to close my mouth. We need more ambition. If we don't say the truth, nothing will change."

Chris is a Warwickshire-based freelance football writer specialising in West Midlands football, the Premier League, the EFL and the J.League. He is the author of the High Protein Beef Paste football newsletter and owner of Aston Villa Review. He supports Coventry Sphinx.

Spoiler warning: This review reveals details from the latest episodes of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has made headlines in today's papers after launching a national campaign on public preparedness for disruption caused by natural disasters and cyber attacks. The Daily Telegraph reports on Britons being asked to make "Be ready" kits for emergencies, "including three days' worth of non-perishable food and bottled water, an FM radio and blankets".

Meanwhile, the Metro warns readers to "prepare for the worst" after websites around the world were taken offline after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a globally-used programming language, PHP. "In the UK, 32 government services were down", the paper reports, before asking the question "are you emergency ready?"

The Independent leads on Streeting's messaging for Britons to be prepared in case "'state-sponsored terrorism' disrupts everyday life". The government's campaign comes as global security flaw knocked dozens of government services offline, the paper says.

Similarly, the Guardian leads on UK households being urged to stockpile enough food and water to "survive 72 hours in a crisis", the Guardian reports. The new guidance from the government follows concerns on "climate change, technological dependency and hostile state threats", the paper says.

Streeting "issues checklist for coping after catastrophe" and to "be prepared with 3 days of supplies", the Times reports. Elsewhere British singer Raye is pictured singing on stage as a "golden wonder" following her Mercury Prize win.

"Don't Panic!" the Daily Mail instructs after ministers were "accused of lecturing families" to stockpile "in case of a national emergency". Elsewhere on the page, Catherine, Princess of Wales, is pictured with her son Prince George, who she is said to be missing while he is at Eton.

Former Health Secretary Matt Hancock has been heavily criticised after another Covid inquiry over "untested patients being discharged into care homes where tens of thousands of residents died", the Daily Mirror reports. "Bereaved families are calling for Hancock to be stripped of his Right Honourable title" following his handling of Covid, the paper says.

Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its workforce, the Financial Times reports. Support roles are predicted to bear the brunt as "AI makes our people more productive", the bank said, according to the paper. It comes as chancellor John Healey prepares to deliver his Budget next week that is likely to tax banks.

A landmark report proposing to create career plans for 14-year-olds and above to help them with their future employment, is the lead of the i Paper. The plan aims to tackle the high number of young people not in education, employment or training once they leave school, the paper explains.

The Daily Star splashes on The Celebrity Traitors and how one contestant admitted their experience was "harder than any war zone".

The Sun reports that Thomas Markle, the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is being investigated by police, after a "huge stash" of child sex abuse images were allegedly found at his home in the Philippines. The paper reports that the discovery was made by the 82-year-old's son, Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Junior. It says he told detectives that "hundreds, if not thousands" of pictures and videos of young girls were "mixed up with innocent family mementos" in four large boxes. There is no response from Thomas Markle Senior.

And the Daily Express headlines on victims of "shocking" attacks wanting tougher sentences for offenders to try to stop records levels of violence against women.

#129. Nanny Burnham won't spend more on defence but is wasting a fortune lecturing us on stockpiling tins, water, loo roll and a wind-up radio in case of a national emergency

By MARTIN BECKFORD, POLICY EDITOR and CHRISTIAN CALGIE, SENIOR POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT-AT-LARGE

Published: 21:55 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 02:27 BST, 23 October 2026

Ministers have been accused of lecturing families on what to keep in their cupboards in case of a national emergency.

The Government is urging households to stockpile bottled water, tinned food, cash and loo roll in a campaign to be prepared for a potential major crisis caused by extreme weather or cyber attack.

Its Be Ready guide recommends keeping nine litres of drinking water per person in case mains supplies are knocked out or shops closed for as long as three days, along with meat, vegetables and fruit that can be eaten without being cooked or refrigerated.

Home survival kits should also include a battery or wind-up FM radio and torch, first aid kit and medication, the checklist says, while blankets are needed in case of power cuts.

In addition, the Be Ready advice includes working out escape routes from houses and agreeing with loved ones where to meet up in case disaster strikes, as well as filling in a form stating everything from insurance policy numbers to the frequencies of favourite radio stations.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the public needed to think about what they would do if a natural disaster struck, if hackers attacked businesses or terrorists disrupted supply chains.

'How would we cope if the payment systems at the local supermarket went down?' he asked on a visit on Thursday.

'Those are the sorts of everyday challenges and threats that we could well face. And it's right that we ask the country to be ready for those things and to ask everyone to do their bit.'

Ministers have been accused of lecturing families on what to keep in their cupboards in case of a national emergency. Pictured: Andy Burnham on Thursday

Security minister Dan Jarvis added: 'The storms last winter and the wildfires this summer have shown how severe weather events can cause disruption to our everyday lives and impact the services we rely on, like phones, power, water and the internet.'

But critics branded the advice over-the-top and said Labour should focus on keeping the country safe by raising funding for the Armed Forces, as well as improving the resilience of critical infrastructure such as power plants.

It comes after widespread anger at the Government sending emergency alerts to every mobile phone in the country during the summer to warn that lighting barbecues could spark wildfires.

Reform MP Danny Kruger, in charge of the party's preparations for government, said: 'Ministers should be doing their job not telling families how to do theirs.

'Government needs to urgently invest in defence to deter aggressors and harden the target.

'With our undersea cables, our military bases and our civilian infrastructure all exposed to Russian or Iranian attack – and all our digital systems exposed to hackers from anywhere in the world – the need for a major uplift in defence spending at next week's Budget is critical.

'Meanwhile ordinary people need help with the cost of living – not bossy lectures about bottled water.'

Tory security spokesman Alicia Kearns said: 'Preparing for emergencies is important.

'But the Government should get its own house in order before lecturing the public. It isn't families that are failing to fund our defence or secure reliable energy, it's Labour.

'With rising threats to our national security, we must all be ready to face all eventualities.

'We each have a role to play, but the Government must lead by example.'

Lord Hannan, director general of the Institute of Economic Affairs, said: 'Britain is not a country on the brink of catastrophe, and ministers should not behave as though it were.

'The last thing we need is a Government encouraging people to panic. The purpose of government is to provide security and reassurance, not to frighten people into stockpiling tins of beans.'

And Dr Valentin Boboc, chief economist at the institute, added: 'There is nothing wrong with encouraging households to be prepared for emergencies, but the Government should be careful not to create unnecessary alarm.

'Talking up the prospect of a national crisis risks undermining consumer confidence at a time when households and businesses are already facing considerable economic uncertainty.

'Ministers should focus on ensuring that our infrastructure, energy supplies and public services are resilient.'

John O'Connell of the TaxPayers' Alliance said: 'Taxpayers want emergency warnings for actual threats, not money wasted lecturing them on common sense.'

The Be Ready website tells households: 'Being ready for three days helps you manage while support reaches those most in need.'

It advises: 'Check your cupboards first to see what essentials you already keep at home' and note down what is still needed.

#131. Next in line? Main contenders for the Manchester United hot seat

With Michael Carrick’s future at Old Trafford a matter of some debate, we examine the credentials of those who could succeed him

The German was of interest to Manchester City while Omar Berrada was part of the hierarchy on the other side of town. He is highly thought of and would come with an impressive CV for a 39-year-old, having taken charge of Bayern Munich and Germany. Nagelsmann is regarded as an innovator who is very demanding of his players and builds teams to press relentlessly, a concept not currently used at United, as Bruno Fernandes will testify. His spell with Germany was underwhelming, concluding with a 2026 World Cup last-32 defeat by Paraguay, and at Bayern – with an exceptional squad – he won the Bundesliga in his only full season and was sacked the following March with the team second and still in the Champions League.

The King of the Europa League is tactically astute and knows about working on a budget. If he is intrigued by the prospect of managing United, it would come down to whether he believes they have more potential than Villa, who are one point and place above them in the Premier League and faring much better in the Champions League, and whether United are willing to pay significant compensation. Emery likes a 4-2-3-1 but has always had a central striker at his disposal, and United lack someone strong in this department. Very calm but with a ruthless edge when required, he has plenty of silverware to back up his credentials. He is regarded as one of the game’s great pragmatists and is happy to play on the counterattack, which would suit the United squad.

The Italian, who left Napoli in the summer, knows the Premier League from spells with Chelsea and Tottenham, winning the title with the former in 2017. A fierce competitor and disciplinarian, he would shake up the dressing room with his high standards. His fiery temper can also result in fascinating interactions with the media, including telling a post-match press conference after losing to Burnley that maybe he was not the right man to manage Spurs. His willingness to speak out when it may not necessarily be wise could put United off. His preference for playing three at the back could be problematic considering the personnel at United, as Ruben Amorim found out.

The Northern Irishman worked within the United academy before stepping up to be part of José Mourinho’s backroom staff alongside Carrick. He stayed when Ole Gunnar Solskjær replaced the Portuguese and was credited with having a strong tactical influence as United secured second place. It is often a strength to have a link to a club but considering the struggles Solskjær and Carrick have endured, an external candidate seems more appropriate. He departed to become a head coach at Ipswich and his work there meant he was linked with a return to United to replace Erik ten Hag. McKenna resigned in June after securing promotion to the Premier League for a second time to take time away from the day-to-day grind of management. Would he want to end his sabbatical by jumping into a precarious situation after five or so months?

The English option and a manager with plenty of Premier League experience who took Newcastle to the Champions League. Arguably this makes him the safest pair of hands. A hard worker, Howe was often first in and last out at the Newcastle training ground as he pored over every detail. A lover of wingers and 4-3-3, he would be reliant on a central striker such as Benjamin Sesko to step up. He likes to work closely with his nephew Andy, who held senior roles at Bournemouth and Newcastle, which would create an interesting dynamic if he wanted similar at United. Howe, like others in contention, would not cost anything in compensation – and every penny counts at Old Trafford.

The 33-year-old has a growing reputation, with his Brighton team third after scoring 23 goals in seven games. This could explain why he is not particularly keen on leaving at the moment. His team are outperforming United with a squad that looks stronger. The size of United is alluring for many coaches but moving mid-season to a struggling club is not always advantageous because it means stepping into a firefight.

#140. DAILY MAIL COMMENT: As the Budget approaches, it is increasingly clear that the Chancellor's strings are being pulled by the unions

Published: 00:59 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 02:26 BST, 23 October 2026

Anyone unfamiliar with John Healey could easily be taken in by his weasel words about the Budget.

Yet hours after promising a pro-business package next Wednesday, he was cosying up to a group of union barons demanding higher spending and punitive taxes on the 'rich'. For one attendee to brag of a 'really good connection' between the Left-wing firebrands and the Chancellor speaks volumes about what transpired.

It also serves as a disturbing reminder of how the unions have grown even stronger since Labour's return to office. From the end of next week, shop stewards and other officials will have the right to march into offices and factories practically at will as the so-called 'right to roam' power comes into effect.

Other provisions under the new Employment Rights Act - which the Department of Trade and Business describes as 'giving trade unions greater freedom to organise, represent and negotiate' - include cutting the notice period for industrial action from 14 to ten days.

Hours after promising a pro-business package next Wednesday, the Chancellor was cosying up to a group of union barons demanding higher spending and punitive taxes on the 'rich'

Any remedial measures for the business sector will struggle against those challenges. But Mr Healey's remarks on improving the environment for trading were disingenuous in the first place.

No one disputes that reducing the red tape suffocating businesses would be a sensible move. But the Chancellor conveniently neglected to mention that almost all the soul-sapping bureaucracy in question was dreamt up by his Cabinet colleague Angela Rayner - who was also responsible for the legislation allowing a new generation of union militants to flex their muscles.

Nor was Mr Healey in any way persuasive with his supposed show of support for entrepreneurs who persevere 'through sheer bloody-mindedness'. If he really wants to demonstrate his solidarity, then the very least he could do is reverse the crippling increases in employers' National Insurance contributions introduced under Labour.

But we won't be holding our breath for that to happen. For all his soothing words, Mr Healey clearly has as little concern for the business community as he does for the hard-pressed taxpayers who stump up for the benefits bill.

That his union guests arrived for their private audience in Downing Street armed with a wish list of extravagant demands is par for the course. But that they left apparently happy at the hearing they received from the Chancellor is a deeply worrying pointer to what we can expect next Wednesday.

It would be interesting to know how much civil service overtime - not to mention taxpayers' money - was involved in drafting the Government's guidance for households in a national crisis.

Practically all of the advice on offer seems like basic common sense. Even the least organised among us had probably worked out that easy access to bottled water, cash and a torch is a good idea.

Quite why any of this requires a radio and social media campaign is anyone's guess. Of course, it is just the latest example of a patronising Labour administration determined to stick their collective nose in where it is neither wanted nor needed.

Announcing the measures yesterday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said they would be vital in the event of wildfires, flooding or cyber attacks hitting Britain. Unsurprisingly, he failed to explain how wet wipes and tinned peas will save us if Vladimir Putin decides to launch a military attack.

#141. Haiti move Nations League home clash with USA to Miami amid gang violence crisis

Concacaf approves exceptional hosting arrangement

Haiti to face US at Nu Stadium on 14 November

Miami’s Haitian community offers home advantage

Concacaf on Thursday announced it has approved Haiti’s request to relocate their Nations League quarter-final first leg against the United States on 14 November from Kingston, Jamaica, to Miami in an “exceptional hosting arrangement”. Haiti have been unable to play nominal “home” games within their borders since July 2021, with the United Nations estimating that 90% of the capital of Port-au-Prince – including the national stadium – is controlled by violent gangs.

Haiti’s match, the first leg of a home-and-away series against the US, had been booked for Kingston. The Grenadiers played their 2026 World Cup qualifiers in Curaçao, Aruba and Barbados. However, the Nations League format slated Curaçao and Jamaica to host their matches on the same night as Haiti’s, shunting Haiti to Sabina Park, the home of the Jamaica national team until their current venue opened in 1962. Now a cricket ground, Sabina Park hosted two of Haiti’s Nations League qualifiers.

While the shuffle sends Haiti within their opponents’ borders, they couldn’t have found a more hospitable home away from home. Miami boasts by far the largest population of Haitians and their descendants in the US, with nearly half a million concentrated predominantly in south Florida. They will play at Nu Stadium, where they played the venue’s first international friendly – a pre-World Cup clash with Peru – in June before a sold-out crowd of 26,700. That support dwarfed the crowds they drew at Sabina Park, where their two matches attracted an average of 297 fans.

The US have won four of their six clashes with Haiti this century, with the other two matches ending in draws.

This will be Haiti’s first trip back to the US since this summer’s World Cup, a hero-making turn for the Caribbean nation in their first tournament appearance since 1974. The Grenadiers were handed a difficult group, losing all three games against Morocco, Scotland and Brazil. Nonetheless, they enjoyed fantastic support from fans at their matches in Massachusetts, Philadelphia and Atlanta.

The second leg of the quarter-final is set to take place on 17 November at TQL Stadium in Cincinnati.

Concacaf added that “this flexibility will remain in place for as long as the security situation in Haiti persists”. Haiti, as well as clubs based in the country, will need to seek approval from Concacaf for each match they look to play in “the territory of its opponents”, a separate arrangement from the neutral sites they have previously booked. The confederation stipulated that the measure “may be amended or withdrawn by the Concacaf Council at any time”.

#149. Nottingham Forest’s false start places early focus on Glasner and Delap

Austrian’s tactics need adapting to but Forest are in the bottom three and their owner is not the patient type

Sitting 19th in the Premier League was not the plan for Nottingham Forest after the arrival of a highly acclaimed manager and a £45m striker to fuel their ambitions. The fates of Oliver Glasner and Liam Delap are intertwined and with the stark stats of zero home goals and a solitary point at the City Ground it is not the dream start they were aiming for.

As Delap prepares to return to Ipswich, where his career ignited, on Friday night, Forest are remaining calm. There is a desperation to get away from the short-termism that caused so many problems; 12 months ago, they were on their third head coach of a disappointing season. This summer they were ruthless with the removal of Vítor Pereira, who had done a fine job to escape the drop, because they saw an opportunity to upgrade with Glasner, hoping he could transform Forest like he did Crystal Palace.

It cost plenty to acquire Glasner and Delap, which many fans believe should lead to instant results, but that is rarely the case in an industry as complicated as football. For the coach, it is a case of learning the club inside out while influencing performance through his carefully choreographed methods. For the striker, he needs to rebuild confidence and that comes via goals.

In Glasner’s first full season at Palace, they won one of their first 13 league matches but ended comfortably in mid-table and FA Cup winners. It was similar at Eintracht Frankfurt, getting one victory in 10, but going on to win the Europa League.

Learning the Glasner way is not straightforward. Playing three at the back is rarely the norm and nor is having two No 10s, all with the background of Forest losing their best player in Elliot Anderson.

The recruitment was measured, targeting positions that required strengthening and avoiding needless purchases that dogged the club after promotion. Replacing Anderson became a priority, but Glasner felt James McAtee could adapt to a deeper role in midfield alongside the shrewd free signing Xaver Schlager. Ousmane Diomande was a coup in defence and Glasner convinced Daniel Muñoz to follow him from Selhurst Park.

Behind the obvious figures, there is plenty of underlying encouragement for Forest. Based on chances created and conceded, Glasner has had the best start of any Forest manager in the Premier League era. His team rank seventh, according to Opta, for expected goals (xG), but have scored the fewest – five – and are the biggest xG underperformers at -6.2. It is a huge discrepancy, missing out on almost a goal a game. It includes 62 shots at home that have come to nothing and if Glasner wants buy-in from the fans, that needs to change quickly. If every team had scored and conceded the goals measured by xG, Forest would be fourth.

It is understandable that Delap is yet to find his feet after a disappointing year at Chelsea and the lack of pre-season set him back. Forest tried to sign him before he went to Stamford Bridge and have great faith in him, but he needs to improve his record of one goal every five league appearances. He is the ideal No 9, possessing pace, power and sharp finishing, but unless he is on peak form, turning that into guaranteed output is not straightforward.

Delap has scored once for Forest, but is putting in the effort through being the front line of defence, relentlessly pressing opposition centre-backs. He has shown plenty of quick thinking, demonstrated by his quick throw-in to set up a goal at Anfield, something almost replicated against Arsenal only for Chris Wood to miss the chance.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Forest allowed Arsenal a single shot on target last Sunday – it just happened to be deflected in for a winner. Glasner can also point in that match to the absence of his captain, Morgan Gibbs-White, the team’s attacking fulcrum. “It feels very unfair,” Glasner said of the result. “We have to accept we are missing some bits. But the performance in many parts was very good.”

In two full seasons at Selhurst Park, Glasner won two major trophies for a club that had gone almost 120 years without one. He has two European titles and his own distinctive formation and execution, something he has harnessed over 12 years in coaching, so he knows how long it takes to develop the complexities.

The picture looks clearer after almost four months together. The hope at Forest is that the endeavour is rewarded with greater luck, the missing ingredient among well thought-out recruitment led by the chief football officer, George Syrianos, and his team and clever coaching. Syrianos is Glasner’s biggest advocate and told fans the manager would be given time.

Friday will be Glasner’s eighth Premier League match at Forest, three more than Ange Postecoglou was permitted before being sacked this time last year by the owner, Evangelos Marinakis. Glasner, unlike the Australian, can show progress and will be justifiably confident points will come.

#151. Private care home investors a risk to public sector, regulator says

Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's ambition to create a universal care service, the regulator says.

The Care Quality Commission's annual report, external highlights how an increasing share of the care home market is owned by large firms - the five biggest have increased their share of the market by 26% in the last two years, driven by interest from US property investors. Between them they own around one in seven homes.

While there could be benefits, there are concerns the trend can lead to higher prices and a reduction in the quality of care - something the CQC says needs to be monitored.

Meanwhile, home care, providing support to help people wash and dress in their own home, has become more fragmented, with a greater number of smaller providers.

The CQC says this could create inefficiencies - nearly a third of these services are providing care to four or fewer people.

In contrast, there are few smaller care homes judged important for providing specialist and personalised care.

Small care homes have always represented a tiny proportion of the care home market, but over the last 14 years the numbers have fallen significantly, particularly those that combine care with nursing support, which are down by a quarter.

The CQC says the funding system remains fragile â people using care services either self-fund or, for the poorest, the state helps to pay for their costs.

And in some areas, providers are increasingly turning to self-funders, making it more difficult for councils to buy the care they need for those relying on state help.

CQC chief inspector of adult social care, Chris Badger, said the reshaping of the market was happening "largely by accident rather than design", driven by a combination of economic pressure and the problems some councils were having in buying services for those relying on state-funded care.

He said this government's renewed focus on social care â Andy Burnham made it one of his key priorities when he became prime minister â was welcome.

But he said it was important the market was "shaped around what's best for people".

Hugh Alderwick, of the Health Foundation think-tank, said the report by the CQC "lays bare the massive challenges" facing the government.

"The prime minister's commitment to reforming the sector provides an opportunity to fundamentally redraw the state's offer on social care.

"But change is needed now to strengthen the fundamentals of the system.

"Councils need enough funding, the right skills and strong leadership to shape services around people's needs."

Prof Martin Green, of Care England, which represents care providers, said: "If the government and regulators are concerned by consolidation in the care sector, they need to take some clear and tangible action to support smaller care home providers."

He said changes to employer national insurance contributions, inflation and the rising cost of energy was making smaller homes unviable.

"Unless we get some real progress in a funding settlement, the trend of smaller homes closing will be a trend that will continue."

The Department of Health and Social Care said the report demonstrated the "scale of the challenge this government inherited", but said it was committed to overhauling social care.

#156. Grandparents should ask for consent to hug their grandchildren, Irish advert says

Published: 18:35 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 02:26 BST, 23 October 2026

Grandparents should ask for consent before hugging their grandchildren, a new government-funded Irish advert said.

A social media video from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) made the 'demeaning' suggestion, but has since been deleted after a storm of criticism.

The video shows two grandparents arriving at a home, where they are enthusiastically embraced by their grandson at the front door while his sister watches on a few feet back, looking uncomfortable.

The grandparents then turn to her, puckering their lips as they bear down, while the girl's unease intensifies.

The video then cuts to text on screen reading: 'Not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them.'

It continues: 'Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely. We-Consent.ie is here to help.'

The clip, funded by Ireland's Justice Department, sparked an immediate backlash, and Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan ordered the DRCC to take it down. Two other videos from the We-Consent campaign were also removed.

He said: 'The video produced by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre involving grandparents does not represent the views of the Government.

The ad shows two grandparents bearing down on their granddaughter to kiss and hug her

The girl looks incredibly uncomfortable - while her brother had enthusiastically embraced the grandparents

'It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my official's engagement with them.

'It goes without saying that having loving grandparents in a child's life is an incredibly positive thing to be cherished and not something to be campaigned against.

'While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive.'

Ridicule of the video came from around the globe, with even Australia's News24 host James Morrow slamming the clip as 'woke'.

Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill said the campaign ad was a 'complete waste of resources', while a member of Ireland's parliament said it 'demonises' and shows 'utter contempt' for older people.

It was funded through Cuan, Ireland's statutory agency for domestic, sexual and gender-based violence, set up by previous Justice Minister Fine Gael TD Helen McEntee.

Speaking on Thursday, she said Cuan was established to support the victims and survivors of domestic and sexual violence, which should have been the focus of the campaign.

'I think it is absolutely essential that we have a very open and a very honest conversation on consent, particularly when the epidemic of domestic and sexual violence, sexual assault, it is still here,' she said.

Critics of the advert said it was a misuse of resources allocated to tackling domestic and sexual violence

'It is still with us, and there is so much work that we need to do. But I think that should be our focus when we're talking about consent campaigns.

'I'm not sure the direction that it has taken, encouraging grandparents to ask permission to hug their [grand]children, is really where I see it being a priority or a focus that is needed.'

The DRCC said it carried out workshops looking at experiences that made participants feel uncomfortable, and that the video reflected this feedback.

'We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland,' they said.

'We created a video series for our social media channels based on feedback from over 20 consent workshops with younger and older people.

'Part of the workshops involved sharing participants' own experiences of instances when they felt uncomfortable. The scenarios depicted in the video series came up very frequently in all the workshops.

'The videos were created with volunteers and staff and reflected these conversations. We do not want that negativity to impinge on and distract from the vital work that we as a centre do in supporting victims and survivors and improving awareness of these important issues across society.'

At Leaders' Questions in the Dáil on Thursday, Aontú TD (MP) Paul Lawless accused the Government of having 'utter contempt' for older people. He said the video was a waste of taxpayers' money.

'I was shocked to see a bizarre advert in recent days funded by the Department of Justice on the issue of consent,' he said.

'This is totally wrong. Firstly, in how it demonises elderly grandparents around the country, but also in terms of the shocking waste of taxpayers' money.

'Consent is very important when it comes to sexual relations between people but equating these two types of relationships with a granny giving a hug to a grandchild is completely inaccurate.

'Why is the state asking grannies to second-guess themselves when it comes to hugging their grandchildren? Why is the state planting a seed in a child's mind that it is somehow dangerous to receive a hug from its grandmother?'

Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill agreed with Mr Lawless that the video was inappropriate but distanced the Government from its approval.

'I just want to be very clear that that is not a Government campaign, and that is not the view of the Government,' she replied.

'Grandparents are an incredibly important part of family life, an incredibly important part of every child's life, and it is both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents.

'It's also important that we clearly distinguish this video, which was an error and doesn't represent the views of Government, from that different body of work entirely. So I want to be absolutely clear, there is no person in Government that viewed this ad, sanctioned this ad.'

Earlier, Fine Gael Senator, Gareth Scahill said the campaign ad was a 'complete waste of resources'.

'What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which at best has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population,' he said.

'The overall We-Consent three-year campaign to inform and engage with all about consent is a good initiative but this publicly funded social media video is a million miles off the mark.

'What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?'

In a statement for Cuan, a spokesperson said the videos were produced at low cost using volunteers and were not approved by Government.

'We-Consent is a programme created and developed by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, aimed at informing, educating, and engaging the public about all forms of consent,' they said.

'Social media videos shared recently as part of this programme were produced by DRCC at a low cost using volunteers and are not part of a Government advertising campaign.

'Cuan understands that DRCC intends to review these videos. They are being removed from their social media channels to enable this review.'

#159. Ex-England defender Bertrand eyes £87m AFC Wimbledon deal

Ryan Bertrand made 19 international appearances for England during his career

Former England defender Ryan Bertrand is leading a consortium that has proposed an Â£87m minority investment in League One side AFC Wimbledon.

Bertrand, who played for Chelsea, Southampton, Aston Villa and Nottingham Forest during his career, is at the forefront of the group with British technology expert Omar Mir, who is the sole funder of the proposed minority share buyout through investment vehicle Sloane Street Capital (SSC).

The Dons Trust board presented their proposals to its members on Wednesday night.

SSC would invest Â£16m on completion for a minority 34% of the shares in AFCW PLC, the company that runs the club.

The remaining Â£71m would be spread over five seasons to the 2030-31 campaign.

If the deal is successful, SSC would oversee football operations, led by Bertrand as senior football advisor, but work within budgets and processes agreed by the AFCW PLC board.

The Dons Trust currently own 50.01% of the voting shares of AFC Wimbledon, which was designed to ensure the club remains fan-controlled.

Bertrand, who won the Champions League, FA Cup and Europa League with Chelsea, said: "AFC Wimbledon's story is unique in English football and it was built by its supporters. We felt at home from our very first meetings.

"We are not here to change what this club is. We are here to help it go further on and off the pitch, for the men's team, the women's team and the academy.

"It would be an honour to join the Wimbledon family and help write the next chapter, and we look forward to meeting members and answering their questions over the coming weeks."

AFC Wimbledon moved to the Cherry Red Records Stadium, close to the site of their old stadium at Plough Lane, in 2020

Under the terms of the deal, the Dons Trust voting rights would be unaffected, plus they would hold veto control of the Cherry Red Record Stadium freehold.

Other proposals include SSC taking two of the 12 seats on the club board, plus an observer position, while the Dons Trust would retain a veto over the club's name, badge, colours, ground and constitution.

Stuart Fiertz, co-founder of the investment management company Cheyne Capital and sports executive Oliver Ward would join the board if a deal is ratified.

Should SSC sell its stake, the Dons Trust would have first refusal and could block who they felt were unsuitable investors.

Also, as part of the terms, if SSC missed a payment, its share of AFC Wimbledon's value would stop growing immediately and control would return to the club within three months.

The voting period for Dons Trust members to decide on the proposals ends on 17 November. Earlier this year, members voted in favour of external investment on the proviso that fan ownership and control were protected.

Since then, the board has considered more than 20 potential investors, with SSC emerging as the strongest.

AFC Wimbledon's lawyers have completed source-of-funds and background checks on the individuals involved in the consortium.

Angus Fox, chair of the Dons Trust board, said: "The deal brings at least Â£87m into AFC Wimbledon over five years, while the Trust keeps a permanent majority of the votes, control of the Plough Lane freehold and a veto over everything that makes us who we are. We have set out the factors to weigh as plainly as the opportunities.

"The board recommends a yes vote, but this is our members' club and our members' decision."
