#163. Items recovered in search for missing fishing boat and crew

Douglas Craigie, Murdo Morrison and Norman Murray had been fishing off the north coast of Lewis

Items belonging to a fishing boat that vanished off the north coast of the Isle of Lewis last week have been recovered as the search for the vessel and two missing crew members continues.

Norman "Tam" Murray, 40 and Murdo Morrison, 23, were on board the Kilda when it disappeared on 13 October.

The body of crewmate Douglas Craigie, 49, was recovered from the sea in the early hours of the following morning by rescuers.

On Thursday, police confirmed that items belonging to the vessel had been recovered from what was described as "an area of interest" off the coast near Port of Ness.

The search was carried out by Police Scotland's marine and dive unit and partners.

A Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) exclusion zone has been in place for divers and vessels in an area between the Butt of Lewis and Port of Ness, but this will be lifted from 23:59 on Thursday.

Insp Neil Taylor, local area inspector for the Western Isles, said the search was a "complex operation" and asked for officers to be given "time and space" to carry out inquiries.

He said: "Efforts are continuing to work with partners and we are doing everything we can to get answers.

"While the Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) exclusion zone will be lifted tonight, we would urge people not to put themselves at any risk.

"Please do not attempt to carry out searches in areas which put you at risk of harm."

A GoFundMe for the families affected by the event has raised more than Â£148,000, against a target of Â£110,000.

#164. ‘It doesn’t look good’: Arteta concerned as Saka limps off against Bayern Munich

‘A player off with really sharp pain is never good news’

Winger forced off 10 minutes into Arsenal’s 2-2 draw

Mikel Arteta made no attempt to conceal his concern over the quad injury that forced Bukayo Saka out of Arsenal’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich, saying it did not “look good at all”.

The manager was delighted with the fight that his players showed, Declan Rice earning a deserved point with an 82nd-minute equaliser. Arsenal had led through Eberechi Eze, who came on in the 10th minute for the stricken Saka, before Harry Kane took centre stage. The Bayern striker set up Alphonso Davies for 1-1 before giving his team the lead from the penalty spot.

It was Saka’s setback that provided the sour note for Arsenal. He collapsed to the turf after a routine battle with Davies and walked off slowly after treatment. Saka was still moving in a very limited way as he left the stadium.

“It doesn’t look good at all but we have to wait and see,” Arteta said. “They [the medics] are a bit concerned. A player who has to come off with a really sharp pain is never good news. Bukayo did not start the game against Lille last Tuesday, then he started at Nottingham Forest on Sunday and it happened very early in this game. The level of intensity that this game requires, as well, is something incredible.

“You could see it on Tuesday night, the PSG-Barcelona game, what happened [with players getting injured]. This is man-to-man for 96 minutes in every action. There’s no breathing. The stress, the quality, the intensity, the level that you need … it’s unbelievable. It’s the highest level. And those things happen, unfortunately.”

Arteta insisted that he wanted more than the draw. “We take it, although that doesn’t mean we are really happy about it as we prepared to win,” he said. “You could see that right from the beginning – the mindset, the purpose and the intention that the team has, to be very dominant, to come here and cause problems to Bayern. To press them and attack them. That’s certainly what we’ve done. We were the better team in the first 25 minutes, we got the goal … unfortunately we also got the injury of Bukayo, which was a big setback.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“The team showed incredible composure, the spirit to keep going, to attack them. The finishers came in and made an impact, as well. After scoring the goal [for 2-2], you see the reaction of the team. We wanted to take the ball and go and attack them again to come and win the game.”

#165. My son was killed by an illegal immigrant. Now I'm exposing the chaos of the system that failed him... and why it MUST be the topic on which the midterms turn

Published: 20:27 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 02:25 BST, 23 October 2026

This November will mark a full year since my son Billy and his sweet wife Jenny were killed in a devastating car crash.

It's the kind of anniversary that no parent ever believes they'll experience, the death of their child. In a different world, our family would be celebrating their one-year wedding anniversary.

But I will never be able to hold my son and see his dimples as he grins or hug my daughter-in-law close.

Billy will never realize his greatest hope – to be a father and have a family of his own. Jenny will never become the piano technician she dreamed of being. And I will never again get the chance to tell them I love them.

Because at just 25 and 24, respectively, Billy and Jenny were beginning their journey as a married couple when their lives were cut short when an 18-wheeler truck, driven by a man who entered this country illegally, jack-knifed across the road.

It sat there with neither hazard lights lit nor warning signs placed in the road, to alert oncoming traffic of the obstacle that blocked both carriageways in the darkness.

Although the driver stayed at the scene, he did not report the highway block.

It wasn't until another driver encountered the truck about 10 to 15 minutes before Billy and Jenny did that 911 was called.

In a different world, our family would be celebrating my son Billy and his wife Jenny's one-year wedding anniversary

At just 25 and 24, respectively, Billy and Jenny were beginning their journey as a married couple when their lives were cut short

I will never again be able to hold my son and see his dimples as he grins

I can remember everything about the night of November 24, 2025. While driving back to Portland, Oregon from Preston, Idaho, Jenny's hometown, Billy and Jenny called us from their Subaru Outback, their cat Bert tucked in the backseat.

They had been married for 16 days. It was a union that felt pre-destined. They'd been inseparable ever since their first date – a blind date where they attended a church event a year earlier. Billy and Jenny had this magical, lightning-in-a-bottle, one-in-a-million kind of love.

When they began dating, Billy couldn't stop smiling – he was simply more alive around her and she was the same around him. On their wedding day, he couldn't stop saying 'my wife;' it was in every sentence he said that day.

After tying the knot at the temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Portland, Oregon on November 8, the newlyweds embarked on a whirlwind tour for the next two weeks, honeymooning at Disneyland and then journeying to Idaho for a second wedding reception with Jenny's friends and family.

On the call that fateful night, we discussed whether they should stay in a hotel for the night or continue driving. It was 8.30pm; Billy and Jenny insisted that they felt well rested and fresh. We decided that they would continue the drive to our home in Springfield – about 200 miles down the road, where I would eagerly be awaiting their arrival. It was a decision I will regret for the rest of my life.

My husband had been tracking their location and at 9.30pm, he noticed they had stopped moving. We tried calling them, but there was no answer. We checked Trip Check, a website for Oregon that reports on road incidents and conditions but initially found no answers.

We kept refreshing the site for more information and later, when an accident was reported on the route where Billy and Jenny's location had stopped, my husband called the Highway Patrol non-emergency number, searching for any answers about our son and daughter-in-law. The information came in dribs and drabs with each call – confirmation that there was an accident, but we heard nothing about who was affected.

Billy and Jenny married on November 8, 2025 - their union felt pre-destined

The newlyweds embarked on a whirlwind honeymoon adventure after they tied the knot

They visited Disneyland before journeying to Idaho for a second wedding reception with Jenny's friends and family

For what seemed like ages, I sat on the couch with my daughter Josie, praying that nothing had happened to Billy and Jenny, that they were safe and out of harm's way. I was in deep denial until two state troopers knocked on our door to deliver a horrific message that would change all of our lives forever.

Here is what I remember about what the two officers told me.

Billy and Jenny died at the scene. There is no way that they could have avoided this accident. They couldn't see it coming. It was instantaneous, which means that they didn't suffer. There were no skid marks, which one of the officers explained, meant that there wasn't even enough time for them to be afraid. These details are comforting, but hollow.

What we learned about what caused the deadly crash still makes my blood go cold. An 18-wheel tractor trailer driven by Rajinder Kumar had jack-knifed across all the lanes of the highway, blocking traffic in both directions. Despite it being pitch black at night, there were no warning lights, flares, cones or emergency signals – not even the truck's hazard lights were on.

Kumar, it was later revealed in police reports, was an illegal immigrant who had a non-domiciled Commercial Driver's License (CDL) in California and a work authorization. He did not follow proper protocol that night when he did not notify the authorities about the jack-knifing. He did not give any warning to oncoming traffic that his trailer was stretched across the entire road, despite having warning equipment. He did not call 911. We later found out that he did not speak English, something that is federally required to hold a CDL.

Kumar was arrested the night of the crash on two counts of criminally negligent homicide - a grand jury later raised the charges to two counts of manslaughter in the first degree - and three counts of reckless endangerment, to which he pled not guilty.

I've never considered myself a highly political person, but the issue of immigration has been blasted into my life as destructively and instantly as the 80,000-pound tractor trailer driven by Kumar that took the lives of my son and daughter-in-law.

I am a life-long Democrat, but my son's unfair and entirely preventable death has me questioning everything I believe in. We are living with the untenable chaos of allowing millions of undocumented people in under President Biden.

Kumar entered the country illegally in 2022 in Lukeville, Arizona, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Biden Administration immediately released him and gave him a work permit. California Governor Gavin Newsom made the unilateral decision to give him a CDL, DHS records show.

We are living with the untenable chaos of allowing millions of undocumented people in under President Biden

Billy and Jenny died at the scene of a terrible accident caused by an 18-wheel tractor trailer driven by Rajinder Kumar - an illegal immigrant

If you allow millions of people en masse into the country, you need to have a plan. I'll be the first to say I don't have all the answers, but we have a major problem with immigration in this country and it's only getting more urgent by the day.

Aided by Oregon's sanctuary state policies and bail policies, Kumar posted bail on April 2 and was granted release. Twenty days later, on April 22, he was arrested by ICE and taken to the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, Washington.

Although Kumar returned to Deschutes County Jail this month, his deportation order to India still stands. He has hearings scheduled that could grant him bail and release once again, leaving him vulnerable to deportation before his criminal trial on January 19, 2027.

When Kumar returned to Oregon this month ahead of his October 23 bail hearing, I was given the opportunity by ICE to speak with him briefly in the parking lot before he entered the Deschutes County jail. I stood a respectful distance, about five to six feet away. I introduced myself to him and he made eye contact. When I told him that I was Billy's mother, however, he looked down and didn't look up again.

'I know you didn't get up that morning planning to destroy three families' lives,' I said. 'I know you have a family in India and I want you to know that I am praying for you and your family. I hope that we can all find peace at the end of this.'

And I truly believe that. I know that it would be important to Billy for me to forgive him, but it's so hard. I still have so many questions.

I think Kumar deserves a fair trial and a chance to defend himself publicly, but I'd also like to find out why he made the decisions that he did. Why didn't he turn on his warning light? Why didn't he call for help?

I can't help but wonder if Kumar did not call 911 that night because he was worried about his immigration status. I'm worried about the next illegal immigrant who's in an accident and afraid to call 911 either for fear of their status being exposed or because they simply can't speak English. I worry about what's going to happen because of that, and who might die.

I have a serious fear that Kumar may be deported before the trial, which would make it beyond difficult to get him back to Deschutes County for trial. If deported, he would need federal permission to return for the trial, not to mention the financing for him to return.

Billy and Jenny had only been married for 16 days when they died

Billy will never realize his greatest hope – to be a father and have a family of his own

The Deschutes County District Attorneys victims' advocate office has been in touch with me, but there are laws saying that they can't communicate with ICE, so once they picked him up, it made things very complicated.

We've lost too many of our youth to people who should not have legally been here in the first place.

An Oregon judge has issued a $1 million arrest warrant for Kumar, ruling that he violated the terms of his release by leaving the state

I truly believe that if Kumar had been here legally, there is a greater chance that he would have followed the correct protocol and my son and daughter-in-law would still be alive. There is a huge lack of support for immigrants once they are in this country. Should we really be surprised at the chaos that results from that?

If we're going to make laws, we should obey them. When I contacted my senators about preventing tragedies like what happened to my son and daughter-in-law by enforcing more immigration regulation, I consistently got the answer that 'nobody in DC is going to listen to us because we're Democrats.'

I'm appalled by the 'why even try' attitude that I got from Democrats and the lack of follow-through with an issue that this party has exacerbated.

With midterm elections and the anniversary of Billy and Jenny's deaths coming up, I made the decision to testify before Congress earlier this year. I could not stand meekly by while the issue of immigration has slipped off the radar. Billy and Jenny deserved justice and I needed legislators to understand that this is a problem that needs to be addressed now.

I told the panel that I was ashamed of how my party was handling the issue of immigration and I stand by that. I can’t help feeling like they created a problem that they’re now refusing to address or take accountability for. Worse, they seem apathetic about the issue.

While I was giving my testimony, Representative Jerry Nadler (D-NY) fell asleep. I wanted to ask him if my grief bored him.

[Editor's note: The Daily Mail has reached out to representatives for Nadler for comment.]

With midterm elections and the anniversary of Billy and Jenny's deaths coming up, I made the decision to testify before Congress earlier this year

Nadler's behavior that day embodies the passivity I have felt from so many of our elected officials, Democrats and even some Republicans, as other victims and I have called for an end to the dangers enabled by the lax attitudes towards immigration in this country. I've called and written letters to congressmen, but it's been an uphill battle to get anybody to pay attention or even get a reply.

This issue should be so much bigger than party politics. My husband is a Republican and I'm a Democrat, and we can work things out without venom and vitriol and fighting against each other, so why can't the people who love this country enough to serve it put their parties aside and talk about what really matters? I pray that they don't have to lose a child like I did to come to this realization.

Every day, I carry the weight of knowing that Billy and Jenny will never get to have the family they wanted, that they'll never travel the world like they dreamed, and never grow old with one another.

Instead of testifying in front of Congress and lobbying for immigration reform, I should be getting to know my daughter-in-law and looking ahead to spoiling my future grandchildren. I shouldn't have had to plan their joint funeral while their wedding gifts were still arriving. This shouldn't have happened at all because Kumar shouldn't have been in the country in the first place.

#172. UK to draft in military aircraft to fight wildfires, Burnham says

RAF A400M planes will be able to fight wildfires if fire crews request them

Military planes and helicopters will be drafted in to tackle wildfires, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to tell the UK's first summit on the issue.

Civilian fire services in all four nations will be able to request the support of the Royal Air Force's Chinook helicopters and A400M planes to fight wildfires on tough terrain such as remote moorland and steep hillsides.

Burnham said the measures were needed because "we cannot put people through another summer like this one".

The government will host its first "wildfire resilience summit" on Friday to discuss how to prevent, respond to and recover from such blazes after a record-breaking summer 2026.

There have been 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales this year, an all-time high and up by more than 300 on last year and more than 1,000 on 2024, according to figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council.

Records for the number of reported wildfires were also broken in 2022 and 2025 - but the UK's Climate Change Committee has warned the risk will rise in the coming decades.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said this was the first time the RAF's Chinooks and the four-engine A400Ms were being equipped to tackle wildfires. Some areas struggled with no air assistance in the summer.

Chinooks have practised picking up and dropping water from firefighting buckets in Portland harbour, UK

RAF Chinook crews have already helped respond, external to wildfires in Cyprus.

In addition to military aircraft, the government said it would also spend Â£45m on wildfire-specific personal protective equipment for firefighters on the ground.

It is lighter than current firefighting equipment which is designed for fires in buildings and not meant to be worn for a long time, the government added.

Ministers are also pledging a Â£25m scheme from April 2027 to April 2029 to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they are natural firebreaks, and financial support for farmers to fireproof their land such as by digging ponds.

"The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high," a briefing ahead of the summit said, following a temporary ban on disposable BBQs.

Burnham will meet fire chiefs, local leaders and experts from tech companies at the summit.

"I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything," he said on Thursday, recounting the night of a wildfire that destroyed 19 homes in the West Midlands in August.

"I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn't have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs."

Earlier this month, MPs on the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said there were weaknesses in the UK's wildfire preparedness, including access to aerial firefighting resources, securing water supplies during major incidents and coordinating resources at a national level.

Firefighters tackled wildfires across the UK over the summer, including here in Ebbw Vale, Wales

MPs said the current system for obtaining aerial firefighting support was "no longer fit for purpose".

At the summit, a "Wildfires AI Unit" will be announced to combine universities, tech firms and officials on the Cobra emergency committee, along with Met Office wildfire forecasts and closer work with devolved governments.

In August, the government convened a Cobra meeting before sending an emergency alert to millions of phones across England and Wales - which sparked a backlash from some.

Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to the Met Office. In a study on how this summer was impacted by human-induced climate change, it said the heat experienced was made 130 times more likely.

"The wildfires that tore through our countryside this summer showed the urgent need to adapt to our changing climate," Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said ahead of the summit.

"Nature is our greatest ally in preventing wildfires starting in the first place," she added.

Major incidents were declared for wildfires this year in areas such as Dunwich Heath and RSPB Minsmere in Suffolk, the Cairngorms, Hampshire and Holme Fen in Cambridgeshire.

#173. Bruno’s betrayal? ‘Toxic’ Fernandes is symptom of United’s culture of entitlement | Jamie Jackson

Michael Carrick must now deal with more dressing-room unrest after Lisandro Martínez’s attack on the board

“Toxic”: this is the damning characterisation of Bruno Fernandes from one highly placed Manchester United source after the captain’s incendiary betrayal of Michael Carrick.

There has surely never been a greater anti-leadership act in United’s history than Fernandes questioning the man who trusts him to unify the dressing room and execute his on-field plan. The Portuguese has proved this faith wrong at the precise moment he was required to step up and exude a defiant togetherness.

Nothing could be more dysfunctional than civil war between United’s head coach and captain, featuring Carrick biting back at Fernandes for questioning his tactics as matters hit a new low in the aftermath of Wednesday’s pathetic 4-1 loss to Como.

A litmus test for any leader comes when the storm arrives. At the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium, Fernandes failed miserably as he squealed about “the staff” deciding the best tactic was not to press Cesc Fàbregas’s bright, emerging team.

For “staff” read Carrick because he decides strategy and bears responsibility for performance. Fernandes is Carrick’s on-field proxy, so his behaviour is the dictionary definition of betrayal. His conduct is not expected to lead to an disciplinary action in the way Lisandro Martínez’s calling out last week of Jason Wilcox as, perhaps, this is a greyer area.

Discussing tactics may be more within Fernandes’s remit, as captain, than a defender suggesting the director of football’s recruitment failed. Provided there is no damage to the team. But even if Fernandes issues an apology, some acts are irreversible. There is a case for Carrick to strip the 32-year-old of the captaincy and appoint a senior man such as Youri Tielemans or Harry Maguire.

Carrick is expected to hold his pre-game media conference on Friday afternoon and be in charge for Bournemouth’s visit on Sunday, so when the team is announced whether Fernandes has the armband will intrigue. Could he even drop the playmaker? Whatever the decision, Fernandes can have zero excuse for his Como outburst.

Fernandes witnessed how Martínez’s criticism of Wilcox became an extra headache for Carrick, whose sole focus should have been on arresting the direst start to a campaign since 1986. Instead, Carrick had to thrash out the most prudent line of action – Martínez is understood to have been fined – then field questions about the episode.

Yet still Fernandes rounded on Carrick after one of United’s poorest displays in a European competition. It was a performance the player was part of, having been on the field until Carrick removed him on 67 minutes. Being replaced by Joshua Zirkzee, who United tried to offload in the last window, shows how ineffective Fernandes was, first as a false 9, then, after the interval, in his favoured No 10 role.

Fernandes’s comments indicate he is seriously disaffected with team strategy and his role within this. But is there, too, a frustration at still being at the club as his prime years – he was 32 last month – begin to expire? This is someone who voiced disquiet last December, during a jarring interview with Canal 11, the Portuguese Football Federation‑owned channel, at United’s desire to sell him.

Fernandes was asked whether there had been an offer from Paris Saint-Germain or Real Madrid. He said: “Nowadays, the issue of loyalty is no longer seen the way it used to be. I could have left in the last window and would have earned a lot more.

“At one point I was going to leave and I would have won many trophies that season. I decided to stay not only for family reasons, but because I genuinely like the club. The conversation with the coach [Ruben Amorim] also made me stay.

“But from the club’s side, I felt: ‘If you go, it’s not really that bad for us.’ More than hurting, it makes me sad, because I’m a player they have nothing to criticise me for.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Now the club, and specifically Carrick, do feel let down by Fernandes. But, it is also relevant to ask how Fernandes (and Martínez) have come to feel so at ease with going off-message.

These are highly remunerated employees. Their job is to play and maintain a united front – whatever happens – and for Carrick to allow a culture of entitlement to fester shows up a serious fault in his management. For now, Carrick and Fernandes limp on – just like the team.

It will be some act for Carrick to save his job – even victory over Bournemouth may not do so – and for Fernandes to rehabilitate himself, before the head coach and fans. But this is football, a world that can be unpredictable and illogical.

The measure, though, of the debacle at Como, and the wider malaise at the club, can be found in Fàbregas’s post-victory words when he bemoaned allowing Zirkzee’s added-time strike for United.

“I regret the last 10 minutes because I was the one who told the team to slow down the tempo because there’s another match [Sassuolo, on Saturday] and at 4-0 we could manage things a little,” he said.

“Their goal hurt me because we dropped our intensity and dropped our defensive block, but it was my fault.”

How Carrick wishes this was what he had to contend with rather than a mutinous captain and a ship that seems to be sinking deeper on every matchday.

Four cheeky cheetah cubs have been captured in a series of adorable shots exploring their surroundings - with the help of mum!

The cubs - who live at the Lunaret Zoo in Montpellier, southern France - were pictured curiously roaming around their enclosure, playfully jumping on the grass and standing on top of loose tree branches.

In one picture, the cubs are seen beside their mother, Bastet, adorably poking their heads above the branches that lay scattered across the enclosure floor.

In another shot, the cheetah cubs - who were born in captivity - are captured sitting together, their heads curiously tilted to one side as they take in their new surroundings.

One particularly cute picture shows one of the cubs sitting in a white bucket - with only its fluffy head appearing to surface and furry paws on display.

Cheetahs are known for being the world's fastest land animal, but are now classified as a vulnerable species, meaning they could be threatened with extinction due to factors such as habitat loss.

Only around 7,000 to 10,000 of the big cats remain in the wild, making the latest four additions a welcome addition to the species.

#178. Carrick joins Wilcox under the bus after Manchester United’s latest night in crisis | Max Rushden

Bruno Fernandes followed Lisandro Martínez in revolt after his team’s 4-1 defeat to Como in the Champions League

You have to credit Manchester United. Your local rivals have turned the Premier League into an almost meaningless farce. We are questioning the validity of anything we’ve seen over the past 20 years; wondering how many goals Erling Haaland will get in the Championship. We are looking at the league table from second position down and wishing we’d invested in inflatable bananas a month ago.

And yet here comes the Old Trafford machine: from players to the captain to the manager to the director of football, to the director of the director of football, to a minority owner who feels the UK is being “colonised by immigrants”, to debt-leveraging majority owners who take vast sums out of the club and are collectively saying hold my Ineos-sponsored high-performance wellness immune boost smoothie.

Yes, it’s time to dust down the Manchester United bin-fire article. Read this and compare and contrast. From 11 August 2022: “Reds rinse and repeat: will we ever break the Manchester United crisis cycle?” There are others.

It is some feat to be more newsworthy than Manchester City, even for an evening. The defeat in Como wasn’t surprising. We’re getting to the stage where the large pieces of furniture Barney Ronay keeps comparing Harry Maguire to are fighting back. @19thCenturyArmoire: “mate i’m a hundred and sixty years old, of course my legs have gone.” @CoffinFridge69: “#BeKind Ronay, appliances have feelings too.”

Everyone knows the problems at Old Trafford lie deeper than the defensive line held by Maguire and Matthijs de Ligt on Wednesday.

Perhaps it was only a matter of time before Bruno Fernandes’s constant on-field complaining spilled off the pitch. An exercise in throwing his manager under the bus, where presumably Michael Carrick found Jason Wilcox, still lying in hiding under the 250 to the Trafford Centre after Lisandro Martínez’s post-match intervention in Madrid.

Carrick did push back on the criticism: “Whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you aren’t going to win.” But it’s hard to throw someone under the bus when you’re already under the bus you’re trying to throw people under.

Poor Carrick, who may well be gone by the time I finish this tram ride, never mind by the time you get around to reading this. It was one of those funereal press conferences: Carrick being as earnest as it is possible to be, while journalists take it in turn to sound even more earnest, as if they’re questioning a man who’s just failed to blow up the asteroid coming to destroy the Earth.

At this rate, that meteor will arrive long before United have recaptured past glories. Ineos presumably has a big blame pie chart constantly updating on a PowerPoint. Spin the wheel – who’s to blame today? Maybe the players?

Does anyone genuinely know any more whether any United player is good? I have analysis paralysis when trying to work out whether Fernandes is world class or why Youri Tielemans never lumbered at Aston Villa. How bamboozled will we be when Joshua Zirkzee has 25 goal involvements for Real Sociedad next season?

As for Carrick, while most of us (me included) felt he’d earned the right to manage the side this season, a more ruthless and efficient ownership would have made a different call. It wouldn’t have been popular.

He may turn out to be a world-class manager – he may not. Football decides pretty quickly about these things. But if he is sacked, there is a path to redemption. Daniel Farke has moved beyond “only good in the Championship”. Frank Lampard could reasonably expect an apology from anyone who comments on the game for his achievements at Coventry.

But at this stage it is fair to say Carrick doesn’t have the tactical ability or experience of almost all his competitors in the division.

Above him, is Jason Wilcox good? Perhaps the last time someone yelled at him like Martínez, it was Mike Newell after an overhit cross at Ewood Park in 1991. What will Omar Berrada’s CV look like after the independent panel delivers its punishments?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It is fair to say that barring the odd All or Nothing documentary, I have almost no knowledge of what happens behind the scenes. But £1bn spent by United to create this squad over the past five years, plus the randomness of Rangnick/Ten Hag/Van Nistelrooy/Amorim/Carrick, gives us limited evidence to suggest high performance.

And at the top, what does Jim Ratcliffe care about? Apart from enjoying the tax rates of Monaco while opining about the fallen British empire. The good old days where you could just colonise and get a pat on the back, eh Jim.

And then there’s the Glazers. Even for someone whose brain shuts down as soon as they hear the words “leveraged debt” the fact they have extracted about £1bn out of the club since the takeover in 2005 is an outrage. Perhaps if they had overseen a period of sustained success, but it is the opposite.

So when you add bad (maybe bad?) players, bad (or at least disrespectful) captain, bad (not great yet) manager, bad technical director, bad chief executive, bad minority owner, bad majority owners – apologies if I’ve missed anyone – it is, well, bad.

So what’s the best plan of action now? Did someone say Antonio Conte? For the wind and the rain make it happen. As Paul Watson said on the latest Guardian Football Weekly, he might resign during his unveiling.

Lots of us who lived through the Fergie success can’t help but enjoy a Manchester United crisis, but it’s possible to laugh and at the same time sympathise with powerless United fans under that dripping roof in the East Stand.

Football is so stupid that Conte, or Eddie Howe, or even Carrick could turn this into a good season. Perhaps everyone’s expectations still cling to a Manchester United that do not exist any more. Perhaps the odd trophy, the occasional foray deep into Europe, may be the new normal. But right now, how many Premier League teams are worse than they are? Did someone say a Manchester derby in the Championship next season? I can hear David Prutton’s excitement already.

Chelsea are rivalled in the hunt for another Seagulls star by Galatasaray

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Chelsea are interested in signing Brighton midfielder Yasin Ayari, but will face competition from Super Lig leaders Galatasary, according to reports.

Contract negotiations are said to have broken down between Ayari and his current Premier League club, with the Blues lurking.

The Swede has already bagged two assists in six Premier League games for Brighton this season, with his current contract set to expire come the 2026-27 season’s conclusion.

Despite Ayari’s contract soon expiring, the Seagulls do hold an option to extend his deal by an additional 12 months.

However, according to a report from TEAMtalk, the club are yet to activate that clause, and Chelsea are prowling for the Swede’s signature, with Galatasaray emerging as clear rivals.

Ayari is well known to the Blues’ sporting director Paul Winstanley, who has been alerted to the contract conflict between the Swede and Brighton.

Winstanley worked as the Seagulls’ Head of Scouting before his exit from the club in late 2022; now, the Chelsea chief, who initially alerted Brighton to Ayari’s potential, wants to experience a reunion with the player at Stamford Bridge.

In recent years, the London club has successfully pilfered more than a dozen members of staff and players from the Seagulls.

According to the report, Chelsea are likely to face competition for Ayari’s signature from multiple other Premier League sides, but they are currently unnamed.

In the Super Lig, Galatasaray, who are shooting high for an unprecedented fifth successive Turkish top-flight title, are among those outside of England hoping to bag Ayari.

Like Chelsea, they are also displaying interest and continuing to monitor developments in the Swede’s situation at Brighton. Saudi Pro League sides are also lurking, too.

As things stand, Ayari’s future with the Seagulls is up in the air; should he wish to move, Chelsea will certainly be among those interested.

#184. Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears

Warning - this report contains graphic content

The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.

Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.

She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset".

The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually.

"He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her.

"He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".

The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.

You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts

She said the woman replied "lots of times".

"She told me that she was in a lot of pain" and that "she couldn't sit down".

Another friend of the same complainant also gave evidence to the court.

From the witness box, she told the jury her friend had told her that she had told him to stop during the alleged rape.

She said her friend had said the worst moment had been after the act, and "she said that Brand told her she'd been dirty and had to clean up her mess".

"She said he was quite cold and keen to get her gone".

The witness said she had given her friend advice after she had confided in her.

"I told her that she should go and get checked out because she had anal tears and a lot of discomfort and to seek guidance from her parents and to go to the police.

"She just wasn't sure - it was all a bit chaotic in her head. She felt like it wasn't worth it."

She told jurors: "She didn't think she would be believed, and she didn't think it would be worth it to go.

Statements from the alleged rape victim's parents said their daughter stayed with them for about two months after the alleged incident with Brand.

Her mother's statement said: "I just remember her saying 'he raped me'.

"She was very worried about HIV," she said, adding that her daughter had started talking about it during a car journey.

"She said she went to his place, went to see him, as she had always admired him."

Her father recalled their daughter being "very upset and very unwell", during the stay, that that she was "upset by something that had happened to her."

The father said in his statement that his daughter told him: "They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted.

"I turned to her in the car and asked if she asked him to stop, and she said 'no' several times.

"I said 'you have been raped, that's rape'."

He said his daughter got a sexual health check, and he said he had only recently learned his daughter is accusing Brand of anal rape.

The woman's former boyfriend also gave evidence, telling the court she was "very upset" whenever she talked about her encounter with Brand, and that "she characterised it as an assault... she called it rape".

Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC cross-examined the woman's former boyfriend and read parts of the statement he gave in June 2025, in which he said the woman had "come round" to having anal sex.

When asked if he had said that, the witness replied: "Yes."

The witness added the woman had "surrendered to the idea".

"If I was being attacked, you either fight back or surrendered, it doesn't negate the attack," he added.

Judge Mr Justice Bennathan sent the jury away until Monday morning, at the end of Thursday's evidence.

He told the jurors that "we aim to finish the prosecution case on Monday", adding the defence case would not begin before Tuesday morning.

#185. Third-longest serving manager in top 92 clubs Woodman leaves Bromley

Andy Woodman won 123 of his 289 games in charge of Bromley, a win percentage of 42.6

Long-standing Bromley manager Andy Woodman has left the League One club following the mutual termination of his contract.

Woodman joined Bromley in 2021 in his first managerial role and oversaw the most successful period in the club's history, winning three trophies in guiding them into the Football League for the first time in their history.

Bromley lifted the League Two title in May this year to secure a second promotion on his watch, with Woodman named the division's manager of the year for 2025-26.

But the Ravens have found life in the third tier challenging as they lie 23rd, just one point above bottom club Wigan Athletic.

They have won just two of their 10 league games this season and conceded an EFL-high 25 goals.

Assistant manager Byron Webster will take charge of first-team affairs on an interim basis with Peterborough United the visitors to Hayes Lane on Saturday (15:00 BST).

Bromley owner and chairman Robin Stanton-Gleaves said Woodman had been "fundamental" in helping the club reach new heights.

"On a personal note, Andy has been a pleasure to work with, and I wish him all the best for the future," Stanton-Gleaves added.

Woodman's five years and seven months in charge of Bromley was the third-longest spell across the 92 clubs in the Premier League and EFL, behind only Arsenal's Mikel Arteta and Nigel Clough of Mansfield.

Pre-match, post-match and topical Ravens content

It certainly comes as a shock to see Andy Woodman departing Hayes Lane but after a 4-0 loss to Leicester City on Tuesday - a third straight defeat in the league in a row and a fifth in a row across all competitions - on form alone, the decision is understandable.

Under Woodman, Bromley have achieved unprecedented success his five and a half year stewardship leading them to an FA Trophy, National League play-off final victory and League Two title last season.

With two years left on his contract, all signs pointed to him being given the chance to lead Bromley through their maiden season in League One but, with only two wins from their opening 10 games, now was seen as the time to be making a change, from both the club and crucially, Woodman himself.

Had this been a straight sacking, it could have been argued that Woodman was a victim of his own success, however the mutual nature of the termination shows that both sides felt that this was the right moment.

It has been an incredibly tough start to the season, compounded by an incredibly long injury list and a large turnover in the squad as mitigating factors, and some truly humbling losses including the 7-2 at Hillsborough and the 5-0 at Hayes Lane to Leyton Orient.

But this all feels sad and shocking in its abruptness, and leaves questions open as to where Bromley go next.

Life without Woodman will feel hard for fans to contemplate, but he will be remembered as the man who lifted them to these heights, and as someone "fundamental" to the club's recent success.

#186. Toddler and grandparents found dead in Ohio home after mystery caller dialed 911 and softly said 'help'

Published: 02:07 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 02:19 BST, 23 October 2026

A toddler and his two grandparents found shot dead inside an Ohio home have been identified after a chilling 911 call in which dispatchers heard someone apparently whispering 'help' before authorities found the trio.

The victims were named on Thursday as Melissa E. Campbell, 51, Gale F. Sanders, 67, and 22-month-old Kozzar J. Lotut, whose bodies were discovered at a property in the small village of Gnadenhutten, south of Canton, on Wednesday.

All three had suffered gunshot wounds, according to the Tuscarawas County Coroner's Office.

Investigators are now attempting to piece together what happened inside the home.

The disturbing discovery followed a mysterious emergency call shortly after 4am that abruptly disconnected before dispatchers could establish where it was coming from.

When emergency operators attempted to call the number back, they heard what appeared to be a faint plea for assistance.

On one of those calls, a dispatcher heard a 'voice softly saying the word "help,"' according to the Tuscarawas County Sheriff's Office.

The unsettling exchange sparked an urgent effort to locate the caller, eventually leading deputies to the home.

Melissa E. Campbell, 51, was among three people found dead inside an Ohio home after a mysterious 911 call prompted deputies to investigate

Authorities discovered the body of 22-month-old Kozzar J. Lotut at a home in Tuscarawas County, Ohio, following a 911 call

Authorities believe the deaths may have been the result of a murder-suicide, although investigators have not publicly established who fired the fatal shots or explained what might have prompted the violence.

A firearm was recovered beside one of the bodies, according to the sheriff, who told Cleveland 19 that evidence gathered so far pointed toward a murder-suicide.

However, the precise circumstances remain under investigation, and officials have not identified a suspected shooter.

The deaths have stunned the small rural community of Gnadenhutten.

According to the sheriff's office, the first indication that something was seriously wrong came shortly after 4am on Wednesday morning.

Emergency dispatchers received a call to 911, but the connection was cut almost immediately.

The caller did not provide an address, leaving operators with no obvious way of determining where help was needed.

Investigators eventually contacted the owner of the number, who explained that he had lent the device to someone else.

Police tape surrounds the Ohio home where deputies made the grim discovery after a mystery caller dialed 911 and softly said 'help'

Kozzar J. Lotut's short life came to a tragic end when the 22-month-old was found dead in a home in the quiet Ohio village of Gnadenhutten

Campbell, 51, was identified by authorities as one of the victims in the mysterious triple death investigation that has rocked the small Ohio community

Three people were found dead at the modest Ohio home after deputies traced a 911 call there

That information led deputies to examine several possible addresses as they worked to narrow down the phone's location with their search ultimately bringing them to the property in Gnadenhutten.

A family member was already at the scene when law enforcement arrived and allowed deputies to enter the home, according to the sheriff's office.

Once inside, officers discovered the bodies of two adults and a young child.

The coroner's office confirmed their identities as little Kozzar, who was just 22 months while Campbell and Sanders were his grandparents, who had played an important role in looking after the little boy.

The pair frequently helped care for Kozzar because he had medical disabilities.

It also remains unclear exactly when the shootings occurred in relation to the initial 911 call, or whether the faint plea for assistance came from one of the three people subsequently discovered dead.

The sheriff has indicated that investigators are examining the possibility that one of the deaths was self-inflicted and the others were homicides.

#187. Paris Saint-Germain sparkle on the pitch while the city of light burns around them | Barney Ronay

PSG, pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfect

Those who sought to bring down the Republic will have to answer for it.

Tell you who would have loved this? Who would have been utterly engrossed scrolling the hashtag #Paris on Tuesday night as two things happened simultaneously, the harrowing of the Barcelona defence at the Parc des Princes, and the harrowing of Paris itself via tales of city-centre thuggery and end-of-days political doom‑mongering.

The big man, Guy Debord himself. The Society of the Spectacle, you say? Actually, I think we’re past that now. Hold the society bit. We’ll just take the spectacle.

The great Parisian Situationist philosopher wasn’t really one for managed fun. But it was impossible not to be bowled over by the extraordinary pre-match show for Paris Saint‑Germain versus Barcelona, Champions League Matchday Three.

The wild pyrotechnics, the plumes of smoke, the full-wrap light show, the lime-green robo‑text spelling out every player’s name on the pitch. Although not the Barcelona names, sadly, for anyone with an unrealised desire to see the words “ANTHONY GORDON” projected in vast letters for the delight of a shrieking crowd.

Admittedly, the Halloween‑themed tifo banner showing a masked Paris Saint-Germain serial killer-type literally butchering the Barcelona badge to death with his bloodied chainsaw was perhaps a bit much. As were the Barça Puta signs, which are now reportedly the subject of a complaint to Uefa.

But it was a wild and all‑consuming spectacle, annihilating every other impulse in your head to a green thought in a green shade. And in the process capturing the profound sense of cognitive dissonance in the city.

Just walking around the streets of central Paris earlier in the day generated its own mild whiplash. On the face of it this was still the same city of flâneurs and tourists and everyday bistro business, and not, repeat not, a civil war drama or some kind of emergent military caliphate.

But the sense of dread was also tangible. You still got the occasional crunch of glass underfoot. Here and there charred bikes and scooters had been politely piled to one side. Even close to the Parc, away from the main hotspots, shopkeepers could be seen emerging warily into their doorways at the sound of a police siren.

By Tuesday night, a total of 2,513 people had been taken into police custody after the events of the weekend. At least 420 rental bikes had been destroyed or maimed. Liberated high-value retail goods were already being sold on Vinted, a commendable show of entrepreneurial energy from the maligned younger generation.

Not that you’d suspect these two worlds had any kind of overlap, lost in the booming triumphalism around PSG’s 4–2 win, one of the most beautifully luminous football matches you’re ever likely to see. Or indeed reading the coverage of an event that seems to have been treated in France like its own clear, clean space, floating above the flames, all the chat about the brilliance of Monsieur Dynamite, Désiré Doué, the wonderful television audiences on Canal+ TV, the whole of European football “kneeling before the machine” (are we sure this isn’t to do with anarchic rejection of social control?). “Paris est insubmersible!” was the headline in Le Parisien. But is it?

Remember when football used to reflect the world? Or just provide clues, a commentary, some kind of metaphor? This is no longer the case. At a time when even the most thunderous of commentators is struggling to summarise all this in suitably trite and damning terms, it was hard to avoid the feeling Paris Saint-Germain, the pet power football project of the state of Qatar, expresses this dualism perfectly.

Sometimes you just have to let football tell you things. “People who want to cause trouble in the city centres next Saturday will be prevented,” Emmanuel Macron announced on Tuesday evening, speaking, as it happens, from Doha, where he met Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, ultimate owner of PSG.

Macron is said to be considering deploying the French military to keep the peace on the streets before the next planned protests, although even here he may have to ask Qatar’s permission if he wants to deploy any of the French troops currently deployed working its missile systems, or embedded in the Doha security services.

The key event Macron is tooling up for is this Saturday night, 24 October, the date the gilets jaunes social media feed has set for an even greater swell of disorder. And again this will be football adjacent, with PSG playing Lyon at home on Sunday, a top‑of‑the-table capital‑city clash played out against whatever wreckage is left, however many thousands of Dot bikes are savaged, whatever guerrilla skirmishes are still playing out in the Marais.

What does this really have to do with football and the Ici C’est Paris brand appropriated by a state outreach project? Well, what are these demonstrations anyway? There have been many theories put forward as to what exactly is happening here, what is the spark, the kindling, the fire behind this disorder. School protests were the original line. Others have now roped in some kind of nebulous omni-cause, Instagram-activism, perhaps even a barbarian takeover, the decline of the west, savagery at the gates, of the type Donald Trump pretends to see.

Do you need a single reason? Take a look around. Modern life is pretty alarming on a minute‑to‑minute basis. Disaffection, alienation, a sense of being transformed in real time into a passive economic consumer unit, a set of eyeballs, an avatar of consumption. French youth unemployment is close to 20%. Robots nobody wants are being lined up to take jobs that don’t exist. Why don’t these young people want to join a youth club? Why don’t they sign up for the Liberal Democrats? Why are they enjoying empowered disorder? Maybe because nothing is yours around here, not even the things thrust into your brain as digital distractions. So why not grab something when you can? Debord would have called this “a vicious circle of isolation”, lonely crowd, technologies based on isolation.

On the other hand, what is PSG in Paris, other than the perfect expression of this? It often seems to surprise people that celebrations of PSG victories end up with riots and burnt-out cars. But Paris is both a beautiful and deeply dysfunctional city, a place of make‑believe and deprivation, where the centre is a perfect, performative relic, the suburbs shunted out to the ring roads, a life lived inside a box, noses pressed up against the glass, peering through your binoculars at the city of someone else’s love.

Paris is the divide between overclass and churn expressed in a single city. It’s everything you might have had but never will. And PSG represent this like no other entity, a football club owned as an act of outreach by a staggeringly rich inherited monarchy, weaponised passion, borrowed culture, engineered spectacle, deeply cynical but also deeply seductive.

Why are the Qataris splurging hundreds of millions into this project? Because they just really like high-pressing positional football? Qatar is the indentured labour state that employs Colin Kaepernick to promote its outreach projects. It will hymn its connections to the footballers of the banlieue, which is true and real and valuable, but not because of anything this political project wants or needs other than public relations.

It is in its own way a perfect human lab experiment, synthesised beauty, collectivism, with a cold, cold hand at its heart. And this is why there weren’t two versions of Paris in evidence on Tuesday night, just the same one, the dark side and the shiny side, an engine of the same divisions, the same kind of violence, right down to the sight of kids in PSG training gear dodging the police or taunting the barricades at the Place de la République.

And now we have Sunday night to come, more Ici C’est Paris, more PASSION. What kind of background will it be played out against? Does it matter under the lights? Will anyone notice?

Le Monde has described these events as a very basic test of the republic, its ability to bend, to remain essentially itself, the state’s willingness to pit itself against its own people. Football, as ever, holds these answers already. PSG’s Qatari owners have spent the past 15 years flaunting this city like a global luxury brand, extending its reach, creating its own ideal of conspicuous consumption, spectacle, triumph, son et lumière, bread and roses. As ever, if you want to know how and why, football has the answers.

#199. ‘We can go all the way’: Jonas Eidevall on life at San Diego Wave and lessons learned from Arsenal

The Swede’s team are second in the NWSL and hope to create special memories at their Snapdragon Stadium

“I love the ocean,” Jonas Eidevall says, and he references walks along the beach at Del Mar. “People are very relaxed, life is lived at a slower pace here. I’m a very simple person. I like to read a book, go to the gym and spend time with my wife and kids, that’s sort of all I need.”

The former Arsenal head coach is revelling in a calmer world as the head coach of San Diego Wave but it is not merely the beaches that are lowering his stress levels; his team are on a five-game winning streak in the NWSL and sit second in the table, one point off top spot, with two matches to go before the playoffs. Winning feels good and the club are targeting silverware, as he tells the Guardian: “It would mean everything. There are no guarantees in the playoffs, but the exciting part is saying: ‘We can also go all the way’ – that’s a possibility for us and we need to believe.”

Success did not originally look destined, when the Swede took charge 21 months ago, at a time when San Diego Wave were enduring something of an exodus of senior players; the United States defender Abby Dahlkemper’s sale to Bay FC in August 2024 and Alex Morgan’s retirement a month later were followed by the USA forward Jaedyn Shaw’s departing for North Carolina Courage and her international teammate Naomi Girma joining Chelsea in January 2025. A reconstruction was needed.

That is why, on a video call that winter, when Eidevall spoke to his players for the first time after taking charge, he began by quoting a proverb: if you want to go fast, go alone, but if you want to go far, go together. “My ideas are not worth anything if we don’t believe and buy into them altogether,” he says. “We focused everything on just building connections as human beings.” Detailed tactical discussions were initially kept to a minimum. They spent – as he recalls – around four weeks of their six-week pre-season focusing entirely on passing out from the back, to develop their style. Fast forward to the present day and it has paid off, with the Wave defenders Kristen McNabb and Kennedy Wesley being the division’s top two players for passes completed this season. More notable, though, has been the development of young players, such as the 18-year-olds Melanie Barcenas and Kimmi Ascanio.

“From 2024, when the club was not performing well on the pitch and it led to a complete rebuild, we had to find an edge, finding players that could fit into the way we wanted to play,” Eidevall says. “Back then it was a bit different to many other teams in the league, because the NWSL was seen as being dominated by athleticism and transitional play, which obviously then requires really fast players and maybe didn’t put a premium on technical supremacy.”

He adds that the club therefore eyed players who are “really, really good technically. We had some young, talented players already – that has given us a really good advantage because we’ve been able to develop players in a salary cap league. That’s huge, because if you only buy readymade players, you will run out of salary cap space pretty quickly.”

It is not just the salary cap that differs in the NWSL, compared to Eidevall’s previous jobs at Arsenal and Rosengård. The broad competitiveness of the American league means that, despite being second in the table, San Diego have lost almost as many games this season as Eidevall’s Arsenal across three English campaigns, and he says: “This was new for me. In European leagues the top teams very rarely go two games in a row without winning. Here, even the team that wins the league might go through spells where they don’t pick up points, so the way you handle those moments becomes very important.

“Training [here] is also a challenge – sometimes it’s very hard to get 22 players because you have a limited roster size. The moment you start to have injuries … there’s no real second-team academy system like we have in Europe, where you can always have the numbers that you want. Here you might not, here you would like to do something XI v XI, but you have 18 players and you just have to be creative with how you coach.”

Trying to play entertaining football has been a target in a campaign during which they have already set new club records for regular-season wins and goals scored. They have done it with the second-highest average possession share in the division, more shots on target than any other team and while facing by far the fewest shots on target.

“That’s the most pleasing part, results through an identity rather than getting results the other way around,” Eidevall says. “The identity we have is to allow the players to be creative.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

We are speaking around two years after Eidevall resigned as Arsenal’s head coach on 15 October 2024, following a disappointing start to that season. In his three full campaigns at the helm in north London he had won two League Cups, reached a Champions League semi-final and secured a second-placed top-flight finish in 2022 – but was unable to win the WSL. Reflecting on what he learned from that spell, he says: “We had a lot of fluidity with how our wide players could play in Arsenal, which at times created too few central options. So, how do we get better central connections? How do we get more players central on the pitch? That was a long-term reflection on my time at Arsenal. And that’s also led to some tactical changes that we’ve done here with San Diego.”

There is an aspect of his Arsenal tenure that he is determined to take inspiration from at San Diego, with his team having secured a home playoff quarter-final at their 35,000-seater Snapdragon Stadium.

The 43-year-old fondly remembers the first sellout crowd for a women’s match at Arsenal’s 60,000-seater Emirates Stadium, for their Champions League semi-final against Wolfsburg in 2023: “We want to sell out Snapdragon Stadium and in order to do so we need to do exactly what we were doing at Arsenal – we need to create special experiences at the stadium,” he says. “That is what’s going to draw people into there. Yes, play exciting football, but we also need to play games that mean a lot to be there. The ripple effect of that, that’s so big.”

#206. Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds

The Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing family

Viewed in 2026, Nathan Barley, Chris Morris’s 2005 sitcom, shows remarkable prescience about the last two decades of metropolitan life, from smartphone addiction and digital derangement to sheer existential vapidity. When Barley’s character referred to his occupation as “self-facilitating media node”, Morris and co-writer Charlie Brooker were way ahead on the creator economy. What the pair failed to predict was ex-footballers joining the sector in droves. These days, if you are a former footballer without a podcast or YouTube channel, then did you ever really play the game?

Setting aside the Gary Lineker Goalhanger empire, manspreading its centrist-dad agenda into issues way beyond guffaws with Micah Richards and Alan Shearer, there is Gary Neville to rule them all. Manchesterism’s second-most influential practitioner has been on heavy manoeuvres. Unlike Lineker’s productions, the Overlap’s output continues to stick largely to football; a rugby podcast was mothballed in February, though its cricket equivalent continues.

Having snatched Wayne Rooney from the BBC in the summer for a Manchester United-based two-hander with the YouTuber Mark Goldbridge, last week the Overlap went daily, extending the output to 4pm Monday to Friday. An online launch had Jamie Carragher baiting Goldbridge, real name Brent Di Cesare. The former policeman shunned a “no comment” approach during his interrogation, biting back during an exchange that had Neville choking on his Huel in laughter. Clipped up, the send button pressed, job done.

The Overlap has gained a TV family dynamic, a chorus line of familiar characters. Neville and Carragher are mummy and daddy bear, football’s Richard and Judy. Jill Scott is the dotty aunt, Roy Keane the irascible uncle, smirking along with Ian Wright in picking over the latest gossip. It has been highly popular, occasionally agenda-setting, softening Keane’s image, even making a cultish figure of production hand Kiaran Saunders, supplier of biscuits and blueberries. Neville’s empire-building, though, is boundless, his tanks bulldozing into the already packed football podcast space, with newsletters to follow. The Overkill, anyone?

The family has been extended. Mondays have Steven Gerrard reviewing the weekend’s action with Becky Ives, this week offering a defence of Florian Wirtz: “Don’t give up on him.” Tuesdays have Kelly Cates and Ashley Young in tandem. Tim Sherwood and Jamie Redknapp are Wednesday’s pairing. Not the first time the Sky mainstays, one-time Tottenham midfield partners, have diversified. In the mid-2000s, they ran Icon, a lifestyle magazine initially only available to professional players. A combination of high-end advertising, onanistic photography and Redknapp’s purring interviews with A-list sportspeople fell flat, even after it became available in airport first-class lounges.

Two decades on, such cologne-fragrant exclusivity has been swapped for the ubiquity of Bury’s most famous son piling it high. The quarter-zipped ex-Spurs duo are not alone as 1990s footballers taking the Neville shilling. Mark Crossley and Duncan Ferguson make an unlikely – but promising – pairing. Previously most famous for being the only goalkeeper to save a Matthew Le Tissier penalty, Crossley has made a successful after-dinner speaking career of Brian Clough anecdotes and “young man” impressions. “Big Dunc” completely refused to speak to the media when a player but he was a hit within ITV’s World Cup 2026 coverage.

On last week’s edition Ferguson suggested Gianluigi Donnarumma might be over the hill. “He’s 27, actually,” said Crossley before a classic game’s gone discussion of video assistant referees ruining the sacred art of smashing into the opposition at goal-kicks. Just what the listener came for, eating perhaps into the Under The Cosh’s market share of real football man podcasts. Whether Ferguson’s appointment as Glentoran manager breaks up the band is unclear, though management never halted Robbie Savage’s many media ventures.

Two further goalkeepers have signed up. Last week’s Friday edition had Joe Hart and Peter Schmeichel entering the Manchester City charges chat. While admitting to mistakenly burying the lead when Lisandro Martínez was willingly dishing the dirt on Manchester United while serving as CBS’s Champions League interviewer in Madrid last Tuesday, Schmeichel gave Hart a far harder ride. “It’s tough to be a Manchester City person,” Hart said. “I love the club … we’re in it together.” Schmeichel stayed insistent on City’s owners: “They’re letting Manchester down, they don’t understand what this place is. They have built a lot of towers and homes and all that but they don’t get this place.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“I’ve worked closely with Khaldoon [al-Mubarak] and he does get this place, that’s my reference point,” said a hesitant Hart. “He’s an incredible person.” More good, strong, clip-up content.

The City affair will ask former players to intersect with uncomfortable issues for some while yet. That Neville’s further business interests include building projects running parallel to the Abu Dhabi-funded developments in Manchester is another example. Overlaps have become unavoidable in more ways than one.

#208. Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in remarkable defeat

Harry Brook hit the fastest 200 in the history of one-day internationals

Just under a year ago, Harry Brook was left wondering if he would be sacked as England white-ball captain and what damage he had done to his international career.

What a turnaround in 12 months. From whacked in Wellington to the run-fest in Rawalpindi, Brook is undeniably England's most important cricketer and probably the best multi-format batter in the world.

Brook's 202 in England's defeat against Sri Lanka was an astonishing display of stroke-making. There can be no higher praise than to compare Brook's dismantling of the Sri Lankan attack to the sort of innings once played by South African genius AB de Villiers.

It was the first double hundred scored by an Englishman in an ODI, passing England's previous best individual score of 182 by Ben Stokes against New Zealand in 2023. In reaching 200 in 114 balls, Brook registered the fastest double ton by anyone in an ODI, bettering the 117 deliveries of India's Shubman Gill against West Indies only last month.

Brook has joined one of international cricket's most exclusive clubs. In completing the set of a hundred in a T20, double hundred in an ODI and triple century in a Test, Brook has matched the previously unique treble of West Indies' legend Chris Gayle.

In the moment, the collection of another landmark might not mean a great deal to Brook. Despite his efforts, his team were beaten as the spirited Sri Lankans pulled off the second-highest run-chase in history in one of the most astonishing ODIs ever played.

For a man who has previously spoken about prioritising match-winning contributions over individual achievements, Brook the captain was left dejected that his innings ultimately counted for nothing. He is the first man to make a double ton in an ODI and end up on the losing side.

Still, it further underlined his status as the premier run-getter across all kinds of international cricket. Perhaps only Australia's Travis Head can challenge Brook for the crown.

Ranked by the International Cricket Council as the best Test batter in the world, Brook averages 53.08 in the longer format of the game. No England player with a minimum of 20 innings since 1968 has a better average than Brook â he stands above Joe Root, Alastair Cook, Geoffrey Boycott, Graham Gooch and everyone else to have batted for England in the past seven decades.

In T20 internationals, Brook averages 36.21 at a strike-rate of 164.92. No batter to have played at least 20 innings for a major nation averages more at a better strike-rate.

Brook is learning to play List A cricket in one-day internationals. Sri Lanka was his 61st List A match, 45 of which have been ODIs. After a slow start to his international 50-over career, Brook averages just under 50 in his past 29 matches and almost 57 in 2026.

The responsibility of captaincy suits him. In ODIs, Brook averages 31 runs more as captain compared to when not. In T20s, his average jumps 19 runs when wearing the metaphorical armband.

'That's life' - captain Brook on England defeat

Brook's workload is an issue, the Yorkshireman having played in every England fixture since being rested for a T20 series in Ireland last September and, fitness permitting, he will be the only man to play in every game this winter â that's five tours to four countries across three continents. He left home last week and will not again see his own bed until mid-January.

He says his time to rest is during the Indian Premier League, the riches of which he has turned down in order to focus his energy on England. Brook probably does not get enough credit for making such a decision.

There is the question of how good Brook could become. Ben Stokes revealed that, at the end of the Ashes, he took Brook to one side to say he should be averaging 60 or more in Test cricket.

Speaking to the BBC in August, Brook admitted to not being the "finished article".

"I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games," he said.

In terms of improvement, Brook has already shown a willingness to do the hard yards to become a better cricketer.

As a youngster, he struggled with his fitness, but has worked hard to become one of the best athletes in the England team. He has spoken at length about being better able to run twos â he is one of the best runners between the wickets in the world. Brook has also turned himself into one of England's most reliable catchers.

As for the batting, well-qualified judges don't hold back in their praise. Last month, Stokes said Brook may have more talent than Kevin Pietersen. In 2024, James Anderson said Brook could surpass Root as England's highest Test run-scorer. Just last week, Chris Woakes labelled Brook as "next level".

Harry Brook hit 21 fours and 10 sixes against Sri Lanka

The missing achievement is a starring role in winning a major series or tournament.

Brook's magnificent century should have been enough for England to win the fifth Test against India at The Oval last year, only for him to throw away his wicket with victory in sight. He has not made a century in 10 Ashes Tests against Australia and was only a bit-part player as part of the England team that won the T20 World Cup in 2022.

Maybe his moment is approaching. Next summer is a home Ashes, followed by the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. Brook will be 28 and at the peak of his powers. There is the chance to play a major part in regaining the urn and to become one of the few British athletes to lift a World Cup in any sport.

To do that, he will have to iron out the flaws that have arisen in England's one-day cricket across the first two matches of the tri-series in Pakistan.

In the opening match, against Pakistan, dropped catches and poor strokes left them well beaten in a contest they could have won.

Against Sri Lanka, England somehow lost from what seemed an impregnable position, their bowling and fielding falling apart amid a growing realisation they were in danger of failing to defend a target of 430.

There was some mitigation. Dew made the ball incredibly slippery, while their attack was weakened by the absence of the rested Jofra Archer and benched Adil Rashid.

Nevertheless, the bowling was awful, particularly Sam Curran, who conceded 103 from nine overs to return the worst figures by an England bowler in an ODI. It was an error by Brook to continue to show faith in the left-armer, while not using the full allocation of 10 overs from either Josh Tongue or Gus Atkinson.

It is one of the first major missteps of Brook's captaincy career and the sort of performance that shows England still have some way to go to be seen as serious World Cup contenders.

Now, England will have to win their next two matches to reach the tri-series final, to be played on 31 October, exactly 12 months on from Brook's horror show in Wellington.

#212. Sheff Wed forward Lowe racially abused on social media

Jamal Lowe has scored five goals in 10 League One appearances this season

Sheffield Wednesday forward Jamal Lowe has revealed his wife was sent a message racially abusing him on social media.

The comment was posted multiple times on his partner's Instagram photos after the 32-year-old Jamaica international was sent off in Tuesday's 2-0 defeat at Notts County.

The League One club released a statement, external on Wednesday saying "racism is abhorrent. It has no place in football or in society, and we condemn this abuse in the strongest possible terms".

"Bad performance or not, racially abusing a player from the team you 'support' is miles off it," Lowe posted on his Instagram account.

"Parents educate your kids, call out family members who display this type of sick behaviour.

"To think we're only one bad result away from being called a monkey is actually insane.

"This is happening way too often! Do better."

The UK Policing Football Unit have confirmed to BBC Sport that they are investigating the matter.

"As we have said repeatedly, there is absolutely no place for racial abuse, either online or in person, and anyone who believes they can hide behind their keyboards should think again," they said in a statement.

"The UKFPU condemns this abhorrent behaviour and we will ensure that, through our dedicated team of officers, we do everything possible to identify those responsible and bring them to justice."

It is the second time this year that racist abuse has been directed at a Sheffield Wednesday player in the aftermath of a game.

In April, an unidentified Owls player was targeted by what the club called "disgraceful and completely unacceptable racist messages" following a 1-1 draw against Leicester.

Wednesday's club statement added: "This is not the first incident of its kind involving our players, staff and their families this season. The continued targeting of individuals and their loved ones is utterly unacceptable.

"Only last weekend, we stood alongside the EFL in supporting its Together Against Racism campaign. Incidents such as this reinforce why collective action and meaningful consequences remain so important."

In 2024, the club was fined Â£12,500 and an Owls fan was banned for five years after Kasey Palmer of Coventry was subjected to a racist gesture during a Championship match.
