#213. Meghan Markle's father Thomas 'is being probed over huge stash of child abuse photos found at Philippines home': Thomas Sr is reported to police by his own son - but daughter Samantha says it's 'all lies'

By CAROLINE GRAHAM, US EDITOR THE MAIL ON SUNDAY and PATRICK HARRINGTON, UK NEWS REPORTER

Published: 23:35 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 03:13 BST, 23 October 2026

Meghan Markle's father Thomas is at the centre of a child sex images storm after being reported to police by his own son.

Thomas Markle Sr is being investigated over a hoard of 'sickening' images that are said to have been found at his Philippines home.

But the family are furious about the allegations, with Meghan's half-sister Samantha telling the Daily Mail her brother Thomas Jr, 60, had invented the story to make money – and even suggesting that their father, 82, had been framed.

Thomas Jr told police he stumbled across 'hundreds' of child sex abuse images in four large boxes at his father's home in the city of Cebu, The Sun reported.

Amongst the material was said to be a 15-minute video of young girls, who appeared younger than 11, performing sex acts – alongside a number of still pictures of scantily-clad children.

Thomas Jr said his father's desktop was 'full of row-upon-row of thumbnail pictures linking to the most sickening child abuse imaginable. The worst of the worst.'

There were said to be pictures of pre-school children, toddlers in some cases, either nude or engaged in sex acts, and images of a man engaged in a sex act with a very young girl on the pages of an antique book.

He claimed one of the images was a photograph of a laptop, in the background of which he recognised a room in his father's former home in Mexico.

Thomas Markle Sr, pictured with nurse Rio Canedo, 46, is the subject of a child sex investigation after being reported to police by his own son

Meghan and her father Thomas, pictured here together, have been estranged since 2018, the year she married Prince Harry

Thomas Markle Jr, Meghan's brother, claimed to have found the child-abuse material packed up in boxes at his father's Philippines home

He made the discovery over the summer, after Thomas Sr had been forced to return to the US by a stroke and blood clot that led to the amputation of his left leg.

Thomas Jr said he had been searching for a mobile phone for his Filipino girlfriend, when he came across the stash his father had allegedly left behind.

He said he saw the first of the material after switching on an abandoned LG mobile, and on July 10 reported his discovery to the FBI Hotline, the US-based National Centre for Exploited and Missing Children, and the state police in Pennsylvania – where his father was living.

But after growing concerned by the lack of action, Thomas Jr said he later returned to the four boxes and enlisted a local IT expert to access three computer hard drives – which contained the bulk of the material.

Thomas Jr has submitted his sworn statement to Filipino police, who have launched an investigation and are preparing to seize the evidence.

A source close to Meghan reportedly told the paper: 'Now maybe people will finally understand why she has had nothing to do with her father since 2018.'

The Daily Mail has contacted the Sussexes for comment.

But Samantha, Meghan's sister, has furiously hit back, branding her brother's allegations about their father as 'disgusting' and 'having no merit in them whatsoever'.

Samantha, who is her father's main caregiver, called her brother a 'liar' and claimed he was making up the allegations to make money.

She said: 'There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.

'My brother first came out with these lies a few weeks ago when the cash from my dad was cut off. He has used dad as a cash cow for years and once the money stopped he made up the most outrageous lies he could to try and make money from the media.'

Samantha said The Sun's story is factually incorrect. The accusations claim the boxes were found 'at Tom's house in the Philippines'.

She said: 'That is not factually true. The computers were packed up in Mexico and put on a cargo ship. They were then in storage in the basement of a building in the Philippines. Dad had no access to them.

'The boxes were then in Tom Jr's house. Dad had no access to those computers for two years. Who knows who could have had access to them? I don't believe any of it. Anyone could have set dad up.'

A young Meghan pictured with her father back when they shared a loving relationship

Meghan and Prince Harry in Sydney in 2018 - the year she became estranged from her father

Meghan has not made any comment on the allegations that have sent shockwaves through the family

Samantha Markle (left) pictured with her father Thomas Snr and brother Thomas Jnr

Meghan with her father on the day of her marriage to her first husband Trevor Engelson in 2011

She said: 'There is no proof my dad downloaded any images. Those computers were out of his possession for two years. That leaves a lot of room for tampering. These are unsubstantiated allegations.

'Anyone could have been in contact with those computers over a couple of years. Dad was in a rehabilitation facility and did not have access to those computers.'

Samantha is Thomas Jr's sister from her father's first marriage to Roslyn Loveless. Award-winning Hollywood lighting director Thomas Sr then married Meghan Markle's mother Doria Ragland and Meghan was born in 1981.

Thomas Sr became estranged from Meghan on the eve of her 2018 wedding to Prince Harry after he suffered two heart attacks and was unable to attend the ceremony at St George's Chapel, Windsor.

He has never met his grandchildren Archie, seven, and five-year-old Lilibet.

Samantha said her 82-year-old father is in poor health and 'hanging on by a thread': 'Dad has severe physical and cognitive issues and is too frail and sick to defend himself. It's disgusting that my brother is trying to destroy a man who has done nothing but support him his entire life. My brother needs money. That is what this is all about.'

Thomas Sr had his left leg amputated below the knee last December and has suffered several heart attacks and a stroke.

Samantha accused her brother of nursing a 'vendetta' against their father.

She said: 'My brother has had this vendetta against my dad for years and when the money runs out he makes up stories for cash. He made up a story a few years ago about my dad snorting cocaine with hookers in Thailand. My brother makes up lies about dad and sells stories because it's the only way for him to make money fast.

'When you talk to dad he shrugs and says: 'It is what it is'.

'My brother has a track record of lying about dad which our father does not deserve because he has always supported Tom and has given him tens of thousands of dollars over the years. He has helped him get jobs and dad bent over backwards to help him.

'It was never enough for Tom. He thinks dad didn't love him enough.

'When Meghan came along she got everything but my father was in a better financial situation then. My dad always gave me, my brother and Meghan everything he could afford at the time.'

Thomas Jr moved from his home in Oregon to live next door to his father in Rosarito, Mexico after Thomas Sr suffered a devastating stroke in 2022.

The two men moved to the Philippines 'for a fresh start' at the beginning of 2025 but Thomas Sr returned to the States earlier this year to be fitted with a prosthetic leg and for ongoing medical treatment for a series of health issues.

He recently had another stent put in his heart after tests showed it was operating at 30 per cent efficiency.

Samantha said: 'I remain fully in support of my dad who is very fragile. He will always have my support. I love him and will always love him and think it's shameful that his final years should be marred by all of this drama. He doesn't deserve it.

'Tom isn't saying these terrible things to support anyone. He's doing it to destroy dad and make money. He wants revenge on dad because the money he was making off dad has stopped flowing. When Tom was living in Mexico and the Philippines dad was supporting him fully. Tom could drink and party as much as he wanted. Dad got upset at the way Tom was drinking.

'Dad totally indulged my brother and helped him live beyond his means. My brother is jealous of dad because dad had a successful career and Tom only has an eighth-grade education. Tom didn't want to put in the work in any of the jobs dad helped get him in Hollywood and elsewhere.'

Samantha said she blames her brother for not getting her father adequate medical care in the Philippines.

She said: 'Dad's foot was turning blue and he was complaining of pain and I was begging Tom to take him to the emergency room but he didn't. By the time he finally called an ambulance it was too late and dad had a massive blood clot which meant his left leg had to be amputated below the knee. I hold my brother somewhat responsible for that.

'My brother needs money and since my dad will no longer give it to him he has to extrapolate it from the media somehow. The bigger the lie, the bigger the buzz, the bigger the pay-day.'

Samantha said: 'Without any evidence that those images were not put there by someone else because those computers were out of my dad's possession for a couple of years, I don't believe that they are his.

'I have no reason to believe those are his because anyone could have been handling those computers.

'I think this is absurd and vengeful that my brother would do this. My dad has been through two heart attacks, a stroke and an amputation and his life is hanging in the balance and it's incredibly cruel that my brother would do this.

'There is a suggestion that Meghan knew about this. I can't speak for Meghan but she publicly bragged at the UN and on her website Tig about what a wonderful father he is and she wouldn't have done that if she suspected anything like these allegations she would now have been bragging about him on the world stage.

'Tom has a history of lying about dad. He said my dad did cocaine with hookers in Thailand. That was a lie for money too. He lies to get money. Tom has a history of drinking. I think this is just revenge.

'I love my father and I will continue to support him because this has no merit.'

Samantha added: 'You can't accuse someone of being an offender when the alleged tools of the crime have been in other people's hands. There is no way to prove any of this. I believe my dad is innocent. He was not in possession of those computers for two years. Who knows who has had access to them?'

#214. Does anyone feature on more than two clubs' all-time top-10 scoring charts? | The Knowledge

Plus: the longest kit supply partnerships, more own goals (part II) and consecutive goalless draws

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“Harry Kane is now Bayern’s seventh-highest scorer of all time, as well as being Tottenham’s highest scorer. The man he overtook at the top of that list, Jimmy Greaves, is also Chelsea’s seventh-highest scorer of all time. Do any other players feature on two (or more) clubs’ all-time top-10 scoring charts?” asks Owen Powell.

A trawl through the Knowledge archive reminded us that we have previously looked at players who are the record goalscorer for more than one club. This question is slightly different, as we’re focusing on goalscorers who are in the all-time top 10 for the most different clubs. There are dozens of players who appear for two clubs, including Sergio Agüero (Atlético Madrid and Manchester City), Kenny Dalglish (Celtic and Liverpool), Jimmy Greaves (Chelsea and Tottenham), Lionel Messi (Barcelona and Inter Miami), Cristiano Ronaldo (Real Madrid and Al-Nassr) and Alan Shearer (Blackburn and Newcastle).

There’s one more worthy of mention. “Harry Johnson is all-time top scorer for both Sheffield United and Mansfield,” writes Darren White. “He played for the Blades between 1919 and 1931, scoring 201 league goals. At the age of 32, he left for Mansfield, scoring 104 goals for them over three seasons. He didn’t play for anyone else, so he has the possibly unique record (for someone with more than one club) of being top scorer for every team he represented.”

And so to those who are among the top 10 goalscorers for more than two clubs: “Romário (Vasco da Gama, Flamengo and PSV) and Delio Onnis (Monaco, Tours FC and Gimnasia) feature on at least three clubs’ all time top-10 scoring charts,” writes Dirk Maas. “Onnis also played for Toulon, but I could not find an official source to confirm that Onnis is in their top 10 as well.”

Elsewhere, Rhys Shakeshaft suggests Robbie Keane, who is among the top 10 goalscorers for three of his clubs (Tottenham, LA Galaxy, ATK), and André-Pierre Gignac (Marseille, Toulouse, Tigres UANL). And Tom Stuart was among those who nominated John Aldridge (Newport County, Oxford United, Tranmere Rovers). The striker is also the Republic of Ireland’s fourth-highest goalscorer.

As well as being Cameroon’s all-time leading goalscorer, Samuel Eto’o is potentially in the top 10 for four clubs: Mallorca, Barcelona, Anzhi Makhachkala and Antalyaspor. “I’m not 100% sure if I can trust the Antalyaspor record,” writes Rhys Shakeshaft, who sent in the answer, “but I’m happy with the other three.”

Historical goalscoring data isn’t always 100% reliable, but we think Sam Kerr is among the top 10 leading scorers for five teams: Perth Glory FC, Western New York Flash, Gotham FC, Chicago Red Stars and Chelsea.

Even five clubs wouldn’t be a record. “I’ve managed to find one male footballer who, amazingly, is in the top 10 for six different clubs!” writes Ben. “Morocco’s Abderrazak Hamdallah is the all-time top scorer for OC Safi (Morocco), second for El-Jaish (Qatar), fourth for Guangzhou R&F/Guangzhou City (China), fourth for Al-Nassr, seventh for Al-Ittihad and 10 for Al-Shabab (all Saudi Arabia). He’s 35 years old and has just joined Al-Taawoun, so it’s entirely possible he’ll add another club to that list.”

“The German national kit is not going to be made by Adidas any more, going to Nike after 70 years. Is this the longest kit supply partnership in history, and what’s the longest current run in club football?” asks Paul Savage.

Dirk Maas has unearthed a couple of club sponsorships that have lasted more than 60 years. “Adidas has been Bayern Munich’s kit sponsor since 1965,” writes Dirk, “but the first time the Adidas trefoil was visible on the shirt was 17 October 1973. HJK (from Helsinki) also started a partnership with Adidas in 1965, one that has continued uninterrupted ever since. The first HJK shirt with the Adidas trefoil I could find was in 1976.”

We can’t find anything to beat the 70-year relationship between Germany and Adidas. We think that, when that deal officially ends, the longest partnership in international football will be between Austria and Puma. That goes back to 1977 and includes some memorable kits – most of them for the right reasons.

In the Knowledge last week we looked at players who scored more own-goals than goals during their career. A number of you pointed out the omission of Des Walker, a magnificent defender for Nottingham Forest and England in particular, but one who wasn’t renowned for his goalscoring exploits.

Walker famously scored only once in more than 800 games, an improbable belter for Forest against Luton in 1992. But he scored at least seven own goals – four for Forest and three for Sheffield Wednesday. The Forest collection included the winner for Spurs in the dramatic 1991 FA Cup final. He also scored at the wrong end when Sheffield United came from 2-0 down to beat Forest in a First Division playoff semi-final in 2003. His other own goals came in the League Cup: against Crystal Palace in January 1992 (a week after he scored against Luton) and Portsmouth in 2003.

He also managed at least three own goals during his time at Sheffield Wednesday, against Liverpool (1994-95), Tottenham (1995-96) and Preston (2000-01). That gives him a career balance of -6 goals: an unbecoming legacy for one of England’s greatest central defenders.

“After Lahti’s fourth consecutive 0-0 draw last night, does anyone know of a similar run?” tweeted Finnish Football Show back in 2017.

This question was made for George Graham, and he hasn’t let us down. His Arsenal team played four league games in October 1993 and drew the lot 0-0. In Arsenal’s defence (or should that be attack?) they did score some goals in cup matches during the month. Still, four consecutive 0-0s in the league is pretty impressive.

Surprisingly enough, Arsène Wenger’s Arsenal also managed a quartet of 0-0s in the league during the 2008-09 season – though they also scored and conceded in cup games during that period.

Goalless George did it again at Spurs, with four consecutive 0-0 draws in January and February 2001. They were all in the league but as no cup games were played in that period it counts as four consecutive 0-0s in all competitions. Serhiy Rebrov was guilty of appalling statisticide when, in the next league match at Manchester City, he scored the only goal in the 90th minute.

Wolves tested the will of season-ticket holders with four consecutive 0-0s at Molineux at the back end of the 2015-16 season. Udinese managed four in a row in the 1982-83 Serie A season, a campaign in which – and you’ll like this – they drew 20 of their 30 games. Como matched that feat in Serie A in 1986-87. That season, they played 30 games, scored 16 goals and conceded 20.

Best of all, earlier this year [in 2017 – ed] FC Rostov followed a 6-0 win at Tom Tomsk with five consecutive 0-0 draws in the Russian Premier League, though they were punctuated by a Europa League goalfest at Old Trafford: Rostov lost 1-0.

“Burnley have gone a calendar year without a home league win. What is the longest home drought, in the league or in all competitions?” asks our own Niall McVeigh.

“Last week, Justin Seven-Seven came on in the 75th minute and then scored in the 77th minute for West Brom Under-21s against Sutton United in the National League Cup. You have probably already guessed my question, but has anyone else ever scored in the same minute as their name?” wonders Peter Skilton.

“Since the advent of squad numbers, has any club used every number from 1 to 99? Which British club comes closest to using all 99 one and two-digit numbers?” asks Vasko Wackrill.

“With the constant talk of the golden boot and how unstoppable Erling Haaland is for Manchester City, wouldn’t a team be more dangerous if all of the outfield players, including substitutes, scored at least once or perhaps a few times during a season? Have there been any teams in which all of their outfield players have scored at least once in a particular season? If not, which group has had the most players score in a season?” asks Bob Zoellner.

“In the third round of the Portuguese Cup, played last weekend, six clubs from the Primeira Liga were eliminated by teams from lower divisions,” begins Cláudio Gameiro. “Is this a record for a European league? And has a national cup final ever been contested by two teams from lower divisions? I’m betting France.”

“By my reckoning, Ross County have already scored 81 goals this season: 38 in 10 league games (including beating poor Queen of the South 8-0 and 7-1), 30 in six Challenge Cup group games, 13 in six League Cup games. They may well have scored a century of goals by the end of October! Surely that cannot be bettered. What is the earliest a team has hit a century of goals in a season?” asks Stephen James.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

While Bayern had a roller-coaster week, Arsenal's was much more straightforward. The Gunners beat Lille 3-0 last Tuesday to make it two wins from two in the league phase before edging out Nottingham Forest 1-0 in the Premier League on Sunday, courtesy of Noni Madueke's late strike.

The England winger came off the bench to seal the three points in what has become a common theme for Arsenal, which could give them the edge against Bayern if the game is in the balance.

Arteta's men claimed a statement 3-1 win over Bayern in last season's league phase, en route to reaching the final, and if they repeat that result they will be just the second visiting team to triumph at the Allianz Arena since April 2025.

The Arsenal manager is unlikely to have any of his injured players back for the trip to Bavaria, although winger Christos Tzolis is closing in on a return to action.

Bayern's attacking quality and Arsenal's defensive solidity makes this an intriguing game. We reckon it will end level.

#217. Austin track bumps out of control - Verstappen

Max Verstappen has won the past two grands prix, in Malaysia and Singapore

Max Verstappen says the bumps on the track that hosts this weekend's United States Grand Prix are "unacceptable" and "out of control".

The Dutchman said drivers had complained about the condition of the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, and attempts by the organisers to resolve it had not worked.

Red Bull's Verstappen said: "I love this track, I love this place. It's one of the best layouts ever and it's one of the best venues, best city to be at.

"But for me the bumps are unacceptable. Over time they've been grinding a little bit here and there but it's just putting a plaster on the big problem.

"But that of course means you need to really fully open up the track. That costs a lot of money and time but that's the only way to get rid of it because these bumps are not natural and they are out of control."

Antonelli to 'just have fun' as he aims for title

Approach African GP with humility, says Hamilton

The track is built on former marshland and that has made it difficult for organisers to keep it in good condition, but the four-time champion rejected that as a reason not to try to solve the issue.

"You can use the excuse that the soil is the problem but then you should have known that and you need to make sure that you reinforce it more," Verstappen said.

"Last year, for example, you pull around 5-6G in a corner, but I had some impacts, vertical load, which was over 9G on my spine, which I can tell you is really not fun, and especially the older you get, you think about that more and more."

Verstappen said the problem was likely to be exacerbated this year because although the cars from 2022-25 had lower ride-heights overall, the way the cars are run under the latest regulations means they are running lower in corners than last season.

That's because of the switch between having the front and rear wings open in drag-reduction mode on the straights and closing in corners means the cars drop down towards the ground when they brake.

"You bottom out way harder, because when the wings close and the ride-height comes down, under braking is actually a very stressful moment, and I know around here in some places, it's very bumpy under braking," he said.

"Especially when it's like these kind of awkward bumps, not just bumps from the track getting older, but the surface underneath the soil just moving up and down, sometimes (it's) very hard to expect, or if you're like a tiny bit offline, you don't know what is there, because no-one really drives here sometimes.

"I can tell you from the checks that I've done from my spine, the bottom end doesn't look that great.

"I know that's part of racing. I know that can be part of sport, but it's also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years.

"And now if we continue with finding this acceptable to drive on, then you are going to suffer with that much more."

Verstappen won last year in Austin while Lando Norris finished second

World champion Lando Norris, of McLaren, backed Verstappen's opinion, saying: "The regulation of building a new track, the tolerances you have to be within are pretty small. It certainly doesn't fit anywhere close to what those regulations are now.

"It's an old track, not a new track so it's pretty bad. There's a lot of places I need to take headache tablets before I go out simply because it's so bumpy and you're hitting your head pretty hard against the headrest and things because of the bumps so it's certainly not a nice thing. There's not much we can do. I mean, we complain about it so it's stuff we've brought up many, many times but there's only so much we can complain about things. But he's right."

But Mercedes driver George Russell said: "It's bumpy, but I think it's just part of racing. I'd say my general view is F1 tracks probably need to be repaved every couple of years just to make it a bit more consistent. Because we're going to tracks now where Tarmac's coming up, it's falling apart, it's causing more issues than not.

#220. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk midfielder Marlon Gomes is on three yellow cards, putting him on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

Benjamin Sesko won't feature for Manchester United for a while yet, following the reveal that the Slovenian's recent knock is worse than first feared

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko won't be back until next year, following his recent injury.

That's according to one report that has ruled the Slovenian out for months, with a more precise timescale for his return to be revealed in the coming days by under-pressure manager, Michael Carrick.

With Manchester United having only picked up a single win in the Premier League this term, the news will come as a huge blow to the Red Devils, as they look to turn their fortunes around tonight away to Como.

Carrick initially sounded hopeful that Sesko's absence in the 1-1 draw with Fulham last month was nothing too serious, noting that, “He just felt a little bit of pain after the game [against Brighton & Hove Albion in the Carabao Cup]: hopefully, it's not too bad, but we will have to see.”

Slovenian outlet Ekipa via Sport Witness reported, however, that the diagnosis “doesn't look good”.

Now, The Sun have claimed that Sesko is looking at a return in February.

Another Slovenian outlet, Planet Nogomet, reported last month that the striker would undergo an MRI scan in London to diagnose a “repetition of problems that have plagued” him previously.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Sesko returned for pre-season with a shin injury that he picked up in May, with Carrick starting the season without the 23-year-old leading the line – after missing six games for club and country last winter with a knee issue.

The worry is that given there is no fracture or break, the star may have a chronic problem that needs an extended period of time to heal, with United having to rely on Matheus Cunha, Marcus Rashford and unfancied Joshua Zirkzee to lead the line in Sesko's absence.

Zirkzee is yet to start a game for Carrick this season, with less than an hour under his belt in the Premier League and three cameos in the League Cup and Champions League in which he struggled to impact proceedings.

With United looking to move the Dutchman on over the summer, it remains to be seen whether Zirkzee will get a second chance at Old Trafford or be offloaded in January, with the club considering replacements for the injured Sesko.

#226. Wedding venue refused to refund woman's $15.9k payment when her fiancé died suddenly - and told her she could apply the amount to a future booking instead

Published: 00:15 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 03:30 BST, 23 October 2026

A Texas wedding venue refused to return nearly $16,000 to a devastated bride-to-be after her fiancé died suddenly, instead suggesting she could use the money toward another celebration in the future.

The dispute erupted after Diego Hernandez, 25, died unexpectedly in April, seven months before he was due to marry his fiancée at Posey Meadows, a picturesque countryside venue outside San Marcos, southwest of Austin.

Rather than refund the $15,909.28 the couple had already paid, the business initially offered alternatives, including to transfer the reservation to another date or to put the money toward an entirely different event.

When the grieving family asked for their money back, the disagreement escalated into a bitter legal battle, with the venue even filing a countersuit against the woman whose wedding had been shattered by tragedy.

The business has now backed down, dropping its counterclaim and agreeing to refund every penny - but only following a wave of negative publicity.

The dramatic reversal comes after Hernandez's heartbroken mother, Lucy Hernandez, publicly condemned the venue's handling of the ordeal.

'Where are their morals? Where are their moral principles?' she asked KSAT.

'We don't have a fight in us. We don't. We're emotionally drained. This is just weighing heavily.'

The couple had been preparing to exchange vows on November 20 at Posey Meadows, a wedding destination set amid the rolling countryside of Hays County.

Diego Hernandez is pictured proposing to his fiancée before his sudden death at just 25. The couple had been due to marry in November, but their wedding plans ended in tragedy

Diego, 25, died unexpectedly in April, seven months before his planned wedding. His grieving fiancée was forced into a legal battle over nearly $16,000 paid toward their big day

Their plans came to a devastating halt when Hernandez died in late April, leaving his fiancée mourning the man she had expected to spend the rest of her life with.

His family contacted the venue to explain that the wedding could no longer take place and requested the return of the substantial deposit that had already been made.

But rather than hand the money back, venue owner Julie Campbell instead put forward several possible alternatives.

She suggested the family could move the booking to another date, or the money could be credited toward a different kind of gathering.

Campbell also indicated that some money might be returned if the venue succeeded in securing another customer for the couple's original wedding date.

For Hernandez's grieving relatives such proposals only added to the stress and offered little comfort.

His mother said she had initially expected the situation to be resolved with a straightforward telephone conversation.

'I'm very surprised,' she told KSAT. 'I honestly felt that it wasn't going to go past a phone call.'

Posey Meadows, a picturesque wedding venue outside San Marcos, Texas, initially refused to refund the couple's $15,909.28 payment

Diego's heartbroken mother, Lucy Hernandez, spoke out against the venue's handling of the dispute, questioning its 'morals' and 'moral principles'

Instead, she described a particularly distressing exchange with Campbell in early May, shortly before she was due to see her son's body for the final time.

According to Lucy, the discussion became heated and ended with Campbell telling her the wedding payments would not be returned.

The confrontation added another painful burden to a family already struggling with an unimaginable loss.

'I've planned other funerals. I've lost my mom and my dad and a brother, but planning a son's funeral is very different,' Lucy said. 'It weighs very different.'

By late June, the disagreement had become serious enough for an attorney representing Hernandez's fiancée to send the venue a formal demand for repayment.

When that failed to resolve the dispute, the woman filed a lawsuit in Hays County district court in late July.

Her legal complaint accused Posey Meadows of securing an 'unjust and ghoulish windfall built on a young man's death.'

But the venue responded with legal action of its own.

Posey Meadows filed a counterclaim alleging that the bride-to-be had breached the wedding contract by seeking to recover the money already paid while refusing to hand over the remaining balance.

The contract stipulated that payments would be forfeited in the event of cancellation.

It did not contain any specific provision addressing what would happen if either member of the couple died before the wedding.

The venue also raised questions about whether Hernandez's death had been adequately documented.

In its counterclaim, Posey Meadows alleged that the family had failed to supply proof of his passing.

The business initially suggested the money could be used toward a future booking or another event rather than refund the deposits which. had already been made

On Facebook many people appeared to have left negative reviews highlighting the story

The family say they offered to provide a death certificate before litigation began but received no response from the venue's legal representatives.

As the controversy attracted mounting attention, Posey Meadows insisted it had been attempting to resolve the situation compassionately.

In an October 16 statement, the business said it had previously granted full refunds to families facing similar tragedies, regardless of the terms of their contracts.

'Our company was heartbroken to learn of a private and tragic situation involving a couple scheduled to be married at our wedding venue,' it said.

The business maintained that it was already working toward a refund when the lawsuit arrived, adding that litigation had complicated the process.

On Wednesday, an attorney for the bride-to-be confirmed that she would be receiving a full refund.

In a lengthy statement, Posey Meadows defended its handling of the dispute, saying it had sought official confirmation of Hernandez's death before making an exception to its cancellation policy.

'Our thoughts continue to be with Diego's family and loved ones, and we extend our deepest condolences,' the venue said.

It claimed the family had been asked for a death certificate in early May but that the document did not arrive until mid-August, after legal proceedings had begun.

While waiting, the business said it had searched for an obituary, funeral announcement or other publicly available confirmation of his death.

'Our efforts were never meant to diminish the family's loss,' the statement continued.

'We regret that the litigation process has complicated what we hoped would be a speedy and compassionate resolution.'

The venue also confirmed it was no longer seeking additional money from the grieving woman.

#227. The rising French star whose dad won Rugby World Cup with England

Felix Balshaw has climbed more than 500 places in the ATP rankings since the start of 2026

Accents quickly reveal a lot about a person.

So speaking to Leeds-born Felix Balshaw - the 20-year-old son of England Rugby World Cup winner Iain - it soon becomes clear why he is representing France on his climb up the professional tennis ladder.

There is no mistaking a strong Gallic twang as Balshaw, who celebrated the first ATP Tour victory of his career this week, discusses his journey.

Balshaw was born in West Yorkshire while his father played for Premiership club Leeds Tykes, before the family moved to Biarritz when Iain - an electrifying full-back/wing who scored three tries in England's iconic 2003 campaign - joined the cross-channel exodus to the French Top 14.

The Balshaws have remained in the luxurious Basque coastal city, known for its Belle Epoque architecture, Atlantic seafront casinos and world-class surfing.

"We came down in Biarritz in 2009 and we just loved the place," said Felix, who broke into the world's top 200 last month for the first time.

"I grew up in France and, as each day went by, I felt more and more French.

"Since I've been little, from when I started playing in Tennis Europe juniors, I have always had the French flag by my name."

Vickery's journey from World Cup winner to bodybuilder at 50

Balshaw pledging allegiance to his adopted country is understandable given the limited contact with his birthland.

Trips back across the English Channel have been "very rare" for the Balshaw children, largely restricted to Christmas family gatherings.

Their maternal grandmother lives in Bath, although Felix has never visited his father's hometown of Blackburn.

But the world number 178 is fully aware his dad will forever be ingrained in the fabric of English sporting history.

The then Bath player scored three tries in the pool stage of England's historic 2003 World Cup campaign, helping secure a 20-17 victory over Australia in the final when he came on as a second-half substitute.

On the eve of the biggest match of his career - facing fellow Frenchman Corentin Moutet in the Lyon Open second round - Felix tried to draw inspiration from watching highlights of his father playing in 2003.

"I just had a massive smile [watching] because I can say 'this is my dad'," he said.

"When he was at Biarritz I was always stood in a little corner in the stands with the rugby gang. It was very, very inspirational to watch him.

"As a father he's tough, but it's always important that he has a lot of experience in rugby, so he's got a lot of stuff to teach me.

"He's always been a great, great part of my life. He's always had my back."

Iain Balshaw won 35 caps for England and played three times for the Lions on the 2001 tour to Australia

Balshaw started playing tennis at the age of four, but unsurprisingly also had a talent for rugby.

At 13, he needed to make a choice about which sport he wanted to pursue more seriously with the prospect of a professional career looming.

"When I was little, and your father is a rugby champion, of course you always want to follow in his steps and do the same journey as him," Balshaw said.

"But I just felt that rugby was not going to be my sport.

"Tennis, I guess, is more difficult for me than rugby because it's an individual sport, but there was a little more fire in me [playing tennis].

"That meant it was the right choice to choose tennis."

Balshaw is essentially an inverted Arthur Fery - the French-born British number one who became a household name with a stunning run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.

The pair actually met for the first time at this week's ATP 250 event in Lyon, where Balshaw beat Portuguese world number 56 Jaime Faria for his maiden win at tour level.

Possessing a Roger Federer-style one-handed backhand, and a Thor-inspired hammer celebration, Balshaw announced his arrival in some style.

Next week Balshaw will rise into the world's top 180, having starting the 2026 season ranked 718th.

His success will no doubt catch the attention of Lawn Tennis Association (LTA) chiefs, who are desperate to increase the pool of British players at the elite level.

Was Balshaw ever approached by the LTA to represent the country of his birth?

And was there ever a conversation with his parents about who he should represent?

"Maybe my parents are hiding stuff and I don't know, but I have never been personally contacted by the LTA," Felix said.

"I think for [my parents] the most important thing is if I'm happy, they'll be happy as well."

#230. Paz, Fabregas and Como teach Man Utd a lesson

When Manchester United savoured the last of their three Champions League triumphs in 2008, Como were a Serie D club, playing in one of nine semi-professional regional leagues.

On Wednesday, at a rainy but picturesque Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on the banks of the iconic Lake Como, the Serie A outfit showed how far they have come.

In fact, on the evidence of their 4-1 thrashing of the English side - and with progressive coach Cesc Fabregas in the dugout - you could argue the European newcomers have leapfrogged the Old Trafford outfit and then some.

Time and again, Fabregas' side sliced through United - who are now winless in their past seven games in all competitions for the first time since 2015.

At the heart of Fabregas' team is the brilliant Nico Paz, signed from Real Madrid in 2024, who scored twice and set up another.

Since the start of September, the 22-year-old Tenerife-born Argentina international has been directly involved in more goals in all competitions than any other Serie A player.

"It was a historic night because we played against one of the best teams ever, to do this at home is incredible, we are very happy for our performance," said Paz.

Wednesday's superb showing took him to nine goal involvements in eight appearances - four goals and five assists - he is also the youngest Argentine player to be involved in three goals in one Champions League game since Lionel Messi against Bayern Munich in April 2009.

"Paz really runs, he covers a lot of ground. He's melded the old-school Argentine creative number 10 style with the physical demands of modern football," said journalist Lars Sivertsen on Champions League Match of the Day.

For Como, this is the most high-profile victory since their project began.

"It's Manchester United. We are only just getting our heads around the fact we are playing Inter, Milan and Juventus," said one member of staff.

"This is without doubt the biggest night in the club's history."

The picturesque setting of Como's Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium, by the banks of Lake Como

According to chief executive Mirwan Surwaso, it was Como's status as an amateur club - they returned to Serie D in 2017 after being unable to convince the authorities of their financial wellbeing - which first attracted the London-based media company Sent Entertainment, owned by Indonesian billionaires Robert Budi Hartono and Michael Bambang Hartono.

When they concluded a deal in 2019, the Hartono brothers were planning a TV project, with the idea of screening matches involving young Indonesian players back home. A visit from Manchester United was not part of the plan.

Fabregas,film stars and Disney: How Como are disrupting Italian football

There cannot be many Champions League stadiums you can walk around and in addition to seeing an iconic tourist attraction. Lake Como is 29 miles long and 2.5 miles wide in some parts - you also come across a yacht club and an 'Aero Club' for the sea-planes that take off at regular intervals.

The clubs themselves have been there for a long time. But Como also use their natural surroundings to offer one hour Lake Como tours, followed by 'pre-match Lakeside hospitality'.

The Aero Club at the back of a stand at the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium

In town - Como's population is just over 83,000, which means 90% of them could fit in the San Siro Stadium - there is a plush new club shop, selling all kinds of branded merchandise. There was no need for that in Serie D.

"Somehow the team got promoted, we had to go professional, and the plan had to be scrapped," Surwaso told Piers Morgan's Football Uncensored Podcast this month.

The alternative plan is still being amended substantially.

Initially it was expected this season would be a selling year, when some of the developing talents Como thought they could cash in on would be sold.

Instead, manager Cesc Fabregas steered his squad to fourth place in 2025-26, capitalising on AC Milan's shock defeat at Cagliari.

It meant in the space of five seasons from Fabregas' arrival as a player, Como had gone from Serie B to the Champions League. Earlier this week, Lionel Messi's son Ciro gave Como his seal of approval by being pictured with his dad wearing a replica Como kit. Tangible evidence of a meteoric rise.

Former France internationals Raphael Varane (left) and Thierry Henry (centre) are both investors in Como

Como head coach Cesc Fabregas with Argentine forward Nico Paz

"Compared to when I finished my career here, it is completely different," said Fabregas. "It is not even night and day. It is another world.

"Playing Manchester United is a historic day once again for the club, the city of Como and fanbase.

"When I retired as a player, I coached to get experience. I explained what I thought of the club and my vision and put the plan to work. We are a family here. Even when we lose, fans come and celebrate. We need to be humble and remember who we were because the story of Como will be beautiful, and we will remember it forever."

Europe's next great coach? How Fabregas led Como to Champions League

The captivating nature of the Como story does bring with it some questions.

In the short term, some wonder how they can possibly comply with Uefa's financial rules, which European football's governing body does not intend to amend despite Como's rise from Serie B.

Surwaso told Morgan: "The scrutiny is on us but we always have our books in order, so we are not too worried."

The other point is that three quarters of the 12,300-capacity Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia is uncovered and was exposed to heavy rain during the fixture.

Growing both sides of the club is essential if Como are to maximise their potential.

For Fabregas, whose responsibility is clearly on the playing side, there is a balance to be struck between celebrating the spectacular journey Como have been on, and ensuring his players are not resting on their laurels.

"We were at minus 10 when we started, but we don't want to spend time thinking about what has passed," said the former Arsenal, Barcelona and Chelsea star.

"If you want to do that, retire and go write a book about what Como did. We must look at what is in front of us."

Como fans show their support before the club's Champions League debut against RB Leipzig on 10 September

While Como now attract thousands to their games, those who followed the club when crowds were in the hundreds remain.

"I had an uncle who supported Como," said Marco Melillo, an out-of-town fan.

"He showed me the sticker collection, I saw the blue shirt and the blue colours and totally went crazy about it.

"I know in England a lot of people support teams in lower leagues, but that is not so true in Italy, where people support bigger teams. I do not like that that much. I was not really interested in supporting a team that was winning something. I liked the colours. I liked the stadium and when I came here and saw the lake, it was 'wow'.

"We know the club is in the best situation ever in its history but when I see the faces of the guys and ladies that were also here in Serie D, we just see in our eyes and say, 'OK, we hope that this story will go on as long as possible, as best as possible, but if it maybe abruptly ended, because in the past we had also some bad things, we know we will be there'."

Federico Borghi is a local, and despite the weather, came with his huge Como 1907-2007 history book.

"In 2008, I had just started to go to the stadium to attend games," he said. "Not even in our best dreams could we think of playing Manchester United. I get chills even thinking about it.

"As soon as I entered the stadium for the first time I realised this was going to be my faith. I was there in the bad times and that has strengthened my faith and my relationship with the club.

"The Premier League is my inspiration and to face one of the top three or four biggest clubs in the world, it's a big honour."

#237. Militant doctors' union criticises NHS single-sex guidance and backs hospitals allowing trans women on to female wards

Published: 18:42 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 02:11 BST, 23 October 2026

The militant doctors' union has rejected new NHS guidance that protects women-only spaces, claiming it is 'exclusionary to trans and non-binary staff and patients'.

The British Medical Association (BMA) said it is 'deeply concerned' by the rules that say hospitals must stop letting transgender women on to female wards.

Women's rights groups have welcomed the guidance but warned that some trusts could continue to flout the law, spurred on by activist staff.

The BMA criticised the rules on Wednesday and said it supports trans staff and patients accessing NHS accommodation and services 'according to their gender', rather than their biological sex.

The doctors' union, which has unleashed 15 rounds of strikes in the past three years, demanded that any hospitals revising their policies must do so 'in collaboration with trade unions and the trans and non-binary workforce'.

The BMA added: 'We are calling for urgent clarity from NHS England on how employers can implement the guidance in a way that is safe and inclusive of trans and non-binary people.'

Darlington nurses Tracey Hooper, Annice Grundy, Lisa Lockey and Bethany Hutchinson

Maya Forstater, chief executive of sex-based rights charity Sex Matters, criticised the BMA's stance.

She said: 'Comparing clear NHS guidance with 'transphobia' is a sign of just how far activists at the BMA have gone from their medical training and their pledge to do no harm.'

Under the guidance, patients must be accommodated according to their biological sex and staff must use single-sex changing rooms and toilets that align with the sex they were born.

The changes follow the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that 'woman' and 'sex' in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex, and subsequent guidance from the Equality and Human Rights Commission.

The guidance applies to acute, mental health and community NHS trusts as well as NHS-funded patients in private settings, but not A&E departments, urgent treatment centres or paediatrics.

#241. Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared

The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer

Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons

Key ins: Bruno Guimarães (Newcastle, £75m), Ezri Konsa (Aston Villa, £51m), Piero Hincapié (Bayer Leverkusen, £45m), Christos Tzolis (Club Brugge, £34m)

Key outs: Leandro Trossard (Besiktas, £15.3m), Jakub Kiwior (Porto, £14.5m), Gabriel Jesus (Barcelona, £8.6m), Fábio Vieira (Hamburg, £7.7m), Christian Nørgaard (Everton, £7m), Ethan Nwaneri (Borussia Dortmund, loan)

It is all change at Villa and, although a little trepidation is inevitable, a refresh was probably overdue. At the same time, Unai Emery did not want to lose so many key players and Villa’s manager has made clear there is no such thing as a transition season in his eyes. Villa have generated about £300m from the sales of nine players and brought in 10 at a cost of about £250m. Villa have lowered their wage bill and changed the profile of their squad. Zion Suzuki, Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi, names on the lips of Villa’s rivals, are particularly exciting signings. Last summer there was concern Villa had gone stale and 12 months ago they ended up fretting on deadline day – Harvey Elliott and Jadon Sancho joined on loan – but there was no such chaos this time. Ben Fisher

Perhaps Bournemouth’s best business was keeping hold of their coveted key players, chiefly Eli Junior Kroupi, Rayan, Alex Scott and Tyler Adams. Bournemouth rejected bids from Chelsea for Scott and stayed true to their plan of resisting offers to give Marco Rose the best chance of succeeding, with the club attempting to juggle European competition and the league for the first time. The arrival of the Portugal centre-back António Silva, 22, from Benfica looks a typically smart replacement for Marcos Senesi, 29. Kroupi’s freak foot injury, which will probably keep him out until November, may have proved a blessing in disguise in terms of retaining the 20-year-old. BF

Avoiding a repeat of last year’s upheaval was a major boost. Keith Andrews held on to his best players and made smart additions to a solid squad. Mamadou Sangaré has added quality in midfield since joining from Lens and looks the bargain of the summer. Callum Wilson has brought experience up front after signing on a free and Jaidon Anthony provides cover on the flanks after his £15m move from Burnley. El Hadji-Malick Diouf, signed from West Ham, offers potential at left-back. Jacob Steinberg

Deadline day deals to bring in the exciting Nigeria forward Femi Azeez from Millwall and the Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés from Stuttgart made it 12 signings in another summer of transition, Azeez’s arrival being announced almost 12 hours after the window shut. The departures of Jan Paul van Hecke, Carlos Baleba and Carl Rushworth brought in more than £140m as the Brighton model continues to deliver big profits, although losing last season’s top scorer, Danny Welbeck, to Chelsea for a mere £5m may be the biggest loss if the new striker Promise David cannot bring the goals. Xabi Alonso’s appointment as manager was the biggest signing of the summer. Chelsea have been sensible since turning to the Spaniard. Morgan Rogers has started well after joining for £117m. Maxence Lacroix adds power in defence, Marco Palestra versatility on the flanks. Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson can raise standards in the dressing room. But there was the usual revolving door. Money was made on a host of outgoings. Marc Cucurella, one of the world’s best left-backs and sold to Real Madrid, looks a bigger loss than Enzo Fernández. However a worry is that Chelsea did not replace Fernández after selling him to Manchester City for £125m, their late £47m move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara collapsing at the last. JS

It remains to be seen whether Coventry have struck the right balance in the market. Frank Lampard wanted to maintain momentum but add power and physicality. Coventry also sought to address their lack of Premier League experience with Taiwo Awoniyi and Ethan Pinnock. Coventry were the highest scorers in English football’s top four tiers last season but the step up means the pressure is on Awoniyi, never prolific for Nottingham Forest, Sidiki Cherif, a promising 19-year-old, and Ellis Simms to deliver before Haji Wright returns from injury. Stephen Mfuni, a teenage loanee from Manchester City and their 11th and final summer signing, increases their left-back options. BF

The lost tug of war with Sunderland over Malick Fofana summed up another chaotic deadline day for Palace, who were still scrambling for signings in the final minutes and confirmed the arrivals of Ben Chilwell, Quinten Timber and Darío Osorio after the window shut. The new manager, Pierre Sage, will at least be pleased to have secured more defensive reinforcements after losing Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea, with the loanees Honest Ahanor and Axel Disasi adding much-needed depth. It was a window that revealed the extent of The Friedkin Group’s ambitions, the strength of the club’s finances after the move to a new stadium, the state of the relationship between the manager and chief executive and the expertise of the senior leadership team; and none of it was positive. The owners deserve some credit for listening to fans and halting the self-defeating sale of Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest but otherwise it was a modest window that descended into a shambles. The club’s best player was sold for a below-market fee, a move for Folarin Balogun collapsed and although the equally desperate search for a right-back ended with Ainsley Maitland-Niles signing, David Moyes was left with one striker and a smaller squad than he started the day with, despite repeatedly urging his employers to strengthen. Gonzalo García, César Palacios and Manuel Ángel followed Arbeloa from Real Madrid and Shea Charles is an exciting signing from Southampton. Some stalwarts have left. “Think of us like a volcano,” said Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, in early July. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” Two months on the Ilicali has presided over 18 signings, investing more than £150m and his manager, Sergej Jakirovic, has choreographed two Premier League wins. The horizon looks infinitely brighter than in June, when the playoff winners sold two players for a combined £8.5m to avoid breaching English Football League spending rules and a near-certain six-point deduction. Hull, remember, spent last season under a two-window EFL transfer embargo. They have compensated for that this summer and, although time will tell whether all those new faces are compatible, reasons for optimism remain real. Not least because last season’s cult hero loanee forward Joe Gelhardt has signed permanently from Leeds. Louise Taylor

The late addition of Burnley’s striker Zian Flemming brought Ipswich’s summer spend close to £200m. That appears to be the cost of giving yourselves a genuine shot at survival. Arrivals such as Exequiel Palacios and Julio Enciso should have no business in the lower reaches, and the former Fulham pair Sasa Lukic and Issa Diop add crucial experience. Gary O’Neil can call upon enviable depth in midfield and speed on the flanks, where Abdul Fatawu and Daizen Maeda look sharp. In an ideal world Daniel Farke might have wished for one more high-calibre attacking recruit but that should not detract from a very decent window, featuring seven extremely sensible signings. The importance of the acquisition of the England goalkeeper James Trafford from Manchester City should not be underestimated. Trafford will almost certainly provide Leeds with a few more extra points – not to mention enhance their play courtesy of his stellar footwork. Just in front of him Tarik Muharemovic looks an outstanding defensive buy. Harry Wilson raises creativity levels and the attacking tone. LT

The final window of Richard Hughes’s spell as sporting director raised more questions over Liverpool’s direction under Fenway Sports Group, owners soon to be enriched by a £2bn investment from 1892 Holdings. #244. The Times apologises to Gianni Infantino after ‘second salary’ claims and FIFA backlash

The Times has published a correction to and apologised for their story about the FIFA President’s alleged 'second salary’

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Times has issued a correction and apology to both Gianni Infantino and FIFA for a story published on October 13, containing false information about the body's President.

In that article, it was alleged that the FIFA President had taken a “second salary” that had not been disclosed, which The Times now admit was incorrect.

FIFA responded to the apology on X (formerly Twitter) by claiming: “It is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President.

The statement continued: “FIFA urges the media to act responsibly and carefully verify all sourcing to prevent the publication and subsequent reproduction of false and defamatory information.

In their apology, The Times accepted that regulations do not require FIFA to include certain expenses and reimbursements received by its President in the annual report.

That is because they are not considered to be “compensation” under Swiss reporting requirements, making the publication’s “second salary” claim false.

Their apology and correction read: “On 13 October 2026 (Sport), we reported that Gianni Infantino received a “second salary” from Fifa, which Fifa had failed to disclose.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“This is incorrect. There was no ‘second salary.’ Regulations do not require Fifa to include expenses and reimbursements received by Mr Infantino in its annual report as they are not considered “compensation” under Swiss reporting requirements.

Additionally, The Times apologised for a second false claim, related to Infantino purchasing, alleging, a Miami property at a suspected undervalue.

“We also accept Mr Infantino did not purchase a property in Miami at a suspected undervalue as we reported,” continued The Times’ statement.

“And neither he nor his family are the legal or beneficial owners of Shadi LLC and have no control over that company, as we suggested.

“We are happy to make these corrections and apologise to Mr Infantino and Fifa for the errors.”

In response, an outraged FIFA clarified that they “welcome legitimate scrutiny,” but that The Times crossed that line.

“Scrutiny is not a license to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate, misleading, or totally false, as in this case, FIFA will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.”

#245. Azaz confirms he will continue playing for Republic of Ireland

Finn Azaz has played 16 times for Republic of Ireland

Southampton forward Finn Azaz will continue to represent the Republic of Ireland despite reports that he may retire from international football.

The 26-year-old told BBC Radio Solent, external that he would carry on playing for the country where he holds citizenship and has made 16 appearances since his debut in 2024.

Azaz, who was born in England, represents Ireland through his father but also qualified for Israel through his mother.

Azaz was an unused substitute when the Republic of Ireland met Israel in two recent Nations League matches - games that were embroiled in controversy - and reports afterwards suggested he could call time on his international career.

The Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games due to the ongoing Israel-Gaza war.

A campaign called "Stop The Game", organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine, staged protests before and during the Republic's game against Austria in Dublin, prior to their second match against Israel.

However, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) decided to fulfil the fixtures, which had already been moved to neutral venues, with the Republic of Ireland winning the first match 3-0 before playing out a 1-1 draw.

The side wore black armbands for the matches and bowed their heads when Israel's national anthem was played before kick-off, while the two teams did not shake hands.

Manager Heimir Hallgrimsson said following the second match that the period had been "tough" on Azaz "mentally".

"It is probably the most difficult situation for him of all of us," he said.

"He deserves a lot of credit for being in the squad and showed desire to be a part of this team."

Republic of Ireland denied by Israel in draw

Republic of Ireland defeat Israel in Debrecen

Azaz has had an impressive start to the campaign and has emerged as one of Southampton's most important players.

Since signing from Middlesborough last summer, the Irishman has scored 14 goals with 15 assists having played 60 times.

Azaz has called for more from the group as they push for promotion back to the Premier League.

"It's been a good start by the team but we're not there yet," he told BBC Radio Solent.

"There's still space to get to another level, we've been pretty consistent but it was never going to be the same as the end of last season straight away.

"You have to build that mentality, it's now about us wanting to keep improving and not just being content with how we're doing.

"We have high aspirations and the mindset has to be to keep getting better."

#246. Azeez to Andrés: seven smart-looking Premier League deadline day deals

An 18-year-old who has played at two major international tournaments and the division’s top clearance maker from last season also feature

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

He is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

He also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more big chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons

He is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

He was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

Danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

He could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

But dribbling ability became increasingly important in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

With the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

Fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

The Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

Fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

He contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

Fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

Comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

It’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).

#247. This Country star Daisy May Cooper reveals she and brother Charlie were dropped by ITV and left in crippling debt before the BBC rescued them

By JOANNA CRAWLEY, DEPUTY SHOWBIZ EDITOR (NEWS)

Published: 15:47 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 02:06 BST, 23 October 2026

Daisy May Cooper has admitted it 'was the last straw' when ITV dropped her and her brother after years of 'sacrifice' to try and get their show This Country commissioned.

The comedian, 40, rose to fame creating and starring in the mockumentary, which followed her character Kerry Mucklowe and her cousin Kurtan, played by her brother Charlie, during their day-to-day life in Cirencester, Cotswolds.

The siblings were inspired to write about their upbringing whilst they were living together in London, with Daisy enrolled at drama school RADA whilst Charlie worked at Topshop after dropping out of university.

The 'homesick' pair spent their spare time doing impressions of people back home before honing their characters when they moved back to Cirencester.

Speaking to Davina McCall on her Begin Again podcast, Daisy explained how they worked as night cleaners back home because 'we were so ashamed to do anything in the day, where somebody might come in and go, "Oh, I thought you were going to be at uni and you were at drama school and now what?"'

During their night shifts, the pair wrote their first scripts for This Country before filming some scenes to send to production companies. 'We had to be at that kind of rock bottom with everything else to to be able to gamble like that,' Daisy explained.

Daisy May Cooper has admitted it 'was the last straw' when ITV dropped her and her brother after years of 'sacrifice' to try and get their show This Country commissioned

ITV eventually gave the pair a pilot but the comedian explained once the broadcaster  'saw the pilot, that was so awful, they were like no'.

They were dropped by both ITV and their production company, with Daisy admitting she feared for Charlie's mental health.

'I remember getting that phone call and Charlie just said "I'm going to go out for a bit". And I remember thinking he's going to do something stupid to himself because it was the last straw and it had been so many years and we sacrificed everything for this.'

There was more bad news after Daisy called their agent who explained to them 'you've signed a contract, so you can't take this idea to anyone else because if you do, you have to pay for the rights, which they have bought for something like £500'.

'They bought the rights off of us. It was such a bad deal. So we'd have to buy them back and it would be £300,000. We didn't have a pot to p***  in. We could barely afford to buy tobacco just to have a rolly that day.'

Despite the setbacks, Daisy explained 'I just knew that everything was going to be OK.'

A determined Daisy went 'straight to the commissioner of the BBC and I sent him the clips and the original script that we had done and I said "I will stand outside your office please come and talk to me."'

'He emailed back that night and said come in for a meeting.'

The comedian, 40, rose to fame creating and starring in the mockumentary, which followed her character Kerry and her cousin, played by her brother Charlie, during their life in Cirencester

Daisy said in a 'bizarre' twist of fate 'we went in for a meeting and the person that had just been in before us was Phoebe Waller-Bridge who was selling Fleabag. So Fleabag and This Country got commissioned within the same hour.'

Daisy added: 'We said "we've got all this debt" and he said "don't worry about it we'll pay for it, we'll sort it". We could have just spent £300,000 to buy our own characters back.'

This Country aired for three acclaimed series from 2017-2020 and won Daisy a Best Female Comedy Performance Bafta.

Last year Daisy admitted This Country won't be making a return due to her dramatic weight loss.

Since the show finished Daisy has undergone a dramatic health transformation and has lost ten stone. She has joked she would never be able to play Kerry again unless her character 'had a tapeworm'.

Speaking to the Radio Times, Daisy revealed her and her brother are working on something new: 'It's early days but we're working on something unscripted.

'We can't do This Country, though, because I've lost so much weight and I've had my lips done. We'd have to say that Kerry's had a tapeworm and been stung by a bee.'

Daisy has been on a dramatic weight loss journey over the last three years but previously revealed she has since been flooded with messages telling her that she's 'no longer funny' since changing her appearance.

ITV eventually gave the pair a pilot but the comedian explained once the broadcaster 'saw the pilot, that was so awful, they were like no'

Discussing her appearance, the mother-of-two told the BBC podcast How To Be In The Spotlight: 'I'm so for body positivity but when I was at my biggest I was at my most miserable and I had a massive food addiction.'

'I wasn't healthy. I couldn't breathe when I was walking up the stairs. I was so unhappy. And I've had some messages like, "Well, now you've lost the weight you're not funny any more".

'What the f**k? Why do women have to be f**king fat to be funny? That makes me so angry. I champion anybody. I think everybody should be happy with their body. But I wasn't.'

Daisy's weight loss caused a similar issue during the filming for season two of her BBC comedy Am I Being Unreasonable?

Filming had to be delayed due to Daisy's new slim physique and lip filler treatment as the star joked: 'Series one is meant to be 30 seconds before series two and in that 30 seconds I've lost about ten stone and had my lips done.

'I saw the rushes and I said to the BBC, "God, we're going to have a disclaimer at the beginning saying - Daisy has had her lips done, go with it and please don't judge".'
