#250. Coach banned until 2048 for training children in DR Congo while suspended for sexual abuse

Jonathan Bukabakwa gets extra five-year ban from Fifa

DR Congo’s FA must improve education and compliance

A coach in the Democratic Republic of the Congo who was banned from football for 20 years by Fifa for sexual abuse of a minor has had his ban extended by five years to 2048 by the world governing body.

Jonathan Bukabakwa, known as Messi, has also been ordered to pay an additional fine of $15,000 (£11,200) after the Guardian revealed he had continued to work with young players despite his suspension.

The Congolese Association Football Federation (Fecofa) and Racing Club Baki, where Bukabakwa was coaching, have been fined $50,000 each by Fifa’s ethics committee for failing to comply with its decision to ban him for 20 years in 2023.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Fecofa has also been instructed to introduce a “comprehensive education, compliance and monitoring programme for its officials, affiliated clubs and registered members” to try to ensure there is no repeat.

“The Congo DR Football Association, the club Racing Club Baki (formerly known as Esperanto FC), and the coach Jonathan Bukabakwa were found responsible for failing to comply with the decision rendered by the Fifa ethics committee on 18 October 2023,” said a Fifa statement.

Bukabakwa, who previously coached youth teams in the Limpopo and Malabo regions, was convicted of sexually abusing minors by authorities in the DRC and was released from prison last year. A Guardian investigation in August revealed there was video footage of him coaching young players at Esperanto in the Limete district of the capital, Kinshasa. Local sources confirmed he had regularly been seen taking charge of players on a school field.

Bukabakwa did not deny continuing to coach young players but claimed he had not been informed of his Fifa ban. He said he had not been questioned or received any communication from the governing body. He has denied the allegations against him.

The case has raised further questions about safeguarding in Congolese football and the ability of authorities to ensure that suspended individuals do not continue participating in the sport. Bukabakwa was provisionally suspended by Fecofa in November 2022 after media reports of alleged widespread sexual abuse in the DRC. Several other coaches were provisionally suspended at the time, although investigations into some of those other cases did not establish sufficient evidence for further action by Fecofa or Fifa.

Véron Mosengo-Omba, elected as Fecofa’s president in May, has promised to look into the previous cases once he has re-established a disciplinary committee. Fecofa was under a Fifa-appointed normalisation committee from 2023 until his election. “We will make sure that no one who is behaving like this will be involved in football in this country,” he said.

#252. Why do Man City fans boo pre-match anthems?

Manchester City fans held up literal 'boos' during a Champions League game at Sevilla in 2015

The cacophony of boos that greet the Premier League and Champions League anthems before kick-off have now become a fixture at Etihad Stadium.

The jeers from Manchester City fans were turned up a notch against Ipswich last Saturday when the side played their first home game since being found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

"I can't remember a Premier League or Champions League home game where the anthems haven't been booed," City season-ticket holder Dave Wilson told BBC Sport.

The pre-match dissatisfaction towards top-flight chiefs can likely be traced back to February 2023, when the 115 charges for breaching the rules were first announced.

Later that same year, Everton had 10 points - reduced to six on appeal - deducted after being found to have broken profit and sustainability rules.

In their first game back after the sanction, Toffees fans displayed their ire at Goodison Park by loudly booing the league's pre-match anthem as well as holding up red cards with the word 'corrupt' printed underneath the Premier League logo.

Though City supporters did not organise a similar display, their anger was clear.

"The Premier League anthem has been booed by City fans for many years," said Wilson. "It was probably heightened on Saturday because it was the first home game since the [guilty verdict] announcement.

"There hasn't been much love lost between City and the Premier League for a long time. For certain games it will be louder than others, it definitely wasn't co-ordinated for that [Ipswich] game but a symptom of everything coming together."

There was audible booing before Tuesday's Champions League fixture against AEK Athens too.

No Haaland, no problem - can Foden be Man City's alternative goalscorer?

Everton fans held up cards with the word 'corrupt' printed underneath the Premier League logo and booed during the top-flight anthem in November 2023

City fans' displeasure towards Uefa goes back even further, there being a litany of disputes with Europe's top brass.

In 2012, Porto were handed a fine, external of around Â£17,000 by Uefa after City made a complaint of racial abuse towards striker Mario Balotelli to the organising body.

In that same season, City were given a fine, external of around Â£24,000 for being one minute late back on to the pitch for the second half of a game against Sporting.

In 2014, Uefa fined City Â£49m and capped their squad size for the Champions League after they failed Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules.

Six years later, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned City's two-year ban from European club competitions after clearing them of "disguising equity funds as sponsorship contributions" - Uefa initially ruled City had committed "serious breaches" of FFP regulations between 2012 and 2016.

Wilson adds: "City fans generally feel there is a conspiracy against them, like the booing of the Uefa anthem too. There is a feeling of being targeted, rightly or wrongly.

"City fans just don't seem to like the competitions we play in!"

City and their supporters are currently in limbo as they await the outcome of the appeal and any potential sanctions.

The side are currently top of the table having won all seven league games so far and that 100% record will be given a stern examination with a difficult trip to Aston Villa on Saturday (kick-off 12:30 BST).

Nick Clarke is interim chair of The Citizens Trust - Manchester City supporters' union, a member-led trust that was set up earlier this year at a time when the "potential biggest issue affecting City fans in the club's history" had transpired.

Though it has been a "difficult time", fans are "completely behind the team" and he says his job is to ensure their views are heard amid the external noise.

"The booing of the anthem on Saturday was totally organic," says Clarke. "Whereas the bananas at Liverpool was a fan-led initiative co-ordinated by the 1894 atmosphere group and they did great work handing those out before the game.

"Even though there are fans who are conflicted about what has happened with the club, there is still a general feeling among the majority [of City fans] that the Premier League is not fit for purpose in regulating itself and how it is ran."

Whatever the outcome of the appeal, City fans are likely to continue making their feelings clear before kick-off.

Kvaratskhelia to undergo surgery on right knee

Paris Saint-Germain’s Khvicha Kvaratskhelia ⁠will undergo surgery after rupturing the anterior cruciate ⁠ligament in ⁠his ​right knee in the Champions League win over ⁠Barcelona.

#256. How England hopeful Acheampong is giving Chelsea a big decision to make

Acheampong has made 52 appearances since his debut for Chelsea in 2024

Chelsea's academy has been a production line for England defenders, and Josh Acheampong could become the latest to take that step.

Since John Terry broke through in the early 2000s, Chelsea have produced Levi Colwill, Trevoh Chalobah, Marc Guehi and Fikayo Tomori for England, while also developing international centre-backs Andreas Christensen and Nathan Ake.

Acheampong has started six of Chelsea's past nine matches in all competitions.

Only four players - attackers Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, and defenders Colwill and Maxence Lacroix - have played more than his 581 minutes under new manager Xabi Alonso.

Much of that has stemmed from Alonso settling on a more consistent side.

Chelsea had conceded a league-high 12 goals before the international break but have let in only one since, including recording their first clean sheet of the season away at Everton on Saturday.

Acheampong, 20, has operated as a roaming centre-back in a back three alongside more fixed options Colwill and Lacroix, stepping into midfield or moving wide to perform the role of a traditional full-back when in possession.

He has also developed a promising understanding with right wing-back Pedro Neto, combining with him in the move that led to Joao Pedro's goal against Bournemouth, while keeping Â£75m signing Wesley Fofana out of the side.

Alonso has been keen to emphasise Chelsea's defensive improvement as a collective effort, with the return of Moises Caicedo from injury and his partnership alongside 36-year-old Jordan Henderson adding greater stability.

During a pre-season tour of Australia and Asia, Alonso also hammered home his policy of giving minutes to those who most deserve it, rather than on reputation.

It's in this environment Acheampong has begun featuring regularly, while also starting eight of England Under-21s' past 10 matches.

Increasingly, the young defender appears to be knocking on the door of a senior call-up should manager Thomas Tuchel seek a versatile option on the right side of defence.

'He's going to be the next great English centre-back'

Acheampong is under contract until 2029, meaning decisions need to be made between now and next summer.

Across recent transfer windows, the defender has been repeatedly linked with moves away from Stamford Bridge, only for sources within Chelsea to insist he was "untouchable".

That message has remained consistent, although it has occasionally raised eyebrows.

Chelsea seriously explored moves for now-Real Madrid defender Dean Huijsen in the summer of 2025 and Liverpool centre-back Jeremy Jacquet in January 2026, who possess similar attributes and are only a year older than Acheampong.

At one stage during the summer Chelsea had 10 senior centre-backs on their books, before ending the transfer window with six.

In a season without European football, there were genuine doubts over how much Acheampong would play. Potential loan moves were explored, including a switch to Crystal Palace.

Palace instead signed Chelsea's Axel Disasi on loan, with Premier League rules permitting only one domestic loan signing from another top-flight club.

Despite being with Chelsea since Under-8s, Acheampong has come close to leaving on more than one occasion.

In 2023, he did not sign a professional contract on his 17th birthday, which is typically the norm for elite academy prospects. The club's current ownership later moved to secure his future in January 2024, avoiding the risk of losing him for only a nominal compensation fee.

Twelve months later, Acheampong again appeared to be heading towards the exit in what former manager Enzo Maresca described as a "bad situation".

Before the conclusion of lengthy and ultimately successful negotiations, the club's hierarchy withdrew him from selection at both academy and first-team level before he eventually signed a contract until 2029.

That agreement, signed in December 2024, remains the deal he is on today.

Chelsea could face important decisions next summer, when Acheampong and Fofana will all enter the final two years of their contracts. Colwill's contract expires a year later in 2030.

Chalobah and Tosin Adarabioyo were sold to Como and Tottenham Hotspur respectively this summer after entering the final two years of their deals.

The policy stems in part from lessons learned following Chelsea's 2022 takeover, when Antonio Rudiger and Christensen departed on free transfers to Real Madrid and Barcelona respectively.

Those exits triggered a scramble to reinforce the centre of defence, contributing to expensive moves for Fofana and Marc Cucurella.

Acheampong's recent performances have begun to attract wider recognition among Chelsea supporters and have raised the stakes surrounding his future.

At present, there are no active discussions over a new deal, although the idea of a seven-year contract has been floated previously.

There is caution within Acheampong's camp about rushing into negotiations until there is clearer evidence that he can become a regular starter at Chelsea.

However, the first-team football provided by Alonso has given the club its strongest chance yet of persuading one of its most promising academy graduates to commit his long-term future.

#259. Will that do? Lamine Yamal conjures another magical spell as Barça pass first test | Sid Lowe

The 19-year-old scored a cracker in Seville, days after his ‘almost rabona’ at Galatasaray, as La Liga leaders beat Real Betis

When at last it was time for Lamine Yamal to leave, the 19-year-old’s number going up before the 90th minute for only the second time since the opening day, Real Betis fans whistled him all the way to the touchline where Barcelona’s coach was waiting. His work here was done, Hansi Flick invited him to take the weight off his feet and his shoulders, not that he wanted to. First, though, he took Lamine Yamal’s head in his hands and, leaning in away from the amateur lip readers, tried to make himself heard over the noise. “I told him I was proud of him because he played a fantastic game,” he said.

At least he could think of something. When Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring just nine minutes into the match that was supposed to find out how good Barcelona really were, it hadn’t been easy. Nothing erudite, anyway. On the morning that Barcelona went to Betis – first v third, a proper opponent at last – Jorge Valdano had lamented that sometimes he doesn’t have the words, and he always has the words. Valdano had just watched Lamine do that, whatever that was, in Istanbul – an “almost rabona”, the kid called it – and now he had a problem. “If he keeps doing strange things, we’re not going to be able to explain it,” he wrote.

To which Lamine Yamal responded by doing another strange thing that same afternoon, scoring another brilliant goal to set Barcelona on the way to a 5-2 win over Betis in a game that made history. And if Lamine Yamal had been a little lucky three days before, momentarily losing control only for the rebound to bounce back to him like the ball knew where it would rather be, this was all him and very him. The move started with Gerard Martín losing his boot and ended with pretty much everyone else losing their heads. In Martín’s momentary absence, Rodri dropped into defence and began it from there, the ball moved across the box and back until it was played up to Lamine Yamal. His superb pass with the outside of the boot unlocked everything and then, receiving again just inside Betis’s half, he set off.

There’s a moment, Lamine Yamal says, when you can sense the anticipation, feel people getting up one after the other all along the stand, a wave accompanying you, moving with you. At that moment, he says, there’s some inner power and you feel like Superman or Spider-Man; the defenders are robots, he says, and however good a robot is, however well programmed to stop him, a human is better. Too fast, too agile, too inspired. Too much thought gone into this, too much psychology. Man against the machines, code this. He rolled the ball one way with his left foot, flicked it the other with the heel of his right, and from the edge of the box, sent it flying into the far top corner.

Somehow. Sometimes you have nothing new to say, you know? It’s not big and it’s not clever but sometimes only swearing will do: sometimes only holy shit! hits the spot. Sometimes you can be sitting alone on the sofa and still shout: “Oh, my God!”, call them in to watch this. But it won’t be the same when they do, even if it’s sort of better: a chance to slow it down and break it down, see the detail, work out how he did it, like you’re ever going to do that. Because for all the expectation, it’s still a shock seen live, the purest reaction of all.

Words? Pah! This weekend, Gabriel Jesus put it best: as the ball passed him, he just held his head in his hands. Lamine Yamal ran to the corner. Fermín López chased, wiping his brow: woah, what was that? Karim Adeyemi went wagging his fingers. On the touchline Flick almost took off his assistant’s hand with the hardest high five. Teammates ran towards him not so much celebrating as laughing, so good it’s funny and even funnier for being repeated, an outrageous goal his catchphrase. Lamine Yamal sat alongside Jules Koundé on the advertising board, arms crossed like it was easy, like “what are you lot losing your heads about?” Maybe it is. And there is something in the way he hit it that felt a little like he put it in the top corner because, well, why not? Might as well.

Lamine Yamal got up, stood holding the corner flag, looking about: will that do? If this was the first test Barcelona have faced, it hadn’t taken him 10 minutes to score again, and like that. And that’s the thing. Who knows, this might not even have been the best goal of the weekend: there were glorious moments from Arda Guler and Kylian Mbappé in Real Madrid’s win against Sevilla. Javi Rodríguez’s run was wonderful for Celta Vigo against Alavés. And Pablo Martínez’s shot in Málaga’s 2-5 loss to Real Sociedad was ridiculous. It might not have even been the best shot of this game had Gio Lo Celso’s “goal” not been ruled out. And it definitely might not even be the best Lamine Yamal has scored, but this keeps happening. Statement after statement.

He didn’t stop there either: there was an absurd pass from which Adeyemi should have scored. A run through three. Another assist. And the moment that got the Betis fans whistling him: when, with López on the ground and Lamine Yamal going over, Facundo Bernal pushed him, he took a run-up and pushed Bernal back, and the defender head-butted him, seeing red. The game hadn’t stopped with his first either; instead, Rodri said afterwards, it had “everything”. Always watch Betis, especially when they’re playing Barcelona: unbeaten in 15 home games, the last time anyone beat them here was Barça too. And it finished 5-3. This time they were only one short.

Barcelona had dominated the first 25 minutes, the ball theirs alone but Valentín Gómez headed in to make it 1-1 before Rodri made it 2-1. Within two minutes, Lo Celso had smashed in an extraordinary 25-yard shot on the bounce and the turn to make it 2-2, only for it to be ruled out for a handball 14 seconds earlier. All that before half-time. And yet it was summed up better by the 30 seconds that passed between Álvaro Valles making a superb save at one end and Joan García matching it at the other; by the 59 seconds that passed between that and Jesus getting the third. Or the two minutes 59 seconds between that going in and Abdessamad Ezzalzouli making it 3-2. Then the fight that followed it, Lamine Yamal tumbling maybe a touch too hard and Bernal walking.

By the time Lamine Yamal did, at last encouraged to rest, Eric García had scored the fourth and it was done. “With this result, we had to make the change,” Flick said; with tensions rising too. Dani Olmo added a neat fifth and it finished. Betis were furious. Asked how it had left him feeling, their manager, Manuel Pellegrini, said: “impotent”. Lo Celso’s goal shouldn’t have been ruled out and Jesus’s should, he said. Ask how he felt, Fran García said “frustrated, angry … and tired”. They had given everything, the ovation as generous as their effort had been. “This is one of the hardest games in La Liga,” Rodri said, but Barcelona had won again.

That’s nine from nine, a new record. Now, a word of advice from Mr Wolf. When it comes to historic starts, Barcelona’s previous record was under Tata Martino, who you may remember but probably don’t. “This is a nice thing but we want to win titles,” Flick said; Martino did not. Betis were the first team Barcelona have played in the top half of the table. The rest currently sit in 19th, 18th, 17th, 16th, 15th 14th, and 11th. Harder games are coming: Paris Saint-Germain next, then Real Madrid. They also have an injury crisis at the back. But no one is playing like them, and certainly not scoring like them. They have scored 39 league goals, 48 in 11 matches in all competitions.

Deportivo A Coruña 1-1 Levante, Espanyol 0-1 Atlético, Villarreal 0-0 Elche, Real Betis 2-5 Barcelona, Valencia 0-0 A Bilbao, Osasuna 2-0 Racing Santander, Celta Vigo 2-1 Alavés, Málaga 2-5 Real Sociedad, Real Madrid 4-1 Sevilla

When Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford went in the summer, when they didn’t manage to sign Julián Álvarez, you couldn’t help asking where the goals were going to come from. The answer was everywhere. Thirteen different players have scored. It turns out that they have the best striker in Europe: Raphinha, the man who is just filling in there, has scored more than anyone else. They may also have the best player at 19, the kid who came back a World Cup winner and still wasn’t satisfied.

“After the game against Elche at the start of the season, people were saying: ‘He’s not right,’” Lamine Yamal said. “But I was calm at home, thinking: ‘I’ve just won the World Cup, I’ve not had a break, I know my body: bit by bit I’ll get to the point where I explode and start to score. And those same people will suddenly be saying I’m the best.’” In the first two games, against Elche and Athletic Bilbao, Lamine Yamal did little. Since then he has scored or assisted in every match. Nine goals, 10 assists, and most of them brilliant. He went to the international break and scored after 104 seconds at Wembley, 70 in Seville, and 320 in Oviedo. Here, on the day they said this time it’s for real, it took him 530, heads in hands, words stuck in throats, and another win on the way.

“It was amazing, a match for all the people who love football,” Flick said. “For me Lamine is the best in the world. I’m happy about his performance; this is what I love to see. And when you see the first goal, it’s unbelievable.”

#261. How Enzo Maresca stepped out of Pep Guardiola's shadow at Man City: 'Fire' in his team talks, heart-to-hearts with Phil Foden, rejecting old boss' office and a new attacking philosophy

Published: 02:00 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 23 October 2026

Stalking the room, Enzo Maresca is demanding answers. Demanding to know that his message is seeping in, demanding his players answer in the affirmative.

Maresca commands the space, down on his haunches complaining about Manchester City’s attitude towards second balls and defending. He’s loud, possesses what modern-day managers describe as ‘fire’ and players do not allow their gaze to divert inside that dressing room haze.

The scene, from a team talk earlier this season, reminds you of somebody. Pep Guardiola might be gone but the process of replacing him had to lead City towards a successor who while his own man, carving his own way, does bear a reasonable resemblance. And no, not just physically.

This decision, taken by director of football Hugo Viana with the blessing of Txiki Begiristain – who championed Maresca’s cause more than anyone else – is one that needed to strike a balance of continuity and change. Maresca has moved the dial without new concepts feeling completely alien. That’s the trick – a refresh, not reset.

Guardiola was back in town last week, far earlier than expected after waving a teary goodbye in May. The seismic guilty verdicts accelerated a return, as Guardiola sat in the directors’ box for the defeat by Paris Saint-Germain and had a debrief with Maresca in the inner sanctum afterwards.

Once it was security green-lighting requests for Noel Gallagher to enter the area around the dressing room to see Guardiola and now it was the same staff doing it for Guardiola himself.

Enzo Maresca has moved the dial at Manchester City after Pep Guardiola's exit without new concepts feeling completely alien

The Italian has led City to seven wins from seven to begin the Premier League season

Maresca is not in constant contact with his predecessor, as he has reiterated on a number of occasions. They spoke following the emotional one-goal victory at Old Trafford last month but Guardiola is mindful of staying out of the way and thought long and hard before accepting the invite for PSG, fearing his appearance might prove a distraction.

Given the pair are close, Maresca the assistant during the Treble campaign, the situation must be taking some getting used to.

Guardiola is watching City at home religiously and, more pertinently, paying close attention to the fallout of the guilty verdicts handed down for serious breaches of financial rules that could see the club relegated to the Championship, pending an appeal.

He will have noticed the consummate way in which Maresca handled the scrutiny in media briefings, with an authoritative charm and dry humour. A slight detachment certainly helps – something Guardiola could not have utilised were he still in the chair, where the exchanges would likely have been considerably more adversarial.

The way a sanguine Maresca addressed the charges with the players, ‘we have a title to win’ and ‘let’s make our own noise’, was designed to insulate the squad from a hurricane of comment and censure.

In 2023 when the charges dropped, Guardiola used it as fuel. No one likes us and all that. Clearly both styles have their merits and the one three years ago kickstarted a phenomenal run ending in Istanbul.

Maresca was a picture of relaxation as he flicked through his phone while leaning on the Etihad’s breeze blocks down the tunnel on Tuesday night after hammering AEK Athens 5-1. Guardiola looked identical, propped on exactly the same spot hundreds of times before.

Maresca is content at the start, surprised at the consistency of results – City will attempt to go eight from eight in the Premier League at Aston Villa on Saturday – and knows there is room for serious improvement.

Maresca is content at the start, surprised at the consistency of results and knows there is room for serious improvement

Guardiola is mindful of staying out of the way and thought long and hard before accepting the invite for the PSG game, fearing his appearance might prove a distraction

‘When you lose important players, many important players, and you lose the manager after 10 years, it always takes time to compete again,’ Maresca said, referencing the exits of Rodri, John Stones, Bernardo Silva, Nathan Ake, Manuel Akanji and more. ‘But we are competing at the moment. This is already a great achievement. We want more.’

There is a degree of pride in that statement from a man who is aware of the need to change certain bits of day-to-day life at the City Football Academy and how they tactically go about winning trophies – for however long that remains a possibility.

So keen is Maresca to subtly alter the messaging that instead of assuming Guardiola’s office he moved to one down the hall. He’s held heart-to-heart conversations with Phil Foden in a bid to recapture his form, with the previous boss having once visited the academy graduate’s house for similar reasons.

Undoubtedly, the 46-year-old wants a more aggressive City. A City more in the image of the 2018 Centurions than the Treble winners. An invitation for the wingers to go at their markers with more regularity, owning their individualism, and the general sense of attempting to force the ball into the box for Erling Haaland with added urgency.

Players keep saying that the messaging is clear – even if Maresca claimed recently that he’d rather win 1-0 than the basketball 5-3 against Sunderland, which is a position at odds with their swashbuckling performances. ‘I think we can attack better, we can defend better,’ Maresca said. ‘It's a matter of finding balance.’

While Maresca bristled at suggestions they gave up a few too many chances when beating Ipswich Town, the 4-2 home defeat by PSG a few days earlier gave stronger answers on the balancing act.

He talks about needing the build-up to sharpen up – meaning more control and retaining midfield stability – and removing Rayan Cherki at half-time for teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi when three down offered that.

The midfield trio of Bouaddi, Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez appeared more symmetrical and could represent a blueprint in the tougher games – especially away from home.

Maresca has held heart-to-heart conversations with Phil Foden in a bid to recapture his form

He wants control and balance in midfield, exemplified by bringing on Ayyoub Bouaddi at 3-0 down to PSG and getting a foothold

‘One of the best in Europe in the right position,' Maresca said of Rayan Cherki. 'I also like simple things. I think the most difficult thing in football is to do easy things, don't complicate.’

The Cherki flicks and tricks were mesmeric in midweek against AEK, with another spectacular goal to boot. ‘Top player,’ Maresca said. ‘One of the best players in Europe when he is in the right position. I also like simple things. I think the most difficult thing in football is to do the easy things, don't complicate.’

We’ve definitely heard those words before, delivered from the same seat last season. Maresca says he learnt more from PSG than any other game and some of that will be down to the mentality of his leaders from the break onwards. The second-half dominance, when City created scores of opportunities, taught him something tactically but also about the fortitude of certain players.

‘We don’t like to lose games, but the mood in the dressing room afterwards was very positive,’ he said. ‘The players can see with their eyes that if we compete in the way we did in the second half, we are there. It was a nice feeling because yes, we lost the game, but we can be there, we are there.’

Again, that sort of summation sounds familiar. And that is definitely no bad thing for City. Just don’t call him Diet Pep. Somebody tried that once and it didn’t end well. This is Enzo Max.

#265. Will Khvicha Kvaratskhelia play before the end of the season following ACL blow?

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

The Paris Saint-Germain star’s season is over… or is it?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is set to miss the remainder of the 2026-27 season after enduring an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in the Champions League on Tuesday evening.

PSG prevailed against Barcelona in a 4-2 win. After nearly 80 minutes, Lamine Yamal tied the scoreline at 2-2; two late strikes from Vitinha and Fabian Ruiz won the game for the Parisiens.

Kvaratskhelia collided with Barcelona’s other goalscorer, Xavi Espart, after 59 minutes, and was carried off the field by PSG staff in the aftermath.

It has now been confirmed by the club that Kvaratskhelia will undergo surgery on his right knee “in the coming days” as the first step of the Georgian’s rehabilitation.

"Having suffered a rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee during yesterday's match against FC Barcelona, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia will undergo surgery in the coming days,” read a statement issued by PSG.

A date for the PSG winger’s return has not yet been revealed; ACL injuries typically lead to sidelining periods of, at least, nine months.

As such, Kvaratskhelia, who has been hyped as a possible 2026 Ballon D’or winner after his dominant run of individual performances during PSG’s title-retaining Champions League win last season, will likely not play again in 2026-27.

Sign up for our free live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest matches, their kick-off times, channels and streams

2025 Ballon D’or winner Ousmane Dembele was also withdrawn against Barcelona through injury, as was club captain Marquinhos.

PSG also shed additional light on the nature of their injuries, revealing that the pair, who are suffering with thigh issues, “will remain under treatment for the next few weeks.”

For Kvaratskhelia, his best hope will be to mimic the abnormal return of Zlatan Ibrahimovic from an ACL injury in 2017.

The Swede recovered from a similar setback in just seven months, two months ahead of the likely nine-month rehabilitation period.

In this scenario, the Georgian’s best case, he would still only make it back to play in PSG’s final league game of the season, versus Toulouse in May 2027.

Should the Parisiens make it back to the Champions League final for a third successive time, Kvaratskhelia would also be available, should his body recover as well as Ibrahimovic’s did.

#266. Houdini act in Venice leaves Massimiliano Allegri searching for an escape at Napoli | Nicky Bandini

Manager’s latest setback exposed growing doubts about his squad and his approach as Davide Nicola began his Venezia tenure with a remarkable win

“I’ll love you even if you win,” promised the Venezia supporter’s banner. More gallows humour from a fanbase that proved long ago that its relationship with the club could survive a defeat. They had endured six already in the first six rounds of this Serie A season: the only team in the division without a win or even a single point.

The last time they were in Serie A, in 2024-25, Venezia finished 19th. The time before that, in 2021-22, they finished bottom. Deja vu all over again? A 3-1 defeat by Atalanta in the first game back after this month’s international break pushed Venezia to breaking point. The club fired the manager Giovanni Stroppa, who had led them to the Serie B title and promotion the previous season.

His replacement, Davide Nicola, is a renowned survival specialist, though his most recent appointment at Cremonese ended with his dismissal last March, when the team were 18th. If Venice’s Lagoon has a deep end, then Nicola was thrown into it, beginning this latest job at home to last season’s runners-up, Napoli.

But a man whose past relegation escapes have drawn comparison with Harry Houdini could hardly be afraid of the water. Nicola’s first Venezia team sat in a patient low block, refusing to be drawn out. And when an opportunity was casually presented to them at the start of the second half, they took it.

A long punt down the left by Simon Sohm took a kind bounce off the head of the Napoli defender Amir Rrahmani, who lost track of it in the air. Venezia’s Akor Adams took a touch to his right before striking back across his body from the edge of the area, wrongfooting Napoli’s goalkeeper Alex Meret.

Stung to life, Napoli introduced Kevin De Bruyne, Alisson Santos and Rasmus Højlund from the bench. None of them could find a way past the Venezia goalkeeper Filip Stankovic, who saved a penalty from De Bruyne and made a sensational one-handed stop from Stanislav Lobotka before denying Alisson in the 90th minute as well. The game ended 1-0, Venezia’s first win of the campaign.

A dream start for Nicola and a result that left some people wondering whether this could be the beginning of the end for Napoli’s manager, Massimiliano Allegri. Appointed to replace Antonio Conte in the summer, he has presided over five defeats in nine games.

Losses to Inter and Como might, in isolation, be excused. The failure to pick up any points at home to Arsenal or away to Villarreal in the Champions League group stage has put qualification for the knockouts at risk, but Conte also fell short on that front. The big picture takes on a different complexion, however, when you follow all that up by losing to pointless opponents.

We can say Napoli were unfortunate against Venezia. They created more than enough chances to score. Stankovic was inspired, and Juan Jesus made a brilliant last-ditch tackle to stop Højlund from prodding the ball into an empty net moments after the forward’s introduction as well.

It is also true that Allegri’s substitutions changed the game. De Bruyne initiated that chance for Højlund, pinching the ball form Ridgeciano Haps in midfield and feeding Alisson, whose excellent cross took Stankovic out of the picture. Why, though, had all these players been on the bench to begin with? Were Napoli presumptuous to think they could beat Venezia without their standout creative talent, their first-choice centre-forward and one of their most able dribblers?

Any team competing in Europe must make tough decisions about squad rotation. In Allegri’s case, though, it is hard to ignore the context of his appointment.

Conte quit Napoli last summer, walking away from a well-paid third year on his contract, because his assessment of the playing squad diverged from that of the owner, Aurelio De Laurentiis. The Partenopei spent more than €150m between 2025 and 2026’s summer and winter transfer windows, bringing in the likes of Lorenzo Lucca up front, Sam Beukema at centre-back and Noa Lang on the wing.

A further €60m was committed to making Højlund and Alisson’s initial loan signings permanent this summer. For De Laurentiis, this was enough.

The choice of Conte’s successor followed this same line of thought. Allegri has embraced his reputation in Italy as an “aziendalista” – a company man. At his introductory press conference, he said “that word, to me, is a compliment”, and stressed his belief in the strength of the existing squad.

He has backed those words with actions. Napoli have used 23 players already this Serie A season. Lucca, who started against Venezia, is almost halfway already to his total minutes from last season. Lang, who was sent on loan to Galatasaray in January after clashing with Conte, is back in the fold and scored in a recent win over Frosinone.

But what if Conte was correct in his assessments all along? Lucca is yet to score and struggled to make any impact on Saturday. Lang, an unused sub against Venezia, was seen being chastised by teammate Frank Anguissa on the sideline, reportedly for cutting short a warm-up after Allegri opted to send Alisson on before him.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

One area in which the new manager was widely thought to have improved on his predecessor was in the handling of De Bruyne. It was no secret that the Belgian did not see eye to eye with Conte.

Frosinone 4-2 Sassuolo, Venezia 1-0 Napoli, Bologna 1-3 Inter, Roma 2-0 Genoa, Udinese 0-3 Lecce, Fiorentina 1-3 Como, AC Milan 3-2 Atalanta, Juventus 0-3 Lazio

In an interview with Il Corriere dello Sport this month, De Bruyne described Allegri as “a little bit more relaxed, a bit more informal, and from what I’ve seen he takes more care of the personal connection with the players.” During Napoli’s games this season the manager has several times been observed conversing with De Bruyne, strengthening the impression that the two were forming a strong working relationship.

During the defeat by Villarreal, however, De Bruyne appeared to resist Allegri’s instructions to drop into midfield and make space for Scott McTominay to get forward, both men gesturing frustratedly in opposite directions. Allegri played the incident off as a result of their language barrier. But there is little indication yet of De Bruyne warming to his manager’s publicly stated belief that he might extend his career by reinventing himself as a deep-lying creator.

These situations do not appear yet to be at breaking point. De Laurentiis will know he is unlikely to find another manager of such experience with such willingness to toe the line. Allegri has bitten his lip thus far about the fact that the one player he did request this summer – Gabriel Jesus, available at a relatively modest price tag – is averaging better than one goal for every 60 minutes at Barcelona.

Perhaps the pressure was even alleviated in some small way by Lazio thrashing Juventus 3-0 on Sunday night, transferring the media’s attention to another former Scudetto-winning manager struggling at one of Italy’s biggest clubs.

Luciano Spalletti, a year into his project at Juventus, may well be on thinner ice. The Bianconeri are a point worse off than they were after seven games last season under Igor Tudor, who was sacked after losing the eighth (by coincidence also against Lazio).

These are separate stories, each with its own dynamics, but as two of four current Serie A managers who have won the competition previously, it is inevitable that parallels will be drawn and questions asked about whether each of Allegri or Spalletti still know how to deliver results. That conversation might extend to Maurizio Sarri, too, who has lost four of his first seven with Atalanta.

The Venezia supporter with the sign may love their club come what may. For football managers, wherever they work, such affection is rarely unconditional.

#268. Manchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their roots | Philipp Lahm

City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward

Do we have to reassess Manchester City now? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra.

I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri.

As a player and a columnist, I never had an issue with Manchester City – precisely because, for many years, the club avoided buying the most obvious superstars. Guardiola said it himself: the most valuable of the valuable do not go to a club such as City, who aren’t even the biggest football brand in their own home town.

Many became world stars in Manchester. Kevin De Bruyne had been discarded by Chelsea, Rodri’s true class was overlooked in Madrid for a long time, Gündogan’s career was on the brink after injuries, and most recently Gianluigi Donnarumma was no longer wanted in Paris. In Germany, City signed players from Hamburg, Frankfurt and Wolfsburg. Erling Haaland in 2022 was the first player they targeted who was also pursued by Bayern Munich. City did not operate like Paris Saint‑Germain did in the era before Luis Enrique.

From the outside, City fundamentally did not do much differently from the other 10 or so top European clubs. But what are achievements on the pitch worth if they are accompanied by rule-breaking? The club have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. It allegedly invested almost €1bn more than allowed and declared. The league leaders face potential forced relegation or titles being stripped. City continue to deny wrongdoing and are appealing against the decision.

It is right for the Premier League to crack down on unfair competition. I also appreciate that Germany is holding on to the 50+1 rule, which the federal cartel office recently upheld. It ensures that the majority of voting rights must remain with the parent club – the non‑profit section of a professional club. The exceptions that have applied to Leverkusen and Wolfsburg are under review.

The bedrock of our football culture is 50+1. This rule exists only in Germany, yet it speaks to a spirit that fits perfectly with the European sports model: 50+1 maintains a balance; on the one hand it allows for investment, on the other it guarantees participation. It strengthens the rights of members and fans. Perhaps it is because of this rule that the average attendance in Germany is higher than anywhere else in the world.

What is the ultimate purpose of football? It is a business, but its infrastructure is still developed by the general public. That is how I have always understood sport. Even as a professional, it was clear to me that my privileged life was made possible by many people working on a voluntary basis. Through my role as tournament director of the European Championship, these political connections have become even clearer to me.

The stadium and football clubs can remain the final places where people gather and society debates its issues only if the elite and the grassroots stay connected, and the public is involved in the process. Football must not be detached from its roots, as was the case with Manchester City. This becomes possible when rules are enforced by an institution. Ideally, not by a commercial entity but by a non-profit one such as Uefa.

In business, as in politics, I am observing a shift in mindset. Today, it is deemed necessary to invest in non‑profit institutions. More and more companies realise that football allows for a genuine exchange with the population – that it provides the perfect vehicle to set up corporate social responsibility projects.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

This is what is needed in these politically turbulent times. In our fragmented world, political parties, churches and the media have lost credibility. In sport, however, people still come together. It is a tool to foster social cohesion. Therefore, I consider 50+1 to be a distinct competitive advantage for the Bundesliga.

I also welcome the fact that rules mean something in another case. Uefa is standing firm against Gianni Infantino, who recently wanted to privatise the World Cup and its profits. Along with his friend Donald Trump, he was seen by many as breaking the normal rules when Folarin Balogun’s suspension was lifted. The outcry from the global football community was loud, and it is possible that the Fifa president will fall.

When behaviour such as that in Manchester and at Fifa is punished, it is a good thing. Football must prevent questionable ideas from distancing it even further from its grassroots. Only then can it drive engagement in civil society, and only then can it strengthen Europe.

Philipp Lahm’s column was produced in partnership with Oliver Fritsch at the German online magazine Die Zeit.

Arsenal are lining up a new striker to act as Kai Havertz' deputy

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal are interested in a ‘complete striker’ to challenge Kai Havertz for the No.9 role.

That's according to a new report, which casts Viktor Gyokeres' position at the club in further doubt, with the Swedish hitman failing to start a single Premier League fixture this season.

Despite being the Gunners' top scorer in all competitions last season as Arsenal won the Premier League and reached the Champions League final, Gyokeres has struggled at times in North London – and now, it appears that he could have even more competition up front.

Gyokeres has already noted this season that he wants to “play football as much as possible”, but with Havertz returning from an injury that sidelined him for much of last season, the Swede has found himself playing second fiddle.

Disappointing cameo appearances in the Champions League and Carabao Cup have led to rumours that the 28-year-old will be sacrificed in the coming months, as Arteta looks to bring in a more rounded centre-forward able to hold the ball up.

Sport Witness, meanwhile, have relayed a report from Italian newspaper Gazzetta dello Sport today that link Arsenal with Monza frontman, Gustavo Varela.

Varela arrived in Serie A from Benfica over the summer and has already struck six goals from six in the division, with Napoli said to be leading the race for his signature at this early stage.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Arsenal, meanwhile, have an eye on the situation, with transfer expert Gianluca Di Marzio adding that “major offers could be on the way for the striker”.

Benfica have the right to match any bid for the 21-year-old, but could well choose not to make an offer if Arsenal propose a deal out of their range.

The Gunners may well have to look for left-field targets in their bid to improve a squad that reached the latter stages of three competitions last season, as they struggled to land their big targets over the summer.

Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez both opted to remain in Madrid, with the Gunners only strengthening in attack by signing Christos Tzolis – with that sole deal perhaps indicating the direction that the club must go in to outsmart rivals.

Varela is worth €5m, as per Transfermarkt. Arsenal face Bayern Munich tonight as Champions League action resumes.

#274. Elite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael Carrick | Barney Ronay

Getting rid of head coach is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different

At the final whistle at Elland Road the TV cameras cut to a lingering shot of the Manchester United chief executive, Omar Berrada, looking down pensively from the stands, deciding, it is to be hoped, on a little clemency, a re-sheathing of the managerial shotgun.

Here we have the man who hired the man. The man who fires the man. The man who also hired or rehired the previous two men he had to fire. Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble.

How do you solve what is, on revenue versus results, the worst-run club in world football? By changing the name of the latest patsy on the touchline, of course. For now a hard-fought point is perhaps enough to stave off that pre-programmed emergency response.

Stand down the cowboy cops. Call off the blue and white saloons. Although with a run of Bournemouth, Chelsea, Aston Villa and Liverpool next up in the league it will no doubt soon be time to go out there and arrest Lee Harvey Oswald again. What’s that you say? OK, well, dig him up again. Re-arrest him. Whatever it takes. Someone has to stop these lone gunmen, these managerial magic bullet merchants from derailing the Manchester United supremacy.

This was a dual-track football match between Leeds and Manchester United, on the face of it a good, even game between two teams of well-matched players. A 1-1 draw was fair in the end, although Leeds played well and probably should have won. But of course they won’t be the story.

Instead this game had already been billed as that familiar thing, a referendum on the future of Michael Carrick. A stay of execution for a week or two. Or another livestreamed firing squad for the Super Sunday cameras.

There has been a predictable sense of low comedy about Carrick’s own transformation in the United dugout this season. It was always going to be the case that his widely praised qualities in victory, blazer, T-shirt, jawline, inscrutable sense of calm, would become his fatal flaws in defeat.

Where’s the passion, the whirling arms, the range of tailored collars? At Elland Road Carrick simply looked drained in the second half as United were pegged back and overrun at times, the beard a little more ragged, the hair unkempt but still sweeping, the look of a brave, doomed tugboat captain resigned now to the approaching tsunami wave on the horizon.

A point leaves United 13th in the league and still struggling to reverse a dreadful start to the season. But it was a good game for two people. First for Carrick, who remains a million miles away from creating the problems afflicting this club, even if you accept that his presence as head coach is one of them.

Michael Carrick did not hire Michael Carrick. Getting rid of Michael Carrick is, by definition, not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. But it might just help to prolong them. Whatever his ultimate ceiling, it is surely worth keeping him just to try, for once, to do something different.

This was also a good game for Lisandro Martínez, who went off injured at half-time with United 1-0 up, and who was also vindicated in his allegedly controversial (translation: entirely correct) comments on the club hierarchy in midweek.

United’s energetic first-half performance clarified one half of this. The players are committed in support of the manager, at least to the best of their ability. The second half made the other half of the argument, that this remains a mismatched, lopsided, cut-and-paste squad, always likely to be pulled apart by opponents as urgent as this Leeds team, which fully deserves its current seventh place in the table.

The problems are so obvious it is barely worth repeating them. But here goes. The third-richest club in the world played a second half with three of its back four out of position. Harry Maguire, signed under Ole Gunnar Solskjær, remains the best straight defender. But Maguire is also essentially a man-shaped solid wood armoire in a pair of shorts at this stage in his career, always the slowest person on any pitch, which means you will not be able to cover space, play a high line or counterattack without leaving yourself exposed to the counter-counter.

So good luck, guys. And remember Omar, who gave you this whisky bottle and loaded pistol of a squad, will be watching.

This was made painfully clear after half-time as Martínez went off and Noussair Mazraoui came on. Leeds scored an equaliser that felt structurally inevitable. They found space down their right side repeatedly. At times they seemed to be constantly peppering the seats behind the United goal, like a group of kids hammering a ball against a garage door. By the end Leeds had more possession, more shots on target and just looked a happier, better structured entity than the travelling heritage exhibit at the other end.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The key point here is to accept that all of this is entirely logical. This is not a mystery, a haunted house, a place of bad voodoo. Why do we talk about Manchester United so much? For obvious reasons. It’s a massive part of the English football landscape. Mainly, though, because this is a story of mind-bending waste, real-time elite-level incompetence played out on a weekly basis.

Yes, you could sack Michael Carrick. It won’t change much. Let’s destroy Eddie Howe for a bit instead. But the available evidence suggests every single person making executive decisions here is outmatched and outmanoeuvred.

There is a reason Manchester United feels like one of those high street legacy chain shops just before it collapses, piles of Quality Street by the door, a rat in the lingerie department, destined to become a pop-up vape shop run by Albanian money launderers. There’s a reason it feels so badly run. This is because: it is.

We know the Glazer ownership has zero interest in minding the details, that this has been a wonderful acquisition whatever the performance on the pitch, an asset supremely sweated. We know also that Sir Jim Ratcliffe is pub-level incoherent on the details he promised to fix. Remember when he was going to sit down and decide what the “style of football” would be? How’s that working out?

Instead Carrick is left shuffling a first XI acquired by endlessly revolving administrations. Here United had four defenders signed under Erik ten Hag, two Ruben Amorim recruits, two from the mist-shrouded age of Solskjær. No players were recruited under Ralf Rangnick, of course. But then Rangnick wanted to sign Erling Haaland, Luis Díaz, and Julian Álvarez, which all sounds far too sensible.

An organisation can be built with many hands. But not when so many of those hands appear to be so far from best in class it’s hard to work out which class they’re supposed to be attending. John Murtough, the former Manchester United football director, is currently director of global development at Atalanta, who have a 24,000-seat stadium and almost zero global presence. Meanwhile Berrada, the axeman, seems entirely invulnerable from the axe himself, despite the fact his job seems to orbit around resolving the consequences of his own mistakes.

United probably will sack their current manager before the year is out. This is the way this machine has to operate, always looking to buy itself, and those in the executive seats, a little more time on the payroll, an entity that has been hollowed out and allowed to rust, run on buzzwords and brown paper and string. Meanwhile, over to you Michael. We’ll see you next week, and maybe even the week after that, for more of exactly the same.

#280. Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a Premier League super-club I Jonathan Wilson

The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically

The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free.

Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.”

This was everything Sunderland fans could have wished for from their first European away game in 53 years and more. They had seen other fans experience these things, and now they could tick off the checklist: complicated travel to a pretty foreign town they would otherwise never visit, a fussy Albanian referee and a great sense of togetherness and community. There was even an injury-time winner from, miracle of miracles, Noah Sadiki.

Ask any of the 5,000 or so Wearsiders who made the trip to Portugal if the Europa League was worth it and the answer would be unanimous. Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Brighton fans would surely say something similar: European football, especially for clubs who are unfamiliar with it, is a joy and an adventure. It generates experiences that will be remembered for ever, and if the cost is that the risk of relegation goes up, that’s a price worth paying. Others at those clubs may see things differently.

The four Premier League clubs involved in the lesser two European competitions play each other on Sunday. Brighton are thriving; the other three are not. Palace were 12th before the weekend fixtures but not playing well. Bournemouth against Sunderland is a battle of third- and fourth-bottom. Whether the Europa League football can yet be blamed is debatable. Brighton surely can’t be bucking the trend just because of the lesser demands of the Conference League. Thursday’s was only the second round of Europa League league games, and the clubs involved bypassed a round of the Carabao Cup; fatigue may come but it shouldn’t be an issue yet.

There are other factors at play. Sunderland have already played Manchester City, Arsenal, Brighton and Brentford, the top four going into this weekend. They could easily have been a couple of goals up by half-time at Brentford. They missed a penalty to go ahead against Arsenal. They registered an xG of 2.72 in losing 5-3 at Manchester City. Only in the defeat to Brighton last weekend have they really disappointed. In the equivalent six games last season (substituting Ipswich for Burnley), Sunderland took only one point; in that sense, they are actually three points better off this campaign.

But that can’t alter the fact that four points from six games leaves them beginning to fret. There is pressure on this next run of fixtures: after Bournemouth, they are home to Leeds, then away to Coventry. Sunderland’s transfer business left a major question on the right of the forward line that has yet to be resolved. A lack of depth in certain areas has been exposed by injuries to Brian Brobbey and Habib Diarra, although both players were on the bench on Thursday.

Bournemouth have also lost key players to injury. Eli Junior Kroupi, who scored 13 league goals last season, has not played this campaign. Neither has Amine Adli, although he came off the bench on Thursday, as did Justin Kluivert, who had been out for a month. Most damagingly of all, perhaps, after impressing for England against Croatia, Alex Scott has been ruled out with a thigh injury.

The transition away from Andoni Iraola was always likely to be disruptive and, while Saturday’s 5-1 defeat at Chelsea was a jolt, their other losses this season were to Manchester City and Liverpool. There has been a sense of margins going against them, of draws that might have been wins. The concern, as with Sunderland, comes if that affects morale, and decent displays that have yielded disappointing results curdle into disappointing performances.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Palace are in a slightly different position. Other than City, their fixture list has been relatively kind. Seven points from six games would constitute comfortable survival if extrapolated over the season as a whole, but Opta’s expected points table, which has Bournemouth ninth and Sunderland 10th, has them 18th. A new manager is settling in, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Múñoz were sold over the summer, while Jean-Philippe Mateta hasn’t played since the opening weekend.

For none of those three sides can unsettled starts be blamed entirely or even primarily on Europe. That said, the evidence is clear: over the past five years, teams who did not play in Europe the previous season see their league position fall when they do play in Europe: Palace dropped from 12th to 15th, Nottingham Forest from seventh to 16th, Newcastle from fifth to 12th, Brighton from sixth to 11th, West Ham from sixth to seventh. Of those examples, only Forest even came vaguely close to relegation, but the fear nags away.

Although winning the Europa League would bring the vast rewards of Champions League football, losing in the final would probably bring in not much more than £20m for a Premier League club, plus gate receipts and whatever intangible benefits there might be from increased exposure. To put that in context, that’s roughly the difference between finishing ninth and 14th in the Premier League.

Which is to say that while fans revel in trips to Milan, Prague or Lyon, for club executives a few nice mini-breaks do not balance out the potential financial headaches.

#281. 'They've lost that edge': How Bath fell back down to earth thanks to stars departing and second-half woes - as bitter rivals Gloucester smell blood

Published: 02:00 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 23 October 2026

‘Never too high, never too low,’ is one of Johann van Graan's most-used phrases. Win or lose, Bath's head coach doesn’t get too carried away. That remains the case, even though the latest evidence suggests his team is simply not at the elite level that saw them claim a brilliant Treble in the 2024-25 season.

A 71-48 hammering at reigning PREM champions Northampton saw Bath drop out of the top four for the first time in more than three years. Then came an even more disappointing defeat in Europe – a 32-14 loss on home soil to Montpellier last weekend.

In their past 11 competitive matches, dating back to and including May’s Champions Cup semi-final defeat by Bordeaux, Bath have lost seven and won four. Not a crisis yet, but certainly a drop-off from the high standards Van Graan has been used to setting since the South African's brilliant overhaul of the club began in summer 2022.

'You can't deny, Bath are not playing to their full capacity,’ club legend and former England prop Gareth Chilcott tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘What's slightly concerning me is that they're creating chances and not taking them.

'Their discipline is a little bit wayward and they seem off the pace slightly. Bath have won lots of games by overpowering teams late on in games. They seem to have lost that little bit of an edge.’

When Van Graan joined Bath four years ago, he took charge of a club that was criminally underachieving at the wrong end of the PREM. He has since worked wonders, winning a first league title for 29 years in 2025 while also lifting the European Challenge Cup and PREM Rugby Cup in the same season.

Johann van Graan won't be getting carried away, but his side have been in a rut in recent weeks

Northampton thumped Bath 71-48 last time out in the PREM, in a reminder of who the standard-bearers are in the English top flight

And that was followed by Montpellier hammering Bath on home turf in the opening round of the Champions Cup last weekend

Now, though, there appear to be a few chinks in their armour, just in time for a mouth-watering West Country Derby at bitter rivals and the PREM's early leaders Gloucester on Friday night.

'It’s not a crisis for Bath yet, but when a team that has been a high-flier starts to look like they're faltering a little bit, then it’s understandable people ask questions,’ Chilcott says. ‘Once teams see you are beatable, it can be very difficult to win games.’

Bath’s success under the no-nonsense, methodical Van Graan has been built on the power of their forwards and a clinical edge. Bath used to be unstoppable from close range through the likes of hulking forwards Thomas du Toit and Alfie Barbeary, but both left the club in the summer.

The Montpellier game summed up Bath’s current travails. Their defence and set-piece was inconsistent and they missed a host of opportunities, summed up by wing Joe Cokanasiga dropping a sitter of a pass for what would have been a certain try had he collected. Star No10 Finn Russell was intercepted for a French score and his team conceded 15 penalties.

Bath are still creating opportunities – in each of their past three games, they have had more than 12 entries into the opposition 22. But against Montpellier, their average points per entry was just one.

‘If you don’t use your chances, you’re not going to win rugby games against top quality opposition,’ Van Graan admitted. ‘We had multiple opportunities five yards from their try line which we didn’t finish. It’s up to us to be better.’

Where Bath were once ruthless, there is now a degree of profligacy. The departure of juggernaut, try-machine Springbok prop Du Toit cannot be underestimated. When the likes of Ollie Lawrence, Guy Pepper and Ted Hill saw their salaries increase after initially signing on meagre terms, Bath had to juggle their squad and that meant there was no room for Du Toit and Barbeary, now with Saracens.

‘They were two really big players – Bath’s two biggest ball-carriers,’ Chilcott says. ‘That will take its toll. Du Toit was unbelievably good. There is no doubt they’re missing him and Barbeary.

Star No10 Finn Russell (right) has not quite hit the heights since Bath won the league in 2025

Springbok prop Thomas du Toit was a massive loss over the summer as he headed back to his homeland

‘Will Stuart has come back from a long-term injury. We know he’s a great England international and a Lion, but he’s a different type of prop to the big South African. He’ll take a while to get back into the swing of things.’

Van Graan lost his highly-rated attack coach Lee Blackett to England and replaced him first with Martin Gleeson and then Irishman Mike Prendergast. The club’s former head of recruitment Rob Burgess also left to become general manager at Gloucester and will now have eyes on beating his former employers.

Injuries have undoubtedly played a part too. Unheralded but hugely influential wing Will Muir hasn’t played since the Bordeaux loss, while captain Ben Spencer, Henry Arundell, Tom de Glanville, Miles Reid and Billy Sela have all had fitness issues at the start of the season.

Stuart is still working his way back to peak form after a serious achilles problem. His club and England team-mate Sam Underhill ruptured his bicep in the PREM-opening win at Harlequins.

New signing Dan du Preez, Barbeary’s replacement, has torn his hamstring and starting prop Beno Obano has already confirmed he is leaving for France, with Saracens' Rhys Carre a leading contender to replace him.

‘They need to get back to winning ways as quickly as possible,' says Chilcott. 'It’s maybe ridiculous to say this so early in the season, but I think the Gloucester game is massive for Bath.’

One worrying trend for Bath fans has been their team’s tendency to fall away in the second half of matches.

In their shock home PREM semi-final loss to Exeter last season, Van Graan’s team conceded 17 unanswered second-half points to fall to a 26-27 defeat. Such a situation has not been a one-off.

One worrying trend for Bath fans has been their team’s tendency to fall away in the second half of matches

Joe Cokanasiga has lost his place for the trip to Gloucester on Friday night

‘We’ve not had everybody available and that’s been the theme of our season. But we never make a big issue out of it,’ Van Graan said. ‘We just back the next man. We are very comfortable with the way we do things and there is a lot of rugby to be played. There are still loads of players to come back.’

Van Graan, who has never lost at Kingsholm, has overhauled the team for the derby with eight changes, bringing in England Under 20s wing Tyler Offiah on the wing in place of Cokanasiga and starting young Italian Enoch Opoku-Gyamfi at lock. Offiah and Louie Hennessey get their first starts of the season.

With Bath not quite at the races and the Cherry and Whites the league’s most improved team by some distance, an enthralling game is anticipated – though a severe weather warning is in place.

Another loss for Bath would mean the storm clouds already gathering over them darkening even further.

#285. Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership | Jonathan Liew

Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club

Heartbreaking: the worst defender you know just made a great point. And no, nobody would describe Lisandro Martínez as the ideal person to scrutinise Manchester United’s indifferent start to the season, given that his high-profile defensive errors against Fulham and Tottenham are partly responsible for it. “We’re all trying to find the guy who did this,” Martínez burbles on Amazon Prime after United’s 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid on Tuesday night, dressed in a hot dog costume and throwing his arms out in mock innocence.

For those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast.

But traducing the messenger will always be easier than hearing the message, even if Martínez’s views are widely shared within the United dressing room. If the fallout from the Manchester City legal case has demonstrated anything, it is English football’s ingrained reluctance to scrutinise the owners and executives who hold more influence over the sport than anybody else. Men in boots, not men in suits. Hey, watch the ball. It’s going to move!

All the same, it’s worth parsing exactly what Martínez was complaining about, because it’s a good deal more complex than it may appear on first viewing. Player calls out board – and specifically “technical director” Jason Wilcox – for failing to invest sufficiently in the squad over the summer. This was a summer in which United brought in three midfielders (Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba), a reserve goalkeeper (Karl Darlow), nobody up front and nobody in defence. So far, so simple.

But let’s begin to unpick the threads. Why did United not buy a defender in the summer, despite pursuing deals for Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly? Because they were unable to sell a defender. There was no interest in Diogo Dalot or Noussair Mazraoui, nor in Harry Maguire, nor in Luke Shaw or Martínez, whose contracts are up next summer in any case. This is the product of recruitment decisions made and deals signed years ago. But why do United, one of the world’s most lucrative clubs, need to sell to buy in the first place?

Perhaps for the same reason they baulked at the asking price for Elliot Anderson and decided to sign the inconsistent Santos and the adequate but overpromoted Tielemans instead: this is a club in austerity measures, whose part-owner Jim Ratcliffe has been furiously cutting costs and raising ticket prices, determined to curb the years of excess that preceded him, where mediocre players were signed on ridiculous money, where failing coaches were paid to leave. But why would United, one of the most commercially successful clubs in footballing history, ever need to cut costs?

Perhaps as a result of the more than £1bn drained out of the club by the Glazers in their 21 years of ownership, not just in dividends but share sales and interest payments on the debt they undertook to buy the club, while neglecting the maintenance of Old Trafford and the training ground at Carrington. Whether he knows it or not, when Martínez is criticising the lack of investment he is in effect holding the Glazers accountable for more than two decades of avarice and mismanagement.

All of which lends a certain significance to Martínez’s intervention that goes beyond the churn of the weekly news cycle. Has any serving United player spoken out so frankly about the ruins of the Glazer ownership? Ole Gunnar Solskjær made a minor stand in early 2005, before they had arrived at the club. Cristiano Ronaldo threw some hand grenades over his shoulder a few days before he left for the second time in 2022. Countless others waited for the safety of retirement, when their disgruntlement could be monetised for personal gain, rather than used to stigmatise them, as Martínez will doubtless be stigmatised in the coming days.

Does any of this help United to win games in the short term? Almost certainly not. Martínez attempted to clarify his comments in a social media post on Wednesday night. He may still be dispatched to the bomb squad anyway, for the crime of pointing out that the emperor secured his throne almost entirely through the use of payment-in-kind loans.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Inevitably Michael Carrick too will be gone before long, away to the great Overlap podcast in the sky. A few months ago I wrote hopefully that Carrick might be the ideal man to cut through the noise and nonsense. I was wrong. The noise has beaten him; the nonsense always wins; any accumulated credit from last season has long since evaporated.

Of course it’s not Carrick’s fault that United haven’t signed a new defender in almost two years, that Bruno Fernandes is so clearly playing through discomfort, that Joshua Zirkzee is still somehow hanging around the place, that the ownership decided to embark on a purge of season-ticket holders in the summer, generating a huge wave of ill-feeling and apathy that can be felt at Old Trafford on matchdays: an entire fanbase trying to work out whether they actually still care about this.

But accountability is for the little people, and far easier to replace a coach on a modest 20-month contract than to oust Ineos or the Glazers, to replace Wilcox or Omar Berrada, even if we now know they partly built their reputations on the success of a club that has been found to have serially cheated. Bumper returns for the owners, price hikes for the fans, corners cut on the pitch; this is the story of the modern Manchester United, which by no coincidence is also the story of modern football.
