The Bournemouth and England midfielder make a big shout that worked out big time as a young man

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Alex Scott had an unconventional route to where he is now.

The England and Bournemouth midfielder spent his formative years flying from Guernsey to the English mainland to train in the youth system Bournemouth and then Southampton.

Scott could have gone to find another club after being let go by Southampton's academy - but instead took a conscious decision to play senior football on the Channel Islands instead.

Scott told FourFourTwo: "I thought I could still be a footballer, that I might get another chance, but knew it would be tough.

"At that point though, I wasn’t enjoying it and if I’d stayed, I don’t think I would have progressed the way I did after going back home. It was the right decision.

"I was training with the team quite a bit when I was 15, doing bits after our under-16s sessions.

"I’d go over to the first team and fill spaces basically, but you couldn’t play until you were 16, so I had to wait.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"In the first game after my birthday, I got thrown on, wearing number 14 – that was also my first number in the Premier League for Bournemouth, so it came full circle.

"It was a lot different quality-wise for sure. Physically when I was that young, it was important for me to play men’s football and I learned a lot. In the youth teams, I’d almost just take the ball and dribble, but when you go into senior football, you’re going to get hurt doing that.

"I learned that the hard way, training with the Guernsey lads and playing in games, but that experience definitely benefited me, especially when I later went to Bristol City and broke through.

"I can remember one game – I can’t recall who it was against, but it was at home. I was playing at eight or 10, and every time I got the ball, this number six for the opposition was just nailing me every time! I was thinking, ‘Yeah, this is proper…’

"But I enjoyed it – I embraced it, gave him a bit back and started trying to do skills.

"That’s probably where it started for me, my way of playing, the freedom to play and enjoy football. Those moments brought that on."

Scott was speaking at PUMA’s new store on Oxford Street in London, the brand’s first European flagship store.

Steven Chicken has been working as a football writer since 2009, taking in stints with Football365 and the Huddersfield Examiner. Steven still covers Huddersfield Town home and away for his own publication, WeAreTerriers.com. #291. The keeper doing 'Premier League' things for EFL's last unbeaten side

Jed Ward was an ever-present on loan for Yeovil in the National League last season

New Walsall goalkeeper Jed Ward is producing "Premier League" contributions with both his hands and feet, according to his dazzled manager and team-mates.

The 23-year-old has kept eight clean sheets in 13 games in all competitions - making a string of superb saves in the process - since joining the Saddlers from hometown club Bristol Rovers for an undisclosed fee in the summer.

And he added another string to his bow with an outrageous assist in Tuesday's 3-0 League Two win over Oldham Athletic - pinging a pin-point 50-yard low through-ball for Tai Sodje to score the Saddlers' opener.

"The pass from Jed is different level - I was shouting at him to play Tai in, but I didn't think he'd do it in that way," said impressed Walsall top-scorer Aaron Pressley.

Ward leads League Two in percentage of shots saved - 86% with 43 stops from 50 efforts on target faced, which is almost four saves a game on average.

Only Swindon's Connor Ripley (58) has made more saves while Exeter goalkeeper Jack Bycroft (seven) is the only keeper to have kept more League Two clean sheets than Ward's six.

He has spent much of the past two seasons on loan at National League clubs Yeovil and Forest Green, but did make 18 League One appearances for Bristol Rovers in 2024-25.

In addition to his unexpected assist, Ward made three stops at key moments of Tuesday's game to continue to delight Saddlers boss Lee Grant, himself a former goalkeeper for Sheffield Wednesday, Burnley and Derby during his playing days.

"In terms of what he's bringing at the moment, [Jed] is very, very high level," Grant told BBC Radio WM.

"There's a big save at 0-0, a big save at 1-0. There's an incredible assist, then there's distribution in the second half which is just so well thought-out and executed. His level of performance has been so high."

Grant: 'We got to see both sides of the group'

The Walsall job is Lee Grant's second head coach role after eight months in charge of Huddersfield Town last season

Walsall's collective level of performance under new boss Grant - with a largely overhauled squad - has been just as high as their last line of defence.

After 11 games, they are the only unbeaten team remaining in the EFL, although a surplus of draws compared to wins - seven to four - means they only sit fourth.

Two goals from Pressley, including one from the penalty spot, after Sodje's opener, comfortably saw off Oldham despite Walsall playing the final half hour with 10 men after Elicha Ahui's red card.

"We got to see both sides of the group - we got to see a team that was really going after the game in the first half, dominated and controlled large parts," added Grant.

"Then we got to see the other side of the group which is becoming a clear trend in terms of the character, the fight and the determination and I think in some ways that feels sweeter."

Walsall have led League Two at Christmas in both of the past two seasons, only to fall away and fail to gain promotion on either occasion.

Pressley, who joined in the summer of 2025 and was part of last season's slide, has already overtaken his goal tally from last term with eight so far - including seven in the league.

Both he and his manager, however, pointed to Walsall's strength in depth - Grant has regularly tinkered with his starting XI, never fielding an unchanged side despite their solid results - as a beacon of hope they can last the course this time.

"I've just trusted my whole group," said Grant. "So, for the long run, it's good to have this sort of depth and be able to utilise that."

Pressley added: "We made four changes on Tuesday and that's the strength of the squad. The players coming on have been outstanding and the way we can change the team from game to game is such a strength."

Arguably, Walsall's biggest test of their unbeaten start will come in their next home game when they host leaders Salford on Monday.

"Obviously it's quite a big game next Monday, but we just need to focus on what we can control in a way on the training pitch and prepare properly," Pressley added.

"That should put us in a good place for next week."

#292. Jordan Henderson's Chelsea revival: How he's still running Premier League midfields at 36, why Xabi Alonso is so enamoured with his role as dressing-room mentor and referee whisperer, and why he hasn't given up on England dream

By RIATH AL-SAMARRAI, CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 02:00 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 23 October 2026

Wherever Jordan Henderson has travelled in his long career, his fittingly no-frills nickname follows, and it’s also how he is addressed by his manager at Chelsea.

All of which is vaguely interesting for a single reason – Xabi Alonso almost never uses soubriquets. But with Henderson, there’s an exception.

According to sources on the staff at Chelsea, if you want to see Alonso’s eyes light up, mention 'Hendo'. His responses tend to be revealing, too. Alonso doesn’t rave about the two goals in the recent 5-1 win over Bournemouth, or what the rest of us say about Henderson’s primary function at the club. His preference, instead, is to drift towards the nuances.

As a midfielder, Alonso was capable of spectacular moments but those close to him cite his deeper obsessions with tempo control, positioning and the minutiae that doesn’t make for exciting reels. In Henderson, he sees a kindred spirit and a master of the subtle arts, which has evidently survived into a 16th season as a Premier League regular.

If Henderson starts a fourth straight game against Tottenham on Saturday evening, it will come as no shock. But the surprise, beyond Chelsea, is the comfort with which he can still control a midfield in the frenzied hothouse of our top flight at 36.

An athlete excelling into their mid or late thirties is not as uncommon as it once was. But a fact lost on no one at Chelsea’s Cobham HQ is that Henderson is thriving in the physical battle.

If Jordan Henderson starts a fourth straight game on Saturday evening, it will come as no shock. But the surprise is the comfort with which he can still control a midfield at 36

If you want to see Xabi Alonso’s eyes light up, mention 'Hendo' - one of the few players the Spaniard calls by their nickname

Alonso has kept him on the field for every minute of the past three games – a hiding by Brentford and strong wins against Bournemouth and Everton – and Henderson covered more distance in those fixtures than any player from either side. Against Brentford, whose squad rank third in the Premier League for this metric, that was notable.

Henderson’s engine has always been one of his defining qualities. When he was taken on a free from Brentford in the summer, in a move largely driven by recruitment executives Paul Winstanley and Sam Jewell, his physical capacity was one of the pull factors.

Granit Xhaka, 34, had been their first choice on a brief to land an experienced midfielder for a young squad, but even before the Swiss rejected the move, it had been established that Henderson’s numbers offered no evidence of a declining output.

Last season, at Brentford, he ranked in the Premier League’s 95th percentile for his distance stats, but in isolation it can be a misleading data point – a player running to bad spots is no use to anyone. Keith Andrews never came close to levelling that complaint against Henderson.

There is a famous irony here – Sir Alex Ferguson once rejected the chance to sign Henderson for Manchester United in the early stages of his career on the basis of an idiosyncratic running style. He feared it would make him prone to injuries but 466 Premier League appearances in, that case has long since been put to bed.

Naturally, the conversation around Henderson these days goes to broader places, and namely his role as a mentor to a young group that was awfully ill-disciplined under Liam Rosenior and Enzo Maresca.

The initial evidence suggests that an emotionally volatile squad has benefited hugely from a strong leadership figure – it has been observed internally at Chelsea that he carries more weight with referees and team-mates.

Two examples came up in the Everton game. He was able to instantly silence his captain, Moises Caicedo, when the latter launched into a rant at Jack Grealish, and then when he led a retaliation against a rough challenge from James Tarkowski. Walking the line between aggression and a red card has often been a problem at Stamford Bridge, so an old head will add value.

It has been observed internally at Chelsea that Henderson carries more weight with referees and team-mates

It is common for him to still be at the training ground at 5pm or 6pm, when most will head for home mid-afternoon, and he spent the recent international break honing his free-kicks

Curiously, Henderson seems to bristle at any depiction of him being recruited purely as a ‘vibes’ man and has admitted the notion has fired him with a point to prove. But he presumably knows it was part of the club’s thinking. Just as it was for Thomas Tuchel during the World Cup and for Andrews at Brentford.

Henderson’s value to the dressing room ranked among the reasons why Brentford had rescued him from his post-Liverpool wilderness, which saw a poorly-judged move to Saudi Arabia followed by a fractious, uncomfortable period at Ajax. Some sources at Brentford thought he might reward the club by sticking around; that he decided to leave once Chelsea came calling will have stung.

At Chelsea, there have been predictable tributes around Henderson’s influence. One source said it is common for him to still be at the training ground at 5pm or 6pm, when most will head for home mid-afternoon, and it is known that he spent the most recent international break honing his free-kicks with set-piece coach Austin MacPhee and Cole Palmer.

Henderson celebrated his strike against Bournemouth by running to MacPhee on the touchline; it was MacPhee who impressed upon Alonso that Henderson was a good option from that 25-yard range.

For Alonso, the strike served as a measure of public vindication for a transfer that, at first glance, seemed quite strange. No doubt he would say the move for ‘Hendo’ was always about a bigger picture and smaller details. But for now, it is working well either way.

Time will tell where it leads for Henderson – he still believes he can do a job for England heading into Euro 2028. Betting against it somehow feels like the riskier choice.

#296. Beer & Blackpool beach was how British players bonded - Pulis

Hearing about Tottenham's team-bonding trip to Marbella last week made me think about the similar methods I used as a manager to build team morale.

While some things have changed from my day, the idea behind taking your players away to a new environment where they will benefit from spending a lot of time together has not.

I wrote a few weeks ago about how Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi needed time with his players on the training pitch after their poor start to the season, to bed them in and build a proper team.

He will have used their warm-weather camp in southern Spain to do more of that, getting to know what is almost a new squad of players.

With De Zerbi being cut from Italian cloth, I am sure the players will have been working mornings and afternoons to drill in the manager's principles in respect to team shape and direction.

But that's not the only purpose of taking them away. De Zerbi will also have been able to monitor the different personalities within the group away from the grass.

If the trip has worked then, as well as getting them ready to face Coventry on Monday night, I am sure he will now, for the first time, understand the strengths and weaknesses of each individual, on and off the field.

Tottenham spent more than Â£250m on new talent over the summer - adding 10 players to De Zerbi's squad

A few eyebrows were raised about Spurs going away so early in the season but it makes perfect sense to me when you consider so many new players arrived there this summer, with several signings late in the transfer window.

When I was Stoke manager, I often took my teams away to Austria in our pre-season for the same reasons De Zerbi and Spurs have gone to Spain.

Those trips were set up not only to test the players' fitness, but also to see how the group worked together.

I have always believed in building a family togetherness within the dressing room, with a commitment from every player to the benefit of the team.

The extreme tests that we asked our players to do over that 10-day period brought out an inner determination to fulfil the tasks given them and, in my opinion, helped us through some tough times early on in our Premier League campaigns.

Watching the lads slowly bond together on the training pitch and at meal times was great to see and I found out a lot about all of them, good and bad.

Yes, I have to admit one or two players were short of the character we wanted and needed, but they didn't last long and left with no bad feelings on my side.

A bucket and spade were not required when Pulis went to Blackpool for pre-season training with Bristol Rovers

Today, whether it's pre-season or a winter break, most Premier League clubs who take their players away go first-class and enjoy great hotels, great facilities and wonderful food.

Wherever the team bus goes, it is followed by an even bigger bus with all the non-playing staff on it.

It is very different to my experiences in my early years as a player, when we would be taken to Blackpool for three days' pre-season training.

Again, the idea was to bring the lads closer together, but that happened in a different way than today's professionals are used to.

We stayed in a guest house with three-quarter beds that we all shared - that certainly brought us closer together! - then trained on the beach each morning, doing our running sessions on the sand.

Then we played seven-a-side games in the afternoon on a local park pitch, after clearing the dog muck off first.

In the evenings, we were allowed out for a few beers, with no time stipulated for our return - apart from having to be downstairs and ready to hit the beach again at 8am the next morning.

That is where things have changed most of all, right through football, during the past few years. In the 1970s and 80s, there was a massive drinking culture right through the leagues - just listen to the stories that came out of clubs as big as Liverpool, Manchester United or Arsenal, when they had teams who not only dominated English football but the European game too.

In my early years of management, the bonding I've been talking about used to happen right through the season through the lads meeting in pubs after games and after training on week days as well.

Winter breaks were rare and, rather than for a training camp, the only time most players I knew went to Spain was at the end of the season when more alcohol would be consumed.

That was what British players classed as bonding sessions and, as I've written about before, even the ones at the top level were much more connected to normal society, rather than living in an eternal bubble.

Now, while they are certainly more aware of the dangers of drinking to excess, as a manager you have to find other ways for them to connect when there are other distractions to contend with.

One item I am very glad my generation was not brought up with is mobile phones. I used to go mad if I walked into a dining room at the training ground or a hotel to see a group of lads looking at their phone and not engaging with each other.

I sometimes think that, as a young player, I had nothing compared to the players of today but, really, we had everything.

The stories, the friendships and the memories of the togetherness I remember from every dressing room during that time still resonate with me and recreating them was always my aim as a manager.

You're in the army now, Harry... Pulis is not the only manager to take his players to a military boot camp - Gareth Southgate did the same in 2017 when he took his England squad to a Commando Training Centre in Devon

Some other things have changed too - I am not sure De Zerbi has ever considered taking his team away to an army camp like I did on many occasions early in my managerial career, where we worked on the players in different ways.

One year, I took Stoke down to Exmouth, where the lads were put through their paces doing cross-country circuits.

That probably doesn't sound too bad on the face of it, but it was freezing cold and chucking it down and the circuits incorporated climbing and swimming under water in a darkened tunnel - I did all of it too by the way - while trying to keep up with the Army PT Instructor.

That was just the morning, the afternoon was spent indoors, where the boys were set different kinds of tasks, where their minds were tested with more practical team-building exercises where they had, say, 20 minutes to use some drums and planks to cross an area without touching the ground.

At night, they slept in bunk beds with only plastic sheeting over the mattress, and one very thin blanket.

Like my own trips to Blackpool as a player, it was spit and sawdust but everyone bought into it and attacked every challenge with great gusto and spirit.

As I moved onwards and upwards as a manager I was allowed to take teams abroad, to locations that were a little more lavish.

Goals in each half from Raul and Roberto Soldado left Stoke a mountain to climb when they faced Real Madrid in a pre-season friendly in Austria in 2007

Irdning in Austria is my favourite destination, and somewhere I have taken many clubs over the years.

It is a small town in the Alps that is ideal in every aspect of what I wanted as a manager, and not just because of the mountains I made my players run or cycle up!

We have almost always stayed in the same place there, too - a 1,000-year-old building I call 'The Castle'. It has swimming pools, a large gym, saunas, steam rooms, a spa and a golf course - you get the picture.

Real Madrid stayed there all the time too - it led to us playing them in a friendly in 2007 because we had already booked it and they said they would play us if we swapped hotel - yet my first time there could have turned out to be a disaster.

It was in 2004, during my first spell as Stoke manager, when I was having a tough time under the Icelandic ownership who were at the club at that time - I liked them as people but we all tended to largely disagree when it came to football.

My first-team then was made up of some really strong characters, but who were also great lads and old-school to the core, in the ways I've been talking about in this column.

During our first three days in Irdning, they had worked their socks off. The fourth day was meant to be the rest day where, fishing, golf or shopping was on the agenda but the players had other ideas.

Gerry Taggart, who was a fantastic lad, came and asked if the boys could borrow the team bus and go somewhere to have a few beers away from our hotel.

Now, being a manager and not in the dressing room as a player, my responsibilities had changed. The group had been brilliant in responding to all the hard work I had thrown at them, so I agreed - well, kind of!

Knowing what a 'fun-loving' group the lads were, and the fact they would be out of my sight, and control, the alarm bells were going off in my head, loud and clear.

So, without the lads' knowledge, I paid the bus driver a few quid to make sure he didn't find any really exciting places, and they ended up coming back to the hotel.

The players eventually worked out that I had instigated this under-cover plot but I know it didn't stop them having a great time because it was at our hotel, where I could keep an eye on them.

That's probably not something De Zerbi had to worry about last week!

Erling Haaland's goal started City's comeback against PSG but the French side won a thrilling game 4-2

I wanted to end this column by talking about a football match.

Manchester City's Champions League game against Paris St-Germain last week was an absolute throwback, which provided so many crosses, shots and goalmouth action.

PSG were fantastic in the first half but City really showed their teeth after the break and, in my humble opinion, were unlucky not to get anything out of the game.

Both teams played football through the pitch, got the ball to the most talented players - the forwards - as quickly as possible and produced unbelievable excitement.

There was no passing backwards or square, and hopefully any young coaches watching will have been influenced by both teams' urgency to play forward.

You cannot mention City at the moment without referencing what is going on with them off the pitch.

When news broke that they had been found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, I wrote tongue in cheek, asking City to send over the FA Cup and winners medals from 2011 to my old club Stoke.

Surprisingly, they have not arrived... but as the fall-out continues from the verdict of the independent commission, I'd like to add some further thoughts on the whole saga and ask some questions of my own.

Football has not been the winner and the whole game has been soured by this story, not just the Premier League.

But one thing I would like to ask people to explore is why, after the Premier League discovered that City first broke these rules, it has taken so long get to this point.

Why were the Premier League top-brass still standing on the podiums, presenting City with the many trophies they have won in this time? The situation now has cast a shadow over the entire game.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

#299. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

#300. Why Nottingham Forest are standing by Oliver Glasner despite Austrian sidelining influential players in his dressing room - and the numbers that back up George Syrianos

Published: 02:00 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 23 October 2026

It is awfully quiet at Nottingham Forest these days.

At any other time in the last four years, five points from seven games and 19th in the Premier League would have had alarm bells ringing at the City Ground and possibly cost the manager his job. By this time last year, Forest had already sacked Nuno Espirito Santo and Ange Postecoglou.

If things feel different now, that is probably because they are. Oliver Glasner was hired at huge expense to bring his trophy-winning magic to Forest and the Austrian is usually a slow starter.

Besides, despite only one win from his first eight games in all competitions, the underlying numbers say Forest have been unfortunate and are due a run of better luck.

None of that changes the importance of Friday’s trip to Ipswich.

Oliver Glasner has had a disappointing start at Nottingham Forest, with his side sitting 19th in the Premier League after one win in seven

Some doubt whether Glasner can harness a free attacking spirit like Morgan Gibbs-White in his rigid tactical framework

Forest’s chief football officer George Syrianos drove Glasner’s appointment and will likely stand or fall by how it proceeds.

In recent meetings with supporters’ groups, Syrianos emphasised that this was a long-term project. According to Forest's modelling, Glasner is the third-best coach in the Premier League at coaxing his squad to play above their potential. Success with him requires patience.

Good, rational explanations for a good, rational appointment. Yet few things are as difficult as sticking to principles when a team keeps losing.

Syrianos has had various roles at Forest but now arguably holds more power than ever before. He pushed Glasner to Evangelos Marinakis when Steve Cooper was sacked in December 2023, only for the Forest owner to choose Nuno Espirito Santo instead. Glasner would eventually land at Palace and we all know what happened next – three major honours following decade upon trophyless decade.

Forest have hired Glasner to win things. Delivering the FA Cup, Community Shield and Conference League at Palace was a stunning effort and at a club of similar dimension, the hierarchy believe he can do the same.

Forest are already out of the Carabao Cup so depending on their league position in January, we can expect them to attack the FA Cup.

Marinakis wants to be back in Europe as quickly as possible and given the strength of some of England’s wealthiest clubs, a good cup run might be more realistic than a top-six finish. Right now, just moving away from the relegation zone would be a relief.

Forest’s chief football officer George Syrianos drove Glasner’s appointment and will likely stand or fall by how it proceeds

No doubt about it – Glasner deserves time. Few Forest bosses since Brian Clough arrived with a better track record than Glasner’s. Despite never managing among Europe’s elite, he still has four trophies, including two European titles. To rip up those plans after a handful of league games would be impulsive even by Forest’s standards.

Miltiadis Marinakis, the son of Evangelos, is a regular visitor to the club’s training base and was there again this week. He will be aware of the statistics that indicate Forest deserve to be higher in the table than they are.

You can take your pick of the Opta data that suggests Forest are hard done by. According to the Expected Points table, Forest’s performances should have them in sixth. By the Expected Goals metric, Forest should have 11 goals rather than five. No other Premier League club is underperforming those standards so dramatically.

Forest’s defensive numbers are good, but they must sharpen their finishing. They have the fourth-worst big chance conversion rate and those five goals have come from 120 shots, with only Manchester United and Brighton taking more.

Two seasons ago, Forest finished seventh by outperforming their underlying numbers to an improbable degree. Maybe the current sequence is simply payback time from the football gods – not that this will be of any comfort to Glasner.

For much of Forest’s top-flight journey, Callum Hudson-Odoi and Ola Aina have been key figures. No longer.

While Aina’s exclusion is logical as Glasner wanted Daniel Munoz from Crystal Palace to play at right wing-back, the decision to sideline Hudson-Odoi is strange. Glasner seems similarly unconvinced by midfielder Ibrahim Sangare, who signed a new deal only three months ago.

With Morgan Gibbs-White injured, Glasner picked the energetic Nico Dominguez against Arsenal over the silkier Hudson-Odoi and even brought on forgotten man Arnaud Kalimuendo ahead of the former Chelsea winger in the second half.

If Glasner stays in charge, the days of both are likely to be numbered. No huge drama for the finances, either – Hudson-Odoi cost £3million in 2023 and Aina joined for free in the same summer. Both would bring Forest a profit if sold.

Yet in the short term, the pair need careful management. Along with Anthony Elanga, Aina and Hudson-Odoi embodied the unbreakable spirit that nearly carried Forest into the Champions League under Nuno in 2025. They remain strong voices in the squad – just like Gibbs-White.

Gibbs-White wanted to leave Forest for at least part of last summer and duly changed his agents. The 26-year-old is believed to be on the radar of Bayern Munich, should Michael Olise join Real Madrid at the end of the season. Few expect Gibbs-White to be at the City Ground by next September.

Between now and May, though, Glasner must extract the best from him.

(From left) Callum Hudson-Odoi, Anthony Elanga and Ola Aina embodied Forest's spirit under Nuno Espirito Santo. But Elanga has left and Hudson-Odoi and Aina are now sidelined

Glasner is convinced he can turn Liam Delap into an elite centre forward - but the £50million man has just one goal in six games

Some doubt whether Glasner can harness a free attacking spirit like Gibbs-White in such a rigid tactical framework. Glasner would counter that by pointing out that Olise and Eberechi Eze flourished under him in a similar system at Palace.

Ultimately, Glasner needs his big bet to pay off. He is convinced he can turn Liam Delap into an elite centre forward and was instrumental in the decision to sign the 23-year-old from Chelsea.

Delap did well against Arsenal but one goal in six is not what you hope for from your £50m No9.

Delap had his breakthrough season at Ipswich and he will hope that returning there will light the fire – and put a few out at the same time.

#302. 'Not in our DNA' - will 3v3 change the future of English football?

Shortly after England's disappointing defeat by Argentina at this summer's World Cup, boss Thomas Tuchel offered his view on why the Three Lions are struggling to win major tournaments.

"I think ball possession plays a crucial role," he said.

"It's maybe not in our DNA like it is in the Spanish DNA or Argentinian or Brazilian DNA to take the ball, control the game and the ball, which is also a big problem."

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), in scientific terms, usually refers to the master blueprint for life - the hereditary material in humans and almost all other organisms.

In football, the DNA of a team starts out at grassroots level, where young players are shaped and developed.

This season, the Football Association (FA) has implemented a change in youth football that could well result in a change of the DNA of the English game.

For a long time, it was considered normal for children of all ages to play 11 versus 11 matches on full-sized pitches, but in 1999 the FA introduced "mini-soccer" for under-10s.

The idea was that the small-sided variation of association football would provide youngsters with more opportunities to get a touch of the ball, and therefore be more involved than they were in large-sided games.

Up until the end of last season, the smallest variation of the game that served as an introduction to football for children under the age of seven was 5v5.

Last month, that was reduced further to 3v3.

This variation of the small-sided game does away with goalkeepers and there are also no referees - the idea is that fewer players in a "team" means those three will get more touches of the ball, and score more goals.

It is the result of two years of research by the FA in conjunction with Liverpool John Moores University, where over 400 games from under-6 to under-14 level were analysed.

"All of the research done demonstrates that those players having more touches of the ball are more engaged in the game," John Folwell, the FA's head of grassroots coach development, told BBC Sport.

"They are also making more decisions and are engaged in more physical activity, so that is the thinking behind it.

"There are no goalkeeper and no substitutes, so everyone is active in the game. They are not sitting on the side watching their mates play, or they are not standing in goal watching their friends play. They are actually involved in the game."

With the new format having only been introduced a few weeks ago, it will take some time before teams and coaches have been able to fully adapt.

The smaller-sized format can pose logistical issues, with more games and more coaches and volunteers needed to oversee them.

BBC Breakfast recently visited Collingham FC in Nottinghamshire to see how the coaches there were adapting to the new format.

"We have three pitches going on at once and all it needs is one parent to be at work and you are trying to keep an eye on three games and nine children at once," said Michael Bland, coach of Collingham FC's under-7s.

"It is the self-officiating, dangerous tackles flying in and trying to teach the kids what a safe tackle is."

Mick Goodwin has been a youth football coach since the 1990s, so has seen it evolve from 11-a-side games to the small-sided format it is now.

"My concern is you will get one dominant player in the 3v3 where the not-so-good players will not get a touch of the ball," he said.

"What we've seen is the dominant player has been shooting from the halfway line.

"We can absolutely see the concept, I just think it needs a bit of finessing and it will be fine."

The guidelines for football for children under seven is that the sport should not be about tactics or competitiveness, but about enjoyment - that is what the FA believes the new format will provide.

At Collingham FC, that was generally the consensus among those who played, and their parents.

"They are open goals and you can score more," said one child, while another added: "There's less players so it is easier to dribble around them."

One parent, Dean, said: "Before [my son] was just in goal but now he is learning to pass to other players, block stuff and be a better defender as well."

Another parent, Hannah, added: "My son has an older brother so he is used to playing in the more traditional format, so for him it has taken a bit of adapting."

One of the more criticised aspects of the new, smaller format is the lack of goalkeepers, with some concerns over how that might impact their development.

The 3v3 format only lasts for 12 months, so goalkeepers do return from under-8 level when the game progresses to 5v5.

"When you make decisions like this, there are obvious trade-offs but we don't believe it is going to be detrimental to the development of future goalkeepers," Folwell added.

"Obviously playing 3v3, players can't use their hands but they are still going to be developing skills of blocking, sliding across, needing to get between the ball and the goal.

"They will also improve their ability on the ball, which we know for goalkeepers now is an increasing technique they need to have.

"We don't believe that goalkeeping is an early specialisation position. There are lots of examples of players who have come through and ended up being goalkeepers at a later age - England goalkeeper Hannah Hampton, for example, first played outfield for a long time."

Whether the new format improves the development of English footballers will not be clear for a few years yet.

But England are far from alone in opting for 3v3 at under-7 level, with the format already part of the youth structure in Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and other countries.

Indeed, it is a format that is growing in popularity across the world.

"It is the first year of adoption and obviously these things can take time to implement and for people to accept change," Folwell said.

"What we have seen is that once people have experienced it they tend to be a convert and understand why we are doing it, because the children really love it."

#306. Do Manchester City have any grounds to win their appeal?

BBC Sport's Dale Johnson, Dan Roan, Laura Scott and Sami Mokbel assess Manchester City's position

Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, a leading lawyer has told BBC Sport.

City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating "sham contracts" to inflate sponsorship deals by Â£830m.

The club have said they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and they have "irrefutable evidence" the ruling "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

In their appeal, City will argue the payments were made by the United Arab Emirates government as a shareholder of the sponsors, while there are inconsistencies in the Commission's judgement.

Therefore, City say the sponsorship amounts were legitimate and not topped up by the owners.

James Severn, Member of the London Solicitor Litigation Association (LSLA) and Partner at Penningtons Manches Cooper, told BBC Sport the appeal is "not simply an opportunity to invite a new panel" to get the verdict overturned.

"City will need to identify a material error of law, principle or fact, or serious procedural unfairness, which materially affected the Commission's decision," Severn said.

"The Appeal Board nevertheless has broad powers to allow or dismiss the appeal, vary the decision or make any other order it considers appropriate."

Manchester City have been sponsored by Etihad since May 2009

Etihad Airways, one of City's principal sponsors at the centre of the case, had previously stated that the Abu Dhabi government had not paid for its sponsorship of Manchester City.

That came in court documents as part of a US investigation in New York in 2015.

City will argue this does not have the full context of the situation and is not proof they have been inconsistent with evidence.

The club are adamant government documents fully support their case - but, Severn said, if these were already available to the Commission they may not be much use in an appeal.

"The bank statements, government records and contemporaneous payment documents could be powerful evidence if they establish a clear audit trail showing the disputed funds came from the Abu Dhabi government rather than the owners," Severn added.

"However, if that evidence was already before the Commission, which nevertheless concluded that the arrangements were a sham, City will face an uphill struggle to demonstrate the finding was materially wrong."

Shortly before City's appeal was confirmed, Etihad Airways issued a statement saying it had never been "given the opportunity by the Premier League to be represented, to provide relevant information, or to ensure the accuracy and fairness of information relied upon".

Severn said Etihad Airways' complaint "does not, of itself, establish procedural unfairness".

"Etihad was not the respondent and is unlikely to have had an independent right to participate in the proceedings," Severn said. "It is likely to have been open to either party to obtain and present such evidence to the Commission.

"If the Appeal Board is prepared to consider new evidence from Etihad, it is likely to carry greater weight if supported by contemporaneous documents."

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?

Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester Cityâs inflatable banana craze

A key part of City's defence will be that the Independent Commission relied too heavily on the emails obtained through the Football Leaks files.

"If City can demonstrate the Commission fundamentally misunderstood the emails, failed to consider their proper context or reached conclusions inconsistent with other contemporaneous documents, that could amount to a material factual error," Severn added.

"City's difficulty is that the Commission heard extensive witness and documentary evidence but nevertheless made serious findings of sham arrangements and disguised owner funding."

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport the commission found "the documents were retrofitted to fit the crime".

"The Commission must have concluded that the evidence and the credibility of the witnesses put up by Manchester City were poor," Maguire said.

"However, from a legal point of view, this is an area they could attack if Manchester City's team can prove that the commission itself was a flawed construct in the sense that the members were Premier League picks rather than Manchester City's, and therefore the deck was stacked against the club to begin with.

Severn added that the retired senior judges and leading barristers, who sat on the Commission, have "spent their careers interpreting complicated facts, dealing with witnesses and applying relevant weight to evidence".

While adding that it would be "impossible to assess reliably" the chances of City winning their appeal, Severn added that "doing so will not be easy".

But Maguire believes that while it will be difficult for City to be successful, "there is a route".

City have brought in Mark Howard KC to advise the club in their appeal, while Etihad Airways has enlisted the services of respected law firm Quinn Emanuel.

Maguire said: "Given the lawyers that have been recruited by Manchester City, they may go down what's been described to me as a mess and noise approach.

"That means trying to discredit everything to do with the process of the Commission rather than necessarily the evidence that was presented.

"I've seen the documents that Abu Dhabi presented to the New York case. I'm not a lawyer, but from an accounting point of view, they can be seen in more than one way."

Even though Premier League regulations state an appeal must be heard within 12 weeks, or by Christmas Eve, Severn added that "given the scale and complexity of the proceedings, a final outcome may not be known for some time".

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two seasons ago, Liverpool won the Premier League title. They did so with the spine of a Jurgen Klopp-formulated side, and the Herculean efforts of a recently departed Mohamed Salah.

Flash forward to the present day, and Liverpool aren’t anywhere near the heights they reached in the 2024-25 term, despite parting with over £500 million to secure the services of an under-performing Florian Wirtz, an injured Hugo Ekitike, a recently returned Alexander Isak, and others additions.

Ahead of January, FourFourTwo have devised Liverpool’s dream transfer window, with signings made for the midfield and the Reds’ virtually empty right flank.

A bit of an obvious one, right? Liverpool are practically begging for additional cover in midfield. In Scott’s case, this transfer would, naturally, be anything but ‘cover.’

By signing the Bournemouth man, who was recently revealed to be up for sale come January, with Chelsea also lurking, Liverpool’s midfield would entirely transform.

In its current state, it is weak, ageing, injury-prone, and overly reliant on youngsters (looking at you, Trey Nyoni) that should be given greater time to develop, not carry the Reds’ burden.

Scott offers a bit of everything, not least his immense press resistance. There’s a reason he looked so special under a heavy-metal manager in Iraola when the pair combined at Bournemouth, and there’s nothing to suggest it couldn’t be replicated at Anfield.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The fee will be ludicrous, sure, but that’s life in the Premier League, and global, transfer market. Pay up, immediately, and keep Scott away from Stanford Bridge.

Liverpool’s right-back spot will never quite be the same. That’s the harsh reality, Trent Alexander-Arnold was a once-in-a-generation talent; now, he’s gone.

Luckily for Liverpool, that reality can be comforting, if they choose to accept it. Instead of scouring the transfer market far and wide looking for a like-for-like replacement for the Scouser, they should consider adding greater depth to the right-back position.

Jeremie Frimpong is a ludicrously poor option for any Premier League title-contending unit to carry with them at right-back, and that’s where Liverpool want to be. Conor Bradley’s injury woes are a concern; at his best, he was magnificent, but even his consistency, albeit superior to that of Frimpong, was lacking in comparison to the Reds’ ambition.

Bring in Givairo Read. He’s been linked prior, possesses clear defensive talent, can road forward when required, will be available for a reasonable price, and he’ll be the third in an ever-rotating right-back line-up that can receive rest, and grow hungry.

Plus, he has five assists in nine games for Feyenoord this season. That’s nothing to scoff at. Let this trio battle it out to claim the right-back spot, and one might just end up pushing themselves to limits that prove worthy of Liverpool’s standards.

Even more so than Alexander-Arnold, now that Salah has left the club, Liverpool’s right wing will never be the same. Not even close. Again, that’s fine; accept the truth of the situation and move accordingly. The Reds’ only option is to replace the Egyptian ‘in the aggregate,’ and even that’ll be a tough feat.

It’s clear that Liverpool need to bring in a quick, tricky forward that can bag them around 8-10 Premier League goals each season, to add to the 25-40 strikes brought by the likes of Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo.

What Sarr offers is Premier League-proven quality and a clear desire to play at Anfield. He was linked to the Reds in the summer, and they’ll no doubt be keeping tabs on the Senegalese star ahead of January.

His fee will be too high for what he’s worth, but the market is sorely lacking. Liverpool need a natural right wing option, and to let Rio Ngumoha develop in his ideal position, so Sarr is the clear choice. A strong, quick finisher - he’ll surely get at least 20% of the goal contributions for Liverpool that Salah used to bag from the right.

He’s a stronger option than Yankuba Minteh at a comparable price, and, as shown at the World Cup this summer, various Africa Cup of Nations tournaments, and in his exploits versus Liverpool, undoubtedly a better man for the big occasion.

#308. Dwight Yorke: ‘I’m not a kid trying to get into management – I’m a manager’

Ghana may soon come calling for Trinidad and Tobago’s former captain and manager, who is proud of his CV since his days as a Premier League striker

Dwight Yorke wants you to stop calling him a former player. “I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time,” he says from his home in Dubai. “I’ve done that and I want that message to come across clearly.”

The message has a deadline. Carlos Queiroz left his job as Ghana head coach on 1 October and the Ghana Football Association is searching for his successor. Yorke is among the names under consideration, along with Pape Thiaw, Aliou Cissé and Walid Regragui, the former Morocco head coach, according to Ghanaian media.

He is tired of the shorthand way he is described during these high‑profile job hunts. People focus on his playing accolades, including calling him the treble winner, a label he says belongs to one season in a run of three Premier League titles at Manchester United from 1999-2001. “I’m a manager,” he says.

Over the past four years, Yorke has quietly built a coaching résumé far removed from Old Trafford. His first taste of management came in May 2022, taking charge of Australia’s A-League All Stars against Barcelona in front of more than 70,000 people in Sydney. They lost 3-2. “I realised then that I enjoyed it,” he says.

Macarthur, based in Sydney, followed that July. “We went to a relatively unknown team in the A‑League and managed to win the cup.” The Australia Cup success, three months into his spell, was the club’s first trophy.

It did not last. Macarthur sacked him in January 2023, with the club sixth, after a post-match address when he reportedly called the club a “pub team” run by “muppets”.

A Fifa chamber found Macarthur had dismissed him without just cause. The court of arbitration for sport upheld that in 2024 and ordered the club to pay AU$212,500 (£111,300 at current exchange rates).

“I wish I’d had the opportunity to finish what I started,” Yorke says. The job taught him communication and the importance of being transparent. “There was a disagreement. It was resolved amicably and I’ve moved on.”

Between Macarthur and his next role, he kept his hand in. He worked as a pundit for beIN Sports and on the Saudi Pro League and travelled the world watching coaches at work.

In November 2024, Trinidad and Tobago came calling. The Soca Warriors finished third in their World Cup qualifying group behind Curaçao and Jamaica, missing out on the finals tournament, and Yorke’s tenure ended soon after. The Trinidad and Tobago Football Association said talks over revised terms had not produced an agreement and the contract was ended by mutual consent, announced in March. “The decision to end things was out of my control,” Yorke says.

He does not accept that missing the World Cup defines his time in charge. “People can be blind to success because they focus on whether you qualified.”

He lost once in six qualifiers, 2-0 in Jamaica in September 2025. He had been handed a brief: make people care about Trinidad and Tobago again, boost recruitment and qualify. “I was given three tasks and completed two,” he says.

With Yorke as the head coach, crowds came back and a number of US-born players with Trinidadian and Tobagonian heritage, such as the CF Montréal winger Dante Sealy and Real Salt Lake’s Kobi Henry, opted in and made their debuts. Yorke gave a new generation a fighting chance to emulate the team he captained to the finals in 2006. “I left Trinidadian football in a far better place than I found it,” he says.

The TTFA president at the time described Yorke’s mandate as qualification alone. The team were ranked 102nd by Fifa when Yorke was hired, behind Curaçao (91st) and Jamaica (62nd). “I miss management,” Yorke says. “I miss what we were creating.”

The players are understood to want him back because his successor, Derek King, is struggling with two draws and eight defeats from his 10 games. Ghana, though, is the live opportunity. “It’s a job I’d be interested in, given Ghana’s history and the players available.”

The Ghanaian FA has not confirmed any approach. The team are bottom of their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying group with no points, after a 2-0 defeat in Côte d’Ivoire and a 4-2 home loss against the Gambia in which they led by two goals. It is a sharp decline for a side that reached the last 32 of the World Cup this summer, losing 1-0 against Colombia.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“You look at the squad and your eyes open even wider,” Yorke says. He says an agent called to tell him Ghana were interested. “The conversation started there and then reached the media before I really knew it.”

From the outside, he says, Ghana “sometimes looks disjointed”. The GFA has said its women’s head coach, Kim Björkegren, will take temporary charge of the men’s qualifying double-header against Somalia next month. In Yorke’s view, outside noise unbalances things, from the administration to the players. So how would he fix it? Organisation, transparency and everyone speaking the same language. “The talent is there. Build the culture and get the players to buy in and the football will follow.”

He has considered the effect that diaspora players could have in the role, pointing to Ghana’s Antoine Semenyo and Brandon Thomas-Asante as proof that countries can benefit immensely from UK-born talent. It reflects a broader trend: at the World Cup, 23.6% of the 1,248 squad players represented countries outside their place of birth. For Yorke, the approach is simple: identify the players, establish their heritage and quality and sell them a vision. “I’d make sure that what I say is what I do.”

Older managers might have screamed and shouted to get messages across, but he says: “I’m not sure that approach can last in the current environment.” He would not berate a player in public. “That can be done behind closed doors, while still being assertive.” Respect and punctuality are non‑negotiable. He has sat in dressing rooms with big egos and says nobody gets special treatment. “Everyone starts equally.”

He borrows, but he does not copy. Sir Alex Ferguson, who managed him at United, is the shadow over any such comparison. Among contemporary managers, Pep Guardiola offered him the best advice. “He said, in effect, that I can’t be him or any other manager. I have to be myself.”

Other labels have stuck anyway. “People still call me a ‘party boy’. That stigma has been overused and has followed me since I retired from football. I’m not saying I didn’t enjoy myself as a player.” But he says: “You never hear that I didn’t turn up for training or wasn’t fit.”

In Dubai, he tends to fast for nearly 20 hours a day and eats one meal. “I’m a fitness fanatic who trains every day.”

Ask Yorke how he wants to be remembered as a coach and he sits up and answers with a list. Committed. Transparent with players. Decisions made for the team, never for an individual. “I’m straightforward. I don’t mess around, take shortcuts or do the job halfway.”

Yorke has the interest and, by his own account, the answers. “If anyone doubts me, I can prove them wrong.”

#311. The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager

Fabian Hurzeler has gone from managing in Germany's fifth tier to being one of Europe's most feted young managers

When Brighton lost at home to Crystal Palace in February, Fabian Hurzeler was booed by his own supporters and subjected to chants of "you're getting sacked in the morning".

"There are only two options," said the German after the 1-0 defeat by their fierce rivals left his team floundering 14th in the table with one win in 12 Premier League matches.

"Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."

Eight months on, Brighton are reaping the benefits of keeping faith with the man who became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in June 2024 at the age of 31.

Palace return to Amex Stadium on Sunday (14:00 BST kick-off) to face opponents who are third in the table after statement wins over defending champions Arsenal and Europa League winners Aston Villa.

Hurzeler's stock has rocketed after 11 wins in 18 top-flight games, a run that has propelled the Seagulls back into Europe and left fans - who shouted "you don't know what you're doing" at him just a few months ago - worried that he could be lured away.

Following last Saturday's win at Sunderland, there was chat on the post-match phone-ins that Hurzeler, rewarded with a new long-term contract before the end of last season and given Â£150m to spend on signings in the summer, could be a prime target for a big club looking for a manager.

"You learn more about yourself and the people around you when you are losing games," former Brighton striker Glenn Murray told BBC Sport in reference to last season's poor run.

"Hurzeler has come out the other side and the way he has got this group of players performing is exceptional."

Scott McCarthy, from the We Are Brighton fan site, said Hurzeler appeared to have lost the crowd to such a degree at one stage last season than even a few wins would not be enough to turn it around.

"He looked like a manager who was out of ideas," McCarthy told BBC Sport.

"Leaving the stadium after losing at home to Palace, the only conversation fans were having was: 'he has got to go'.

"It's totally different now. It's worked out phenomenally."

Will Brighton manage to keep hold of Hurzeler, who has gone from managing in Germany's fifth tier to reported interest, external from Manchester United?

Hurzeler signs to 2029 as Brighton rival elite clubs

Hurzeler's Brighton choice and Barber's favourite moment - fans' forum

Hurzeler (left) has been linked with Manchester United should they decide to replace Michael Carrick (right)

The determination Hurzeler demonstrated in the face of anger from fans following last season's defeat by Palace has been evident throughout his 10-year coaching career.

In 2016, after one injury too many following spells in the reserves at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich, the former midfielder gave up playing professionally to accept a player-manager role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23.

It was the start of a coaching journey that has led to the Premier League.

To make ends meet at village club Pipinsried, which is about 30 miles from Munich, football-obsessed Hurzeler worked for an art dealer selling paintings to wealthy Bavarians.

In an interview with the Guardian, external in 2024, he revealed he was fired from that job because he was spending too much time watching games.

"If you want to sell something to a person, you have to try to convince them by doing something," he said when comparing selling pictures to managing Premier League players.

"And you can't go there and say: 'Look at this picture, it's an amazing picture'. You have to understand the needs and the wishes from the clients.

"That's a little bit similar to being a coach.

"The most important thing is to understand the person behind the player. What are his needs? What are his values? How is he educated? How was his past? Where does he get education?"

Hurzeler's obsession to succeed runs deep.

While managing St Pauli - who he left in 2024 to join Brighton after guiding the Hamburg club back to the Bundesliga following a 13-year absence, external - he was invited to Tottenham's training ground to watch Ange Postecoglou's side train.

Hurzeler - who was born in Houston, Texas, before moving to Germany at the age of two - asked so many questions that Postecoglou had to ask another member of his coaching staff to step in and take over.

Hurzeler is covered in beer by his players after St Pauli's promotion to the Bundesliga in 2024

He also picked up tips from Roberto de Zerbi at Brighton, a few months before replacing him after Kieran McKenna,, external who had been heavily linked with the job, opted to stay at newly promoted Ipswich.

Despite respectable back-to-back eighth-placed finishes, Hurzeler's time at Brighton has not been without its difficult moments.

In addition to fans calling for his dismissal last season, the Seagulls were thrashed 7-0 at Nottingham Forest in his first season in charge, while former Arsenal and England defender Martin Keown labelled Hurzeler "wet behind the ears", external on the BBC's Final Score following Brighton's 4-2 defeat at Chelsea in September 2024.

So what is the reason for the shift in fortunes since his own fans called for his dismissal?

"It's partly because Hurzeler went back to basics," adds McCarthy.

"He relied on an experienced core in the side to get out of the hole, which is testament to him because it shows his pragmatic side. You get managers who are wedded to their philosophy and won't change.

"Hurzeler realised what he was doing was not working and that it could cost him his job, so tried something else. You can now see this is a team more in his image, because they press insanely."

Will Hurzeler leave Brighton if another club comes for him, or stay and attempt to write his name in club folklore by qualifying for the Champions League?

"I personally don't think he will go," says McCarthy.

"The money would obviously be tempting but he is a very intelligent guy. He didn't become a Premier League manager at the age of 31 without having his head screwed on.

"Does he want to go to another club where he isn't going to get time? What has happened at Brighton has shown he needs two-and-a-half-years to build a squad."

Back in Pipinsried, Hurzeler's name is still revered - and he has not forgotten where his coaching journey began.

"Yes, he does enjoy coming back every now and then - to see if everything's in order," Sepp Ankner, their chief finance officer, told The Athletic, external in 2024.

"When he does, he talks to everybody. He's really retained that connection with Pipinsried."

But his rapid ascent means gilded surroundings might not be far away for Europe's hottest managerial property.

#312. Meghan's candles, notebook and $535 hamper: Duchess of Sussex releases second holiday drop of As Ever products - including homeware

By JESSICA GREEN, ASSISTANT LIFESTYLE EDITOR and MAANYA SACHDEVA, ASSOCIATE LIFESTYLE EDITOR and CAITLIN LENG

Published: 21:44 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 03:28 BST, 23 October 2026

Meghan Markle's lifestyle brand has expanded into homeware after months of speculation as she unveiled a new teapot and table mats as part of As Ever's second Christmas collection today.

The Duchess of Sussex, 45, launched her brand's $148 advent calendar earlier this month in her first commercial venture since moving back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

She appears to be rapidly expanding As Ever's offerings; before her new line of home accessories, she debuted three new hampers - including a £180 ($242) Parlour Basket - and playing cards.

Now, the former actress has shared further products she hopes will be a hit with customers this holiday season, such as a new 'tabletop collection' with crockery and napkins, a two-wick candle and reed diffuser.

'Chapter Two' of Meghan's holiday collection includes 'sweet treats', fragrances, the 'Trellis tabletop collection' and 'thoughtful gifts for everyone on your list,' she announced in a post on As Ever's official Instagram account.

The products are currently only available to buy in the US, but there has been speculation that Meghan could eventually bring her £11 tins of tea and £50 scented candles to the UK in recent weeks.

Meghan Markle launched her lifestyle brand As Ever's second Christmas collection on Thursday

'Chapter Two' of Meghan's holiday collection was announced in a post on As Ever's official Instagram account and includes 'sweet treats', fragrances, the 'Trellis tabletop collection' and 'thoughtful gifts for everyone on your list'

In a promotional video on As Ever's Instagram page for the new collection, the former actress can be seen laying a festive-themed table

The 2026 'Holiday Advent Calendar' priced at a hefty $148 - described on As Ever's website as a 'magical celebration of the season'

She shared that her 'secret to hosting with ease' is 'preparation' and told readers to 'take care of the little details before the doorbell rings'.

New launches include a $130 'heirloom handwoven rattan charger set' and a blue-and-white porcelain teapot, priced at $98 - or around £73.

Shoppers can get their hands on the collection's new $98 'Penny for Your Thoughts' leather notebook - branded on the As Ever website as a 'simple luxury for everyday use and enjoyment.'

A 'Signature Two-Wick Holiday Candle' - priced at a whopping $98 - is also on offer as part of the new launch. Described as a 'limited-edition scent of the holiday,' the two wick candle features nodes of pine, berry, cashmere and clove - and is recommended by the As Ever website to be purchased with Meghan's costly $410 'Candle Lover's' basket.

One of the priciest gifts on the site is the $535 'Library Basket' hamper. Coming in at just under £400, the hamper comes with a signature leatherbound notebook, coasters, card set, candle - and matchbox.

Customers can also indulge in a $75 'Trophy Chocolate Bar Gift Set' featuring five 'beloved' bars of the confectionary. The chocolates - described as 'limited edition' -  are created in collaboration with Los Angeles-based Compartés, the chocolatiers behind Meghan's pricey advent calendar.

The new collection features a $98 'Penny for Your Thoughts' leather notebook, which has been branded as a 'simple luxury for everyday use and enjoyment'

As Ever's 'Signature Two-Wick Holiday Candle' is priced at a whopping $98, or approximately £73

One of Meghan's priciest gifts on is the $535 'Library Basket' hamper, complete with her signature leatherbound notebook, coasters, card set, candle - and a matchbox

Also on offer is Meghan's 'curated' popcorn medley, marketed at the high price of $65. The popcorns, listed as a 'luxury taste of nostalgia' on the As Ever page, come in milk chocolate, white chocolate and salted popcorn flavours - and are topped with Meghan's signature 'flower sprinkles.'

The Duchess' Christmas range hasn't been without its controversy, after a British priest faced backlash online from 'Sussex Squad' supporters when publicising a £6 charity advent calendar in contrast to the one promoted by Prince Harry's wife.

Meghan unveiled the £112 ($148) gourmet chocolate calendar in an online advert earlier this month while wearing a reported £75,000 worth of clothing and jewellery.

Anglican priest and London university chaplain the Reverend Daniel French suggested that people could instead buy the charity advent calendar that is almost 20 times cheaper and contains Fairtrade chocolate.

The alternative he recommended also raises money for a leprosy charity and comes with a 'little booklet on the meaning of Christmas', he told his followers.

Sharing an image of Meghan alongside her As Ever product, Rev French wrote: 'For £5.99 you can pre-order a Christian Advent Calendar with Fairtrade chocolate from the Meaningful Chocolate Company. A donation is made to The Leprosy Mission.'

The calendar also comes with a 24-page Christmas story and activity booklet celebrating the birth of Christ.

But Rev French's post sparked a backlash from members of the Sussex Squad, who branded him 'satan spawn' and 'evil', while claiming he had an 'ugly heart for a so-called Christian'.

His Protestant colleague Father Chris Phillips – whose parish is in Benhilton, south-west London – backed the priest on X, prompting a fresh wave of angry responses, to which he replied that he had 'encountered the Sussex Squad on here', adding: 'Wow.'

His defenders have said he has been 'terrorised' by 'deranged trolls' ever since, forcing him to lockdown his account. Trolls claimed he was a 'coward' for doing so.

Meghan's chocolate advent calendar is her first major As Ever product since she moved back to the UK

It was this X post from Rev Daniel French about a Christian alternative to Meghan's calendar that sparked a row

After 24 hours of online abuse, including threats and defamatory suggestions about his character, he was forced to lock his account and blocked a number of pro-Meghan supporters.

Meghan unveiled As Ever's first advent calendar in collaboration with LA-based gourmet chocolate company Compartes earlier this month.

The £112 box of chocolate treats is her first major product since she, Harry and their two children moved back to the UK.

The calendar – 'inspired by her Montecito home and garden' – features a festive illustration of the £11million mansion she and Prince Harry called home for six years.

A press release declared that 'every detail was considered with care, including countdown numbers hand-painted in Meghan's own penmanship using edible gold lustre'.

The 'limited-edition' product includes 24 handcrafted chocolates and flavours include strawberry, raspberry, blackberry and orange marmalade, plus what is described as a 'special chocolate finished with Meghan's own flower sprinkles'.

Compartés' dark chocolate ganache truffle also features in the calendar, with Meghan's writing said to turn 'each day's reveal into a small, personal moment'.

The product is available to order in the US on As Ever's website, with delivery from early November.

Meghan's business described this as the 'latest chapter in an ongoing collaboration between the two brands', after the $12 (£9) As Ever x Compartés chocolate bars.

As Ever explained that the box's design was 'inspired by Meghan's Montecito home and garden', and she worked on it with Compartés creative director Jonathan Grahm.

The product is 'made to be enjoyed through December and treasured long after' and 'brings together the artistry of Compartés and the warmth that defines As Ever'.

Compartés said it was also selling three other cheaper but 'ultra-giftable advent calendars' at $120 (£91) each, including 'Enchanted Castle', 'The Nutcracker' and 'Winter Forest'.

Meghan has also entered the Christmas hamper market for the first time, launching a new 'hostess basket' with her As Ever brand alongside her advent calendar.

The Duchess' $211 'Holiday Collection' basket has a leather As Ever tag with gold lettering and comes pre-filled with peppermint and lemon-and-ginger tea caddies, a trio of spreads, flower sprinkles and Meghan's scented candles.

Other products in Meghan's 'Holiday Collection' include 'botanical confection' chocolates developed by Los Angeles brand Compartes as part of an 'ongoing collaboration' and two decks of 'parlour cards'.
