#313. James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’

The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career

“The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.”

McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.”

But there’s sadness, too, in the way his life and career were scarred by his refusal to wear the poppy when playing games around Remembrance Sunday in England. “It’s completely changed me as a person,” McClean says. “It’s made me a bit of a recluse because I don’t trust a lot of people now. I’ve been stung bad.”

McClean’s autobiography, The Walls, is one of the best sports books of the year. It’s a powerful and sometimes disturbing read elevated by McClean’s willingness to show himself in an unflattering light.

I have written a lot about Derry and boxing, and Bloody Sunday, but it helps to be back here to understand how McClean can respect the millions of soldiers who died in two world wars while refusing to forget how the British army killed so many Irish people in this city.

He comes from Creggan, the estate affected most on Bloody Sunday in 1972 when 14 unarmed civilians were killed by the British army in Derry. Six of the fatalities were from Creggan. In 2010, after the Saville report finally concluded that all the victims posed no threat, the British prime minister David Cameron apologised for the “unjustified and unjustifiable” massacre.

McClean was born in Derry in 1989 and he writes that “learning how to make a petrol bomb was one of my first life lessons. I was 11 before I’d properly mastered it.”

He pauses when asked how he would feel if any of his three daughters or his son, who is 11, ended up making petrol bombs. “I’m very thankful they don’t have to. It’s a different era now. I just want them to be proud to be Irish.”

The 37-year-old spells out the contrast with his youth. “I grew up in a very Republican community still dealing with the effects of the Troubles. You would see gunmen on the street. People got shot, kneecapped. To get access to my street you had to go through a lane where you sometimes saw masked men doing punishment beatings. But you weren’t scared. You knew you’d done nothing wrong. That was the norm … but it’s not normal.”

His biological father, Joe Kelly, was an alcoholic in Creggan and McClean spoke to him only once – when he shouted at him in the street to stay away. But he remembers a happy childhood and, when his professional career began with Derry City, “I was very carefree”.

McClean was 22 when Steve Bruce signed him for Sunderland in August 2011. He made his Premier League debut that December after Bruce was replaced by Martin O’Neill. McClean soon became a regular starter and that first season in English football was full of joy and praise. He was fast, skilful and disciplined. Apart from wasting money his biggest vice was typing his name on Twitter where he would revel in glowing reports of his play.

“It was amazing,” McClean says. “I never thought about the politics when I first got to England so up until November 2012, when the poppy thing started, I never experienced any bother.”

Everything changed when he told Sunderland he wouldn’t wear the poppy because it also represented the British army which had occupied Derry for so long. “There was never a decision for me to make,” he says. “Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen. It was a very difficult year and I felt a lot of that could have been handled better by the club. But Sunderland came out with a statement before the game which drew all eyes on me. It was there to protect the club. They basically said this is James’s personal decision but we, as a club, wholeheartedly support the poppy appeal.

“I wanted to make my own statement but I was constantly told by the club that: ‘No, no, it’ll die over. Just leave it.’ I’d just turned 23 and I thought the club had a duty of care to look after me and that’s what they were doing. I’d won the player of the year the previous season but I felt they hung me out to dry.”

McClean recalls that: “The next game was away to Fulham on a Sunday, on Sky. A threat was made that I would be shot if I came on to the pitch. I remember [his wife] Erin panicking. It sounds extreme and people might say: ‘Oh, wise up, you’re not going to be shot on TV.’ But the night before the game I was assigned two police officers to stand outside my door. So the Met police took it seriously and that made it more real.”

O’Neill brought him on in the second half and his every touch was booed – by the Fulham and Sunderland supporters. The vitriol poisoned his world but McClean kept searching for his name on Twitter. He became furious whenever, after a mutually respectful encounter with a member of the public, the person would go online to abuse him.

Sometimes McClean would track the person down and demand an apology. “Maybe that madness was always there, but it got stronger,” he notes.

McClean moved to Wigan before joining West Brom where, in “the best kind of madness” he earned £42,000 a week while he had his best spell in the Premier League. But as one poppy season blurred into another, the death threats kept coming, as did the warnings that Erin would be raped. McClean says: “My reaction was always to fight fire with fire. I went into some games in the wrong frame of mind. It wasn’t: ‘Can I help the team?’ It was: ‘I hope I score today so I can shush them up.’”

McClean admits: “There were days where I went looking for the conflict.” He posted a photograph of himself listening to his favourite Wolfe Tones song, The Broad Black Brimmer. “I knew exactly what I was doing,” McClean writes. “It was an IRA song – and I was sure it would rile a certain type of person up.”

By the time he reached Stoke, for whom he played 111 games between 2018 and 2021, his problems in English football reached a new low. “Brexit made the idiots louder” and “the poppy season seemed to be getting longer every year”. He had also made a stupid mistake during lockdown when he posted a photograph of himself, wearing a balaclava, with his two eldest children below a caption which read: ‘Today’s school lesson – History.’”

McClean thought he was being funny but his choice not to wear the poppy, in contrast, was heartfelt. “I thought others might have followed suit but it never turned out to be the case.”

Did he feel that a more rounded understating of his stance had emerged by the time he enjoyed his happiest seasons in English football, while playing for a Hollywood-tinged Wrexham from 2023 to earlier this year? “A wee bit, aye. When you explain it to footballers you’ve played with, and to people on a personal level, it opens their eyes and they say: ‘Oh, I understand that.’ But the overall British population? I don’t think so.”

Reflecting on his Premier League years, McClean marvels at the brilliance of Kevin De Bruyne and Eden Hazard. “You had to accept there were lads capable of doing things that were beyond you,” McClean writes. “But there were also games where I thought I was coming up against a physical strength that I found suspicious. Coming back into the Premier League after a break convinced me that some players had to be benefiting from some kind of performance-enhancing support.

“I remember coming up against one player that I’d encountered at Sunderland who I always felt that I’d been able to match in terms of his speed and power. While I’d been away from the Premier League, he’d gone to a bigger club, and now he was a different animal completely.”

These are startling allegations and, while McClean has no concrete evidence to support his doubts, he trusts his gut reaction. “I’ve always been very fanatical about my fitness,” he says. “But when you come against the top Premier League clubs, no matter what height, what size, they’re just faster, they’re stronger, and you’re thinking: ‘How is that possible?’”

After their daughter Willow was diagnosed with global development delay and autism, Erin persuaded him to be tested for autism. He was found to be “at the high-functioning end of the spectrum” but he still struggles with the fact that “I’ve probably got body dysmorphia or some kind of bulimia. Maybe it’s the autism thing, because I’m so strict with my diet 95% of the time. But when I can’t work out I binge. So if I’m travelling and flying, I’ll just eat that much shite to the point where I have to make myself sick. I still feel really guilty, because the next day I’ll punish myself in the gym – which is not healthy.”

Life has become even more complicated since he returned to Derry City in January. “I was meant to be coming home for the fairytale ending. But you quickly realise the promises are just bullshit.”

McClean has not played for the club since July and, asked about the situation, he says: “It’s not good. It’s a player against owner and there’s only one winner. I think that’s it in terms of Derry City. You never think you’ll be betrayed by your own so it’s painful.”

When contacted by the Guardian, a spokesman for Derry City said: “The club cannot speak to, or comment on, how James feels.” He also rejected the suggestion that Derry City had failed to fulfil any promises made to McClean.

Earlier this month, McClean said he couldn’t “understand or accept” the way he was being treated by the club and that he was fit to play despite being left out of the squad by interim manager Mark Connolly. Derry City then released a statement in which they said: “The club has sought to resolve this internal matter privately. Out of respect for confidentiality and the fact that this dispute involves sensitive medical details regarding James’ hip condition, the club have previously refrained from making any public statement on the matter.”

McClean insists he could play football elsewhere but how does he feel if this is the end of his career? “It doesn’t unsettle me because I’ve been boxing off and on for 10 years and in the past 18 months I’ve really thrown myself into it. I’m not going to start a pro boxing career because it’s just not feasible at my age. But I’ve been in contact with Misfits and they want me to fight.”

Misfits Boxing was set up by KSI and the Sauerland brothers, who made their name in the traditional fight game, and it features YouTubers and former athletes who want to become boxers. It is dismissed by boxing purists but McClean sounds enthusiastic about making his debut in the ring once his contract with Derry expires: “Boxing is giving me that purpose to wake up and train hard.”

What kind of boxer would he like to become? “I’m a pressure fighter. I like to be constantly in someone’s face because I’ve got the fitness to maintain that. I’m not saying I’m by any stretch of the imagination a [Gennady] Golovkin or a Canelo [Álvarez], but I love watching them. I’m not looking to have a career in boxing but three or four fights a year is perfect. The dream was always to be a footballer but this is a new excitement, a new challenge.”

As we prepare to step out into a rain-sodden Derry, there seems little chance of any reconciliation for him on the football field. But he looks up and his taut fighter’s face suddenly relaxes into a smile. “It could be a blessing,” McClean says softly. “It could end up a blessing in disguise.”

The Walls by James McClean (Sandycove, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

#320. Wigan pine for FA Cup glory as not even victory can lift them off foot of League One

Gary Caldwell, club captain in 2013 and now manager, needs much more than the weekend win against Reading to disperse the clouds

If the 2013 FA Cup final represented a blip for the Sheikh Mansour-era Manchester City in their quest for total domination of English football, it was a historic moment for their conquerors, Wigan Athletic.

Memories of that famous day at Wembley still endure for Latics supporters despite the relegation from the Premier League that followed. Yet watching the modern‑day Wigan, who remain bottom of League One despite a 1-0 win against Reading on Saturday, makes the toppling of City in a Cup final seem an epoch ago.

The club, perhaps understandably, continue to hark back to their halcyon days. Last season they brought back Gary Caldwell – club captain in 2013 – for his second stint as manager, having led the club to promotion from this division in 2015-16. Choosing to swap Exeter for a return to the Latics was seen as a risky move by Caldwell, considering the shoestring budget imposed upon him by Mike Danson, the owner who is keen to sell.

Finances are ultra-tight at the Greater Manchester club amid dwindling crowds and losses on the pitch and on the balance sheet. The local businessman Danson and his family saved Wigan from liquidation in June 2023 after mismanagement from previous owners brought a points deduction and relegation from the Championship. Three successive mid-table finishes in League One under their stewardship have brought a semblance of stability, but this season they have plummeted.

The problem is the Dansons have been unable to find an ambitious buyer to take the club to the next level. Now the prospect of a first season in the fourth tier since 1996‑97 is a distinct possibility, although victory against Reading – the Latics’ second league win of the campaign, sealed by Scott Hogan’s 71st-minute strike – made the picture a little rosier.

“Some of our play was tremendous,” Caldwell said. “Our spirit, our character, our determination not to let the ball go in the net was fantastic. It was pretty stressful towards the end. We need to try and build on this. You have to keep the players believing and committing. There’s still so many aspects of our game that need to be better, but a result makes you feel better about yourself psychologically.”

The presence of Leam Richardson in the opposition dugout at the Brick Community Stadium gave fans more reason to reminisce about better days. Richardson, who claimed the League One title as Wigan manager in April 2022, was sacked in November of the same year just 16 days after signing a three-year contract.

Caldwell has also found himself under pressure. The former centre‑back has been criticised by fans for his team’s uninspiring style of play, which has produced just six goals in nine games, the fewest in League One. They went 447 minutes without a league goal until Hogan, the veteran forward, converted after Christian Saydee’s cross was parried out by the Reading goalkeeper, Joel Pereira.

And while Wigan’s keeper, Joe Whitworth, was regularly called into action to see out the win, the home team were still good value for three points, allowing Caldwell and his squad to breathe. The manager’s backers will rightly point to the lack of spending by the club in the summer, with the £1.5m generated by the sale of Sam Tickle to Bristol City not yet reinvested on players and an overreliance on young loanees to prop up the squad.

Danson and the club’s hierarchy have issued rallying cries to supporters to return to the stadium in an effort to generate more revenue, thus making the club more appealing to new owners, but why should fans part with hard‑earned cash to watch such insipid football?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Before the game, Caldwell said: “We also recognise the need for points is big, for our supporters to have that feelgood factor, and be able to leave the stadium in a much better frame of mind than they have been.”

The Scot got what he needed against Reading, yet the sense of chaos above Caldwell was evidenced by the abrupt departure of Sarah Guilfoyle from her role as managing director on the eve of the new season, after a 10-year stay at the club. And there are plenty who feel the owners ought to bear the brunt of criticism.

The Wigan Athletic Supporters Action Group is demanding answers from Danson on why selling the club has been such a struggle and the lack of investment. Other fans are more resigned to the idea that some short-term pain may be necessary for long-term gain; most agree a sale would be transformative.

For now, despite a rare victory against a hitherto in-form Reading, the short-term struggles look likely to continue. The hope is that a hero of 2013 can perform miracles on the pitch, despite the constraints off it.

#323. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#324. Savaged by Simon Jordan – and thanks to the algorithm I want to be savaged again | Barney Ronay

The former Palace chair seeming very angry indeed about others’ opinions is just par for the course as football’s age of rage ramps up another level

Yet again the mainstream wokealorium is preachifying from its pulpitrex. It’s egregious. It’s sanctiforial. It’s a wangitude of complete retardifaction.

This has not been an easy column to write. It has been difficult, gruelling in parts, but also warm, exhilarating and at times deeply erotic. Yes. I was SAVAGED by Simon Jordan. And I’ve never felt so alive.

You know who Simon Jordan is. Used to own Crystal Palace. Now a very good and listenable pundit on TalkSport, where he does the grown-up topics. Simon Jordan has strong opinions. This is his thing. His worldview says: the world is bad. The world is in need of correction. And he’s right about that, as he often is about things.

That’s what makes this all a bit surprising because I like Simon Jordan! I listen to his morning show with Jim White and it’s often really good. I respect the fact he has industry knowledge because he ran a football club. And yes that involved lots of dealings with Steve Bruce, Iain Dowie or similar, but it’s still basically the same thing.

I like the way he pops up in clips looking like an exquisitely powdered 17th-century Umbrian count, some gorgeous little angry blond glove-puppet I want to sit on my knee and pet and cosset and whisper in his ear about granditudinous hypocralism, in a way that’s just warm and fond and not, for me, in any way sexual, but which definitely is for him.

I like the way he talks. It reminds me of Jackie Chiles, the lawyer in Seinfeld, saying it’s outrageous, egregious, preposterous. Sometimes this can have a Mrs Malaprop edge. But that’s also fun and even then you get his point, which is usually good, even if you didn’t expect to agree, or can only agree secretly. When you’re right you’re right. When you’re veritudinously superfactual you’re veritudinously superfactual.

By now you’re probably wondering what happened. Well, I was definitely savaged. No one can take that away from me. And yes this was a week ago, but other stuff happened in between and I forgot about it for a while. I also haven’t fully listened to the savaging. It’s two minutes long and life is short.

In fact I only know about it because my friend and colleague Barry Glendenning is very reliable in this respect. If you’re ever cancelled, owned, or significantly beasted on the internet then Barry will let you know, as an act of love and kindness, and not, repeat not, because he enjoys it and is killing time in the pub on his phone. It’s like having a faithful and attentive online Lassie. What’s that? Slow down boy. Wait, you’re saying Michaela Strachan has called me a nonce? On LinkedIn? Good boy. Easy. There you go. Here’s a lovely bowl of vape oil and Guinness.

I have to admit I am also amplifying this, promoting myself as genuinely savage-worthy. In reality I was savaged in a minor, offhand way that I still don’t really get. I was at Croatia versus England in Rijeka. The game was meant to be played without fans as punishment for some Croatia-related disorder in Paris last year, which included accusations of people making Nazi salutes.

In the event the Croatian FA filled the ground with children, which is allowed under a loophole in the rules. It felt a bit weird in the moment. At the very least it didn’t seem to fit the spirit of the offence. Nazism, yes, bad. But also: a lovely day out for Year 8.

I still don’t really get why anyone would strongly disagree with this. It seems obvious enough. Yeah, everyone likes happy jolly children. Personally I believe the children are our future. I’ve always said that. But they’re not some kind of smart bomb that disintegrates the capacity for logic.

The counter-argument seems to be that this is joyless liberal Guardian stuff. It’s the woke mind-virus. It’s being too interested in not promoting nazism, when you should simply enjoy the laughter of little boys.

And yes Simon Jordan is right. It is annoying to be preached at. But we’re not talking libtard snowflake stuff here. We’re talking actual Nazis, people who just like and enjoy swastikas, who talk fondly about the Ustase, arguably the most vicious sect of the Third Reich war machine. I don’t know, man. The more I hear about the Nazis, the less I like the sound of them.

Plus we now have the sight of Hajduk Split fans this week walking behind an actual coffin and chanting “Auschwitz”. Does this seem like the message is being hammered home? At the very least we’re going to need more children. How many is this one going to take? Ten thousand? Maybe if we can get children to carry a coffin through Amsterdam then it’s fine and just a heartwarming event that shows lessons are being learned.

This is how it goes you see. You are supposed to LASH BACK in these situations. But it’s all a bit weird. Suddenly Simon Jordan is attacking me with children. He’s barging me out of the way in Starbucks with his mega-buggy, one hand clutched to his pearl-draped throat, saying, what about the children, the children, the children?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

You see? I’m being sucked in. Because this is what the internet will do to you. I wasn’t even the main savaging that day. I was a side-beef, an afterthought. By now the algorithm is already filling my feed with fresh SJ face-offs, the latest a “heated exchange” with Dale Vince about Robbie Savage, in itself a mouthwatering trio, perpetual savaging motion in action.

In the end this is the only real point of interest here. This stuff is utterly addictive. And with good reason: it’s designed to be. Vast amounts of expertise and resources have been poured into this irresistible machinery. David Squires did a brilliant cartoon this week about the rise of the celebrity football chat-cast, the industrial-scale, seed-funded waffle that must now justify its space by shouting above the noise, and which will always tend towards beef-culture and a narrative of opposition.

I’ve tried really hard to stay out of this. I don’t do radio or TV stuff, because, well, what’s the point, but more because nobody’s clean, nobody escapes, suddenly you’re having a charity boxing grudge-match with Stephen Warnock.

But it is worth logging for the record that we are at fever pitch. The level of rage around football right now is genuinely astonishing. The story of the Manchester City verdict is, in part, a regulatory ruling over a breach of financial rules. But really it’s the astonishing post-truth online response, the urge to assail and objectify and dehumanise over a tribunal’s interpretation of accountancy practices.

Just going to report on a game at the Etihad this week involved BRAVELY DEFYING assorted threats of violence in response to articles written in these pages. And yes, these are clearly the work of a 77-year-old hunchback in Jakarta, or a drunk and bored corporate lawyer taking a break from surfing porn on the family computer.

But it is all part of the design too. This is meant to happen. A new book called Our Minds Under Siege by Bruno Giussani, a former global curator of TED, describes the way algorithm life is actively changing human behaviour. This is not a secret. Marketing has wanted to do this since the early 20th century.

Walter Dill Scott’s Theory of Suggestion. The Drive Theory of Motivation. The deliberate creation of want and anxiety into the way we sell things. And now we have a new and commercially irresistible language. Dopamine craving. Variable social validation. The feedback loop.

The way even random scrolling is controlled and metered, designed to create a craving that’s always there inside your head, and controlled by tech platforms that openly define humans as eyeballs, want, need, hunger.

In the end, this is why Simon Jordan seems to care so violently about someone else’s opinions on the children-washing of Uefa sanctions. It’s why I’m just incredibly excited by this as an outcome, why I want more not less. Savage me again. Make me feel something. Let me exist inside the machine with you, egregious, preposterous, vibramoniously alive.

#328. Football Daily | Post-Ferguson worn-out horror show continues at Manchester United

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

We’re in the midst of what the kids call “spooky season” – or, for our fellow fusty old-timers out there, “autumn”. If you’ve been cosying up with a few horror flicks this month, you’ll know nothing good can come from hanging around a lake at this time of year. And so it proved for Manchester United, who endured an early Halloween nightmare on the banks of Lake Como that may have driven a stake through the Michael Carrick era. Hailed as the interim anti-Amorim not so long ago, Carrick has overseen two wins this season, against Ipswich and Sabah Baku. Como were in Serie D when Carrick won Big Cup with United as a player in 2008 – now, 18 years on, he watched the Italian upstarts dance, twirl and shimmy through the set of training cones he had sent out to represent his storied club.

In the dugout, Carrick appeared frozen by fear. If there had been a sofa perched on the touchline, he may well have crouched behind it to avoid the series of jump-scares served up by his players. At the end, he walked over to the three United fans who had stuck around and held up his hands, looking like a cross between Ole Gunnar Solskjær and a doomed Squid Game contestant. But somehow, things were about to get worse. A week after Lisandro Martínez had taken aim at (or, in truth, just below) United’s hapless hierarchy, Bruno Fernandes decided to swing a little lower. Asked about his side’s tactics, Fernandes said it was “on the manager and staff to see”, before offering a surprisingly detailed dissection of Carrick’s pressing techniques. Now 32, perhaps Fernandes is eyeing the lucrative podcast market, where former United players are busy making hay by stating the obvious. Perhaps he’s just full of it. Carrick fired back with a maxim that works for horror-movie protagonists and lazy footballers alike: “If you don’t run, you ain’t going to win.”

In truth, Manchester United’s entire post-Ferguson era feels like a worn-out horror franchise, a repetitive cycle of diminishing returns that has churned through managerial victims, while still finding new ways of scraping the barrel. United fans might have dared to dream that City’s guilty verdict marked the end of the nightmare; instead, a new team of FFP-baiting waifs in shiny blue shirts have appeared, also led by a crafty Catalan. Carrick might not make it past United’s trip to Stamford Bridge on Halloween, but could Cesc Fàbregas replace him? Asked before the game, the Como head coach snapped back: “I don’t think that shows enough respect to a great footballer and manager like Michael Carrick, at the helm of a wonderful Manchester United side.” Tone it down a bit, Cesc, it’s giving sarcastic. Fabregas is on the bookies’ speculative longlist to replace Carrick, but it’s hard to fathom why he would take the job. At Como, he has total oversight of a talented team, a financial stake in the club and all the perks of Italian lakeside living. It’s a lot to give up just to be pushed around by Jason Wilcox.

Big Website reports that Frightfest tropes Julian Nagelsmann (hipster lost in woods) and Unai Emery (vampire) are the leading candidates. Our personal pick, purely for content reasons, would be Antonio Conte, who would surely combust with rage within a week. Ultimately, will it matter? We all know the big reveal by now: the real villains at Old Trafford are in the boardroom, hollowing out the mistreated mega-club like an overripe pumpkin. Much like reading a tea-timely email packed with too-early Halloween gags, bringing United back to relevance is a tortuous process that nobody has the strength to complete. For now, the nightmare continues.

Join Daniel Harris for an all-encompassing clockwatch taking in the early (5.45pm BST) and late (8pm BST) kick-offs in Bigger Vase, with updates from Lech Poznan 0-3 Sunderland, Bournemouth 1-2 Milan, Celtic 2-2 Celta and more.

“We’re not against anyone and we’re not in favour of anyone” – the president of the Asian Football Confederation, Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, gives no hint about the body’s support – or opposition – to the re-election of Gianni Infantino as Fifa overlord. How very helpful.

double quotation markAny chance the Independent Football Regulator could also force the sale of Manchester United while it is at it? – James Marriott.

double quotation markBelated birthday greetings to Florent Sinama-Pongolle, a player once described (by Big Website if memory serves) as the only footballer whose surname sounds like an art-house trend – Alan Burgess.

#330. The most dangerous crime drama on TV? Wannabe killer is now linked to hit show Dexter after at least SEVEN convicted murderers are influenced by the 'how-to script' of gruesome on-screen slayings, warns criminologist

By ARTHUR PARASHAR, SENIOR REPORTER and JON BRADY, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER

Published: 00:43 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 01:53 BST, 23 October 2026

For millions of ordinary fans, hit US crime drama Dexter has been the perfect binge-watch at the end of a long day.

But for a twisted minority, it has ceased to be entertainment and mutated into something far darker: a twisted inspiration for real-world violence.

Within just three months, two British killers who styled themselves on TV serial killer Dexter Morgan have been convicted of gruesome murders – while a 16-year-old obsessed with the show was convicted of attempting to murder a girl he did not even know in school.

The boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was just 15 when he approached his female victim in a corridor at Thorpe St Andrew School while wearing a balaclava, plunging a knife into her back before fleeing the scene.

His two-week-long trial heard he had a 'dangerous interest in killers and killing'; he created video compilations of both real and fictional serial killers, including Dexter, and craved what he saw as the 'admiration' they got for their crimes.

Just two weeks earlier, forensics student Benjamin Day, 20, admitted to murdering Maria Saceanu, 24, after luring her to a plastic-lined 'kill room' inside a West Midlands Airbnb, inspired by his obsession with the TV show.

His confession came just weeks after another Dexter-inspired serial killer, James Desborough, 40, was convicted of murdering and dismembering two men in his remote woodland cabin in Cornwall.

Astonishingly, two other Brits, Steven Miles and Mark Howe, Canadian film-maker Mark Twitchell, American teenager Andrew Conley and Norwegian Havard Nyflot have all been convicted of killings inspired by Dexter since 2009.

Police on the scene of a stabbing at Thorpe St Andrew School in Norwich - where a teenager obsessed with serial killers including Dexter Morgan stabbed a girl in an unprovoked attack

Benjamin Day was arrested wearing a Dexter-style outfit after murdering Maria Saceanu in a 'kill room' in a twisted 'tribute' to the show about a self-described ethical serial killer

Dexter Morgan, played by Michael C. Hall, wearing a khaki shirt that Day changed into before killing his victim

Canadian filmmaker Mark Twitchell and British teen Steven Miles were inspired to kill by Dexter

Day's confession came just 70 days after James Desborough (pictured) was convicted of a Dexter-inspired double murder

Dexter, which first aired 20 years ago, follows the life of Dexter Morgan, who by day works as a blood-splatter analyst for the police, and by night transforms into a vigilante serial killer who is expertly equipped to cover his tracks.

Criminologists have warned that the show – which has produced three spin-offs – could be providing a 'how-to script' for copycat killers and would-be murderers.

Alex Iszatt, a behavioural criminologist, told the Daily Mail: 'Dexter gives them a ritual. They can fully become him: follow the same code and principles, wear the same clothes, and use the same methods of killing and disposing of bodies.

'Dexter provides a usable identity. They are ready to perform to an imagined audience. They are Dexter.'

In the series, Dexter works as a blood-splatter analyst for the Miami Metro Police Department, but becomes a vigilante serial killer during the night.

His actions are strictly governed by a twisted quasi-ethical set of rules taught by his adoptive father, known as 'The Code'. He can only kill proven murderers that have evaded justice – and he can never get caught.

In the show, Morgan feels an uncontrollable, innate urge to kill – which he describes as his 'Dark Passenger' – and follows a meticulous routine, using his police network to research suspects beforehand.

His modus operandi is to prepare a 'kill room', wrapped completely in plastic sheets, to catch all evidence and blood. He tapes photos of the victim's crimes to the walls, forcing them to look at what they have done.

Finally, he murders them and dismembers their bodies before dumping them deep in the ocean.

'What makes Dexter particularly useful to a violent personality is that he provides a justification for killing,' Ms Iszatt adds.

'You're not a monster with uncontrollable urges; you're a vigilante, with standards, and the people you kill deserve it. It doesn't matter if they happen to be your mother, brother or girlfriend.

'There's something inherently appealing about Dexter's dual identity; he is a dark version of the superhero fantasy, respectable and ordinary by day, secretly powerful and dangerous by night. He is Batman.

'For someone fascinated by control, violence and getting away with things, the fantasy is not simply being a killer, it's doing what everyone else can't, while remaining invisible.'

This week, the series was thrust back into the spotlight after a 16-year-old boy was convicted of attempted murder after stabbing a girl he did not know in the back with a kitchen knife in a horrifying unprovoked attack on March 11.

He was arrested by armed police shortly after fleeing Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich. His victim, who was also 15 at the time, miraculously escaped with only minor injuries to her back and was discharged from hospital the next day.

He was convicted of attempted murder after prosecutors successfully argued that he had intended to kill the girl – backed up by a cache of evidence police found at the boy's home that showcased an obsession with serial killers including Dexter.

Dexter fanatic Mark Howe (pictured) was jailed for at least 21-and-a-half years for murdering his mother, Katrina Wardle, at their home in Leicester in 2014

Andrew Conley strangled his brother to death. He too was obsessed with the US crime series Dexter

Prosecutors said he was obsessed with serial killers and had written in a note to himself that he had 'seen serial killers being admired... I want admiration, gratification. I've wanted this for years. I don't care who I hurt. Not anymore.'

King's Lynn Crown Court was shown video compilations the teenager had made at home of both real and fictional serial killers, including Dexter.

A video, thought to be made using the AI video editor Viggle.AI, showed the character dancing over a map of the show's setting, Florida, and a 'list of names of the victims'.

He made a similar video of actor Jamie Dornan as Paul Spector, a serial killer in the BBC2 series The Fall who, like Dexter, leads a double life: by day he is a bereavement counsellor but by night operates as a sadistic, sexually motivated murderer.

The teen also produced a 'fancam edit' of Dornan in character – a slick compilation  of clips usually made by fans of actors and pop stars to share with fellow admirers – which he captioned 'me btw (by the way).'

It featured Dornan removing a mask he fashioned out of a neck gaiter and a beanie hat – giving him an appearance not dissimilar to the balaclava the teenager wore on the day he attacked his victim.

He also created a bizarre AI-generated video of US multiple killers Edmund Kemper and Ted Bundy dancing on top of a picture of the Earth alongside a third unidentified individual.

Other notes found by police expressed 'hatred for women' following the 'failure of a relationship', and hinted at a possible motive with thoughts on 'misanthropy, misogyny, suicide, bullying'.

He is also said to have made a 'victims list', and wrote an essay on arming himself with a knife and stabbing a man to death in the street.

Some of the material was found in a shoebox that appeared to have been stabbed.

In his opening speech, prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said the boy had an 'obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing' and a 'hatred for women'.

He added: '[He] went to school not to learn but to kill, taking with him a kitchen knife.'

The teenager was convicted unanimously of attempted murder, and faces sentencing on December 18.

It is the third time in recent weeks that Dexter has been linked to horrific crimes of violence in Britain.

The teenager in the Norfolk school stabbing was obsessed with serial killers, and created a 'fancam edit' of Jamie Dornan as murderer Paul Spector he captioned 'Me btw (by the way)'

He also created a bizarre AI-generated video of US multiple killers Edmund Kemper and Ted Bundy dancing on top of a picture of the Earth, alongside a third unidentified individual

Earlier this month, University of Worcester student Ben Day violently stabbed Maria Saceanu 78 times to death before attempting to dismember her in an act directly inspired by the TV series.

He changed into a khaki top similar to that worn by the character and prepared a copycat 'kill room' in what was planned to be a 'tribute' to the show he planned to share online.

The murderer, who changed his university course from journalism to study forensics and applied biology, also had a 'shopping list' of items required for the killing, including plastic sheeting, a staple gun, cleaning chemicals and microscopic slides.

Police said Day 'had an obsessive personality and had become obsessed with the character Dexter'.

Listing 'similarities' between the death and the TV series, prosecutor Rachel Brand KC told jurors: 'Dexter Morgan works as a forensic scientist in a police department – and the broad premise of the programme is that he is a serial killer who knows how to cover his tracks.

'As you know the defendant changed his university course… to study applied biology and forensics.

'He had changed into 'Dexter' clothing before Maria Saceanu arrived at the house.

'In the TV series Dexter prepares a 'kill room' when carrying out his attacks, lined with plastic sheeting which he fixes using a staple gun or duct/gaffer tape.

'And this is exactly how the defendant had prepared the room.

'Dexter wears an apron, a plastic visor and gloves when killing his victims – all such items were found in the bedroom.'

Other similarities with the TV series included a canvas roll containing knives found in the bedroom, the dismemberment attempts and microscope slides thought to be a 'trophy' from the killing, Ms Brand said.

Ms Iszatt, a former crime scene investigator, said the 'kill room' is particularly significant because it turns murder into a ritual of control.

'On the show it's clean, sterile and methodical; the plastic sheeting and protective clothing are presented as solutions to practical problems,' she added.

'For someone interested in forensics, it also feeds a fantasy of competence: not simply being capable of killing, but being clever enough to outsmart the police afterwards.'

Dexter killer Day lying on a hospital trolley with his left hand heavily bandaged on the day he was arrested on suspicion of murder

Dexter was aired for the first time 20 years ago and is hugely popular - leading to three spin-offs including a prequel series

Maria Saceanu, 24, was brutally murdered by Dexter fanatic Benjamin Day

The University of Worcester, where Day studied, boasts of 'state-of-the-art research labs and dedicated crime scene simulation house provides immersive settings for working through real-world scenarios'.

They tell prospective students: 'You'll get to use industry-standard geophysical equipment for detecting concealed burials, crime scene investigation kits and specialist fingerprint-enhancing tools.'

A spokesman for the university said it was 'deeply shocked and saddened by this terrible crime'.

Ms Iszatt said the clothing Day was wearing was 'not merely practical, but a uniform'.

'Putting them on marks the transition from the ordinary person into 'the other' - the forensic-genius killer - creating a psychological distance from the act and making the fantasy feel more real'.

Day's guilty plea came just 70 days after another Dexter fanatic James Desborough was convicted of murdering homeless men Claudio Aquilino, 57, and Daniel Coleman, 43, followed by his prison cellmate, Steven Kempster, 65, while awaiting trial.

The former builder befriended the two vulnerable men at a homeless shelter, before killing and dismembering them at his woodland cabin near Sticker, Cornwall. He used their bank cards and made journeys to create an illusion they were still alive.

Desborough was present at various points during police searches for the bodies and mentioned casually to a forensic biologist on the scene that he 'particularly enjoyed the dismemberment scenes' in Dexter.

Prosecutor Ahmed Hossain KC told jurors: 'That is a series which involves scenes of dismemberment and disposal of bodies.

'There are many, many people who are fans of the television programme Dexter but... when you consider that comment by Mr Desborough together with the fact that two dismembered bodies were found on his land, that the comment takes on a particular significance.'

This is at least one of seven Dexter-inspired killings in the last 17 years.

In 2014, British teenager Steven Miles, who was obsessed with the TV serial killer, was jailed for at least 25 years for murdering and dismembering his 17-year-old girlfriend Elizabeth Thomas.

Miles's trial heard that he had a fixation with horror movies and wanted to copy the actions of Dexter Morgan.

The same year, Mark Howe, then 21, was jailed for at least 21-and-a-half years for murdering his mother, Katrina Wardle, at their home in Leicester.

He stabbed her more than 53 times in the face, mouth, neck, chest and arms after a row over his cannabis smoking. The judge described the attack as 'akin to torture'.

It later emerged that Howe had been secretly sending his friends text messages about hating his mother and began stabbing the punch bag in his bedroom while also becoming obsessed with Dexter.

'He was a fanatic for the programme,' the victim's husband, Kris Wardle, later revealed. 'I mean, Dexter is a serial killer.'

Hi, I'm Alex Matthews, Editor of The Crime Desk.

In 2014, we revealed the bombshell evidence identifying Aaron Kosminski as the fabled Jack the Ripper. Now, we can reveal his astonishing connection to the Freemasons and claims this motivated his killings and protected him from life in prison.

Sign up here to get our exclusive piece for free.

Howe had used a photo of Dexter with a blood-splattered face as his own Facebook profile picture and had searched 'Dexter's kill knife' before carrying out the murder.

In 2008, two years after the series first aired, Canadian film-maker Mark Twitchell murdered Johnny Altinger, 38, in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, and dismembered him after luring him to his death on a dating website, Plenty of Fish.

Twitchell was dubbed the 'Dexter Killer' due to his obsession with the show and its lead character.

At the time, Michael C Hall, the actor who played Dexter, denied the show glamourised killers.

'I would hope that people's appreciation was more than some sort of fetishization with the kill scenes,' he said.

Referencing Twitchell, he said: 'I wouldn't stop making Dexter because someone was fascinated by it only in that way. I try to tell myself that their fixated nature would have done it one way or the other, but it seems that Dexter had something to do with it. It's horrifying.'

In May 2013, it was reported that Twitchell had bought a TV for his prison cell, where he would catch up on every Dexter episode he had missed.

In 2010, American teenager Andrew Conley was handed a life sentence for strangling his ten-year-old brother to death in Indianapolis. He strangled him for 20 minutes in the kitchen before wrapping his brother's head in two plastic bags and dumping the body.

Conley told police he had fantasised about killing and a few weeks before, he told his girlfriend that he wanted to be just like Dexter.

Also in 2010, 26-year-old Faiza Ashraf was kidnapped, murdered and buried in a shallow grave in Asker.

During the investigation, one of the killers – Havard Nyflot – claimed he had been inspired by Dexter and had decided the victim was a 'bad person' who deserved punishment.

Nyflot and his co-defendant were jailed for 18 and 19 years respectively.

Ms Iszatt said Dexter 'gives vulnerable individuals a language for explaining their own violence'.

'The narrative of the 'Dark Passenger' presents the violent part of Dexter as something that exists within him and demands expression.

'For someone already experiencing violent impulses, that can become a convenient way of understanding and separating themselves: the violent part of me is not really me; it is something that happens to me.

'The show doesn't explain why these people wanted to kill - they have pre-existing psychology, fantasies and circumstances - but it provides a language, an identity and a practical template through which those existing impulses are expressed.'

Paramount, which owns Dexter series producer Showtime Networks, did not respond to a request for comment.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Manchester United boss, and current AC Milan manager Ruben Amorim has confessed that he blocked Pervis Estupinan’s move to Aston Villa after the Unai Emery-led side made a summer swoop for the Ecuadorian.

Estupinan joined the Serie A side in the summer of 2025, after spending five years at Brighton in the English top-flight.

The left-back was largely overlooked by then-manager Massimiliano Allegri in Italy; however, his new boss, Amorim, has revealed why he never had any intention of letting the Ecuadorian leave amid concrete interest from Aston Villa.

Aston Villa made serious efforts to attempt to bring Estupinan back to England, in need of a new left-back after Lucas Digne’s exit to PSG this summer.

Sport Witness reported in July that the Ecuadorian had agreed on certain terms to set up a Villa Park move; however, Amorim never wanted Estupinan to leave.

The Serie A side coughed up nearly £17 million to secure the left-back’s services from Brighton, and Amorim was far from happy when he heard of Aston Villa’s approach.

Under Allegri, the 28-year-old averaged under 60 minutes per game during the 2025/26 Serie A term. With Amorim as his leader, Estupinan has played 340 minutes in seven Italian top-flight matches, averaging even fewer minutes played at just 48 per match.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Despite using the left-back even less than his predecessor did, Amorim has explained why letting Estupinan depart was never on his mind.

“At the end of the transfer window, we had a list of clubs that wanted Estupinan. But I said no. So, I want the fans to know that it was my responsibility,” claimed the Portuguese coach, who then acknowledged that a section of AC Milan fans aren’t overly keen on the Ecuadorian.

“Even at other clubs, sometimes the fans don’t like certain players too much. We have to help Estupinan, we have to help the fans understand who Estupinan is: and I can assure you that Estupinan works really hard.

“So, I want the fans to know that it was my responsibility. He’s playing because I chose Estupinan, because I believe in him and I’m convinced he'll be truly important for our team.”

“But I understood that feeling from the first game. We simply have to help Estupinan, because we are a team: if one of our teammates suffers because of this, the whole team suffers with him and stands by him,” Amorim concluded.

Unai Emery’s men instead welcomed Aaron Wan-Bissaka to their line-up; however, an injury against Newcastle on Saturday has left the Villans shortchanged at left-back. They return to action against Viking in the Champions League on Wednesday.

#333. How Brazil’s election result could shape women’s football in the country

Female players including Carlinha and Tayla Carolina have spoken out against the far right, who they fear will harm the women’s game as well as wider society

The day before the first round of Brazilian elections, the Estádio do Morumbi hosted the second leg of the Brazilian Women’s Championship final, in which São Paulo drew 1-1 with Corinthians to win 3-2 on aggregate and secure the Brasileirão Women’s title.

It had been an incredible final but after the game the goalkeeper Carlinha used an interview to appeal to her fans: “Never again Bolsonaro in power,” she shouted to a record-breaking TV audience of 23 million people.

Having lost her grandmother during the Covid-19 pandemic, Carlinha recalls the challenges faced by hundreds of thousands of Brazilian families when the far-right president Jair Bolsonaro spread fake information about the virus while ignoring public appeals for the government to buy and distribute vaccinations. More than 700,000 Brazilians died during the pandemic. Now his son, Flávio, is standing against the 80-year-old incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

“I didn’t just think of [my grandmother] when I gave that interview, I think about her and miss her every single day,” Carlinha tells Moving the Goalposts. “I felt relieved after talking about my personal opinion in such an important moment of Brazilian democracy. I’m a journalism student and I know the impact if the right wins the elections.”

Carlinha is one of several female football players who have used social media and their visibility to speak up before and during the presidential election, which will come to an end on Sunday with a second-round vote. The father of the Bolsonaro dynasty is currently under “humanitarian house arrest”, serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt.

Carlinha’s club and international teammate, Tayla Carolina, went viral the weekend after discussing her family’s background and how public policies implemented during Lula’s government were important for her mother and grandmother, who have worked as cleaners throughout their lives and have since passed. “I’m from a very humble family, I’m a Black woman. I’ve studied in public schools and used the national healthcare system … my mum, dona Dora, worked for over a decade for someone who never paid her labour rights … and she worked until she couldn’t walk any more due to the cancer that took her from us. She never saw me play because she never had the time, she never rested,” she wrote. Her story resonates with many Brazilians who fought for shorter working weeks, approved earlier this week in congress.

Tayla elaborates her point: “I’m from a country where most of the people are poor but the country is not seen as poor. It shows there are huge inequalities, which come from exploitation. Years have passed and there’s still a lot of inequality and I come from it … as a public figure, and someone who has lived similar lives to the majority of Brazilians, I feel the responsibility to speak up.”

The player organisation Fifpro has just released a new study showing that nearly half of female football players think of early retirement owing to the psychological and financial pressures of the women’s game (800 professional players took part). With the Women’s World Cup being staged in Brazil next year both Carlinha and Tayla feel the election will have a huge impact on the game going forward.

“There is one side that makes it quite clear how they feel about women’s rights,” says Carlinha, referring to, among other things, politicians such as Eduarda Campopiano, one of the most voted members of the São Paulo Assembly, who calls herself an “enemy of feminists” and has said she does not believe in femicide – that women and girls can be killed because they are women. Tayla also feels the need for policies to support the women’s game at a crucial moment. “We still need government incentives, so it may not be immediate, but the game will be affected, positively or negatively, depending on how the elections go.”

Lula approved the World Cup law in June 2026, which regulates many aspects of the tournament, including how ministries, the Brazilian FA (CBF), state federations and clubs will commit to developing a legacy and supporting the women’s game in the country. The legacy plan, divided into four strands, proposes supporting access and permanence of girls and women in football, developing and professionalising the game, fighting gender- and racial-based discrimination, and enhancing the economic and cultural aspects of women’s football in Brazil. The commitment to the tournament is stated in Lula’s government plan. Bolsonaro’s proposals for women’s sport do not mention the World Cup; instead, he proposes “ensuring that women’s categories, from youth to elite, are played by athletes of the female sex, protecting women and tournaments from ideological agendas”.

Brazilian football, men’s and women’s, has been heavily politicised for decades, and the rise of social media has led to an increase in players publicly supporting their political candidates. In the men’s game, the far right is often championed by the Santos and Brazil forward Neymar, who has showed support for the Bolsonaro family on many occasions. Tottenham’s Richarlison, meanwhile, is positioned on the left and this week accused Flávio Bolsonaro of “taking possession” of an island he says he bought a few years back.

The country’s female players do not have the same number of followers on social media and cannot influence a big audience in the same way as the men. However, it is true that the result of the election is likely to have more of an impact on the women’s game than on the men’s.

Kely Nascimento, the daughter of late football legend Pelé and founder and executive director of the Nascimento Foundation, says: “Female players, female athletes, they don’t have the protection of wealth. What feeds the brilliance of Brazilian football are the players, and they mostly come from communities, favelas and other places that are going to be hugely affected by these elections. Women are more affected by all this, right?”

Carlinha, who played in one of the two recent friendlies against Argentina, says playing for the national team at home is “one of the best feelings ever”. At both stadiums, in Porto Alegre and Recife, the crowd predominantly chanted in support of Lula, which could be heard over the TV commentary during the broadcast.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

The politicisation of women’s football is not new, as Brazilian women’s football historian and author Aira Bonfim explains. “This is a hundred-year-old history, because we have episodes of women playing football in Brazil since 1915, and the women’s game reveals different perspectives of gender inequalities, racial inequalities, class, territory, which will affect the progress of the women’s game,” she says. “By knowing women’s football history, we can look at episodes which are equally as political, such as the ban on the women’s game [between 1941 and 1979], the persecution of women, and lies that were told so that female players would give up on it.”

One of the pieces of history that she has uncovered in her research became a short film, which debuted earlier this month at the Rio Film Festival, The House of Dona Carlota, produced by Mymama Entertainment and directed by Lili Fialho and Bruna Linzmeyer, which tells the story of a woman who was arrested and persecuted because she led a women’s football team, Primavera Atlético Clube.

It shows women’s football as a space of socialisation, sport and resistance to the Estado Novo dictatorship in the late 1930s and early 1940s. The women’s game was banned in Brazil for decades, and the World Cup in 2027 is where many hope its renewed development will be consolidated.

“What’s at risk [in this election] is a waste of all of the human investments in building social legacy plans. There is also the risk of dismantling all political communication that has been done to support [the World Cup] through the ministries, cities and state governments. If you elect someone who did not make any commitments towards it, who did not commit to the World Cup or what it represents to women, it can be a huge loss,” Bonfim says. “Just the fact that during Jair Bolsonaro’s government he removed the status of the ministry of sports reveals how he feels about the sector.”

The hosting of a Women’s World Cup is key in developing public policies and attracting investment and support. As Nascimento says: “There are girls all over Brazil for whom football is not just their dream, but it’s also how they get out of very awful situations. And there are amazing people doing God’s work all over Brazil just to get girls to play, to be educated in another way … for some reason, Brazil just makes football magic, and that’s not gender-specific. And there’s an enormous Brazil that is being ignored and taken advantage of.”

There are many reasons for the international community to look closer at the second round of Brazil’s elections on Sunday, from how it can affect climate change, foreign policy and financial markets to many other issues. Women’s football, and all it represents, is one of them.

#334. How much money do clubs get for Nations League players?

Several Premier League clubs are set to benefit financially from releasing players to represent their country

Uefa will pay clubs a total of Â£205m for releasing players to participate in the 2024-25 and 2026-27 Nations League tournaments, as well as both qualifying and finals matches for the 2028 Euros.

The majority of that fund is reserved for clubs with players released for the Euros finals, with Â£120m being distributed in this instance.

The remaining Â£89m is divided among clubs who have had players participating in either the Nations League or Euros qualifiers.

Of that total, a payment of Â£27m is due to be released this week to clubs which had players compete in the 2024-25 Nations League.

Uefa said in a statement that this will be the first payment under its Club Benefits Programme cycle.

The programme means clubs are paid on a per-player, per-match basis for the Nations League tournament and Euros qualifiers, changing to per-player, per-day for the Euros tournament proper.

A similar system was in place at the 2026 World Cup.

Norway goalkeeper Orjan Nyland's club RB Leipzig are receiving the biggest payout from Uefa for the 2024-25 Nations League tournament

Uefa has said 611 clubs will benefit from the current cycle of payments.

This will likely rise to more than 900 when including the full Euro 2028 tournament, as was the case in the 2024 competition.

The flat rate for each player named in a squad list per Nations League or Euro 2028 qualifying match is Â£3,285. This is a 5% increase on what clubs were paid in the 2020-24 payment cycle for the equivalent games.

According to Uefa, RB Leipzig are the club set to benefit most from the 2024-25 Nations League compensation, earning Â£302,000 after releasing 16 players for the tournament.

While it is not possible to calculate which Premier League clubs will benefit most financially from the current international break until after all Nations League and Euro 2028 qualifiers have concluded, a rough idea can be gathered from looking at how many players each club have released for the 2026-27 Nations League (not including those out on loan):

However, there is no guarantee every player called up will be named on a team sheet, which must happen in order for a payment to be made.

Most Premier League clubs have additional players who have been called for international duty in tournaments outside the Nations League, which will operate a different compensation system from Uefa (if any), as well as those attending under-21s matches.

And while there are obvious financial benefits to having multiple players released for international duty, many clubs sending fewer squad members will benefit from increased rest and training time for players remaining at home.

Uefa announced an equivalent compensation scheme for the women's game in 2022, in time for the 2025 Women's Euros.

More than Â£3.7m was allocated to 221 clubs across European national associations that had released players for the tournament.

Uefa states that the clubs given the financial compensation were "encouraged to use the funds for developing women's football".

#337. Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson

Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team

For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes.

This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League?

Brentford began the weekend in third and with, perhaps, a slight sense of frustration that they had drawn four games. Again, they will feel they might have done rather better on Saturday; they were leading Liverpool 1-0 when Yehor Yarmolyuk foolishly flicked his head towards Jérémy Jacquet and was sent off just before half-time. The result was a 2-1 defeat and a sense of an opportunity missed. Bournemouth have not had the easiest start under Marco Rose, but Sunday’s 2-0 win over Sunderland perhaps hints at a brighter future.

Which left Brighton to carry the charge of the B clubs, which they did in emphatic style, ending a run of four derbies without success with a crushing 5-0 win. Crystal Palace had been extremely fortunate to survive a first-half battering from Nottingham Forest last week. They were thoroughly outplayed in the early stages again, and this time found themselves 3-0 down inside 10 minutes. Perhaps the opening goal, a cross headed into his own net by Jaydee Canvot, was fortunate, but it was an error induced by the intensity of Brighton’s start. The second goal, a perfectly weighted drive from just inside the Palace half from Diego Gómez, spoke of a side playing with immense confidence. Already this season, 11 different players have scored for Brighton in the league. They have become the image of a side without stars, the whole far greater than the individuals who comprise it.

The difference from February, when Brighton last played Palace, is stark. They lost that game 1-0, meaning they had won just one of their previous 12 Premier League games. Generalised grumbling had begun to curdle into calls for Fabian Hürzeler to be sacked. When they lost Carlos Baleba, Jan Paul van Hecke, Danny Welbeck and James Milner over the summer, there were reasons to wonder whether they could keep going with the process of continuous renewal.

There were the usual assorted signings, the usual mix of Premier League experience and exotic unknowns. The 19-year-old centre-back Luka Vušković, who spent last season on loan at Hamburg from Tottenham, already looks at home (and who really thought, when Spurs and Brighton effectively swapped centre-backs, with Van Hecke moving to London, that Brighton would not end up with the better of the deal?). The 21-year-old Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés, who arrived from Stuttgart, sparkled from the bench against Arsenal and has excelled in the two games since.

But the stand-out performer this season has been a far more familiar name: Pascal Gross, who returned in January after a season and a half at Borussia Dortmund. No player in the Premier League has registered more than his four assists this season. Nobody has run further. He has three goals. He averages a league-high 3.0 key passes a game. To bring back a player who is now 35 has been a masterstroke.

The victory over Arsenal before the international break suggested a team capable not merely of accumulating points against the league’s lesser lights, or even of challenging the elite, but of overwhelming them. Arsenal were suffocated by the Brighton press and, while a couple of low-xG long-range finishes in the first half helped, the fact is that Brighton dominated the match to a remarkable extent.

The question is whether they can keep it going. Just as their transfer policy is now an accepted feature of the Premier League, so too is Brighton’s mid-season slump. They haven’t won a game in December since 2023. Is this squad strong enough to sustain the challenge? Europe seems not to be unsettling Brighton as it did on their first foray, or as it appears to be draining Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Sunderland – which may be a reflection on the relative quality of the Conference League.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

They are doing this without Kaoru Mitoma, Yankuba Minteh and Mats Wieffer, all of whom should be back at some point over the next month. That suggests the depth of this Brighton squad. It’s always a major step for a club unfamiliar with the Champions League to haul themselves into the top five. At times it often feels a mental barrier as much as anything.

But if any of those B clubs are ever going to break into the Champions League, they may never have a better opportunity than Brighton do this season.

#338. Who has scored against the most Premier League teams?

Erling Haaland (right) is one of two players to have scored against every team he has faced in the Premier League, while Frank Lampard (left) has scored against the most opponents in the competition

Manchester City striker Erling Haaland has become only the second player in Premier League history to have scored against every league opponent he has played against.

Haaland's second-half goal in City's 5-3 win over Sunderland means the Norwegian has scored against all 25 opponents he has faced. He could move to 26 this season, should he score against Hull City.

The only other Premier League player in history to have scored against every club they have faced (minimum two opponents) is England captain Harry Kane, who netted against all 32 clubs he played against.

However, neither player rank in the top 10 for highest number of opponents scored against in the competition.

That honour goes to current Coventry boss Frank Lampard, whose 178 goals between 1997 and 2015 came against 39 different opponents.

Former Manchester United striker Andrew Cole is second with 38, while ex-England duo Alan Shearer and Jermain Defoe managed to net against 37 different teams.

Wayner Rooney and Teddy Sheringham rank fifth and sixth with 36 and 35 respectively.

Completing the top 11 are Thierry Henry, Michael Owen, Paul Scholes, Steven Gerrard and Ryan Giggs with 34 apiece.

#341. Two more men are charged over the 'murder' of woman, 26, who was knifed to death in the street

Published: 01:49 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 01:51 BST, 23 October 2026

Two more men have been charged in connection with the death of Alisha Samuels earlier this month.

The 26-year-old was found with stab wounds on Dorking Avenue in Manchester at around 2am on October 15, where she was pronounced dead.

Earlier on Thursday, Greater Manchester Police announced three suspects were arrested and were in police custody for questioning.

It has since been reported that Carl Hardy, 19, of Shaldon Drive, Manchester, has been charged with murder and attempted murder, as has Tony Evans, 19, of Dorking Avenue, Manchester.

The pair have been remanded in custody and are set to appear at Manchester City Magistrates' Court today.

A 48-year-old woman was the third person arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender, however has not been charged.

Earlier this week, Lawrence Johnson, 26, of Manchester, was charged with the murder of Ms Samuels as well as the attempted murder of another man.

He was remanded in custody and was due to appear at Manchester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

Alisha Samuels died after being found with serious injuries in Manchester last week

The 26-year-old was found with stab wounds on Dorking Avenue in Manchester at around 2am on October 15, where she was pronounced dead

Tributes have been paid to Ms Samuels by friends, describing her as a 'beautiful soul' and 'beautiful inside and out'

Officers were first alerted to a disturbance in the area after 'screaming and shouting' was heard by locals, with Greater Manchester Police's Major Incident Team since launching an investigation into Ms Samuels's death.

They were being supported by firearms officers from Specialist Operations and officers from the Force Critical Wanted Unit.

Detective Chief Inspector Justin Bryant reportedly said: 'My thoughts remain with Alisha's family and friends as they continue to come to terms with this devastating loss.

'I would also like to thank everyone who has supported our investigation so far. The information we have received from the public has been invaluable.

'I continue to urge anyone with information, no matter how insignificant it may seem, to come forward and speak to us.'

Detective Chief Inspector Bryant earlier spoke of the investigation team working 'tirelessly' after the tragic death of Alisha Samuels.

'We remain focused on establishing the full circumstances surrounding the events of October 15 and want to reassure Alisha's loved ones that we are committed to securing justice for her,' he said.

Tributes have been paid to Ms Samuels by friends, describing her as a 'beautiful soul' and 'beautiful inside and out'.

Her friend Aimee Quinn said in a post: 'How is this real life? How am I going to live without speaking to you every day with all of my problems?

'I can't believe I'm never going to hear your daft one-liners or belly laugh with you again, no more holidays and all the plans we had to travel the world together.'

Another posted: 'Oh Alisha, from the minute I met you, I knew you were special.

'I loved you from the start. You were one of the kindest, funniest people I've ever met and I'll always be grateful I got to know you.'

Donna, a woman laying flowers at the scene and whose daughter attended school with Ms Samuels, described her as having a 'smile that would light up every room'.

She added Ms Samuels was 'beautiful and clever, and she and my daughter were so funny together'.

Putting on this live broadcast is no easy task, thereâs so many different jobs that get the show to air. BBC Bitesize Careers went behind the scenes on a busy Sunday afternoon to meet just a small number of people involved and to find out more about how they got their jobs on the legendary show.

Cue the music. Do, do, do, dooo, do-do-do-do doooooooâ¦.

Joe Hart on why he loves his job on Match of the Day.

Isabelle Anastasiou on finding your next career step.

Departing Arsenal doesn't always lead to greener grass elsewhere, says one ex-player

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Plenty of Arsenal players haven't gone on to better things after leaving the club.

Nicolas Anelka became the Gunners' record sale when he departed for big things in the 1990s, but despite his journeyman career, perhaps never reached the heights that some thought he would during his Arsenal days – while Patrick Vieira, Thierry Henry and Marc Overmars can all safely claim to have given their best form in North London after big moves to Europe.

Now, one Gunner from that era has admitted as much.

While the likes of Ashley Cole, Serge Gnabry and Robin van Persie have all enjoyed silverware post-N5, Emmanuel Petit has now reminisced with FourFourTwo about his time as an Arsenal player.

The Frenchman is still the only Gunner to have scored in a World Cup final, and after signing for mentor Arsene Wenger in 1997, enjoyed phenomenal success at Highbury, winning a league and FA Cup Double in his first full season.

“I have some very good memories. When I first came to England, I really loved the tradition over there,” Petit tells us now, courtesy of Betfred.

“I loved it. Back in the day I loved everything. The football, the speed, the total football at times. You never give up and that’s something I learned in England. Never give up until the end.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The midfielder ended up leaving in 2000 for Barcelona – moving back to the Premier League just a year later to return to London with Arsenal's rivals, Chelsea.

Reflecting on that time now, Petit says that the connection he had with the English supporters was stronger than that at Camp Nou – and that he regrets even moving to Barça in the first place.

“I loved the link with the fans in England and I would pay good money to go back to those days because I miss that sometimes,” he says, adding, “I do believe that my biggest mistake was leaving Arsenal to move to Barcelona.”

Petit failed to win anything in Catalonia, appearing 31 times under manager Lorenzo Serra Ferrer's failed tenure as manager after Louis van Gaal left in 2000.

The World Cup winner retired in 2004 after three years at Stamford Bridge.

He has written cover features for the mag on Mikel Arteta and Martin Odegaard, and is assisted by his cat, Rosie, who has interned for the brand since lockdown.

#347. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Ever wondered who makes sure your footy video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to."

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.
