#349. Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action

Florian Wirtz takes on more responsibility in Liverpool’s attack while Pierre Sage is under pressure at Crystal Palace

Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s physicality overpowering Bryan Mbeumo in Manchester United’s area at a corner grabbed him a fifth goal in 10 outings for Leeds: a pretty respectable ratio. “I just tried to cause a ruckus,” said Leeds’ No 9. “I make it difficult for the defender. I read the flight of the ball and was quickest to react. I feel really comfortable [here]. I feel the support from the club and the fans and it is a great feeling stepping on to the pitch, particularly at Elland Road.” Of the contenders to be understudy to Harry Kane as England’s centre-forward, Calvert-Lewin may be the lead act – if he can stay injury-free, which has been a difficulty throughout his career. Jamie Jackson

Match report: Leeds 1-1 Manchester United

After the defeat to Atlético Madrid last Tuesday, Manchester United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, could at least sit a bit more comfortably watching Michael Carrick’s side battle to a draw at Elland Road. Lisandro Martínez bemoaned, among other things, the lack of squad depth at United in his post-match comments in Madrid, but one area Wilcox did strengthen over the summer was United’s midfield. Carlos Baleba, a £65m arrival from Brighton, started his first game for the club alongside Andrey Santos, a £50m signing from Chelsea, and the pair held their own against Leeds’ combative midfield three. “They’re both young players adapting to life at this football club and I thought both of them were terrific today,” Carrick said. “That’s a massive positive for us.” As for Martínez, he was taken off at half-time with a tight thigh. Billy Munday

Florian Wirtz created nine chances during Liverpool’s comeback win against Brentford. The German’s effectiveness grew when Brentford were reduced to 10 men but it was still one of Wirtz’s better games in a Liverpool shirt. The playmaker took on responsibility in the second half. Andoni Iraola was happy and perhaps sees a connection growing between Wirtz and Víctor Muñoz. Both of Wirtz’s assists in the league this season have been for Muñoz, a £34.5m summer signing from Osasuna who hugs the touchline and stretches the play with speed and directness. Iraola plays positive, vertical football. Wirtz could be more dangerous if his passes are hitting speedy wingers such as Muñoz and Bradley Barcola. Jacob Steinberg

Ayyoub Bouaddi made his first league start for Manchester City in the win against Ipswich but anyone watching would have thought he was an old hand. The teenager belied his years with a mature performance at the base of midfield, controlling the tempo while keeping things simple in possession and spotting danger when required. The Moroccan cost £85m in the summer from Lille to battle for a place in Enzo Maresca’s revamped side, fighting Enzo Fernández and Elliot Anderson for a spot in the team – and he is looking their equal. “Not bad, yeah?” Maresca joked about Bouaddi’s performance. “I think that the manager is always looking to find minutes and space for good players. Ayyoub is very good. He is very young, coming from France, so we need to help him, not put him under pressure every game. I think he is doing well.” Will Unwin

Match report: Manchester City 3-2 Ipswich

If you were at Craven Cottage on Saturday and didn’t know which three players Álvaro Arbeloa had brought with him from the Real Madrid setup, you would have assumed one of them was Josh King. The 19-year-old has started every league game this season ahead of Emile Smith Rowe in the No 10 position and has already taken on the role of chief creator. King has been in Fulham’s academy since under-nine level and became a regular in the first team under Marco Silva last season. Arbeloa has spoken of wanting to help the youngster raise his level, to help him kick on. “He’s a top talent,” said Arbeloa after King’s all-action performance against Hull that helped Fulham to their first league win of the campaign. “The sky is his limit. He has the talent, the mentality, the character – he has everything to become a top, top player.” BM

David Moyes claimed Chelsea got the rub of the green with the two goals that condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season but there was no question it was deserved on the basis of their respective second-half performances. Everton’s response to Pedro Neto’s opener was nonexistent, with Moyes’s decision to introduce a seemingly unfit Christian Nørgaard instead of Hayden Hackney a contributory factor, but they could feel aggrieved about Morgan Rogers avoiding a second yellow card in the 44th minute for leaping into James Garner. With Harrison Armstrong booked for what the referee, Paul Tierney, deemed a reckless challenge on Josh Acheampong earlier in the game, his inconsistency on the Chelsea forward’s tackle was a key moment. “I would love to speak on the referees but I would probably get fined,” said Garner. “All this camera stuff on their heads, you need to keep out of the game. Just let referees ref it and stop making it about them. That’s all I’ve got to say.” Andy Hunter

Sven Botman was extremely fortunate not to be sent off for a nasty tackle on Nicolas Jackson as Newcastle lost 1-0 at home to Aston Villa, with the excellent Johan Manzambi heading the first-half winner. The rash, high way Botman lunged in on Jackson seemed emblematic of the centre-back’s decline since he suffered a serious knee injury three years ago. The moment has surely arrived for the now under pressure Matthias Jaissle to drop Botman and recall not merely Dan Burn but Fabian Schär, too, in a switch to a more stabilising back three. Newcastle’s failure to keep a clean sheet in their last 13 Premier League games at home – a run stretching back into last season under Eddie Howe – emphasises the need for defensive fortification. Moreover Schär’s ball-playing ability, and particularly his dangerous long diagonal passes, would enhance Newcastle’s pretty dismal threat as an attacking force. Tellingly, Jaissle’s team registered only one shot on target on Saturday, paving the way for Unai Emery’s 100th Premier League win as a manager. Louise Taylor

When Arsenal signed Eberechi Eze, it was hard not to be a little suspicious. Though he started his top-level career relatively late, it is rare a player steps up levels at 27 – all the more so given Mikel Arteta is not exactly in love with mavericks and risk. Ultimately, Eze looks better suited to being the main man in a mid-ranking team rather than a cog in a top one which prioritises shape and system above all else. He was anonymous against Nottingham Forest prior to his removal at half-time. Though Arsenal did not explode thereafter, Noni Madueke did offer greater threat, his speed challenging defenders inside and out before scoring a winning goal that, though fortuitous, also reflected the difference he made. There is surely little chance Eze is picked to start Arsenal’s next game, at Bayern Munich, and he is running out of time to establish himself at the club. Daniel Harris

Match report: Nottingham Forest 0-1 Arsenal

Pierre Sage is treading on very thin ice at Crystal Palace after another disastrous defensive display allowed Brighton to equal their biggest win against their arch rivals. A poor start to the season has been marked by Palace conceding 17 goals in seven league matches – the worst in the division. The chair, Steve Parish, admitted during the international break that the Frenchman’s position remains on “high alert” and, judging by the angry reaction of some Palace fans to the 5-0 thrashing at the Amex Stadium, Sage could be in big trouble. But there must be some sympathy given the failure to adequately replace the influential Maxence Lacroix in central defence after he was sold to Chelsea. That is believed to have led to disagreements with Parish, who has shown a tendency to act quickly if things aren’t going his way. It could be a nerve-racking few days for Sage before Thursday’s trip to face Besiktas in the Europa League. Ed Aarons

Match report: Brighton 5-0 Crystal Palace

Sunderland’s problems are stacking up. Brian Brobbey’s continued absence with an injury sustained while playing for the Netherlands is beyond Régis Le Bris’ control but defeat at Bournemouth was self-inflicted. The swift journey from the Championship to the Europa League has become a stumble. Kevin Danso’s red card was by no means the only error committed during a performance where cross words were exchanged between befuddled defenders. Granit Xhaka found himself incapable of exerting anything like the influence he showed last season. Instead, Tyler Adams and Lewis Cook dominated midfield. Trips to Poznan, Milan and Anderlecht await for Sunderland but Le Bris’ squad is struggling to straddle two fronts. A horrible performance at the Vitality Stadium came despite five purported first-team players being rested against Torreense. Play like they did on Sunday and a struggle in the bottom half surely awaits. Just about everything that went right last season has taken a turn for the worse. John Brewin

#351. How to become a football referee

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

The latest Premier League season is in full flow, and the bookies think these managers are on red alert…

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The 2026-27 Premier League season is now well underway, and some teams, and their managers, are struggling more than others.

Michael Carrick has seized headlines recently for his dire start to the term with Manchester United - and persisting with him could, says the noise from Italy, cost the Red Devils their chance to bag Antonio Conte.

Here, as per Sky Bet, are the favourites for the next manager to get the Premier League sack, from ‘Big 6’ to mid-table to possibly relegation-battling clubs.

While many Manchester United pessimists might have seen something like this coming, with the club’s return to Europe introducing a balancing act that Carrick didn’t have to deal with in 2025-26, going from a third-place finish to 12th and out of the Carabao Cup by October is stark.

When a manager reaches the point where a draw, as the Red Devils claimed last weekend against rivals Leeds United, is seen as enough to just about keep them in a job, they’re clearly walking on a tightrope. Manchester United have Como in the Champions League up next, where they will travel to Italy, and another dire result against an at times brilliant Cesc Fabregas-led side could be the final nail in the coffin.

After that, it’s Bournemouth at home in the Premier League, followed by Chelsea away. A nasty three-game swing, and even more motivation for Sky Bet to have him in first as their likeliest manager to exit their Premier League club.

In the seasons prior, Crystal Palace were flying. No, not flying in the way of a bottom-half Premier League side venturing into the European qualification spots, flying in an actual trophy-winning manner, beating Manchester City to the FA Cup, Liverpool to the Community Shield, and lifting the Conference League trophy, all in two seasons.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

When the architect behind that success left, Oliver Glasner, there remained an expectation that the Eagles would continue to soar. Perhaps another trophy would prove difficult, but performances that put them in contention are now the baseline.

Instead, Crystal Palace have taken just seven points from seven games, landing them at 14th in the Premier League standings. Sky Bet have new boss Pierre Sage at second in their rankings, with odds of 13/8.

It’s slightly surprising that the former Real Madrid boss, now Fulham manager, was unable to leapfrog Sage in this list. After all, Fulham are positioned 18th in the Premier League table, with five points from seven games.

A strong 1-0 win versus Hull City last weekend, after falling 2-1 away from home to Ipswich Town the week prior, could be the reason. Instead, Sage is a few inches closer to the guillotine, and Alvaro Arbeloa has bought himself a little more time with the Cottagers.

That and, naturally, expectations at Fulham being less high than they are elsewhere in London. One thing is for certain, the longer that Arbeloa battles relegation, the higher he will move up Sky Bet’s odds list. A slight improvement defensively in recent weeks bodes relatively well for Fulham, but there is a long, long road ahead for the Spaniard to push his side to mid-table.

Hundreds of millions of British pounds spent, off the back of a season spent battling relegation, and a new manager in Roberto De Zerbi, whose previous reign with Marseille in Ligue 1 was mostly solid.

All of this, and Tottenham Hotspur still limped to the finish line against Coventry City on Monday night, to secure their first win of the Premier League season.

Spurs are now positioned 16th in the standings, with six points from seven outings, but De Zerbi’s job is by no means safe. Battling from a goal down at Old Trafford with just 10 men on the pitch was a more impressive result from the North London unit, but anything less than total abstinence from the relegation spots will be the Italian’s downfall, as the 2026-27 term rages on.

Crystal Palace, Glasner, what a match made in harmony. Instead, Sage is second on this list, and the former Eagles man has also managed to make an appearance shortly into his new gig with Nottingham Forest.

Glasner’s new team are 19th in the Premier League, with just five points from seven games; barring an impressive 2-1 away win at Villa Park, the highlights have mostly been lowlights from Forest in England this term.

Still, Glasner arrived with the expectation that he’d work magic - this Forest side, that finished 16th last season, was anything but a superteam before him. Sky Bet has his odds of leaving the club at 9/1, but the City Ground will surely keep the Austrian for long enough to accurately gauge whether he can replicate his London-based success in Nottingham.

#354. World-first cancer vaccine slashes death risk in stunning findings led by Aussie scientist

Published: 00:44 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 03:22 BST, 23 October 2026

A Sydney scientist is leading a world-first cancer vaccine trial that has dramatically reduced the risk of melanoma returning or patients dying from the disease.

The study found the vaccine cut the risk of cancer recurrence or death by 42 per cent compared with patients who received only an immunotherapy drug, pembrolizumab, which is sold under the brand name Keytruda.

The landmark findings could pave the way for personalised cancer vaccines to improve survival rates for patients with melanoma and potentially other cancers.

Professor Georgina Long, medical director of Melanoma Institute Australia and chair of melanoma medical oncology and translational research at the University of Sydney, was the principal investigator in the clinical trial.

'These results show that patients with earlier-stage melanoma can be treated after surgery in a fundamentally new way,' Professor Long said.

'These results are more than a landmark for melanoma. Just as email transformed how we communicate, individualised neoantigen therapy has the potential to transform how we treat cancer.'

The vaccine, known as intismeran, is being jointly developed by pharmaceutical companies Moderna and MSD.

Intismeran is an individualised messenger RNA (mRNA) cancer vaccine designed specifically for each patient, based on the unique genetic characteristics of their tumour.

Professor Georgina Long (pictured) led the clinical trial of a world-first cancer vaccine that dramatically reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death

The study found the vaccine cut the risk of cancer recurrence or death by 42 per cent compared with standard treatment (stock image)

The vaccine targets neoantigens, abnormal proteins that develop on cancer cells following genetic mutations. It is designed to train the immune system to recognise these unique markers and identify and attack the tumour.

By tailoring treatment to each patient's cancer, the approach aims to strengthen the body's immune response and lower the risk of the disease returning.

Professor Long described the technology as a significant leap forward in cancer treatment, combining personalised medicine with advances in messenger RNA (mRNA) technology and data analysis.

'This is a coalescence of an mRNA platform, personalised, and the use of algorithms and data in a way that we've never seen before,' she said.

'It is equivalent to the first email which has absolutely changed communication. This is that sort of change in cancer, in my view.'

The trial, funded by Merck and Moderna, was conducted across 157 sites worldwide and involved 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but who remained at high risk of the cancer returning.

None of the participants had previously received drug treatment for their cancer.

It ran across a host of Australian sites, including Melanoma Institute Australia, Westmead Hospital in NSW, Princess Alexandra Hospital in Queensland, and the Paula Fox Melanoma and Cancer Centre and Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Victoria.

Professor Long described the findings as a major advance in cancer care

Professor Long has dedicated her career to eliminating melanoma deaths and developing treatments for resistant cancers.

In 2024, she was named Australian of the Year alongside her late colleague, Professor Richard Scolyer.

Associate Professor Seth Cheetham, director of the Australian mRNA Cancer Vaccine Hub, described the findings as a major breakthrough that could usher in a new era of cancer research and treatment.

'This is the first really large trial that's shown definitively that this technology works, it reduces the risk of recurrence or spread and results in better outcomes compared to standard of care,' he said.

'This is really the gold standard, and it's what the entire field's been waiting on,' he added.

Professor Long said the results could have implications far beyond melanoma.

'I think track record predicts future,' she said.

'So advances in melanoma transformed lung cancer, kidney cancer, head and neck cancer, bladder cancer, so many other cancers.'

Professor Georgina Long was named Australian of the Year in 2024 alongside her late colleague Professor Richard Scolyer

She said the findings represented a fundamental change in cancer treatment by using the immune system in a more personalised way to reduce the risk of melanoma returning or causing death.

'This has not been achieved before in the history of cancer drug development,' she said.

Moderna's shares reportedly surged by more than 170 per cent in a single trading day in August after news of the trial's promising results emerged.

#356. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#357. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

The 41-year-old previously promised Portugal fans he will “have one or more farewell matches”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Cristiano Ronaldo has been suspended by the Portuguese FA and fined less than £250 after the Portuguese maestro walked out on the national team following a row with Jorge Jesus.

That occurred during the last round of international games, during which Ronaldo exited the Portugal camp in Copenhagen prior to their Nations League clash versus Denmark.

Jesus, new boss in Portugal and former manager to Ronaldo in the Saudi Pro League, was accused of breaking his word twice to Ronaldo; now, the #7 will serve a 30-day suspension.

When receiving his punishment from the disciplinary council, it was not specified whether time already served under a provisional suspension would be removed from Ronaldo’s 30-day period.

As a result, it is unclear as to whether the 41-year-old’s punishment will extend to Portugal’s upcoming Nations League clashes in November; however, further information has since emerged.

According to Sky Sports News, the suspension began on the day of Ronaldo’s walk-out, September 30, making him eligible to face Denmark on November 14.

The news arrives after the #7 took to Instagram and asked the Portuguese FA to spare him any leniency, while revealing the details of his row with Jesus.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The 41-year-old also published a bullet-pointed list of ‘validated’ claims he signed off on Jesus saying in a post-match Nations League presser, which Jesus never read.

“I made the mistake in having someone of the stature of Pele or [Diego] Maradona warm up today and then not putting him in the game. If it were today, I would not do it,” read one point.

The Al-Nassr forward then clarified that Jesus broke two promises made with him, before offering an apology to his Portugal team-mates.

“The consequence of this act of mine must be assessed and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation… Regardless of each person’s status, the rules are the same.

“The Federation wants to give me [a dignified farewell]... I can promise all my fans, naturally and especially the Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches,” concluded the 41-year-old.

It appears that Ronaldo is set to return versus both Denmark and Wales next month; whether that will be the 41-year-old’s farewell with Portugal is still unclear.

#362. Memorial service held for veteran TV presenter Dermot Murnaghan who passed away aged 68 from prostate cancer

Published: 18:26 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 01:42 BST, 23 October 2026

Good Morning Britain presenter Susanna Reid and Sky News journalists Beth Rigby and Mark Austin were among those who paid their respects at Dermot Murnaghan's memorial service on Thursday.

Veteran broadcaster Murnaghan died aged 68 on July 11 following a period of illness with prostate cancer, having first announced his stage four diagnosis last year.

The former Eggheads quiz show host was best known for his 15-year tenure as a lead anchor on Sky News, and he presented news bulletins for the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 during his decades-long career.

Many of Murnaghan's colleagues were in attendance at the memorial in St Bride's Church, London, including Sky's political editor Rigby, along with news presenters Austin, Matt Barbet and Anna Jones.

Sky Sports presenter Jacquie Beltrao also attended the service along with Times Radio presenter and former Sky News broadcaster Adam Boulton.

After his death, Reid shared a selfie of herself with Murnaghan on Instagram, calling it 'utterly devastating news' as she remembered the 'legendary news journalist and presenter'.

She recalled the 'sheer pleasure of presenting with Dermot at BBC Breakfast', and wrote: 'Dermot was a serious journalist who never took himself too seriously.

'He was intelligent and charming and viewers and guests loved him.'

Former Sky News broadcaster Dermot Murnaghan appearing on Sky News in August 2025 in what was his first TV outing after his diagnosis

Good Morning Britain presenter Susanna Reid leaving St Bride's Church in London after a memorial service for Murnaghan

Many of Murnaghan's colleagues were in attendance including Sky's political editor Beth Rigby

Sky News presenter Mark Austin attended the funeral for Murnaghan on Thursday

Sky Sports presenter Jacquie Beltrao attended Murnaghan's funeral

Sky News presenter Anna Jones paid her respects at Murnaghan's funeral

A person holds an order of service outside St Bride's Church for the funeral of Murnaghan

Rigby said she was 'deeply saddened' by the death of Murnaghan, whom she worked with during coverage of the 2019 general election on Sky.

Murnaghan announced his 'incurable but it's not untreatable' prostate cancer diagnosis last year and became a vocal advocate and campaigner in raising awareness of the disease.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast last November, he urged men in high-risk groups to get themselves checked for prostate cancer, as he admitted he delayed getting tested 'because I felt fine'.

A spokesperson for Prostate Cancer UK said the charity was 'heartbroken' by his death, adding: 'He was a passionate and dedicated supporter of our charity, and his work had a huge impact on the hundreds of thousands of men affected by prostate cancer across the country.'

Murnaghan started his presenting career in 1989, hosting Channel 4's breakfast programme and its business segments before becoming one of its lead presenters.

At ITV he hosted the Lunchtime News and News At Ten, and led the coverage of the death of Diana, Princess of Wales, in 1997.

The award-winning journalist was a main presenter of BBC Breakfast from 2002 until 2007 and presented his own show discussing politics and current affairs for Sky News.

He left Sky - where he covered the death of Queen Elizabeth II - in 2023.

Diego Demme explains how playing for Germany's most hated club fueled his desire for success with RB Leipzig

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Across his 16-year playing career, Diego Demme faced some of the world's biggest clubs like Juventus, Barcelona, Inter, Bayern Munich, and AC Milan. However, one of his most daunting challenges came on August 20, 2016, in a DFB-Pokal match between RB Leipzig and Dynamo Dresden.

Demme was 17 when Red Bull acquired the playing rights of fifth-tier SSV Markranstadt and established RB Leipzig. He was 22 when he left Paderborn, who were closing in on a maiden promotion to the Bundesliga, and joined Leipzig, who were already viewed as pariahs by millions of German fans.

These supporters accused Leipzig of using their corporate backing to undermine Germany's 50+1 rule and outspend traditional eastern German clubs like Hansa Rostock, 1. FC Magdeburg, and Dresden, whose supporters had endured years of financial instability.

It didn't take long for rival fans to voice their discontent. Leipzig's team bus was attacked with bottles during their first away fixture, and players were spat at and pelted with beer cups. Five years later, as they celebrated promotion, a prominent Leipzig supporter known as 'Mocke' was beaten by four assailants.

They suffered more hostility in 2015: Erzgebirge Aue fans displayed banners comparing Leipzig fans to Nazis, and Heidenheim fans threw fake banknotes at the team bus. After warning Leipzig fans against attending, Karlsruher hooligans entered Leipzig's hotel, forcing them to hire private security for away matches.

Le bus du RB Leipzig a été accueilli avec des billets customisés pour l'occasion à Heidenheim. [via @BILD_rbleipzig] http://t.co/iQNrdpU6QwSeptember 18, 2015

In Leipzig's opening match of the 2016/17 season, Dynamo Dresden ultras smuggled a severed bull's head into the stadium and hurled it towards the pitch, in protest against Red Bull, whose logo features two charging bulls. Dresden were fined €60,000 and sanctioned with a partial stadium closure order.

Some fans unfurled banners stating that 'tradition cannot be bought.' Another threw a coin that struck Leipzig captain Dominik Kaiser's shoulder, who, after squandering a two-goal lead, missed Leipzig's fourth penalty in a 5-4 shootout defeat.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"We always had fans against us and our project with Red Bull, particularly in the second and third division, and we wanted to give our best to shut them up," stated Diego Demme to FourFourTwo. "Sometimes, there was a little bit of overacting, like when Dynamo Dresden fans threw a severed bull’s head onto the pitch. There were some crazy people, but that gave us a little extra motivation."

If Leipzig thought they would be given a reprieve against Bundesliga fanbases, they were soon proven wrong. In September, 100 Koln supporters staged a sit-in blocking Leipzig's bus and delaying the match. In February, 400 Dortmund ultras gathered before the match and attacked Leipzig supporters with stones and bottles, leaving six Leipzig fans and four police officers injured.

It was Leipzig who had the last laugh, finishing three points clear of BVB in second. Leipzig have finished in the top four in seven of the last eight seasons, and after losing in the 2019 and 2021 DFB-Pokal Final, they hoisted the cup in 2022 and 2023.

Diego Demme has announced his retirement from professional football 💐 Thank you for everything, Diego! Wishing you all the best for the future ❤️ https://t.co/SspHcpi6oISeptember 24, 2026

Just as Leipzig were gearing up for a run to the Champions League semi-final, Demme left in January 2020. Alongside Yussuf Poulsen, he was the last remnant of a team that had gone from playing in Germany's third tier to sitting atop the Bundesliga.

Six years after swapping Paderborn for Leipzig, Demme departed as a German international and a Champions League footballer. He would go on to win the Coppa Italia and Scudetto with Napoli before enjoying a swansong with second-tier Hertha Berlin.

Leipzig might never win over the hearts of rival Bundesliga supporters, but they did give Demme the platform to win something far more important: his place amongst Europe's footballing elite.

After getting his big breakthrough as the co-founder of the football analytics website Breaking The Lines, Zachary Lowy has been able to tap into his footballing expertise for a number of esteemed outlets like ESPN, FotMob, The Times, The Independent and Urban Pitch. Since joining FourFourTwo as a freelancer in 2025, Lowy has been able to cover a wide range of topics from analyzing the sweeping changes to the MLS season to interviewing key figures like Asamoah Gyan and Rob Holding. Fluent in Spanish, Portuguese and Italian, Lowy’s versatile skillset has allowed him to traverse a number of different fields when covering major competitions like the FIFA Club World Cup. In addition to football, he is also a seasoned participant of other sports like pickleball, tennis, and volleyball.

#366. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.

#370. Kathryn Turner is not just any social media star, she's an M&S social media star: Food store boss racks up millions of hits on TikTok and Instagram and counts Stormzy and Gemma Collins among her legion of fans

Published: 00:40 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 01:40 BST, 23 October 2026

Kathryn Turner is not just any social media star – she's an M&S social media star.

The 56-year-old product development manager for M&S Food has become an unlikely hit on TikTok and Instagram after setting up accounts earlier this year to show off the upmarket shop's wealth of quality products.

Her introductory 'Hi, I'm Kathryn, director of product development at M&S Food' has become a social media meme and her fashionable business casual looks are being touted by fans as the must-wear Halloween costume for 2026.

Despite only being active on social media for a few months her videos have been watched more than 50million times, and she counts Boris Johnson's wife Carrie, Stormzy, Nigella Lawson and Gemma Collins amongst her legions of fans.

Marketing experts say the mother-of-three's deliberately unpolished and authentic videos stand out in a sea of corporate-looking adverts and the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI).

And the supermarket is understood to credit her videos for an uptick in sales on a number of products including its mango grapes and unconventional strawberries and cream 'sando' – inspired by Japanese fruit sandwiches made with soft, sweet bread.

However, M&S has also faced accusations that her account serves as a handy loophole ducking the ban on promoting unhealthy food – a claim the firm rejects.

M&S Food product development boss Kathryn Turner has won the hearts of social media followers with her down-to-earth videos

Experts say her down-to-earth, authentic videos lack the slick editing of a corporate advert, making her appealing to watch

Ms Turner's career at M&S began in 1995 following hospitality jobs with British Airways and the BBC and a sales role at confectionery giant Mars.

Within a few years she had scored her first big wins, launching the Teletubbies-themed Tubby Toast croissants in 1998, followed shortly after by the Count On Us range of calorie-controlled meals that are still on sale today.

She became director of product development in 2022, overseeing a team of 80 people as they develop 1,500 new and 1,000 improved products every year. Much of this happened on the quiet – until she joined TikTok in May.

Since then, the food boss's videos have taken viewers behind the scenes of M&S Food, visiting the panettone factory in Italy and potato fields on Jersey that directly supply the supermarket's gargantuan retail operation.

But her most popular videos are those filmed on the shop floor of real M&S shops with her trademark lapel mic attached to her collar, discussing the thousands of new products that the British firm puts out each year.

Fans have called for her to run for Prime Minister against Andy Burnham, and dramatically vowed to 'follow her into war'.

Ben Marder, Professor of Digital Marketing at the University of Edinburgh's Business School, told the Daily Mail that her videos capture what marketers call the 'snapshot aesthetic', meaning viewers see it as looking less staged than a slickly produced ad.

With more than 300,000 followers on TikTok, her following is bigger than that of the official M&S Food account – which some people may see as more 'corporate'.

'She is promoting the product, that is standard marketing - but these videos are going out against a backdrop where nothing is authentic anymore, where influencers are either AI-polished or just AI,' Professor Marder said.

'People are craving authenticity and this is an authentic person: there's no editing, it's obviously been done on a phone, it's what we used to call the "snapshot aesthetic".

'Lots of influencers use this but what's interesting with this case is that I think people see M&S as a very polished, high-class brand that wouldn't do these kinds of videos.

'There's that contrast with what people expect and that the videos are authentic - and she's an older lady on TikTok, who comes across as so genuine.'

Some observers have pointed out that Ms Turner promotes products that would fall foul of rules on advertising junk food, including chocolates and cakes

McDonald's global CEO Chris Kempczinski was lampooned earlier this year after taking what was seen as a less-than-enthusiastic bite of a Big Arch burger in a social media clip

Videos of her gleefully showing off new lines are a marked contrast to the video of McDonald's global boss Chris Kempczinski, whose taste test of the chain's Big Arch burger went viral for all the wrong reasons in February this year.

The fast food boss was widely derided for taking an almost imperceptible bite of the burger – leading to claims that he wasn't willing to eat his company's own wares – and labelling it a 'product' in cold, harsh business-speak.

Professor Marder added: 'As a consumer, you want the CEO of a company to like the products - and we can see that she likes the products.'

She credits her success to M&S food trends manager Francesca Byrne and trainee product developer Brandon Spatcher – who himself moonlights as a food influencer to 150,000 TikTok followers and is represented by an influencer marketing agency.

In a post thanking them on LinkedIn, she said: 'Listen to the brilliant 20-somethings in your team. They’ve been the driving force behind our social media journey - bringing fresh ideas, honest feedback, and plenty of encouragement along the way.'

Not everyone is a fan, however: critics have accused M&S of using Ms Turner's approachable persona to circumvent rules on junk food advertising.

Some of her videos feature her showing off sugary biscuits, chocolate liqueurs, panettone and chocolate bars that would likely fall foul of Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) rules on foods high in fat, salt or sugar (HFSS).

Fans even joke about the calorific foods she promotes, commenting 'Kathryn pls my clothes don't fit' and 'my waistline will not survive this winter'. One even asked if she might consider developing an M&S-branded version of the fat jab Mounjaro.

The ASA banned paid-for advertising for HFSS food, including the use of influencers, in January this year as part of a Government-led obesity crackdown.

But the rules do not cover a company's own social media accounts or posts made by people without being paid – known in the marketing world as an 'organic' post.

Aside from sharing her own videos, Ms Turner also reposts 'organic' clips made by other TikTok users – encouraging M&S shoppers to get in on the act in the hope that their video might make the cut, giving the firm extra publicity for free.

M&S Food is big business, bringing in around half of the Marks and Spencer group’s £671.4million pre-tax profits last year.

Products that appear in Ms Turner's enthusiastic videos often see a sales boost in shops, including a range of 'mango grapes'

But sources at M&S have firmly rejected the suggestion the accounts are a bid to circumvent the rules on HFSS, telling the Daily Mail they were set up purely for Kathryn to express her genuine enthusiasm about the products she launches.

The company openly encourages staff to post about working for the company on their personal social media, having found success during the coronavirus pandemic.

Store-specific accounts proved popular in telling anxious shoppers if essentials like loo roll were in stock but now focus on employees showing off their work.

However, M&S is yet to be drawn on whether there are any bonuses for workers who find viral success – which could spark interest from advertising watchdogs.

Influencers including Molly-Mae Hague and Grace Beverley have fallen foul of the ASA in the past after failing to declare that they had commercial interests in firms whose products they were promoting on camera.

Molly-Mae failed to tell fans she was creative director at PrettyLittleThing as she promoted items for sale, while Ms Beverley did not disclose on camera that she was founder of activewear firm TALA as she promoted the brand.

Experts have suggested Ms Turner, and other salaried M&S workers, may be operating in a grey area around employee-made content where regulation is yet to catch up.

While not 'paid for' ads under ASA rules, such videos may catch the eye of regulators in future, according to Anastasija Vasilevska, of marketing agency Socially Powerful.

She wrote in an article on the topic last month: 'An employee posting a specific LHF (less healthy food) product is a very new kind of situation, so it hasn’t had time to get tested yet.

'As more brands put out employee content, and as the LHF rules settle in, it’s only a matter of time before a regulator has to weigh in.'

And those who have weighed in on the subject on TikTok have found themselves answering to Ms Turner's army of defensive fans.

One TikToker said: 'The Kathryn Turner backlash needs to end. Why as a society can we not just have nice things?'

As it is, the ascent of 'Kathryn, director of product development at M&S Food', is unlikely to be halted for now. Copycat videos recently shared by frozen food rival Iceland have largely been given the cold shoulder on social media.

Professor Marder, of the University of Edinburgh, believes there is a simplicity to her success.

He said: 'As the saying goes, "in Rome, do as the Romans do" - and on TikTok, you have to do what the TikTokers are doing. And that's exactly what she's done.'

#375. 'We will be 20 minutes': Callous lies of 'depraved' killer to lure his student stepdaughter into deadly trap laid bare

Published: 01:37 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 01:37 BST, 23 October 2026

The callous web of lies spun by a 'depraved' killer to lure his student stepdaughter into a deadly trap are laid bare in messages recovered by police.

Jobless Nathan Owens, 34, is set to be jailed for life today after a jury took just over three hours to convict him of murdering Carla Georgescu, 19.

Consumed by sexual obsession and jealousy, on February 4, Owens drove through the night to Carla's university accommodation in Preston, Lancashire.

He had duped her into letting him in with a false story that he needed to pick up a purse, supposedly left when he and Carla's mother had joined her for an early birthday meal three days earlier.

Messages reveal how he falsely told Carla 'we' are on our way – when in reality, his wife Janina was asleep and oblivious, at home in bed.

The depraved 'coward' remained silent throughout his police interviews and his trial, meaning exactly what happened next may never be known.

But irrefutable evidence showed that having tricked his way in, Owens subjected Carla to a brutal sexual assault before strangling her, staging the scene to make it appear she had taken her own life.

He then drove home to Hartlepool 100 miles away, disposing of evidence including her mobile phone and bloodied bedding on the way.

Nathan Owens, 34, smirked and flicked his hair when found guilty of killing his stepdaughter on Thursday

Carla Georgescu, a 19-year-old clinical psychology student at the University of Lancashire, was strangled and murdered by Owens. Source: Lancashire Police

On February 1, Owens and his wife Janina had a birthday dinner with Carla in Preston. She was left alone at one point with her stepfather, where they are both seen looking at their phones

And in a final unimaginably callous act, on his arrival he deleted the last message Carla sent her mother to help cover his tracks.

When Carla's body was found, police initially assumed she had hanged herself.

However they became suspicious when they found footage of Owens arriving alone that night with a blanket over his head.

As the net tightened – with a desperate Owens searching online 'I think the police think I'm guilty’ – he set about deleting his electronic devices.

But thanks to telematics information later downloaded from Owens' Ford Puma, detectives would establish where he had stopped to dump evidence, and recovered Carla's phone.

It revealed how at 1.27am on February 4, Owens sent his 'intelligent, gentle and articulate' stepdaughter a message asking if she was awake.

When Carla replied that she was, Owens wrote: 'Your mum forgot her wallet at yours.

'We are going to come and get it, we should be there from 3.45 to 4.

'I'm sorry but she needs it before you leave.'

Carla, in a fluffy dressing gown, caught on CCTV letting her stepfather into her accommodation

Owens captured leaving the building around an hour-and-a-half later, 'shielding' himself from cameras with an umbrella and face-mask, while wearing Carla's trainers and carrying two bags

On the face of it, the urgency of the overnight dash was because Carla, a talented artist, was due to fly to her native Romania the following day to meet up with a boyfriend she had met online.

In reality, prosecutor Nicholas Lumley KC told his trial at Preston Crown Court it was his 'last chance to catch her before she went to Romania, to have her before anyone else could'.

His motivation was 'to satisfy his sexual needs, come what may', he added.

Totally taken in, Carla responded asking: 'What did it look like?'

After sending her a detailed description to keep up the pretence, at 3.35am Owens followed up by writing: 'We will be 20 minutes.'

Again, it was a lie – there was no 'we', Janina Georgescu was still asleep in bed.

Chillingly, as he prepared his evil plan, at 0.56am Owens had messaged his wife: 'I love you more than anything.'

Police suspect the purpose of the text was to check she had remained asleep.

CCTV caught Owens shopping in Asda with Carla's mother while her body lay undiscovered in her university halls

Police bodycam footage played at Preston Crown Court shows Owens, 34, being arrested

In the meantime, at 2.19am Carla had sent her mother a message in Romanian, asking: 'Where did you leave your purse?'

Finally moments before 4am, Owens messaged Carla 'Hereed' – meaning 'Here'.

Footage shows how he deliberately parked in a side street, rather than in one of the spaces outside the block.

CCTV then shows second-year University of Lancashire clinical psychology student Carla – wearing a fluffy dressing gown and pyjamas – letting Owens into Ribble Hall.

At this stage Owens' head is hidden by a patterned blanket – although he momentarily glances towards the camera, revealing his face.

He may have explained away Carla's mother's absence by saying she was asleep in the car, prosecutors said.

Owens was then captured leaving the building around an hour-and-a-half later, 'shielding' himself with an umbrella and wearing a face-mask.

In a grim sign of the bloody scene which had by now played out, he was wearing Carla's trainers and carrying two bags.

Carla's body was found at her University of Lancashire accommodation, Ribble Hall in Preston, on February 5 after her mother raised the alarm

When he arrived home at around 8.30am, his wife later recalled how he made no mention of seeing Carla in the night and seemed 'his normal self'.

But in a final betrayal, police established that Owens had deleted Carla's final message to her mother from Ms Georgescu's phone lest she become suspicious.

She later told jurors how the couple later went for their regular walk at a nearby beach together and also shopping at an Asda store – all while Carla's body lay undiscovered.

But over the course of the day, Ms Georgescu became worried when Carla did not respond to her messages and calls.

On February 5 – which would have been Carla's 20th birthday – she contacted university security and her body was found.

Police broke the news to the couple, with Carla's death initially put down to suicide.

Yet within hours, Owens was carrying out web searches about how police investigate suspicious deaths while also wiping his electronic devices.

He later gave Mrs Georgescu a false story about having gone to Preston that night because Carla had wanted him to take incontinence pants to her and help tidy her room.

And when police returned to the couple's home to ask about his movements that night, Owens lied that he and his wife had been to see Carla together.

At that stage Ms Georgescu was again asleep in bed and unable to contradict him.

By then, however, detectives had grounds to arrest him on suspicion of her murder.

The trial heard how jobless Owens hid his secret depravity from his psychotherapist wife.

Owens had become 'sexually fixated' with Carla, secretly taking pictures of her dressed in her underwear.

His 'escalating fascination' with Carla included having sex with a life-sized 'effigy' of his teenage stepdaughter which he had clothed in her nightdress.

On Thursday Owens smirked as jurors convicted him of murder and grievous bodily harm with intent.

He previously pleaded guilty to two counts of making indecent images of Carla over doctored childhood images.

#378. Ipswich on 'inevitable' path to WSL - Boswell

Boswell joined Ipswich's academy in 2019 and was made captain as a 20-year-old in 2023

Ipswich Town Women are on an "inevitable" trajectory to promotion to the Women's Super League, according to club captain Maria Boswell.

The Tractor Girls finished ninth in WSL2 last season following promotion to the second tier in 2025, and were in the fourth tier as recently as 2021., external

Under the management of former men's team player David Wright, appointed to the role in April, the Blues are third after five games of the 2026-27 campaign.

"I don't think there's any ceiling to what we can go on and achieve. For me, I just see it [promotion to the WSL] as inevitable," 23-year-old Boswell told BBC Radio Suffolk.

"The way the club's going I don't see it as any other option whether it's this year, or whether it's in five years' time.

"I think that is where this club will naturally belong and fall into just with the intent of the owners and the investment we've had and where they see the club. I don't see it happening any other way and I do hope that I'm part of it when it does happen."

Boswell joined Ipswich's academy in 2019 and was named captain as a 20-year-old in 2023.

The club started this season with draws against Nottingham Forest and Southampton, before winning consecutive league games against Leicester City, Wolverhampton Wanderers and Sheffield United.

On Sunday they will host second-placed Sunderland at Colchester Community Stadium.

"We've brought in such good players and I think looking around we kind of got to end of pre-season and decided that there was no reason why we shouldn't strive for that [promotion to the WSL]," said Boswell.

"I think it's about coming in with that in the back of your mind but not letting it kind of get too ahead of yourself or cloud everything else you do.

"It's just about coming in training with the intent that we do every single session and then hopefully going out on a Sunday and putting in performances that earn us the three points which at the moment we're doing, but it's not given that that just naturally continues just because it's how we started."

#381. Law firm at the heart of Prince Harry's disastrous hacking claim against the Daily Mail's publisher calls in insolvency experts

Published: 21:11 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 01:31 BST, 23 October 2026

A law firm at the heart of Prince Harry's disastrous failed hacking claim against the Daily Mail's publisher has called in insolvency experts, it has been reported.

Thomson Heath Jenkins is said to have summoned the practitioners and its office has closed. One source in the company told The Telegraph it had been 'a shock for staff'.

The law firm fronted one of the biggest legal battles in recent times: the sensational hacking trial brought against Mail publisher Associated Newspapers by the Duke of Sussex and six other well-known claimants, Baroness Doreen Lawrence, Sir Elton John, his husband David Furnish, model Liz Hurley, actress Sadie Frost and former Lib Dem justice minister Sir Simon Hughes.

In July, the High Court exonerated the Mail, throwing out every single one of the 97 allegations against its journalists whom Harry and his fellow claimants had accused of criminal activity by phone hacking, landline tapping, car tracking and other unlawful means of gathering information.

After the three-month trial, the duke and his co-claimants lost comprehensively, with the judge describing Mail journalists as honest, truthful, straightforward, careful, impressive, convincing and credible.

Harry and co were presented with a bill up to £34.5million in costs after the High Court ruled their 'inadequate' case had been 'unreasonable to a high degree'.

Prince Harry, shown here in his most recent interview, comprehensively lost his hacking case against the publisher of the Daily Mail

In August, Mr Justice Nicklin granted a rare 'indemnity order' obliging them to pay extra costs, concluding that not only did they lose their 'speculative' case but they knew even before launching it that the evidence was insufficient.

After the July ruling, the duke issued a statement implying the judge was biased and branding his 426-page ruling 'a complete and obvious whitewash'.

Since then, a deadline has passed for Harry's side to lodge any appeal with the trial judge.

Thomson Heath Jenkins was one of the firms of solicitors who spearheaded the disastrous case.

The claimants lodged it in October 2022 and the damaging allegations were maintained for over four years, in spite of weak evidence, until Mr Justice Nicklin quashed every one of them.

Solicitor Mark Thomson, who founded the company in 2009 and owns 100 per cent of the shares, personally represented Ms Frost and Sir Simon. In total, seven lawyers from the firm worked on the case.

Mr Thomson gave evidence during the case. In the witness box, he told the judge that Dr Evan Harris and Graham Johnson, researchers working for his own clients, were 'overexcited' or perhaps simply 'trying to impress Hugh Grant' when they declared in various messages that they had gathered critical information from a whistleblower.

On Thursday, Thomson Heath Jenkins was contacted for comment but there was no response.

Only last week, the law firm announced it was 'thrilled to share that we have once again secured our high ranking' in industry bible Chambers & Partners UK Guide 2027. It said the firm had been recognised for its 'strong privacy and reputation management department'.
