#402. Growing up as the child of a mother who had an affair with a married man: When I was 14, mum handed me a letter to open when she died. Decades later she killed herself. Her heart-breaking message to me: 'Find the love I never did'

Just before bed one night, when I was eight, my mum told me she had a new boyfriend.

She seemed lighter than usual, excited even. But then she told me that Graham was married.

‘That means our relationship has to be kept secret,’ she said solemnly. ‘Promise not to tell anyone?’

I nodded, a slightly nervous feeling in my stomach. I had always been told not to lie, so this went against everything I had been taught.

But I adored my mum and wanted to do what she asked. I couldn’t have known how significant that moment would turn out to be for me, drawn into a world of deceit before I was old enough to comprehend it.

Understandably, there is rarely sympathy for the mistress in a story of infidelity, but I believe there should be more recognition for how children of the ‘other woman’ are impacted.

Certainly, it shaped me in fundamental ways, from how I saw men and relationships to bottling up my feelings to an unhealthy extent, and struggling with trust in my own marriage years later.

Mum was in her late 20s when she met Graham on a night out, three years after she split from my dad.

Sophie was a child of the 'other woman', and she says it has affected her own relationships including her marriage

'I adored my mum and wanted to do what she asked,' writes Sophie Hunt

She had tried hard to make her marriage work but Dad was an alcoholic who could become violent when drunk. While I rarely saw him, I still loved him and cherished a silver cross he had bought me, which I kept in a blue velvet pouch.

Mum, meanwhile, worked hard so we didn’t go without, and she owned our house and the shop she worked in.

Soon after she told me about Graham, he came round one day.

I didn’t know what to expect but I was surprised by how smart he was, a well-off businessman dressed in a tweed blazer, shiny shoes and an expensive-looking watch.

I could see he was handsome but – a decade older than Mum – I thought he seemed a little dull for my fun, vivacious mother.

However, he was generous and money was no object. He always paid for holidays and showered Mum with jewellery.

He told me he didn’t have any children of his own but was very patient with me and would help with any tricky homework.

Graham would come over a few nights a week. Mum was so happy when he was around and I began looking forward to his visits, too.

He couldn’t take the place of my dad, but it was nice to have a father figure again.

I would get board games ready for us to play and draw pictures for him, even though he could never take them home.

Sophie's mum split from Sophie's dad, pictured, three years before meeting Graham

Sophie enjoyed having a father figure again and would draw pictures for Graham

A few months later, Mum and I spotted Graham and his wife in a supermarket.

Mum seemed shocked but I did as I was told, careful not to make eye contact with either of them. From a quick glance, I saw that his wife was beautiful.

To make sure we didn’t bump into them, it was almost as if we were playing a game of hide-and-seek around the aisles. It was exciting, but also felt wrong.

Life with Mum and Graham could be fun. We went to the Algarve and travelled around Britain in his sports car.

When Graham took us skiing in the French Alps, I was bursting to tell my friends how much fun I’d had, but I had to keep it to myself.

It wasn’t the kind of holiday Mum could afford, so I told people we had been to Spain instead. Mum loved the sun, so it sounded much more believable.

Looking back, I realise what a burden it was for a young child to carry these adult secrets. Unable to talk to anyone about what was happening, I began to internalise the idea that uncomfortable feelings were best kept to myself.

Clearly, Mum hoped that she and Graham would become an official couple. But three years into their affair, he told her he couldn’t leave his wife.

From my bedroom, I heard him say his wife had taken the news of him wanting to leave very badly, and he was worried about her mental health. But Mum was just as distraught. I heard her in hysterics and watched as she ran out into the street after him, howling.

Although I didn’t fully understand what was happening, I began to cry too. Mums were supposed to be strong and it was horrible seeing her like this. I also felt sad because I’d grown to like Graham and see him as a stepdad.

Mum struggled in the aftermath. She began having panic attacks and they were so terrifying I thought she was dying. Aged just 11, it was down to me to cheer her up, but I wasn’t sure how.

About a month later, I was arriving home from a school trip when I saw Mum looking out of the window as if she was waiting for me, still wearing her dressing gown. I knew something bad had happened.

When I stepped into the kitchen, she said, ‘Sophie, your dad has died.’

I burst into tears and we sobbed together. He was only 34, and Mum told me he had drunk himself to death.

Sophie stayed with her aunt's family to finish the school term when her mum and Graham first moved in together

But while I grieved, I found it difficult to speak about Dad with Mum, knowing how much he had hurt her in the past. It was another thing I had to keep to myself.

There was further drama to come. Within a few weeks, Mum and Graham were back together – and this time it appeared he had left his wife for good.

They bought a modest three-bedroom house in a different town, where nobody knew them. Meanwhile, I stayed with Mum’s sister and her family to finish the school term, visiting at weekends.

It felt as though Mum had prioritised her relationship with Graham over me, and I struggled with feelings of rejection, especially so soon after losing my dad.

It was a hellish time, when my own panic attacks – which would continue to plague me for decades, only stopping a few years ago – began.

Once the holidays started, I moved in with them and felt relieved that the affair was out in the open at least. The burden of keeping their secret was finally over.

But it wasn’t the fresh start Mum hoped for. Because, even though Graham said he loved her, he never committed to marrying her. And as the years passed, Mum told me that he was seeing other women, too.

I tried to persuade her to leave him, telling her she could have any man she wanted. I even wrote to Graham – who spent long periods away for work – to say he’d broken Mum’s heart and to leave her alone. He never replied or acknowledged it.

But he was all Mum wanted, and she eventually accepted an arrangement in which he supported her financially and promised not to leave her.

Graham’s wife – I don’t know if he ever actually divorced her – sent Mum hate mail, warning her that he would always be unfaithful, and Mum would read these letters to me.

Looking back, these were not appropriate things for a mother-to-be sharing with her 14-year-old daughter. But Mum needed someone to share the pain and humiliation of her relationship with – and that person became me.

Our lives revolved around whether Graham was around or absent. He preferred Mum not to work, so she would be free to go on holiday with him.

It was around this time that Mum handed me an envelope on which she’d written: ‘To Sophie, Not to be opened until my death.’

I was confused – Mum was only 36, hardly old – but all she told me was to keep it somewhere safe.

By then, I was so used to keeping Mum’s secrets that it never occurred to me to open the envelope before I was supposed to. Bemused, I tucked it away in my diary.

Only now do I realise what a burden it was to be given something like that, planting the thought of losing Mum in my mind at an age when I should never have had to worry about such a thing.

All the while, Graham’s other affairs continued. Mum felt trapped, knowing that she would be left with nothing if they separated. I also felt that she couldn’t bear the thought of Graham’s wife being proved right.

But I watched how his lies and betrayals diminished her. She went from vibrant and sociable to thin and increasingly withdrawn, eventually becoming almost reclusive.

At 15, I began having suicidal thoughts. I was still grieving my father and struggling with everything I had kept bottled up since I was eight. Mum didn’t notice anything amiss, too caught up in her relationship troubles.

So, without telling anyone, I made an appointment to see the doctor. I broke down in front of the GP, who prescribed me antidepressants.

Days later, Mum found the tablets hidden under some drawers and was furious. She told me I didn’t know what depression was. I knew she was suffering, but I needed help, too.

I went straight into work after leaving school, ending up in retail working for a clothing brand.

When I was 22, I secured a transfer from our home in the North of England to one of the company’s London stores. I was excited to start a new adventure. I needed space to discover who I was.

Moving into head-office roles I grew in confidence professionally, though I lacked confidence when it came to men. As a result of my childhood, I didn’t trust that they wouldn’t betray me.

After school, Sophie ended up working in retail for a clothing brand (pictured at 21 with her mum)

But then I fell in love with a guitarist with a big personality, and we got engaged.

At 28, we had a son together. But after his birth, I suffered from postnatal depression and Mum urged me to come home. In the end, I returned north as a single mum with a two-year-old, and it was wonderful seeing Mum so happy to spend time with us.

Graham was still on the scene, too, though was still unreliable.

Within a few months, determined not to give up on love, I signed up to a dating website and met David, then 31, an electrician. He had recently come out of a long-term relationship and, like me, had a son, then seven.

We chatted online for a few weeks before meeting in person and, from that moment, were inseparable.

I was open with David about everything I had been through from the start. He was shocked that I had endured so much yet seemed, as he put it, quite ‘normal’.

I loved that he had grown up with siblings and parents who had been married for 33 years, and who seemed to have no secrets between them.

Fourteen months later, David proposed at midnight on Christmas Eve, hiding an antique engagement ring inside a cracker.

I had never been so happy. I was 31, had my little boy, a fiancé I loved and a wedding to look forward to.

But just seven days later, on New Year’s Eve 2012, Graham – who by then had been in a relationship with Mum for 23 years – knocked on my door looking broken, with a police car parked outside. ‘Your mum has killed herself,’ he said. She was just 53.

I was absolutely devastated. While she hadn’t seemed happy for a long time, I never thought she would take her own life, especially as she adored my son and was excited about my engagement. I’ll never know if there was a final catalyst that sparked her decision.

The next day, New Year’s Day, I remembered her letter, to be opened upon her death, and finally opened it:

When the time comes for you to meet the man of your life, learn by my mistakes and make sure he is the right one. Don’t let men take advantage of you. Find someone who absolutely adores you and loves you so much it hurts. It has to be 100 per cent or nothing.

Knowing that she had written those words almost two decades earlier, when she was only 36, was heartbreaking.

While she had not handled some aspects of my childhood well, she was still my mother and I loved her. And she wanted me to have the kind of love she had never found herself.

In the months that followed, I had grief counselling – the first time I had ever opened up to a professional. It was such a release to let out the emotions I had kept bottled up for so many years.

There were plenty of tears, not only for the loss of Mum but for Dad too. We spoke about how difficult it can be to feel truly secure when you have experienced people you love hiding the truth and telling lies.

Sophie, her son and her mum enjoy time at the park

I was so grateful to have David’s support too and we married in June 2014. But my brain wouldn’t let me accept that I had found my happy ever after.

Mum’s letter stayed with me. She meant well, but I found myself asking was David the right man for me?

For a while, I became convinced that he must be having an affair. After all, growing up watching Mum and Graham, I had been raised to believe people would betray you.

But David remained steadfast, and transparent about everything he did, and told me I had to learn that not everyone acted the way Graham had.

Through grief, time and support, Mum’s letter made me realise that I had, in fact, found my person. David had seen me at my lowest – but through it all he stood by me.

In fact, I’m not sure how I would have coped with everything that followed without him.

Now 45, I’ve started writing my memoir, My Darling Sophie, because I want my son, who is now 17, to understand more about me and the grandparents he never had the chance to know.

When I think about my son when he was aged eight, I can’t imagine asking him to keep a secret like my mother did.

He was so little and it makes me realise just how much I was asked to take on at an age when I should have been allowed to be a child.

I have compassion for Mum, who had been through so much and was chasing her own happy ending. Ultimately, I feel more blame for everything that happened lies with Graham, so I don’t resent Mum. I just wish she had realised what she was asking me to carry and, later, that I needed emotional support, too.

I want my son to know that he can tell me anything. I never want him to feel that his pain doesn’t count because someone else is going through something worse.

Today, Mum’s ashes sit in a ceramic case in my dressing room, alongside a bottle of her favourite Dior perfume. I’m not sure I will ever feel ready to let her go.

As for Graham, I last had contact with him in 2017, and have no wish ever to speak to him again.

More important is what I have to look forward to. I have my son, David, a family, a career in the design industry that I love, and happiness. I was burdened with secrets I should never have been asked to keep, but I won’t let them define me.

For confidential support call the Samaritans for free on 116 123 or go to samaritans.org.

#406. I trusted my boss. But because of his lies, I'm now in £250,000 of debt - and about to lose the family home

Six months ago, Nicky Oakley was packing up her three-bedroom house, buzzing with excitement to move into her dream ‘for ever home’ with her partner and their three children.

The four-bedroom Victorian property, set in sprawling gardens, was supposed to mark the beginning of an idyllic new chapter.

Instead, the move exposed a nightmare scenario. Unknown to her, Nicky had a six-figure debt and her home was in the process of being repossessed, after her signature was forged on court documents.

While she should have been sipping champagne, a stunned Nicky was learning that her boss – and friend of nearly 20 years – had defaulted on loans secured against her property. To cover his tracks, he had forged emails from solicitors and faked Nicky’s signature.

Forced to turn legal sleuth to fight for her home, Nicky discovered she wasn’t the first person to lose thousands to James Kenny. In 2007, he had been handed a two-year suspended sentence after admitting to forging his own wife’s signature on a second mortgage application, even setting up a fake law firm website to trick her. (They have since divorced.)

Further digging revealed he had duped other employees: Nicky knows of at least four other women who say they’ve lost thousands after being conned by the same man.

Shockingly, despite Nicky reporting what happened to Merseyside Police and the Report Fraud service, no action is being taken against Kenny. Meanwhile, she has no idea if she and her children will even have a roof over their heads by Christmas.

‘My life is in absolute tatters,’ says Nicky, fighting back tears. ‘I’ve been used by a man I’d known for decades and am on the verge of financial ruin. I feel like such an idiot for falling for his lies, but I trusted him implicitly.’

Nicky Oakley knows of at least four other women who say they’ve lost thousands after being conned by James Kenny

Nicky says of James Kenny: 'He was such a likeable guy, the life and soul of the party'

Nicky met Kenny in 2007 when they worked for a luxury wedding venue in Cheshire. Charming and ambitious, Kenny was the operations manager. ‘He was such a likeable guy, the life and soul of the party,’ says Nicky. ‘He was a little eccentric, but that’s the kind of person you sometimes need in events. He was good at his job and we worked well together.’

The pair worked closely for around 18 months before Nicky left to have her first child. ‘He’d message every few months, even asking if I wanted to work for him a couple of times. I was working freelance around my children, and although I appreciated James’s offers, the timing was never quite right.’

After a contract ended in 2023, she contacted Kenny to see if he had any jobs that might suit her. He claimed to have the opportunity of a lifetime: he was launching the world’s first pirate-themed festival, complete with pirate ship, working cannons and a crew of actors.

‘James thought it was a multi-million-pound idea and was already looking at rolling it out across Europe,’ says Nicky. ‘It was easy to get caught up with his enthusiasm.’

He offered her the role of director of operations with a salary of around £50,000, plus a £10,000 bonus.

‘I couldn’t resist the opportunity,’ Nicky said. ‘Ironically, I was actually glad to work with someone I liked and trusted again.’

There was just one catch. Kenny explained that the project was waiting on the arrival of a guaranteed lottery grant and he needed a short-term loan to get things off the ground. He claimed he couldn’t take out a loan totalling £60,000 himself because he was living in church accommodation, following the death of his father, a vicar.

He asked Nicky to act as a guarantor, using her home as collateral.

‘I don’t consider myself to be someone who takes financial risks,’ Nicky explains. ‘I went over the paperwork in minute detail, checking a letter confirming the lottery funding [a document Nicky later discovered had been faked].

When Kenny offered her the role of director of operations with a salary of around £50,000, Nicky 'couldn't resist the opportunity'. ‘Ironically, I was actually glad to work with someone I liked and trusted again,’ she says

'James assured me the £4,000 a month repayments would be no problem and I believed him. He hadn’t come to me with the idea, I’d asked him for work. I thought I knew him really well. Now, I feel like such a fool. It was the worst decision of my life.’

While waiting for the festival budget to kick in, Nicky juggled a part-time job as a teaching assistant with meetings with suppliers. But within three months, she received a letter stating that Kenny had defaulted on the loan repayments.

‘I called him in an absolute state,’ Nicky recalled. ‘I was on the verge of tears, asking how he could do this to me and why hadn’t he paid.

‘He assured me that there had just been some teething problems with the payments being set up and that the money was there.’

At the same time, Nicky received a letter regarding the lottery grant, explaining it would not be awarded due to fraud checks. ‘I was absolutely furious with James,’ Nicky recalls. ‘The lottery money was supposed to pay off the loan – I was terrified.’

Again, Kenny had an answer; he claimed to have had a business partner years before who’d been convicted of fraud. Nicky recalls: ‘He was apologising to me. He appeared devastated and as shocked as I was that his connections meant we’d had the money taken away.’

While Nicky looked up his former business partner, she didn’t think to search under Kenny’s name, too.

His solution was simply to take out a second bridging loan – totalling £142,500 – to cover the first and buy Nicky some breathing space. Nicky felt she had no choice but to sign as guarantor for the second loan, to stop her home from being taken.

Kenny claimed to have had a business partner years before who’d been convicted of fraud as a way of explaining the fraud checks

‘James somehow managed to suck me in and reassure me,’ Nicky recalls. ‘He’d be on the phone going, “Don’t worry Nicky, I’m sorting this, I’m not going to let you lose your house.”

‘He’d always managed to solve problems when we worked together before so I trusted him.

‘He was utterly convincing, telling me the loan company must have made a mistake with their letter to me because he’d had communication that it was all in hand. I wanted to – and needed to – believe him.’

To reassure her, Kenny put Nicky in touch with his solicitor. After weeks of anxious email exchanges, in June 2025, Nicky finally received written confirmation from the solicitor that the entire debt had been cleared in full. She also received an official Satisfaction of Charge certificate – confirming that she was no longer responsible for the debt.

‘It felt like a weight had been lifted,’ said Nicky. ‘My house was safe and I even felt a little guilty for not trusting James when he’d told me it was going to be sorted.’

Three months later, Nicky and her partner found their dream Victorian home in Cheshire and put their house on the market.

The brutal truth unravelled just days before they were due to exchange contracts. ‘I was standing in my living room, with boxes everywhere, just a few days before we were due to move,’ Nicky explained. ‘I got a call from our estate agent, saying: “Nicky, we can’t proceed, there’s a repossession order on your house.”

‘My head started spinning. I rang James, sobbing, asking him what was going on. He told me there must be some mistake but I just didn’t believe him any more.

‘I grabbed all my carefully filed documents, walked to my nearest solicitor and begged someone to help me.’ What the solicitor uncovered over the next few hours was horrifying.

The debt clearance letter had been a forgery, a court repossession order was already under way – and Nicky’s signature had been forged on a court consent order in August 2025. This must be signed by a homeowner in the case of a repossession in order to agree that their home is to be forfeited to pay a debt.

Nicky recalls: ‘My hands shook with fury as I read the email chain with messages supposedly from me to the loan company, consenting to them taking my home. The rose-tinted spectacles just fell from my eyes. James wasn’t there to talk his way out of it; I had black-and-white proof that my signature had been forged. Nobody else could have done it. He’d been playing me all along.’

Even the correspondence with Kenny’s solicitor was fake. Although he had indeed had dealings with this solicitor in the past, he’d not practised for years and had no idea his name had been used. Kenny had created a spoof email address in the solicitor’s name, forging legal correspondence – including the Satisfaction of Charge document – to keep Nicky in the dark.

‘I called James in tears and, incredibly, he still pretended he didn’t know anything about forged documents,’ says Nicky. ‘Later, he sent me a number of video notes telling me not to worry – and admitting he had signed the court document, not me.’

Rather than apologising, he was still trying to give the impression they were in it together.

‘My world collapsed. I felt so guilty that I’d got my family caught up in this mess, guilty for the other people in our chain who had lost their houses – I’d been completely fleeced.

‘Not only had we lost our dream home but we were weeks away from losing our current one.’

In November 2025, it transpired that Nicky owed £215,000 to the loan company, which included additional fees implemented by them as a result of non-payment. While she has been fighting the repossession of her home, further interest and legal fees mean the amount she currently owes is well in excess of £250,000, a figure that continues to rise.

Nicky’s solicitor advised her to contact the court to delay the repossession. Furious and terrified, Nicky reported the incident to the police, too. But after months with no movement, she had to resort to using her own detective skills. What she discovered left her sickened. Kenny was not just a dishonest boss – he was a convicted fraudster.

‘I felt such an idiot when I typed “James Kenny and fraud” into Google and found a local newspaper article covering the case of him fraudulently signing his wife’s name on mortgage papers.

‘I knew instantly he’d done the same to me.’

Nicky sat open-mouthed as she found more articles reporting on other fake festivals Kenny had claimed to be running – and other victims who explained how he had also ‘employed’ them and never paid them, or persuaded them to invest before defaulting on payments.

‘I’ve since connected with other women he’s duped. Talking to them has made me feel less alone, but the reality is I am still fighting for my home.’

In May, Nicky attended a court hearing to stop the repossession. Although the judge expressed deep sympathy for her plight, the court ultimately ruled in favour of the lender. Legally, any case against Kenny would be treated as separate to the loan company pursuing Nicky. As the guarantor of the loan, her house was the collateral should he default.

The judge at the first hearing ruled that, regardless of any later deception, the lender was entitled to recoup their money.

A spokesman for Merseyside Police told the Daily Mail that Nicky had reported the incident to Report Fraud but that they cannot comment on the case. Report Fraud said: ‘[This report] was assessed by the Report Fraud Analysis Service at the City of London Police but has not been passed to a police force for investigation at this time.’

Meanwhile, Kenny has pocketed more than £200,000 from the two loans. It goes without saying there was never a plan for a pirate festival. Unbelievably, he has repeatedly told Nicky he doesn’t want to fall out with her over what has happened although he hasn’t been in touch since she confronted him over the forged documents. She has heard that he is now living in France. When approached by the Daily Mail, Kenny did not respond.

Nicky has managed to delay the repossession by asking for an appeal and is arguing that the repossession should never have gone ahead as the order was not signed by her.

With legal fees mounting, she has been forced to set up a GoFundMe page in a desperate bid to save her property before the court deadline passes.

‘I’m embarrassed that I’ve had to set up a crowdfunder to pay legal fees,’ Nicky admits.

‘People have kindly donated almost £2,000 but it barely touches the sides.

‘I want James Kenny to face justice – but right now, my only priority is keeping a roof over my children’s heads.’

#413. JAN MOIR: Meghan, with her sprinkles and faux bonhomie, is hard enough to bear but this is why Prince Harry is far worse... no wonder William looks haunted

Published: 01:00 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 01:00 BST, 23 October 2026

Our dear friends the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been back in the UK for almost 50 days but already it seems like a century – if not two.

Did you think they were going to keep a polite and deferential low profile in respect of King and country? Oh, you poor fools.

Let’s be frank. Re-Megxit has been chaos, a family uprooting that seemed wild and capricious from the get-go.

‘For us, when certain stars align, and it’s clear that this should or probably will end up being the case, then we lean into that,’ Prince Harry blathered to GQ magazine this week, explaining why he shifted continents and moved his family back from California to the Cotswolds on what seemed to be a whim long divulged to no one, least of all his father.

Stars align? Harry sounds like a tweenie journaling his feels in a shiny pink diary and sucking the end of a glitter pen because he doesn’t know how to spell ‘genetic pain’ properly.

To date, the couple went to a pub, the Prince got booed at a rugby match, the children had to change schools, the Duchess launched a range of chocolates that cost £5 each and we all went to Nottingham for a performative charity meet and greet to keep up royal appearances.

At a foodbank in the city, Meghan was coming on strong, acting like Scarlett O’Hara handing out silk kerchiefs to her servants at Tara as she helped pack tins of food into plastic bags.

She was talking and asking a lot of questions to show her bountiful concern, it was really a beautiful moment. Are these baked beans individually wrapped? Is it easy to chunk a pineapple? I love Tesco, it’s always been my favourite opera. Please, allow me to donate a morning’s jam profits to the local Chimney Sweep Society. Here are six packets of my flower sprinkles to give to those who have nothing. When you say just put a tin in the bag and move on, what exactly do you mean?

‘For us, when certain stars align, and it’s clear that this should or probably will end up being the case, then we lean into that,’ Prince Harry blathered to GQ magazine this week

Our dear friends the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been back in the UK for almost 50 days but already it seems like a century – if not two, writes Jan Moir

Meanwhile, Harry gave a grief masterclass online which included a section called ‘Turn Pain Into Profit’. Sorry my mistake – ‘Turn Pain Into Purpose’. We all know that our boy has been giving the world a masterclass in grief for most of his adult life and many are heartily sick of it, particularly since mentions of his mother Diana are increasing exponentially as the 30th anniversary of her death approaches.

No one would argue that it is not a tragedy and a sadness that a boy lost his mother when he was only 12 years old.

Yet, without diminishing anyone’s sorrow, isn’t it also true to say that bereavement is survivable – and the only way through the unbearable is to bear it as best you can.

‘I’ve done different forms of therapy and I put in the work,’ Harry said this week. Good for him, even if it is a remark straight from the Kardashian playbook of luxury struggles.

For me, the worst moment so far has been the Prince’s typically peevish interview with GQ. It was very revealing, just not in the way he likely imagined.

Harry stated that he wants reconciliation with his family because life is too short, then seemed to blame someone – Prince William, Sooty, Shergar, Prince William, Scooby Doo, Simba, Prince William, take your pick – before later insisting he meant nothing of the sort.

Listen. If Harry cannot make himself clear in these interviews, he shouldn’t be doing them. There always seems to be an apology, a pushback, a sly clarification.

Here he revelled in presenting himself as the injured party trying to make peace with his family, yet there is never any talk of reconciliation with Thomas Markle is there?

Harry stated that he wants reconciliation with his family, including his brother William, because life is too short

Think about that, the next time you see Harry and Meghan hugging strangers and acting like God’s greatest gift to the world of charity.

Harry also talked about his fight with the British Press and how he wants to protect journalists. This came as a shock to many of my colleagues, whom he falsely accused of gross misconduct in his recent court case against this newspaper. He and his co-defendants comprehensively lost and now face legal bills in the millions.

But instead of being embarrassed or ashamed or even apologising, Harry is incorrigible, deluded and obsessed.

He ran away from England, he is a loser in court and had few successes in America.

One of the main reasons he has returned is because – like a salmon swimming upstream to spawn – he has a need, an elitist’s desire to have his children educated at the same kind of exclusive, expensive establishments with selective admission policies which he himself attended. He may claim to hate tradition and the Establishment but, at heart, he’s just another posh drone.

Meghan, with her sprinkles and faux bonhomie, is hard enough to bear but Prince Harry is far worse. He has notions.

What Re-Megxit has proved beyond doubt is that he sees himself as a hero who is both righteous and wronged, as both crusader and victim, as a man who is above reproach and beneath the dignity of accountability.

Now I understand why Prince William always looks so haunted, how the King keeps a careful distance, why courtiers pull down the portcullis at the mention of his name.

For Harry is a one-man riot, a looter trying to smash and grab his way back into The Firm, convinced of the imperative and his self-appointed role as moral custodian and hero.

Peacemaker, Prince, pest, the great pretender.

He is just never going to stop until he gets his way.

Marie Curie was the first person – not just the first woman – to win two Nobel Prizes. In two different branches of science. She discovered radium and coined the word ‘radioactivity’.

Her research and work were world renowned. When she was once asked how it felt to marry a genius, she replied: ‘Go and ask my husband.’

Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, yet she does not get a mention on the current GCSE science curriculum

Girls should be learning about her in science lessons – and be inspired by her example. Instead she doesn’t even get a mention on the current GCSE science curriculum – and neither does Lise Meitner, who was involved in the discovery of nuclear fission. However, 85 men do feature. Of course they do.

A report from Cambridge academics has found that girls could be put off taking science and maths A-levels because of the dearth of women and females on the syllabus.

It shouldn’t take a rocket scientist to work that out. Disgraceful.

Kathryn Turner is the director of product development for Marks & Spencer’s food departments. She has become a huge success online, going viral on TikTok and Instagram with more than half a million followers who enjoy her videos featuring new and improved items from the M&S food range.

I say unlikely – but her success is no surprise to those of us who are devotees of her brisk and oddly fascinating content. ‘I want to talk to you about our pasta sauces,’ Kathryn will begin, and I am gripped.

‘Our chocolate is only ever made with cocoa butter and our Belgian range has had a massive glow up,’ is the kind of thing she will say. ‘You’ve probably noticed we’ve gone a little bit wild on grapes this year,’ she says, as the camera follows her down the M&S fruit aisle and we all nod along in happy contentment.

What is the secret of Kathryn’s success? She is a natural – who is so natural. And that is so unusual. It is delightful to watch someone nonweldable, fresh, businesslike, informative – but most importantly, someone who is not trying to be a star. Kathryn is always in her M&S barrel trousers with her lanyard stuffed in her pocket and her specs on her nose.

Kathryn Turner, director of product development for M&S's food departments, has gone viral on TikTok

She is as enthusiastic about her products as she is about her job. I like her sensible jerseys, her crisp blouses, her barely brushed hair. She embodies something decent and steady about the brand and watching her makes one think, maybe things are not so bad.

‘Have you noticed we’ve started selling most of our beans in jars?’ she asked recently.

I hadn’t but felt oddly comforted by this news. Thank you, Kathryn!

Sunday Rose says it is not fair she has been labelled a ‘nepo baby’, just because she is the daughter of singer Keith Urban and actress Nicole Kidman. Yes, she became a model at 16 and made her Met Gala debut in May wearing Dior, but come on. Give a girl a break. Just like mummy and daddy did.

‘I’m very aware that I’m given opportunities that not everyone can have and I’m truly grateful to be able to take advantage of them,’ Sunday Rose said.

‘So, when I’m at work, I make sure to always give my best, never come to work with a negative attitude, no matter how tired or jet-lagged I may be and treat everyone with respect.’

No bad attitudes! She treats everyone with respect!

I’d say this 18-year-old is going to go far – if she hadn’t already got there.

Pop star Dua Lipa and actor Callum Turner are just so damn glam. I love their look! They walk out for dinner and it looks like a scene from a 1950s Italian film.

Dua Lipa, who has a demanding career as a huge pop star, married Callum Turner this summer

They attend the opera in New York and their very appearance is operatic in itself. The couple married this summer and to manage their demanding global careers they have a golden two-day rule – they are never apart for more than 48 hours.

Charming and romantic – but it won’t last.

When you get to my age you can never be together for more than 48 hours! Make the most of it, kids.

#415. I'm horrified by the helicopter parenting at my son's university

'My daughter was crying so much when we dropped her off. Now she’s struggling to make friends. What should I do?’

‘My son can’t find his timetable. Any ideas?’

‘My son is looking for a football team to join. Where can I find the list of clubs?’

The messages could come straight from a Year Seven parents’ WhatsApp group. However, these concerned mums (and occasionally dads) aren’t asking for help with their 11-year-olds.

No. This is a Facebook group for parents of students at a Russell Group university. The darlings in question are at least 18 years old with brains enough to get into an elite institution. And yet, mummy and daddy are still stepping in to solve their problems, sometimes from hundreds of miles away.

They’re tackling everything from friendship issues – including talking to other parents to set up ‘play dates’ – to finding GPs, organising food deliveries or resolving course problems.

How do I know all this? Well, as the parent of a first-year, I’m on the group, too.

Feeling rather bereft without my son, I thought joining last month would be a way to connect to his new life without bothering him.

A Facebook group for parents of first-year students features posts such as: 'My son can't find his timetable. Any ideas?'

I hadn’t thought much about what other parents might post. I expected it might contain helpful information, such as tips on areas to avoid when looking for second-year flats.

I certainly didn’t expect questions about things students could easily look up themselves, such as where an English module was being held. Or how to accost the administration office about a mucky flatmate who keeps pinching cereal.

I’ve found it shocking and, sadly, this isn’t a one-off.

There are Facebook groups for parents at most universities, all with thousands of members. And all, I imagine, featuring similar dilemmas.

While parents may think they’re doing what’s best for their children, it’s a depressing snapshot of how extreme helicopter-parenting culture has become. After all, isn’t a key part of university growing independence and finding ways to deal with issues yourself?

Thirty years ago, when I started university, long queues for the single payphone on the corridor meant speaking to your parents once a week if you were lucky. You certainly weren’t going to embarrass yourself in public by admitting you had no friends or couldn’t work out your timetable.

Did I ask my parents for help when I missed a deadline because I’d been ill? Or when my milk kept disappearing from the communal fridge? No.

Developing strategies to deal with those not doing their washing up is part of growing up. And, yes, nurturing new friendships is hard. Most people don’t find their tribe straight away, which can leave you feeling insecure and lonely.

Given most parents will have successfully navigated their study years solo, why don’t they now let their children do the same?

But that’s got to be better than having your mum find friends for you at 18 – which is both tragic and unlikely to help develop confidence.

As for getting to grips with academic challenges, if a student is disappointed with their course, that’s on them for not having done proper research before applying.

We complain Gen Z is flaky, with no get-up-and-go. Yet Facebook groups such as this provide ample evidence where much of the problem lies: with us, the parents!

We send our children such mixed messages when we encourage them to spread their wings, then cushion their every landing from life’s bumps, inconveniences and stresses.

Given most parents will have successfully navigated their study years solo, why don’t we let our children do the same?

Maybe it’s because university is now such a huge financial investment that we can’t bear the thought that our children won’t have a good experience.

Perhaps we’ve got too used to monitoring their movements – my husband and I did stalk our son on tracking app Life360 during freshers’ week, but soon realised that way madness lies.

And maybe ‘good’ parenting has become synonymous with hands-on parenting – to the point we are just too enmeshed with our children’s lives.

Yet who will pay for it in the long run, when our over-cossetted children are unable to navigate the adult world? Us again.

I’m not completely unsympathetic to the Facebook parents. My mind is racing about all the issues my son – who contacts me just once a week – could be facing alone.

Is he going to lectures? Doing the required reading? Getting on with his flatmates? Going out, but not too much?

I have to sit on my hands not to send multiple ‘just checking in’ messages a day.

And yet, perhaps his scant communication is best for both of us. What I don’t know about I can’t try to solve. It’s hard, but I just have to trust that he will work things out for himself. Eventually.

And it appears he will get in touch if he really needs us.

Take last Friday. Having not heard a dicky bird for several days I got a message at 11pm saying he’d left his driving licence in a corner shop while buying beer. Could I please send a picture of his passport in case that worked as ID to get him into a club?

I admit I did, though he was still refused entry. It was a vital lesson learned, I hope.

Now I need to learn mine and come off the group. And I’d suggest other parents should do the same.

#419. Woman who stood up to Paris looters in viral video 'is 24-year-old actress' - as internet salutes her bravery

By NICK CRAVEN, SENIOR REPORTER and PETER ALLEN

Published: 00:57 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 01:00 BST, 23 October 2026

A woman who went viral for bravely standing up to the Paris rioters, screaming at them to stop looting a supermarket at the height of the mayhem, has been identified as a 24-year-old actress by French media.

Drama student and model Emma Kunstlich, 24, was horrified when youths clad in balaclavas began smashing shop windows and looting before her eyes, according to French newspaper Le Monde.

Clearly distraught at seeing the mob ransacking the shelves of the convenience store near Place de la Republique, while a male assistant watches helplessly, footage showed the woman trying to block the door to the shop.

Eventually she is pushed out of the way by the thugs, as one of them holds onto her and she screams 'Stop, stop why are you doing this? This is not the cause!'

She added: 'Hey, don't touch me! Stop. What's the point of doing this?

'There's a man inside, by himself! Look! Stop this!'

Her identity was first confirmed by the news organisation. She told them: 'They don't even have a political message. They're just breaking things and stealing, without grasping the consequences of their actions.

'And if the RN [far-right National Rally, led by Jean-Marie Le Pen] comes to power, we're all going to be in deep s**t!'

A source later confirmed to Le Monde that they had been able to confirm Ms Kunstlich's identity amid global speculation.

A woman is seen pleading with rioters not to loot a shop, asking: 'Why are you doing this?'

The woman was pushed aside by looters, while pleading to them: 'This is not the cause'

The clip, which quickly went viral on social media, gained traction with many who sympathised with the anti-government protest, but drew the line at the mindless looting and vandalism which has scarred Paris and other French cities.

As the clip rapidly spread around social media, some posters inevitably added their own spin, such as claiming that she was the owner of a boutique and it was her shop being looted.

Others suggested she had somehow been an enthusiastic advocate for migrants and was now being 'repaid'. There is no evidence to back any of these claims up.

It comes as dozens of protesters took to the Paris streets on Thursday despite bans on demonstrations ordered in multiple French cities following a weekend of clashes and widespread looting that marked France's most violent unrest in years.

Organisers of the Paris protest said an administrative court in the city overturned a ban issued by police.

The Paris police prefecture previously said the ban was necessary, given the risk of street violence after groups of masked youth clashed with police forces, looted shops and torched cars over the weekend.

The Paris court ruling was not immediately made public.

More bans were expected in the coming days. French President Emmanuel Macron said such measures aim to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.

A street barricade burns as clashes between riot police and demonstrators continue for the second day during nationwide protests against the high cost of living in Paris, France, 18 October 2026

A protester dressed as Spiderman gestures as a car burns during a demonstration at Place de Republique on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France

The right to demonstrate in France is protected by the French Constitution, and the ban on demonstrations planned for Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble was seen by some as an infringement on French people's right to protest.

High school and university student groups said they will continue to mobilise, even though the autumn school break started this week.

Macron said the strategy adopted for the coming days is to ban protests requested by 'individuals or groups with no legitimate authority.' His remarks came after a special security meeting at the Elysée Palace.

'Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law, but alternative routes will be proposed' to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, Macron said.

'The rules are simple, and I think they're just common sense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days,' he said.

'For those who still want to protest, if they are trade unions, prefects will propose alternative routes.'

Macron blamed the weekend's violence on 'actions led by radical far-left groups who aimed to bring the Republic down,' in addition to criminals who came to loot.

The turmoil in Paris and other French cities has prompted a strong security response from the government.

Demonstrators clash with riot police in and around Place de la Republique in Paris on October 17, 2026

Protesters gather at Place de la Republique during a demonstration in Paris, France, on October 17, 2026

Night curfews have been implemented in some areas of the French capital, as well as in other cities where calm has been restored.

The ban in Paris applied to areas including the Elysée presidential palace, both houses of parliament, and the city's main train stations. Areas in downtown Paris, which were severely hit by the looting, were also covered.

Thursday's planned protests were seen as a prelude to Saturday's big demonstration, when activists from the 'yellow vest' movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, and the CGT labour union, are expected to join.

Some of those protests, including marches in Lyon, will also be banned, local authorities said.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a 'massive' security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.

Union representatives said their meeting with Lecornu did not result in concrete proposals.

They are now focusing on another big day of action scheduled on Nov. 5, and called on private and public sector employees to join.

The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of staff.

French gendarmerie officers intervene as students stage a sit-in protest outside Sciences Po Paris in Paris, France, on October 22, 2026

French riot police officers intervene to disperse demonstrators during a nationwide protest over rising living costs, fuel prices, and education funding in Nancy, France on Saturday, October 17, 2026

#422. 'I've painted more Lowrys than Lowry' says the world's greatest art forger whose 'Old Masters' sell for £25,000

Published: 23:51 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 00:53 BST, 23 October 2026

David Henty has a very strong work ethic. He rises every day at about 5am, has a quick coffee, sets up his easel and palette – sometimes on the roof terrace of his home in Saltdean, near Brighton, sometimes in the kitchen – and then he begins.

'I start by doing lots of special breathing and meditation to open the pineal gland in the back of the brain that lets you look through your third eye,' he explains.

When he's shut out all white noise, he begins channelling. 'I sort of imagine I'm sticking my finger in the light socket of the universe, picking up frequencies and wavelengths until I'm in a sort of 'flow state' of mind and can start downloading the great masters.'

Which is when, finally, he picks up his brush and starts painting. Perhaps a couple of small Lowrys – 'I've painted more Lowrys than he did!' Or a Picasso – 'so quick and easy'.

Or maybe a soothing Modigliani. Or a quick Van Gogh – 'When he's good, he knocks it out of the park. But when he's off, he's not all that.'

But his favourite is Caravaggio. 'I love him. All that light and dark – it's more how I would paint. At the moment I'm working on his St Jerome Writing in my kitchen and, as a mark of respect, I'm finishing it with my left hand, because he was left-handed, even though I'm not.'

Henty is an art forger. By his own account, the very best art forger in the world, and extremely proud of his work.

He has a blue plaque by his front door – fake, obviously – which declares him 'The World's Number One Art Forger'.

Fine art forger David Henty pictured at The Helm gallery in Brighton alongside his paintings

His car has the number plate 'V9OGH' and his home is filled with Banksies, Rembrandts, Vermeers. Somewhere, downstairs, there's a Mona Lisa.

And what makes him so good, he insists, is this unusual ability to immerse himself in whatever artist he is copying. Van Gogh, in his penury. Caravaggio in his dark cloaks.

Picasso and Lowry with their quick strokes and confidence.

Which, naturally, sounds like a right load of old bunkum. But it turns out that Henty is fantastically successful at his (or, perhaps more accurately, other people's) craft, with his work constantly being mistaken for the real thing – not just by collectors, but by auction houses, gallerists and forensic experts.

So much so that we are standing in a new exhibition of his work in the Helm Gallery in Brighton – surrounded by recognisable masterpieces by Modigliani, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Picasso, Hirst.

They add up to about £1billion worth in the original – and many are sporting red 'sold' dots.

Oh look, there's Vermeer's priceless Girl With The Pearl Earring – a snip at £9,000. And Picasso's Women Of Algiers, which went for $179 million (£134million) in 2015, for £25,000. And that's Leonardo da Vinci's Salvator Mundi, which broke all records when it sold for $450million (£336million) in 2017.

There's also a lost Van Gogh – Painter On His Way To Work – supposedly destroyed in a fire in 1946. And Carel Fabritius's The Goldfinch. 'They're always very popular,' he says. 'I've done lots of them. A small flock,' he says with a glint.

As well as this exhibition, Henty features as central character in a gripping new thriller by Rob Starr about art and insurance fraud (he's already been the inspiration for Peter James's novel and play Picture You Dead). And a biopic of his extraordinary life is due to launch on TV in China.

'They reckon it'll get a billion views! Then we've got an exhibition in Shanghai!'

Vincent van Gogh's, The Painter on the Road to Tarascon, painting in oil on canvas

Meanwhile, his email is constantly pinging and his phone buzzing with commissions from clients who include footballers, hedge fund managers, the Cotswolds set, billionaires, shipping magnates, police officers, and a former controversial Tory billionaire donor and pal of Boris Johnson who couldn't stop buying Modiglianis to give away to his pals and still owes him £50,000.

'He'd take them when the paint was barely dry.'

Some want his copies because, rich as they are, even they can't afford the £170 million it would cost for their own Picasso.

Others, because they own the original, but want to keep it safe – perhaps in a tax-free lock up – but also show it off.

His copies are astonishingly good. Too good, some might say. Back in 2016, Henty got a bit of a shock when one of his Picassos turned up at an auction in Brighton – for £1 million.

'It was just a sketch for a bigger work,' he says. 'Picasso's mate Roland Penrose lived down the road from here, so on the back, for a laugh, I wrote, 'To Roland from Pablo' and gave it to a friend. It was definitely one of mine.'

Anyway, he came clean – 'I wouldn't normally, but it didn't seem fair' – and the sale was pulled, but the broker, who'd been set to make £400,000, went mad and threatened to burn down Henty's house.

'I had to get security and everything. But it wasn't my fault. It was them that did the crime by selling it on.'

Just last week, he tells me, a group of four huge Basquiat lost canvases from the artist's 'Congo' period popped up for £39.2 million, plus 10 per cent buyer's fee. A pal was interested in buying, until Henty warned him off.

Johannes Vermeer, Girl with a Pearl Earring, on display in the Mauritshuis, The Hague, Netherlands

'I said to him, 'Don't buy them. They're mine!' I painted them last year on some 1970s canvases I'd got from the car boot at Brighton for £60.'

They weren't copies. Knowing some of Basquiat's paintings were lost, he just knocked them out 'in the style of' in a couple of days and sold them for £5,000 but somehow, in the intervening 16 months, they'd acquired provenance – evidence that they were genuine.

So someone was trying to make a lot of money but, again, he insists it wasn't him.

'Mine are copies, not forgeries – not any more,' he adds with a roguish grin. 'My buyers always know that I painted them.'

So while he signs the front as the grand master, they are sold 'in the style of,' or 'after Picasso', or Lowry, or whoever takes his fancy. Because he's very keen not to end up in prison. Not again.

Back in the mid-1990s, he did five years for forging thousands of fake British passports which he planned to sell to anxious Hong Kong citizens ahead of the Chinese handover.

The ruse might have made him millions, if only the words 'Britanic' and 'Magesty' hadn't been mis-spelt.

'I was doing the watermarks not the spelling, but it was bloody annoying,' he says.

Soon after he was released, he was back inside, in Madrid this time, for selling stolen cars. 'I know I know. Stupid. But I was on to a brilliant scam and it was hard to resist.'

Growing up, Henty had always had a rather flexible relationship with the law. His father, a 'completely bent' antiques dealer, was often absent.

His mother wasn't really on the scene at all and Henty and his four siblings ran wild in a council house on the outskirts of Brighton.

'There was very little school, no discipline and we'd nick anything that wasn't nailed down,' he beams.

So when he followed his father into antiques, it wasn't surprising that a bit of fiddling crept in. A touched-up picture here. A forged signature there.

'I'm very good at matching paint,' he says.

But it was in prison that he really honed his craft. Joined art classes, started reading up on the great masters – 'I'd always wanted to study fine art' – and, with the help of two of his brothers, selling dodgy paintings at Bermondsey market.

A quick picture of a cottage garden. A few faked signatures. All when he was in prison. He tells the story of one little picture he bought at the car boot at Arundel and re-signed as a Vanessa Bell.

'I got £700 for it and a couple of years later, I spotted it in a Mayfair gallery for £16,000!'

So he set up on eBay. Selling, selling, selling. At least 1,000 'masterpieces' – Lowrys, Picassos, Singer Sargent. 'I've done so many of some, they're like old friends,' he says. All signed. All, presumably, still out there.

Perhaps because, while his 'channelling' sounds a bit of a shaggy dog stretch, he's always done the legwork. 'You've got to be an art historian – to really know your artists – to be a good forger,' he explains.

So he spent thousands of hours immersing himself in the art world. Studying the works up close in art galleries and auction houses, burying himself in art magazines.

And for one birthday, he booked in for two full days to study Caravaggio's 1601 painting, Supper At Emmaus at the National.

'I just sat there looking at it for hours. To see how he did it. How it made me feel. And when I started dreaming about him, I knew I was ready to start painting.'

Which, he did using correctly pigmented paints. Old canvases from the right era as the artist. And developing clever ageing tricks.

He also has endless 'ageing' tricks – 'I was just ageing a Vermeer this morning with some furniture polish – it's very effective!'

Mostly though, he just stashes them down the side of his log burner until teeny cracks appear in the paint. For the patina, he used to drop the paintings off with his late pal 'Lennie the Bag', a chain-smoker who lived in such a thick smog that it would add a lovely 18th century patina to fake a Rembrandt in a couple of weeks.

And if he's really going to town, he might accidentally drop a fibre from an 18th century apron, or similar, into the paint, so it dates itself.

It must have been a massive blow when it all came crashing down in 2014 following an investigation by a national newspaper and he was banned from trading on eBay.

Though not prosecuted because, legally, he wasn't doing anything wrong – though of course some of the people paying hundreds and thousands for his copies, clearly were. 'If they sell it on, it's their crime, not mine.'

But as luck would have it, instead of heralding the end, the exposure attracted a whole new set of buyers, with a lot more money.

'It was brilliant!' he says. Because today, they come to him, paying £25,000 for a Picasso that might take him half a day which seems bonkers but one thing is certain, he is exceptionally good at his craft.

As a result, there are hundreds, perhaps thousands, of his fakes masquerading as the real thing and bristling with security, alarms and infra-red lights.

So finally, for the billion dollar question: Does he feel guilty? 'No! It's not really my problem is it? It's just a bit of fun.'

#425. Moment appalled bystanders confront man after he 'breaks goose's neck' in public park - as police launch probe

Published: 00:51 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 00:52 BST, 23 October 2026

This is the moment a man is confronted by appalled bystanders after a goose allegedly had its neck broken in a public park.

Police are investigating a report of animal cruelty at Ward End Park in the suburbs of Birmingham on October 19 after a video of the distressed bird circulated online.

The clip sees a hooded man staring blankly at the camera with a box – containing bread to attract geese, according to witnesses.

'He's feeding ducks [sic] and he has just killed one,' the person filming the video says. 'He's just broken the duck's neck [sic].'

Panning to the goose, the disturbing footage shows the animal slumped on the turf while still twitching.

'This is what he has done to it,' the cameraman adds as the bird lets out several pained squeals.

The man – wearing a navy Nike hoodie, black coat and trousers – then calmly picks up his box and continues staring down the lens.

Footage shows the man being confronted by appalled bystanders after a goose allegedly had its neck broken in a public park in Birmingham

Police are investigating reports of animal cruelty in the suburbs of Birmingham after a video of a distressed goose circulated online. Footage shows the animal slumped on the turf while twitching

The clip sees a hooded man staring blankly at the camera while holding a box - containing bread to attract geese, according to witnesses

The alleged goose killing comes just days after two opportunistic thieves were filmed picking up a much-loved pet rabbit which was later found dumped in a car park.

The pair were caught on camera stealing eight-year-old Peter from his front garden pen in Hull, East Yorkshire, on Saturday afternoon.

They were seen laughing and joking and could be heard saying, 'We'll make shashlik out of it,' as they walked off with the distressed rabbit.

West Midlands Police confirmed officers are probing the Birmingham video as part of their investigation into reports of cruelty towards a goose in the park.

A spokesman for the force said: 'We received a report of animal cruelty at Ward End Park in Birmingham on 19 October and are making enquiries to establish the circumstances around what happened.

'Officers are working with partners including the park's management and the local authority and are looking to speak to anyone who might have seen what happened and might know who was responsible.'

The clip garnered outrage on social media with users claiming community officers had warned the man in the clip about similar behaviour in the days running up to the incident.

Animal rights activists told the Daily Mail the luring technique allegedly used in the video is occasionally used by farm poachers but is rarely deployed brazenly in broad daylight.

Animal rights activists said the luring technique allegedly used in the video is occasionally used by farm poachers (Pictured: The man with his box)

Animal cruelty investigator Joey Alexander said he had recently conducted an investigation into a phenomenon which saw people at a large free-range turkey farm in Essex taking the birds by the neck and swinging them in circles, before throwing them in the bin.

Mr Alexander insisted the cruelty of what appeared to be happening in the video rivals these previous incidents, especially the fact the alleged killer appears to lure the animal with food.

'There are just shocking and callous parts of this. The bird was likely still conscious when it was flailing on the floor. It is a horrific act of serious animal cruelty.

'It is completely needless and there is no reason for someone to do that. I can understand why the whole public is sickened by it. Only a monster could do that.'

The animal rights activist added that he thought the individual in the clip looked 'disturbed' and did not seem to 'express normal human emotion'.

He said: 'I have heard stories like this before of people killing wild animals in parks to take them home and eat them. I have not actually seen someone doing it.'

The latest set of statistics showed that reports of cruelty involving wild birds hit a five-year peak in summer 2025, according to the RSPCA.

Some 359 incidents involving wild birds – including 26 in the West Midlands alone – were reported during July and August 2025 – almost double the 179 received during the same period in 2024, the charity revealed.

The RSPCA added that this year was shaping up to be just as worrying, with the charity having already received 474 reports involving cruelty to wild birds as of July.

The birds most commonly targeted included pigeons, corvids (such as crows, magpies and ravens), gulls, swans and ducks, with many incidents involving catapults, air weapons and other deliberate acts of violence.

A spokesman for the RSPCA said: 'It's extremely distressing to hear about an attack on a goose. We'd urge anyone with first-hand information about this incident to contact us on 0300 1234 999.

'All wild birds are protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and it is illegal to deliberately kill, injure or take one, except under licence.'

Mr Alexander added that he believes the consequences for harming animals are insufficient and that people might be deterred if they were made more severe.

The current maximum sentence for animal cruelty is five years' imprisonment, an unlimited fine, or both.

'It feels like a brazen act that really highlights the fact that laws protecting animals in this country are not strong enough,' he said. 'People like this need to be made an example of.'

The animal cruelty investigator said that the normal human emotion when confronted with such an incident would be to intervene, but added that the person in the video might have been 'dangerous', in which case it can be best to keep one's distance.

He also expressed concerns that cases of such cruelty seemed to be on the rise in the UK.

'There's a cultural mentality towards animals that they are here to serve our ends,' he said. 'But if someone overtly abuses an animal in front of us, it hits home too hard and we react like this but when it is hidden we are not going to emotionally react.'

The incident comes only days after two men were caught filming themselves grabbing a rabbit from his family home

Single mother Amy Ulliott, 38, and her teenage children were finally reunited with their pet on Sunday after being alerted to a small brown rabbit answering to Peter's description had been found in a car park around a mile away.

Humberside Police are investigating the theft, with Ms Ulliott claiming the CCTV shows them speaking Russian and potentially 'planning to make a stew' out of her pet.

Ms Ulliott said her family were shocked to find the family's pet was missing when they got home and were even more disturbed when they viewed CCTV which showed Peter being callously handled by the ears before being carried away.

Ms Ulliott, a carer, told the Daily Mail: 'No one with an ounce of humanity would do a thing like that to a defenceless rabbit, when I saw what they had done I felt physically sick and had very little hope that I would ever see Peter alive again.'

The family immediately called Humberside Police to report the theft and Ms Ulliott and her family took to the streets to search for him themselves, also posting the shocking video on social media.

The person who eventually found him had taken him in and given him food and water while trying to find his owners – and then, seeing missing posts, got in touch with the good news.

She said: 'Both of them were speaking in what sounded like Russian. And we've been told that one of the men may be called Oleg.'

Ms Ulliott said when she uploaded the footage, she was contacted by a Russian speaker who said he had been able to translate what the men were saying to each other.

She added: 'He told us that one man said to the other, "We'll make shashlik out of it".

'It seems they were saying it was their intention to have him on a skewer like a kebab, which is just a horrifying thought.'

The Daily Mail showed the clip to a Russian translator who confirmed that the language being spoken was Russian, possibly with a Ukrainian accent.

They said the man who grabbed Peter, turned to his friend and said: 'Take a picture of me.'

He then sings a tune and says 'whoa' when the rabbit kicks out at him.

By STACY LIBERATORE, US SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR

Published: 00:46 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 00:46 BST, 23 October 2026

Sailors have reported a mysterious sighting as they crossed the Atlantic this month.

A submission to the National UFO Reporting Center (NUFORC), dated October 11, detailed an encounter with glowing UFOs that the ship's crew said moved at impossible speeds and patterns.

For about 40 minutes, two sailors watched through binoculars as a single orb appeared 12 to 16 miles away, which 'rose and fell rapidly, bearing right and left, periodically shooting at hypersonic speeds, for about 5-10 minutes.'

The report, posted on October 21, claimed that three or four more orbs appeared, which looked the same as the first.

'All twisting and turning, rising and falling together in no set pattern,' the report states.

'Every so often they went somewhere else altogether, at a speed I can only call unreasonable, and then were simply there again.

The NUFORC report included screenshots of the boat's radar, reportedly taken during the encounter, showing nothing on the screens that would suggest objects were in the sky.

A submission to the National UFO Reporting Center (NUFORC), dated October 11, detailed an encounter with glowing UFOs that the ship's crew said moved at impossible speeds and patterns - but did not show up on the boats radar (pictured)

The witness said the encounter began around 3:25am, when the ship’s second mate spotted a strange light low above the horizon, slightly to the left of the vessel’s bow.

The ship was crossing the Atlantic roughly 400 miles south of Nova Scotia, heading east at about 20mph, according to the report.

The witness described clear skies with only a thin crescent moon, saying ‘visibility was great.’

The vessel was not noticeably rocking, and there was ‘no traffic whatsoever’ nearby.

After seeing the first orb, the sailor said: 'The others appeared, 3-4 more. They were like the first in every respect.'

Another startling NUFORC report was submitted last year, featuring a video showing a clear image of what one witness believes was a giant UFO flying over California.

The April 27 video taken by an unnamed resident in Twentynine Palms followed what appears to be a brightly-lit hexagonal craft as it flew over the desert.

The report, posted on October 21, claimed that three or four more orbs appeared, which looked the same as the first. The witness shared screenshots of the radar to show no objects in the sky when they saw the UFOs

The UFO reportedly appeared out of nowhere around 10:27 pm PT while the witness was staying at a remote cabin.

According to the report, the suspected spacecraft was moving very slowly and irregularly, like it was in a daze.

'It seemed to move arbitrarily with no clear path. The movements were jerky and at varying speeds,' the witness wrote in their NUFORC report.

The large object also appeared to pulsate, giving off a bright light from its edges, as it moved through the sky for approximately 15 minutes.

'Tonight is the new moon - so it was definitely not the moon, and in any case was much brighter than even a full moon,' the witness continued.

'The striking thing was its great brightness and irregular shape and path,' they added.

Another startling NUFORC report was submitted last year, featuring a video showing a clear image of what one witness believes was a giant UFO flying over California

As the witness in Twentynine Palms followed the UFO, they added that the strange craft began to change shape - morphing from a six-sided object into a circle.

The person taking the cellphone video was the only witness at the cabin that night, so no one else was able to confirm their story.

However, they declared in their report to NUFORC that they hadn't taken any 'mind-altering substances' during the sighting and had clear vision the entire time.

Officials at NUFORC tried to find an explanation for the sighting, noting that a SpaceX rocket launch had taken place that day, but that Falcon 9 took off from in Florida three hours earlier.

A previous rocket launch created a similar phenomenon over the UK in March.

That bizarre shape was caused by illuminated frozen fuel expelled from the SpaceX rocket, experts revealed.

The light blue spiral is formed when excess fuel that has been released from the fast-spinning rocket turns to ice.

It then reflects sunlight in the upper atmosphere, giving it an otherworldly gleam before becoming water vapor.

The picture, taken by photographer Michelle Cowbourne, was taken at dawn on Thursday, October 22, looking up to the tower of St Michael's Church perched upon the ancient Somerset mound.

The breath-taking snap shows the church against a vivid sky background of red and a deep blue, with an orange rainbow cutting through its centre in perfect symmetry.

Describing how she captured the resplendent shot, Ms Cowbourne said it came just following 'torrential rain'.

She said: 'As the sun rose the clouds rolled in from the west, the torrential rain came just as the sun cleared the horizon and the sky lit up with orange to the left of the scene and dark to the right.

'Then a vivid rainbow appeared above and lasted for just a few moments. It's always exciting when a rainbow appears as it is fairly fast moving, trying to keep the camera as dry as possible and still get the photos. I was absolutely drenched myself.'

In an equally beautiful picture, Ms Cowbourne managed to photograph the rainbow from inside St Michael's Church - with the rising sun casting a yellow glow across the hill and into the town below.

Ahead of Storm Austen's arrival in Somerset, an incredible snap at Glastonbury Tor has captured the site's full majesty as a rainbow appears from an illuminated sky

The beautiful scene was also photographed from inside St Michael's Church upon the hill

The shots come as Storm Austen is forecast to bring gusts of 50 to 60mph to Somerset from Thursday night into Friday, with gusts exceeding 70mph possible in exposed coastal areas.

The Met Office has warned of potential travel disruption, damage to buildings and power cuts across parts of southern England and south Wales.

Forecasters issued an amber wind warning for the far South West ahead of Austen's arrival around midnight, as well as yellow warnings for much of the rest of England.

The amber warning is in place from 1am to 10am tomorrow for Devon and Cornwall, where gusts of 60 to 70mph will develop with some exposed areas expecting 80mph.

Power cuts may affect homes, while some buildings may be damaged and a 'danger to life' is likely from large waves and beach material being thrown onto coastal roads.

A yellow warning for wind is in place for a wider region of the South West as well as South Wales and along England's South Coast between midnight and 5pm on Friday.

Strong winds are also expected to spread across southern England on Thursday and Friday, with gusts of 50 to 60mph likely and some exposed areas seeing 70mph or above.

#447. Don't make life harder for Britain's beleaguered businesses, Sainsbury's boss warns Chancellor

By EMILY HAWKINS and JOHN-PAUL FORD ROJAS, DEPUTY BUSINESS EDITOR

Published: 00:01 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 00:43 BST, 23 October 2026

The boss of Sainsbury's has urged John Healey not to make life even harder for Britain's beleaguered firms.

Simon Roberts said the Chancellor must use next Wednesday's Budget to ease pressure rather than 'adding further taxes or further regulatory impacts to an industry that's already very heavily taxed'.

It came after Mr Healey told a newspaper that he will aim to deliver a boost to 'bloody-minded entrepreneurs' and 'back business in Britain making a profit'.

That is likely to include cutting back red tape for smaller companies. But many bosses are sceptical given the record of his predecessor Rachel Reeves, who imposed national insurance hikes on employers – despite a previous campaign to woo business.

Mr Roberts said that in meetings with the Government he has been 'very clear about the drivers of inflation and why it's so important we don't see any repeat of what we've seen in previous Budgets'.

He said the shock rise of NI within the 2024 Budget had increased costs in retail and hospitality – and the Government should 'make sure we don't do anything to further aggravate that situation'.

Andrew Murphy, boss of toy retailer The Entertainer, told the BBC Ms Reeves had courted businesses but made 'the biggest 180' and ultimately did 'the exact opposite' of what they had suggested.

And on the prospect of any possible help for business, he added: 'If it's just tinkering around the edges, then it is not going to make a decisive difference.'

Sainsbury's chief executive Simon Roberts pictured outside 10 Downing Street in 2024

Chancellor John Healey during a visit to Shell UK's St Fergus Gas Terminal in Peterhead, Aberdeenshire

Mr Murphy joined a chorus of other bosses – including those from Marks & Spencer and JD Sports – urging for a roll-back in the NI hikes.

He said this would help his firm employ more people on eight and 12-hour contracts.

The rate has been raised from 13.8 per cent to 15 per cent and the threshold where employers start paying was cut to £5,000 from £9,100 – making more people on part-time contracts eligible.

Meanwhile, banks are concerned that a tax raid they are expected to face next week would have a damaging impact on their ability to lend to the wider economy.

Chris Hayward, policy chairman of the City of London Corporation, said the Square Mile would welcome Mr Healey's promised action to reduce business costs.

But he added: 'If he taxes banks, domestic banks will then lend less money to SMEs [small and medium enterprises].

'If you're not careful, you make one move to help small businesses but on the other hand, by taxing the banks, you damage their opportunity to borrow to grow.'

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said of Mr Healey's comments: 'Business will be right to be thoroughly sceptical but the acid test would be repealing Labour's job-destroying Employment Rights Act.'

Separately, the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) urged the Chancellor to reduce employment costs as figures showed 71 per cent are facing difficulties hiring staff.

The BCC's Patrick Milnes said: 'The Chancellor must use his statement to give firms breathing space.

'Cutting employer national insurance contributions for under-25s would lower the cost of taking on young people.'

Meanwhile, the pub and restaurant trade bodies called on the Government 'to act to reduce our tax burden and remove barriers to support investment, growth and jobs in every postcode'.

A new name for Ilhan Omar has been revealed in a Justice Department filing.
