The reference has renewed attention on longstanding allegations surrounding Omar's first marriage and immigration history.

The filing emerged as US Attorney Jeanine Pirro moved to prevent the search warrant for Omar's Washington, DC, home from being made public.

Pirro filed a motion on Wednesday asking a federal judge to keep the warrant sealed after several media organizations requested access to the records.

Her office argued that the government was not yet finished executing the warrant.

The filing doesn't explain why prosecutors used the name or establish that Omar has committed any wrongdoing.

Fox News has separately reported, citing people familiar with the investigation, that investigators believe 'Ilhan Nur Said Elmi' is her real name.

Omar has repeatedly denied the allegations, and the latest filing does not establish that they are true.

Citing sources familiar with the probe, the New York Post reported on October 19 that authorities are examining whether Omar's 2009 marriage to Elmi was fraudulent and whether the two were siblings.

The DNA evidence is among several lines of inquiry being pursued by investigators, alongside whistleblower accounts and government records.

No DNA results have been made public, and the allegations have not been proven in court.

Omar became a US citizen in 2000 as a teenager through her father's naturalization.

Investigators are reportedly examining questions about information contained in immigration documents relating to Omar and her family.

Omar has accused President Trump's administration of politically targeting her, arguing that the investigation is an attempt to intimidate one of his most vocal critics.

Her lawyers have challenged the search and demanded the return of seized property, alleging that authorities exceeded the limits of the warrant.

The Justice Department has disputed claims that officials violated court orders.

The controversy has also unfolded amid scrutiny of Omar's financial disclosures and her household's reported assets.

The Daily Mail has reached out to Omar's office for comment.

Published: 22:41 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 03:37 BST, 23 October 2026

The infamous 'beer and sandwiches' were replaced by 'cheap unbranded' biscuits and tea.

But one thing about Wednesday night's backdoor Downing Street summit between union bosses and the Chancellor hadn't changed since the sixties: the barons were apparently in charge.

And their demands ahead of next week's Budget were straight from the same socialist playbook of decades yonder: hike spending while soaking the rich with more taxes.

One attendee boasted of a 'really good connection' between union chiefs and John Healey, who was clearly keen to impress Labour's 'paymasters' having rushed back to Westminster from Scotland to grant them a private audience that evening.

The Chancellor had been north of the border to announce approval of drilling at the Jackdaw gas field.

While attendees of the No11 gathering confirmed no beer or sandwiches were on offer, it had the hallmarks of the behind-closed-doors 'stitch-ups' between Harold Wilson's Labour government and union barons in the sixties and seventies.

Those talks, which often ran late into the night in smoke-filled rooms, focused on brokering pay deals to avoid crippling mass strikes and became known as 'beer and sandwiches at No 10'.

One attendee boasted of a 'really good connection' between union chiefs and John Healey, who was clearly keen to impress Labour's 'paymasters', having rushed back to Westminster from Scotland to grant them a private audience that evening

'There was no buffet. No booze. No sandwiches. It was a sparse show,' one attendee of Wednesday's meeting said, adding that just biscuits, tea and coffee were offered

The Chancellor had been in Scotland announcing approval of production at the Jackdaw gas field before flying back to Westminster for Wednesday night's summit with union barons

This was after Mr Wilson's wife, Mary, famously served beer and sandwiches made from bread in the Downing Street kitchens to create a working-class atmosphere during talks.

However, times have changed in some regards, according to one attendee of Wednesday's gathering.

'There was no buffet. No booze. No sandwiches. It was a sparse show,' they said, adding that just biscuits, tea and coffee were offered.

'They were poor-quality cheap biscuits - unbranded. They were the kind of biscuits you get in a hotel room.'

The brand of tea and coffee on offer was also unclear as it was pre-made and served from jugs and caddies.

But what the meeting lacked in fare was made up for in grace-and-favour access.

More than a dozen barons filed into No11 from 5.30pm and were each granted two questions in which to pepper the Chancellor with demands in a bid to strong-arm him into eleventh-hour changes ahead of next Wednesday's Budget, the first of Andy Burnham's premiership.

Among them was the hard-Left boss of the Unison union, Andrea Egan, who is said to have led calls for new wealth levies to pay for more spending splurges.

This was after being left disappointed that Mr Healey ruled out raising capital gains tax on assets such as shares and second homes.

In an interview ahead of the meeting, she told the Mirror newspaper: 'It's time to tax the rich.'

Another baron who called on Mr Healey to turn on the spending taps was Daniel Kebede, the firebrand boss of the militant NEU teachers' union.

He pressed for more school spending to be included in the Budget and is said to have warned the Chancellor: 'Seventy-four per cent of schools in England have less funding in real terms than in 2010.'

Meanwhile, GMB boss Gary Smith lobbied for greater spending on defence and support for energy-intensive industries amid sky-high energy bills crippling Britain's industrial sectors.

Under the proposals from campaign group Fairer Share for an annual 0.48 per cent tax on all homes, families in London and the South East would see their bills rise by hundreds of pounds per year.

Replacing council tax with a property value levy would see an average home in England liable for an annual bill of about £1,410 per year. This would mean somebody currently paying average Band D council tax would pay about £870 less per year.

But families living in an average home in London would be liable for an annual property tax of about £2,660 – leaving somebody currently paying Band D council tax almost £700 a year worse-off.

Under the proposals a house in the North East would get an average annual charge of about £748, while the equivalent bill in the South East would be £1,824.

Andy Burnham has previously backed a property tax based on the value of land, but since becoming Prime Minister he has played down the prospect of imminent reforms to council tax.

Labour MPs are calling on Chancellor John Healey to consider replacing council tax and stamp duty with a so-called Proportional Property Tax at the Budget

Now a number of his MPs are urging him to reconsider. Luke Myer, the Labour MP for Middlesbrough South and East Cleveland, said that council tax is ‘crying out for reform’.

And Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, said: ‘A Proportional Property Tax would end the postcode lottery, make the system fairer and put money back into the pockets of struggling households, giving our high streets a much-needed boost too.’

Fairer Share said that, without reform, low and middle-income households face a £900 increase in their council tax bills over the next decade.

Andrew Dixon, founder of Fairer Share, said: 'A property tax review is the key first step to a fairer system.

'It must explore a revenue-neutral Proportional Property Tax, which could put much-needed cash in people’s pockets to cover rising food and energy bills, spend supporting local high streets or help them get on the housing ladder.'

#460. Give millions more weight loss jabs, MPs demand - as report shows just 6% of eligible patients are offered Mounjaro

Published: 00:00 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 00:02 BST, 23 October 2026

Millions more Britons should be offered the blockbuster weight loss jab Mounjaro on the NHS , MPs have warned the Government.

A damning cross-party report shows just 6 per cent of the millions of eligible patients will get access to the injections as part of the NHS' three year roll-out, which began in 2024.

The Health and Social Care Committee (HSCC) warned that the 'woeful' situation will likely drive many desperate patients to turn to the black market, risking serious harm.

Meanwhile, others seeking access to the treatments privately are plunging into debt to do so by spending upwards of £300 a month.

This has created what MPs described as a 'two-tier system' that may block those at greatest need from affording treatment.

Mounjaro – referred to as the 'King Kong' of slimming jabs – was approved for use by NHS drug watchdogs in late 2024.

National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) promised a gradual roll out, committing to delivering the drug to 200,000 patients over the course of three years.

The staggered access was said to allow the NHS to cope with high demand and avoid placing undue pressure on GPs services.

The rollout of the blockbuster fat jab Mounjaro on the NHS is 'unambitious', MPs have warned

However, MPs say the target does not go far enough.

'Current plans to rollout Mounjaro are unambitious given the scale of the challenge of obesity and reach a woefully small number of people who could benefit from this lifechanging treatment,' MPs wrote in the HSCC report.

'We acknowledge there are challenges relating to capacity and funding.

'However, given the much larger number of private prescriptions of GLP-1s, we believe there are opportunities to learn from the private sector and better use the capacity of digital providers.

'The system needs to be designed to support wider access now and be ready for the future.'

The HSCC argued that expanding NHS access to the drugs could prevent dangerous complications from obesity.

Committee chairwoman Layla Moran said this could 'save the NHS billions in the long-term'.

Obesity – classed when a person has a body mass index (BMI) of more than 30 – costs the UK economy more than £74billion a year, and the NHS more than £9billion. Around two-thirds of English adults are classed as overweight or obese.

MPs are now calling on the Government to 'urgently reassess the pace of rollout of Mounjaro'.

It is the most powerful approved weight loss jab, helping patients shed around a fifth of their body weight after 17 months.

But currently, patients must meet strict criteria before being given weight loss jabs on the NHS.

Mounjaro can be prescribed by GPs to people who are severely obese – a BMI of more than 35 – who also have at least four serious weight-related health conditions like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnoea and high cholesterol.

Wegovy, meanwhile, can only be accessed through specialist weight-management clinics and cannot be prescribed by a GP.

Another popular jab, Ozempic, is prescribed on the NHS for type 2 diabetes rather than obesity.

The report did not propose specific changes to prescribing criteria for GLP-1s, but MPs said more could be done to improve access to obesity treatment more widely.

Instead of every patient needing repeated GP appointments, for example, they suggested that the NHS could work with already approved digital providers.

These could help to prescribe, monitor and support people taking weight-loss drugs at scale – freeing up NHS capacity while expanding access.

They also argued that a significant change would be recognising obesity as a chronic, relapsing disease that needs treating, similar to conditions such as type 2 diabetes and asthma, rather than being viewed as a lifestyle issue.

Furthermore, MPs called for greater use of bariatric surgery, which they branded a 'cost-effective underutilised treatment for obesity'.

They said just 6,550 procedures were carried out in 2024-25, reaching fewer than 1 per cent of eligible patients, and called for this to be doubled.

The committee also warned of a 'postcode lottery' emerging, with access to specialist services and surgery varying depending on where patients live.

For example, there were 785 bariatric procedures in the North East and North Cumbria compared with 340 in south-east London.

Overall, the report concluded that 'people living with obesity are being let down by the NHS'.

Ms Moran said: 'Our report urges the Government to make improvements to obesity care a priority – both to improve public health and quality of life, and to save the NHS billions in the long-term.'

NHS England and the Department of Health and Social Care were approached for comment.

'Obesity is one of the biggest challenges facing our health service, and this government is determined to end the obesity epidemic to help drive the shift from sickness to prevention.

'We expect NHS Integrated Care Boards to be making these drugs available as part of a phased rollout, starting with people in the greatest clinical need, while building the workforce and capacity needed to expand access safely and sustainably.

'We will carefully consider the Committee's recommendations and respond in due course.'

#462. Summer 2026 was Europe's deadliest on record: Over 50,000 people died in urban areas - with climate change responsible for two thirds of deaths, study estimates

By SHIVALI BEST, SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR

Published: 00:01 BST, 23 October 2026 | Updated: 00:01 BST, 23 October 2026

Summer 2026 was Europe's deadliest on record, a new study has confirmed.

Scientists from Imperial College London predict that over 50,000 people died in urban areas across 30 countries, including the UK, as a result of extreme heat.

According to the experts, climate change was responsible for about two thirds of these deaths.

Dr Clair Barnes, Extreme Weather and Climate Change Researcher at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London said: 'I think we can be quite confident in stating that the summer of 2026 is likely to have been the worst on record for heat–related mortality across much of Europe.

'These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health.

'Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them.'

Summer 2026 was Europe's deadliest on record, a new study has confirmed. Scientists from Imperial College London predict that over 50,000 people died in urban areas across 30 countries, including the UK

Looking at specific regions, southern and western Europe had the highest death rates, while 4,500 deaths occurred in typically cooler countries, such as the UK

Over the summer, Europe was hit by a series of extreme heatwaves.

Western Europe had its hottest summer on record, with average temperatures reaching 2.9°C above the 1991–2020 average.

In two studies, researchers from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine set out to understand exactly how many excess deaths this extreme heat caused.

The team looked at 854 urban areas that make up about 40 per cent of the population of the 30 countries studied.

Using temperature records and modelling, they were able to estimate exactly how many heat–related excess deaths occurred in each area during the summers from 2000 to 2026.

Their results revealed that over this summer, 50,391 excess heat deaths occurred in the 854 areas studied.

That figure is substantially higher than the previous worst years of 2003 and 2022, during which 28,000 and 29,000 excess heat deaths occurred, respectively.

Late June was especially severe, with almost a third of all deaths estimated to have occurred between 17 June and 1 July, when daily average temperatures were a staggering 5°C above average.

Over the summer, Europe was hit by a series of extreme heatwaves. Western Europe had its hottest summer on record, with average temperatures reaching 2.9°C above the 1991–2020 average. Pictured: wildfires in southeastern France on July 28

To understand the role climate change played in these excess heat deaths, the researchers compared the temperatures that occurred in each urban area with those that would have been expected without the addition of greenhouse gases. The results suggest that climate change was responsible for two–thirds of heat–related deaths this year

Looking at specific regions, southern and western Europe had the highest death rates, while 4,500 deaths occurred in typically cooler countries, such as the UK.

In terms of the victims, the majority of people (44,000) who died in the heat were elderly, while the reamining 6,000 were under–65.

'We know that those who are older, very young or have pre–existing morbidities face the highest dangers from exposure to extreme heat,' said Professor Andrew Hartle, from Imperial College.

'But the temperatures we are increasingly seeing pose a threat to healthy people too.

'We need to ensure we are informing the public of this, and rolling out measures to protect people during the most extreme temperatures.'

To understand the role climate change played in these excess heat deaths, the researchers compared the temperatures that occurred in each urban area with those that would have been expected without the addition of greenhouse gases.

The results suggest that climate change was responsible for two–thirds of heat–related deaths this year.

For comparison, earlier in the century, it was estimated to be responsible for about 40 per cent.

Dr Pierre Masselot, from London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine said: 'This summer has been another dramatic reminder that climate change is everybody's problem.

'It is not just hot regions that are suffering anymore with some parts of Western and Northern Europe experiencing extreme heat and historically high health burden.

'And the whole population is affected, as shown by the significant death toll among younger age groups.

'It is becoming increasingly clear our cities are poorly adapted to rising heat, and it is critical we improve our efforts towards adaptation.

'This means cooling the cities through more green spaces and less pollution, and providing health care for affected populations.'

#463. Dazzling headlights forcing one in four drivers off the road after clock change

By FREDA LEWIS-STEMPEL, SENIOR MOTORING REPORTER

As the clocks go back this weekend, a huge chunk of drivers fear the dazzling effect of other vehicles' headlights, research claims.

It causes so much concern that one in four motorists affected by glare plan on reducing or even giving up driving when the time adjustment happens.

Four in five drivers say they are concerned about the impact glare will have on their driving as darkness falls in the late afternoon, research by the RAC has found.

And three-quarters of those affected by glare think the problem is getting progressively worse.

This is because the vehicle headlights designed to show drivers the road ahead are leaving many others struggling to spot hazards, signs and road markings, as well as making it harder to judge the position, speed and distance of oncoming vehicles, the RAC's research has uncovered.

Last year, an independent study on headlight glare commissioned by the Government confirmed that some brighter modern headlights are more likely to cause glare to drivers.

Three quarters of drivers struggling to see due to headlight glare say the problem is getting worse

Among drivers who get dazzled, half say overly bright headlights make it harder to spot other road hazards, while a similar proportion (49 per cent) struggle to see road signs and markings.

Nearly half (47 per cent) find it difficult to judge the position of oncoming vehicles and four in ten (43 per cent) can’t easily judge other vehicles’ speed and distance.

Worryingly, a third say they get temporarily blinded by oncoming bright headlights and one in seven dazzled drivers admit they've narrowly avoided a collision.

Similarly, nearly two in three say they find it difficult to see the indicator lights of some oncoming vehicles because headlights are so strong.

Concern about headlight dazzle is causing some people to change their driving behaviour altogether.

Of those affected by glare, a fifth (21 per cent) say they plan to drive less once the clocks go back as a direct result of being dazzled, while 3 per cent plan to stop driving at night altogether.

For those who've given up driving at night or curtailed their driving at night, the impact on their lives is stark.

Three in ten (28 per cent) say they see friends less as a result and 20 per cent see family less, while a fifth (21 per cent) report feeling much more isolated.

But 6 per cent have cancelled medical appointments because of the difficulties they face driving in the dark, while the same proportion have postponed them.

Drivers want action to be taken to reduce glare caused by existing vehicles already on the roads, as well as by future models.

Three-quarters of 1,208 drivers surveyed by the RAC think future research should examine both existing and future vehicles, while only 14 per cent think it should look solely at vehicles not yet for sale.

Following on from last year's independent study on headlight glare, further UK research is expected to get underway shortly after a commitment made in January’s Road Safety Strategy, and work continues at an international level where regulations for future vehicles are agreed upon.

Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at RAC, said: 'The shorter days are here, which means millions of drivers will once again have to contend with the unwelcome effects of headlight dazzle.

'While nothing can stop the nights drawing in at this time of year, drivers continue to feel strongly that more can and should be being done to reduce the dazzle they experience.

'We welcomed the Government’s commitment to carry out further research into the problem, but drivers will only be satisfied when they know meaningful changes are coming that will tackle the problems they experience.'

If the glare from an oncoming vehicle at night is so bad that you temporarily can't see anything, you should slow down to reduce the risk of the impact on your impaired visibility.

However, avoid slowing or stopping abruptly as you don't want a car that is travelling behind you running into the back of you.

2. Don't look directly at oncoming headlights

To prevent yourself from being dazzled, never look directly at the headlights of other cars.

Look to the left-hand side of the road and follow the white line marking the edge if there is one, so you can keep track of your position, the RAC recommends.

Windscreens are particularly susceptible to steaming up on the inside, especially in cold weather, while car heaters can blow dirty air at the glass, causing a hazy film to build up on the inside.

This can increase glare from oncoming headlamps, so ensure yours is clean and clear.

Drivers at night should dip the rear-view mirror to reduce the risk of being dazzled by motorists following them.

Many new motors in showrooms today have an auto-dimming rear-view mirror function. If your car doesn't then you should be dipping the mirror manually.

If being dazzled by other drivers' headlights or street lighting is an issue, motorists should consider anti-glare glasses when driving at night.

These are not simply glasses with yellow tints, which can help reduce glare by also make darker areas of the road less visible and are therefore not recommended.

Specsavers has a product called SuperDrive lenses for varifocal wearers, while all of its glasses can be fitted with a clear 'SuperClean Smart' treatment, which is specially designed to help reduce reflections and dazzle caused by oncoming headlights and street lighting — helping you have a safer journey.

Motorists suffering from glare at night should consult with their optician.

6. Use low beams where possible to safeguard other drivers

Use your low-beam headlights instead of high beams when driving in well-lit areas or when approaching other vehicles as high beams can significantly increase glare.

Ensure that your headlights are correctly aimed, especially if you are often travelling with heavy loads, which can impact the height of your lights beam.

Misaligned headlights not only contribute to blinding other drivers but will also reduce your own visibility.

#464. Almost half of landlords put up rent in last year - and most of those that did earned £100,000 or more

Almost half of landlords put up their tenants' rent last year, research shows – and the majority of those who did earned £100,000 or more per year.

In a poll by the Tenancy Deposit Scheme Charitable Foundation (TDS), 48 per cent of landlords said they had increased rents at least once in the past 12 months.

Of those, 55 per cent earned £100,000 or more per year including income from their properties and other sources.

In addition, 60 per cent owned five or more properties and 54 per cent employed a letting agent.

Under the Renters' Rights Act which came into force in May, landlords can now only raise rents once per year and tenants have stronger rights to challenge them at tribunals.

Some landlords therefore raised rents prior to the legislation coming in.

In a case published this week, a tenant challenged their landlord's £50 per month rise but the judge went even further and ordered they cut the rent by £200.

The TDS Foundation's research found that almost seven in ten landlords earn over £50,000 in pre-tax income annually, and approximately a third of landlords (31 per cent) earn over £100,000 per year.

The UK’s median pre-tax household income is £38,948.

On the rise: Nearly half of landlords put up rents in the past 12 months, data shows

The proportion of landlords who earn over £50,000 has increased significantly within the past two years, from 51 per cent to 69 per cent.

While the proportion of landlords upping rental costs for tenants was higher among higher earners, the overall number of landlords who increased rental prices last year dropped slightly.

The survey of more than 2,000 private landlords found that 50 per cent had kept their rents unchanged in the past 12 months, compared with four in ten, or 39 per cent, last year.

According to the research, the most common reasons landlords gave for upping rents were higher running costs, increased property maintenance expenses and increases in the cost of living.

Dr Jennifer Harris, head of policy, research and social impact at The Dispute Service Group, said: 'Our research shows that decisions about rents are rarely straightforward.

'While retaining good tenants and recognising the financial challenges they face are important considerations for many landlords, they are facing pressures of their own, with rising running and maintenance costs continuing to influence decisions about rents.'

Since May 1, 2026, the Renters' Rights Act has been in force. Under the new law, landlords can only increase their tenants' rent once per year and it must be no higher than the open market rent.

Landlords also have to give tenants written notice of the proposed rent increase at least two months before the hike takes effect.

If a tenant thinks their proposed rent increase is above market rate, they can challenge it at the first-tier tribunal.

Existing rent review clauses in tenancy agreements also became void after May 1, 2026, meaning landlords could not use them to hike tenants' rent after this point.

Within the survey results from TDS today, there may well have been a flurry of landlords who increased their tenants' rent before May 1, 2026.

Twenty-six per cent of landlords surveyed via TDS said they had at least one tenant in rent arrears, a slight fall from 29 per cent in the previous year's survey.

When dealing with arrears, landlords most commonly reported engaging directly with tenants to discuss their options or providing information about their rights and available support services.

Twenty-one per cent of landlords surveyed said they had agreed a repayment plan with tenants, while 17 per cent had offered a rent-free or reduced-rent period to provide some financial breathing space.

The outcome of a legal case this week sparked concern that the Government has introduced rent controls by the back door.

A tenant successfully challenged a £50 rent increase for rent from £1,650 per month to £1,700.

After listening to arguments from both parties, the judge went even further and ruled the market rent was £1,450 a month, forcing the landlord to reduce it by £200 per month.

Labour's housing minister, Matthew Pennycook, took to X on Tuesday to highlight the case as an example of how the Government was 'standing up for renters'.

While tenants could challenge unfair rent hikes before the Renters' Rights Act, they had to prove the rent was significantly higher than what the landlord could expect for a comparable property.

Tenants can also challenge their rent, irrespective of any increase, at the tribunal within six months of moving into a property.

Tenants have to pay £47 application fee to challenge a rent increase but the tribunal can order the landlord to reimburse it if they win.

Ashley Osborne of Lexit, a service that helps analyse buy-to-let properties for landlords says of the recent case: 'The landlord asked for £50 more and the tribunal cut the rent by £200, below what both sides agreed at the start.

'The tribunal called the flat attractive and high specification. It still set the rent £200 below the rent agreed at the start of the tenancy, and £250 below the proposed rent, on its own reading of the comparables. The agreed rent is no longer the floor.'

He added: 'I warned a year ago the Renters' Rights Act was rent control by the back door. Its defenders said this wouldn't happen.

'But when a third party's view of market rent can override a rent two people freely agreed, that's rent control in substance, whatever the act calls it.'

#473. RICHARD LITTLEJOHN: Trump is toast? Don't ask me, just listen to what the voters are saying in the local Cheers-style bars of the US

Published: 23:00 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 23:00 BST, 22 October 2026

Trump’s toast. Don’t take my word for it, just overhear the conversations in Bobby’s, the Last of the Great Pioneer Town bars.

I’ve been drinking in there for decades, ever since my immediate family moved to the States 50 years ago with my Dad’s job in the motor industry.

(And no, I didn’t relocate with them, despite what that lying, smear-mongering, far-Left public school tosseur Jimmy O’Brien maintains every other day on LBC radio. I don’t ‘live’ in America.) But it’s no secret that I spend a bit of time in Florida.

And just as Bruce Springsteen insisted that you learn more from a three-minute record, baby, than you ever do in school, so you learn more about the state of American politics from Bobby’s than you ever do from watching the biased American TV networks – or the BBC.

If you can remember Cheers – the Eighties TV sitcom set in a Boston Common dive bar, starring Ted Danson and his elaborately elevated syrup – you’ll get some idea of the clientele in Bobby’s. The punters range from retired, self-made billionaires to the local tennis coach.

Not that anyone talks politics or religion – unless they want to be shown the door, the street and eventually, the ocean. It’s a sports bar. Go Dogs, that kind of thing. But you pick stuff up by osmosis.

There’s Dottie, a retired nun who has an impressive selection of Pearly Queen-style badged MAGA hats, and a life-size cardboard cut-out of President Donald J Trump in her living room. She’ll go down with the ship. But there’s also a gentle buzz, a nervous rumble round the bar. Even though this is ostensibly, albeit sophisticated, MAGA country, you pick up a sense of unease. Has The Donald lost it? Is he going into Crazy Joe Biden mode?

Never mind the bizarre AI video with the tiger, or that gormless Lady Godiva lookalike who lasted about five minutes as this week’s latest White House press secretary. There’s a growing body of opinion that Trump is, well, getting on a bit, entering a marbles-free zone.

Even though this is ostensibly, albeit sophisticated, MAGA country, you pick up a sense of unease. Has The Donald lost it? Is he going into Crazy Joe Biden mode? asks Richard Littlejohn

If you can remember Cheers – the Eighties TV sitcom set in a Boston Common dive bar, starring Ted Danson (centre) and his elaborately elevated syrup – you’ll get some idea of the clientele in Bobby’s

And this is Cocoon Central, where Viagra and HRT-fuelled octogenarians are still knocking their knees out on the pickleball court. (And knocking them together on golf carts behind the clubhouse.)

Lifting that narco-crook Madura out of Venezuela was a doddle. Blowing up the drug smugglers in the Gulf of Mexico was the starting-pistol for trebles all round in Bob’s Country Bunker, outside of the usual bien pensant salons.

Yet the fallout from the Iran war is backfiring, bigly. It was never going to be easy. Yes, those with long memories – Jimmy Carter’s humiliation in the desert, etc – agree that Tehran’s Mad Mullahs should be wiped off the face of the earth.

And majority US opinion – evangelical Christians, especially – are steadfast in their support for Israel. But failure to think through the knock-on effects, such as the oil and gas crisis caused by the Straits of Hormuz shutdown, and his man-crush on Russia’s crazed, dead-eyed tyrant Putin, are baffling to most Americans.

When push comes to shove, everything boils down to Bill Clinton’s political guru James Carville’s dictum: ‘It’s the economy, stupid.’

Couple of days ago, I was in a discount warehouse in Florida, admiring a well-marbled ribeye steak priced at 25 dollars a pound or thereabouts. A little old lady fingering what the Americans insist on calling a ‘filet’ turned to me and said; ‘Remember when steak cost eight dollars a pound?’

Yep. About five minutes ago, seems like. And even in low-tax Florida, petrol is around $4 (£2.99) a gallon – a bargain next to UK prices and high-tax Democratic states like California – but still historically a strain on the purse strings.

Here’s what tells me Trumpism has run its course. The Donald has always enjoyed huge support in the Sunshine State, where he has his Mar-a-Lago estate. Republican governor Ron DeSantis – who declared that Florida is where woke goes to die – is term-limited and having to stand down after eight years. His chosen successor – endorsed by Trump – is just two points ahead of his Democratic challenger.

Frankly, I never buy into the polls, but among the Bobby’s regulars like my mate Roger – who thinks I’m a dangerous liberal – there’s trepidation. Roger’s stocking up on ammo from Wal-Mart, just in case.

In swing state Michigan, my sister lives outside Detroit and works as den-mother to a 20-something bunch of Big Bangers in a finance house.

Last time out, these young thrusters were all gung-ho for Trump. Today, not so much. Trump’s stupid squabble with Canada has gone down like a Led Zeppelin in Michigan.

Slapping punitive tariffs on America’s nearest northern neighbour was the act of a madman. In 2016 and again two years ago, Michigan’s car workers defied their UAW union leaders and turned out in droves for Trump. The auto industries of Detroit and Canada are joined at the hip, mutually inter-dependent.

Windsor, Ontario, is Canada’s Motown, without the Four Tops or Bob Seger. You can see it from Joe Muer’s seafood place on the Detroit river. My mum used to go there to buy cumberland sausages from the Canadian wing of Marks & Sparks.

The trucks carrying components rattle backwards and forwards over the Ambassador’s Bridge linking the two countries every ten minutes. Why the hell would Trump want to screw up that relationship?

Michigan’s senatorial race – which could decide control of the House in a couple of weeks – is a razor-edge toss up. The Democrats’ front-runner is a far-Left headbanger called Abdul El-Sayed. If he wins, the blame will be laid at the door of Trump’s hideous new golden ballroom. Full disclosure: this column is a bit of a mea culpa. Even though I considered Trump a joke candidate when he declared in 2016, I came to quite admire him, like a lot of people, on the basis of: My enemy’s enemy is my friend. He irritated all the right people.

He humiliated his Veep, JD Vance, by refusing to back him at a press conference only this week

He’s an Anglo/Jockophile, who was all in favour of Brexit. My old mate Nigel Farage, who campaigned for Trump, assured me he wasn’t as bonkers in private as he seemed to be in public. Trump also got the measure of Mother Theresa May, who turned out to be our hopeless, tone-deaf version of Hillary Clinton.

Trump stopped biological men competing in women’s sports, was rock-solid behind Israel and read the riot act to craven European leaders – including our own – who shamefully refused to fund Nato and our domestic defence forces. Was he right, or was he right? The defiant bottle he showed after assorted assassination attempts was impressive.

That was before Iran, the Tony The Tiger meme, the attempted annexing of Greenland and renaming Lake Ontario the ‘Lake of America’.

Then there’s his family’s crypto thing, which I don’t pretend to understand, but people who do say will blow up in his face once he leaves office.

My great Bobby’s drinking buddy John Addison, who ran a serious US corporation and is a full-on Georgia Bulldog Republican, predicts a bloodbath for his GOP (Grand Old Party) in November. And he’s rarely wrong.

That still leaves another two years of lame-duck Donald, who will spend his last days fighting off impeachment and firing off increasingly insane executive orders.

America’s biggest problem is what comes next. The Dems are torn between virtual-communists like the headbanger who runs New York and that preening spiv Gavin Newsom, from California, who makes Councillor Burnham look like, nah, never mind.

Newsom’s so vain, he probably thinks this song’s about him. And Trump won’t nominate a successor. He humiliated his Veep, JD Vance, by refusing to back him at a press conference only this week. Mrs Vance apparently thinks the game’s up. Best get out while the getting’s good.

My pick, expressed a decade ago in this newspaper and a cover story for The Spectator magazine, would be Florida’s Marco Rubio, who has ridden the Trump tiger in style as his respected Secretary of State.

But, then again, what do I know? And I don’t have a dog in this fight. So, if you want me, I’ll be in Bobby’s, the Last of the Great Pioneer Town bars.

#475. Tommy Robinson 'retaliated' to Daily Mail's race-riots expose by hiring private investigators to track down two journalists to their homes, court hears

Published: 17:46 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 22:45 BST, 22 October 2026

Tommy Robinson hired private investigators to hunt down two Daily Mail journalists to their homes, he told a jury today.

The far-Right activist, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, said he wanted to 'put pressure on them' after the Mail angered him by publishing an article saying he was 'stoking race riots from his sunbed'.

He is on trial accused of using 'bullyboy, intimidatory tactics' to threaten the two reporters in 'retaliation' for their journalism.

Entering the witness box at London's Southwark Crown Court, wearing a navy waistcoat, blue shirt and tie, the activist gave his name as Stephen Lennon and stated his occupation as 'journalist'.

Lennon described his anger after the Mail published a front-page picture of him, on his mobile phone on a sunbed in Cyprus, in the summer of 2024.

It was during the riots engulfing England triggered by the murder of three schoolgirls at a dance class in Southport, and he had been tweeting about it.

At the time, the Prime Minister was denouncing individuals 'who were whipping up trouble and running away'.

Tommy Robinson arriving at Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday as he prepared to go into the witness box at his trial, where he denies two charges of harassment causing fear of violence

Lennon, 43, a founder of the English Defence League, agreed when his barrister Alisdair Williamson KC said he had made a 'rather intemperate statement' about the anti-migrant riots. But he insisted that really he had been 'trying to calm the situation the whole time'.

He is accused of two charges of harassment causing fear of violence, which he denies, against Mail journalists Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, who had revealed how Lennon was using his Tommy Robinson account on X to tweet about the riots from his Cyprus holiday resort.

Today he said that after reading the Mail's report: 'I was angry, I'm not going to deny.'

Lennon allegedly sent Mr Dirnhuber the message: 'I'll be knocking on your door.'

And after a photo of Mr Dirnhuber was subsequently posted on X outside his home address, Lennon reposted the tweet on his Tommy Robinson X account with the words 'Got ya', adding: 'I got all three of you tagged & bagged in 1 day.'

He allegedly phoned Mr Young 'swearing and shouting', saying he had researched Mr Young's family and telling him: 'I'm coming to get you.'

A man identifying himself as 'Tommy Robinson' also left a voicemail on the Editor-in-Chief of the Daily Mail's mobile phone saying: 'I've already located every f***ing one of you.'

Court artist's sketch of Robinson - real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon - giving evidence today

Lennon has millions of followers, and one post from a follower directed at Mr Dirnhuber read: 'Can't wait to see your face and beat the ever-loving f*** out of you.' The defendant said he had no knowledge of this.

During his spell in the witness box, Lennon said he had been 'shocked and scared' after the article, because he claimed the Mail had taken pictures of his family and had revealed his hotel location. He claimed this had led to 'six or seven' groups of men 'looking for' him.

The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told that no identifiable photographs of Lennon's children were ever published in print or online.

Prosecutor Ben Holt said: 'You do realise, Mr Lennon, how the Daily Mail worked out where you were - from your own posts?

'It follows that, had you been relaxing with your children, not posting on X, they would not have found you.'

Lennon replied: 'I didn't realise. I thought they had a tracker.' He added that Mr Dirnhuber, a junior editor, must be 'the best tracker there is', adding: 'He is obviously a skilled investigator.'

He also admitted he had not actually asked the Mail to remove a photograph said to show his ex-wife – which did not name her, and was captioned only as 'Robinson and his friends'. He explained not asking for it to be removed by saying he 'didn't want to draw attention to the picture'.

Nor did he complain to the Press regulator IPSO, or instruct libel lawyers, because they cost him too much. Instead, he said, he had decided to send private investigators to the journalists' homes because 'I didn't see any other option'.

Video played in court showed Lennon saying of his approach: 'What is good for the goose is good for the gander.'

He later added: 'I am giving warnings to journalists.'

Mr Holt said: 'Mr Lennon, I suggest you knew full well what you were doing, posting these messages, putting out their whole addresses, so they would be afraid, fearful of violence.'

Lennon replied: 'They are fearful of the camera. I am asking the questions on camera, that is what they are afraid of.'

He said he had hired private investigators to find the journalists at their home addresses. 'It's what they've done to me,' he told the jury.

He said it was 'not done to intimidate them'. Lennon said he wanted to track down the journalists who wrote the story about him to 'question them on camera', and did not want to cause any harm to their families. He added: 'I would find the men and get them on camera.'

Lennon said he had hired a private investigation company to find Mr Young and Mr Dirnhuber and take photographs of them outside their homes.

He said: 'I wanted to find the journalists', adding he wanted to 'put pressure on them'.

He further told jurors he had requested photographs 'to confirm the identities' of the journalists he was tracking down, and to know: 'Is he in the house, is he there?'

Asked what he meant when he said he had 'tagged and bagged' the reporters, he said: 'I got the location of the journalists within 24 hours. I looked forward to asking questions.'

Asked if he thought his course of conduct was 'reasonable', he said: 'I felt it was totally reasonable, under the circumstances.'

Prosecutor Mr Holt asked Lennon about a phone call to Mr Young, during which the activist allegedly said: 'I know where you live.'

'That's a typically threatening thing to say,' said Mr Holt. Lennon replied: 'I told him [Mr Young], I told everyone, "I don't want to be doing this".'

'You were just threatening them,' said Mr Holt.

'It really wasn't like that,' Lennon replied. When Mr Holt asked if he was 'bullying' the journalist, Lennon replied: 'No, I was trying to pressure him.'

Mr Holt asked if he screamed down the phone at Mr Young, to which he replied: 'I did raise my voice, yes. I was panicked. I was angry, I'm not going to deny.'

Lennon denied that having private investigators take photographs of the home addresses of Mr Dirnhuber and Mr Young was 'designed to intimidate them', saying: 'It's what they've done to me. It was not done to intimidate them.'

The activist accepted he had never identified a picture in the Mail's online article showing his ex-wife as 'the real problem' or asked anyone to take it down. He said he had not wanted to draw attention to it.

He told the court: 'I was in a mad panic, I wasn't really thinking about them or their families to be honest.'

The defendant said taking pictures of Mr Young's family was 'a bargaining chip for me', adding: 'I purposefully didn't do to them what they had done to me.'

A British teenager has been seriously injured after plunging 100ft off a glacier during a ski trip in Austria.

He then plunged around 100ft – or 30 metres – down a steep precipice, resulting in serious facial and back injuries, according to reports.

Mountain rescue attended the scene to provide the boy with medical treatment and he was airlifted to hospital shortly thereafter.

The accident took place on Wednesday October 21 at 11.30am local time at Hintertux Glacier ski resort in Zillertal Valley, west Austria.

The boy had been attempting a red run classified as intermediate difficulty at the time of the incident, with the safety fence erected to stop skiers from leaving the marked slope.

Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt unleashed a sharp and blunt verdict on Katie Zacharia's week-long stint in her old job.

'The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well,' Leavitt told Fox News Digital backstage at a Turning Point USA campus tour stop at California Polytechnic State University.

She added that President Trump was continuing to consider his options for the position and that she had offered her expertise to help him find the right replacement.

Leavitt, who served as President Donald Trump's first press secretary during his second term, opened up about the preparation that went into her first press briefing to the crowd of campus students.

'I prepared like heck for that first briefing,' Leavitt said.

'I poured myself into my preparation. I read, I studied, I talked to every Cabinet member, I talked to the president. I just absorbed as much information as this noggin up here could.'

The comments come after Zacharia's tenure ended just days after she took the White House briefing-room podium for the first time with a wobbly performance.

Trump announced Zacharia's appointment on October 9, after first contacting her about the role on October 7.

'The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well,' former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said about her successor, Katie Zacharia

Zacharia's debut briefing lasted just 14 minutes, taking questions from only three reporters

Trump announced Leavitt's appointment on November 15, 2024, while he was still president-elect. She didn't deliver her first White House press briefing until January 28, 2025, giving her more than two months between the announcement and her debut

She officially began the job on October 12 and faced reporters for the first time the following day.

Her debut briefing lasted just 14 minutes, with questions from only three reporters.

Trump subsequently praised her performance, telling reporters: 'I thought she did excellent. She did very good.'

But the appointment quickly became a talking point, with questions raised about Zacharia's limited preparation time and her experience handling the White House press corps.

Zacharia also faced questions over her legal credentials after it was brought to light that she had failed California's bar exam in 2011.

She then moved to Beijing with her husband and worked at a Chinese law firm.

Despite never passing the bar exam, Zacharia frequently appeared on news channels as a legal analyst, offering commentary on legal and political issues while identifying herself as a lawyer.

Zacharia's rocky debut was followed by an uncomfortable appearance on Sean Hannity's Fox News show on October 15, just hours before she was pushed out of the job the following day.

Hannity delivered a notably tough grilling, confronting her over her widely criticized briefing, pressing her on why she had repeatedly described herself as a lawyer despite failing the California bar exam.

He challenged her explanation for the short briefing, asking: 'Why only three questions in 14 minutes?' before warning her that the White House briefing room would 'never be a friendly room to you.'

Zacharia defended herself by blaming the whirlwind hiring process and lack of preparation time, but the combative interview added to the scrutiny surrounding her brief tenure.

As Leavitt reflects upon her first briefing, the lack of preparation on Zacharia's end gave a major disadvantage.

Trump announced Leavitt's appointment on November 15, 2024, while he was still president-elect.

She didn't deliver her first White House press briefing until January 28, 2025, giving her more than two months between the announcement and her debut.

Leavitt, who was 27 when she took the job, became the youngest White House press secretary in history.

Her first briefing lasted around 46 minutes, during which she took questions on the administration's agenda and media access.

Leavitt announced her departure from the role on August 12, attributing the decision to wanting to spend more time with her growing family.

Trump praised Leavitt as one of his most trusted aides and said he understood her decision to spend more time with her family.

She also agreed to remain an outside adviser to the president.

Now, however, Leavitt is preparing for a return to the national spotlight.

Fox News announced on October 5 that she would join the network as an on-air contributor, providing political analysis and commentary across its platforms beginning November 1.

#481. Unlikeable characters spouting tired gags... this Gen-Z sitcom's just a mess: CHRISTOPHER STEVENS reviews Channel 4 comedy It Gets Worse

Published: 22:16 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 22:18 BST, 22 October 2026

No generation has ever faced such struggles as Gen Z... or so they love to think.

Truth is, everything now is much the same as it's always been – including the jokes.

Workshy Ethan (Leo Reich, the writer and star of It Gets Worse) claims he's living on money left to him by his mother.

When he gets caught out, he admits she's alive and adds, 'It just sounds way better than saying she gave it to me.'

That gag is at least a generation old. Steven Moffat used it in his comedy Coupling, more than 20 years ago, when geeky Oliver spun the same lie about an inheritance, and trotted out the same justification when the lie was discovered.

Coupling and It Gets Worse are versions of the same set-up, sitcoms about young people who have to grow up whether they like it or not.

Unlikeable characters spouting tired gags... this Gen-Z sitcom’s just a mess: CHRISTOPHER STEVENS reviews Channel 4 comedy It Gets Worse

'All I want', whines Ethan to his therapist, 'is ten years of my life where I wouldn't have to worry about anything.

Ethan shares a flat with two friends from uni, Abi (Emily Fairn) and Sam (Olive Gray).

Each episode follows one character's viewpoint, so we don't yet know much about Sam.

This is a blessing, because the opening double bill told us far more than anyone could ever want to know about the other two – particularly their sex lives.

Abi is an HR intern at a media start-up, which is a fancy way of saying she sits at the reception desk, counting the minutes till it's time to take a coffee to her obnoxious American boss (Lena Dunham).

Ethan has sex with anything in trousers, including that therapist (Andrew Scott).

Channel 4 must imagine that Gen Z viewers are going to relate to these people, but all I can see is a derivative, aimless mess with delusions of relevance.

Since Phoebe Waller-Bridge had an unexpected hit with Fleabag ten years ago, it feels as though every new comedy has looked like this – a bunch of shallow, unlikeable, promiscuous characters, estranged from their families and cobbled together as friends.

They're always broke, and they never stop complaining.

Each new series arrives with great fanfare, promising to break the mould of comedy when in fact they're all identikit flop-and-forget products.

It Gets Worse does feature star names in cameos, but a single scene is never enough to create more than a cardboard cutout with a few forced one-liners.

You've just got time to say, 'Oh look, that's Vicki Pepperdine as Ethan's stereotypical, homophobic, fusspot mum,' and she's gone.

Novelist Zadie Smith supplies a voiceover that tries to be satirical, pointing out that Ethan has 'one of the easiest lives in recorded human history'.

But Zadie is the archetypal Millennial. It's not so long ago that her generation thought they were the special ones.

And when Sri Lanka found themselves 24 for two, with captain Kusal Mendis run out at the non-striker’s end without facing a ball, they looked doomed.

Pete Hegseth's aides punched a hole in a globe used by General Dwight D. Eisenhower during World War II after trying to lug the relic into the defense secretary's office.

His moving crew lost control of the 30-inch floor globe in early February, sending it crashing onto its base and tearing a gash several inches wide near Antarctica, according to the Washington Post.

The Army confirmed the damage, saying the fall also knocked the sphere off the metal frame it spins on. The globe never made it to Hegseth's office.

Hegseth's staff had requested the artifact, which a plaque dates to the 1930s, because of its wartime pedigree, sources told the outlet.

Historic pieces are normally moved around the Pentagon by trained curators, and the Army office that keeps the globe had planned to call in experts from the US Army Center of Military History to pack it safely and document the transfer.

But those historians were furloughed during a partial government shutdown triggered by a congressional standoff over the Trump administration's immigration policy.

Rather than wait, Hegseth's team sent in its own crew, and one source said impatience appeared to have played a part.

However, the government shutdown ended on the same day the globe was wrecked. It is unclear whether Hegseth personally ordered the move or whether another senior official in his office gave the green light.

The globe is thought to have been used by Eisenhower, pictured here with then-vice president Richard Nixon, when he led the Army's War Plans Division during World War II

Pentagon officials refused to let The Post photograph or inspect the damaged globe, but the paper obtained images showing the hole and specks of debris littering the carpet below.

Hegseth, a former National Guard officer who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, now calls himself secretary of war after carrying out Trump's order last year to revive the department's pre-1947 name, a switch Congress has never approved.

The botched move comes as Hegseth faces mounting fire over his handling of the war with Iran, which began just weeks after the globe moving incident.

Hegseth declared this spring that regime change had already happened in Iran, but the Islamic Republic is still standing, with the Revolutionary Guards tightening their grip at the expense of civilian and clerical institutions.

The war is deeply unpopular with Americans and has helped drive up costs at home, a growing headache for Republicans heading into the midterms.

But instead, the toddler risks death if he even shares a laugh or smile with those around him.

Rupert, from Broughton in Wales, is one of only approximately 50 children in Britain living with Alternating Hemiplegia of Childhood (AHC) - an ultra-rare neurological condition often described by specialists as a 'time bomb' due to its unpredictable and life-threatening nature.

The condition - for which there is no cure or treatments for in Britain - causes sufferers to have 'attacks' triggered by day-to-day activities, meaning Rupert's parents, Dave and Siobhan Smith, must closely monitor their son at all times to mitigate the risk of injuries - or even death.

What began as 'abnormal' eye movements quickly progressed into seizure-like episodes and choking for Rupert, who has siblings George, six, and Henry. But it was not until he had a choking fit which stopped his breathing that his parents pushed for answers and he was given the devastating diagnosis.

Diagnosed at just seven months old, the toddler's young life has been governed by invasive medical procedures, including lumbar punctures, MRIs and CT scans.

Rupert's best hope rests on experimental therapies and clinical trials only offered in the United States which, unfortunately, come at a mammoth cost.

Fifteen-month-old Rupert Smith is one of only approximately 50 children in Britain living with Alternating Hemiplegia of Childhood (AHC)

Rupert's every movement must be closely monitored to mitigate the risk of fatalities as for sufferers of AHC, there is no cure nor approved treatments for the condition

Rupert pictured with parents Dave and Siobhan, and siblings George and Henry

In the months since his diagnosis in January, his family has set up a fundraiser aimed at raising the £1.5million needed to send Rupert across the Atlantic for the potentially life-saving treatment.

Mr and Mrs Smith spoke to the Mail about the fragility and uncertainty of their son's condition - but how they will do whatever it takes to ensure his life is as normal as possible.

'When Rupert was a few weeks old, we noticed some abnormal eye movements, his eyes would roll around, flicker and deviate outwards,' Mrs Smith, 36, said. 'We'd taken him to Wrexham Maelor Hospital and they said they couldn't find a reason for it and it could just be his age.

'Shortly afterwards, he started having really rigid episodes where his whole body would just spasm. He would become very rigid and have abnormal posturing, which looked like seizures.'

The family, concerned with his alarming symptoms, brought Rupert back to hospital where tests kept returning as normal - baffling medics.

But at the end of 2025, the boy's situation was life or death - leaving Mr and Mrs Smith desperate for answers.

Mrs Smith, a former pharmacy technician turned full-time carer, explained: 'In November, he'd gone into Wrexham Maelor Hospital again with a choking episode and just as we were about to leave hospital, Rupert turned blue and stopped breathing. He had to be resuscitated by the doctors and a crash team.

'We spent a couple of weeks in hospital, and that is where he had a whole genome sequencing. On January the 5th this year, we got his diagnosis of AHC.'

Following a choking episode in which he had to be resuscitated, Rupert was put forth for whole genome sequencing. He was given the formal AHC diagnosis in January this year

Rupert's AHC can be triggered by 'day-to-day' actions like laughing or being tired

Alternating Hemiplegia of Childhood (AHC) is an extremely rare neurodevelopmental condition caused by a gene mutation and characterised by recurrent 'attacks' and episodes of weakness or paralysis.

AHC episodes are often triggered by various stressors and can affect either one side of the body or both. While the condition does not typically limit a child's life expectancy, affected individuals are more at risk of serious or fatal complications caused by the episodes.

At present, there is no cure nor treatment for AHC on the NHS. Care is typically focused on managing symptoms and reducing the severity of AHC attacks.

For Rupert, Mrs Smith explained, AHC attacks can be triggered by simple 'day-to-day' things, making management of his condition particularly difficult and distressing to manage.

'For example, an episode can come on if Rupert is tired, hungry, too hot or too cold, or even if he is exposed to water,' Mrs Smith said. 'His top trigger is actually excitement, and that is the worst part of it for us because we can't allow him to become too happy.

'It's terrifying because it happens so, so quickly. One minute he's playing and the next minute he could stop breathing or he's having a life-threatening seizure or he's completely paralysed and can't move anything but his eyes.

'For us, it's just terrifying, we're constantly on edge, you can't take your eyes off him. It's just the fear that one day we could lose him. We carry oxygen with us everywhere we go and he's got rescue medication.'

And in addition to the AHC triggers, Mr Smith added, Rupert also faces various physical difficulties, meaning he has multiple medical appointments per week.

AHC is an extremely rare neurodevelopmental condition caused by a gene mutation (Rupert pictured with his siblings Henry and George)

Rupert can't crawl or walk, and also has very low muscle tone. He is pictured here having pysiotherapy

He said: 'He has his daily struggles, he's developmentally delayed globally, so he's far behind where he needs to be. He also has very low muscle tone. So, he can't crawl or walk. He's just learning to sit up by himself and things like that. But he has lots of physiotherapy to try and help with that.

'In day-to-day life, he struggles with what he should be doing. But it is the triggers - the medical emergencies - which can take him from us.'

The family are now working to raise the £1.5million needed to send Rupert to America for treatment which could potentially suppress and control his AHC - giving the tot the best chance of a normal future.

The money - of which they have raised just over £380,000 so far - also factors the cost of any potential cure for AHC that could be developed in the future.

Mrs Smith explained why Rupert's journey to America is so important. She said: 'In this country there are no treatments, only symptom management. He's on anti-aphylactics, and has medication to try and prevent the paralysis. But there is currently no cure.

'There is a treatment and a cure being developed by Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard University in the USA, which is what we're fundraising for. It has had some really positive results, but will cost a fortune.

'They have been awarded a huge grant to push forward a cure for AHC - because in theory, once AHC can be cured, any condition that's caused by a single gene being affected can be treated.

Rupert's family are now working to raise the £1.5million needed to send him to America for treatment which could potentially suppress and control his AHC

The treatment, she added, should be ready next year.

Mrs Smith explained: 'The treatment kills the bad genes. It is essentially a protein that attaches to the bad gene and stops it from working, so the good gene can carry on. This will then allow Rupert to develop the way he should, and minimise or stop the symptoms of AHC altogether.'

Mr and Mrs Smith added they are so 'grateful' for the immense outpouring of support Rupert's cause has generated so far.

'The support has been overwhelming,' said Mr Smith. 'The way people come together has been phenomenal. It makes us feel as though we are not alone.

'We have never met another family who has a child with this condition, only spoken to them.  So knowing we have got all these people fighting for Rupert with us - I can't put into words how much it means to us and our family.'

Wrexham Maelor Hospital is overseen by Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board. Interim chief operating officer Matt Powels said the Trust is 'absolutely committed' to supporting families like the Smiths.

He said: 'Firstly, I want to pay tribute to Rupert's parents for raising awareness of his extremely rare condition. We all look forward to a day when a cure is found for AHC.

'More generally, our children's services are absolutely committed to supporting parents and young people who find themselves having to deal with rare and life-limiting conditions, often in partnership with our colleagues at Alder Hey Children's Hospital.

'It is vitally important parents and children with life-limiting illnesses feel supported at every stage of their child's healthcare journey. That is the ethos which drives our colleagues within children's services.'

A high-ranking Democrat in Virginia who has been indicted on drug trafficking and money laundering charges claimed she is being unfairly targeted by President Trump in a defiant statement.

Virginia state senator L. Louise Lucas, 82, was charged on Thursday with racketeering and money laundering conspiracy connected to her family's marijuana business.

The allegations center around a cannabis company owned by Lucas and her family, The Cannabis Outlet, through which she allegedly 'disguised the proceeds of illegal marijuana distribution,' prosecutors said in her indictment.

In a statement shared to social media following the indictment, Lucas wrote: Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother.'

'I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back and I’m not stopping now,' she wrote.

'I'm not new to this. I'm true to this. I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.'

The 82-year-old reportedly surrendered to authorities on Thursday, and Lucas is charged along with a half dozen other co-conspirators including her two daughters and her grandson.

One of those daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke, is running for Portsmouth City Council after serving as the vice mayor there for years.

At a press conference on Thursday, FBI Director Kash Patel accused Lucas of accumulating almost $5 million 'in ill-gotten gains through her criminal enterprise.'

Virginia state senator L. Louise Lucas, 82, was charged on Thursday with racketeering and money laundering conspiracy, as part of a wide-ranging public corruption probe

FBI Director Kash Patel and US Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the charges on Thursday at a press conference

A vocal proponent of marijuana legalization, Lucas is accused of pushing for the move in the Virginia Senate for her own benefit, and prosecutors alleged in her indictment that she sent text messages about making 'a lot of money' through legalization.

In a phone call from February 2026, Lucas also allegedly told a co-conspirator she had her 'last chance at generational wealth,' and said she had 'gotten too old not to be greedy.'

Lucas, the president pro tempore of the Virginia state senate and one of the most powerful Democrats in Virginia, allegedly 'used her political position' to 'insulate' herself and her family from prosecution, per her indictment.

In May, federal agents searched Lucas's office and The Cannabis Outlet store, located in Portsmouth, Virginia.

Although Lucas characterized the action against her as being directed by the Trump White House, the investigation into Lucas predates the Trump administration and began during the Biden administration, according to NBC News.

According to the indictment against Lucas, members of the alleged conspiracy 'used various business entities' to carry out 'illegal marijuana distribution,' with the ultimate goal of 'wealth accumulation.'

Prosecutors say that Lucas and her family created a number of businesses and corporations to further the alleged scheme, including 'Hair for Dayzzz,' 'Freedom is Dope,' and 'Mama's Chicken LLC.'

Lucas, the president pro tempore of the Virginia state senate and one of the most powerful Democrats in Virginia, allegedly 'used her political position' to 'insulate' herself and her family from prosecution

Federal agents seen raiding Lucas's office in Portsmouth, Virginia in May

Pictured: A copy of a cheque that prosecutors say was handed to Lucas, per the indictment

Lucas's daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, who is currently running for the Portsmouth City Council

Lucas has been a leading proponent of marijuana legalization in Virginia.

in addition to serving as president pro tempore, she leads the powerful Senate finance committee, which oversees all legislation with any budget impact. According to prosecutors, Lucas used this position to enrich her family's booming cannabis empire, including through obtaining legalization in 2021 and statewide retail sales by July 2027.

Despite pushing through legalization legislation, Lucas allegedly bought huge amounts of marijuana via a co-conspirator from outside the state's five licensed cannabis growers.

According to Lucas's indictment, the Democrat allegedly paid $750,000 to an unindicted co-conspirator in August 2022 for a 100% stake in a shell company called 'Mama's Chicken LLC', which she 'expected to obtain a Virginia recreational marijuana license.'

When it became apparent that state laws meant licensed marijuana stores wouldn't open in Virginia until 2027, Lucas then began pressuring the co-conspirator to return the money within months, according to the indictment.

Lucas seen with former President Joe Biden and ex-Virginia Governor Terry McAuliffe

In November 2025, she allegedly texted that same person telling them she would be pushing forward legislation that would ensure licensed pot stores in Virginia.

She allegedly sent in the message: 'You know I will be carrying the legislation as the Chief Co-patron. Yes, we can make a lot of money but, before we start down that road again; how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me with arrangements for the balance. Then we can talk about future business plans.'

On February 9, 2026, Lucas allegedly called the person to update them on the pending cannabis legislation, telling them: 'This is our last chance at generational wealth… I’ve got too old to not be greedy.'

On March 9, Lucas also allegedly called another Virginia legislator to ask for a recreational marijuana license, because she 'got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling in because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.'

Lucas, who is not up for re-election until 2027, was accused by US Attorney General Todd Blanche of using her influence to put her financial interests above her constituents.

'The Department of Justice intends to prove that Senator Lucas violated the trust of the people of Portsmouth and Chesapeake, Virginia, and of her state senate colleagues,' Blanche told a press conference.

'Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself.'

The case comes as the Justice Department has also brought a high-profile investigation against Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar in Minnesota.

The Justice Department typically does not bring political cases within 60 days of elections to avoid allegations of bias, however Blanche dismissed those concerns when speaking to reporters on Thursday.

'It’s not even a rule, it’s a practice,' Blanche said, noting that while many of Lucas's fellow Democrats may be facing incoming re-elections, she is not on the ballot again until next year.

'The justice manual speaks very clearly about what the Department of Justice can and can’t do, and we cannot bring a charge if our purpose is improper,' he said, saying he believes this case was correctly brought.
