#494. Prolific stalker, 38, who installed multiple listening devices, trackers and cameras at ex and her new partner's home and workplaces amid 'despicable and devious' two-year harassment campaign is jailed

Published: 20:52 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 20:56 BST, 22 October 2026

A prolific stalker who waged a 'despicable and devious' two-year harassment campaign against his ex-partner and the father of her child has been sentenced to a year behind bars.

Craig Newton, of Newham, relentlessly stalked Danielle Dowles and Alex LeGrand between June 28, 2023 and November 23, 2025, Snaresbrook Crown Court heard on Monday.

The 38-year-old, who has been convicted 13 times for 30 offences since April 2007, installed listening devices in their home by four-way cables, and cameras outside the victims' residences as well as their offices.

Numerous covert tracking devices were found on both of their cars on five separate occasions, the court heard. Their vehicles were also repeatedly damaged in various incidents between August 2024 and July 2025.

On July 15, 2025, Mr LeGrand described his car as being 'blown up' in an arson attack he said was carried out on his car by Newton, the court was told.

Dashcam footage shows a black Mercedes driving towards Mr LeGrand's car. Smoke appears to fill the vehicle, and shortly after, a male gets into the vehicle's passenger seat before driving away.

The terrifying campaign also extended to the victims' relatives, and on July 28, 2025, Mr LeGrand's mother's windows were 'smashed' by two individuals. The same happened to his sister on August 5, 2025, the court heard.

That same month, 'bricks were thrown' at his mother's home again, and three months later, his sister-in-law's vehicle was also 'targeted and damaged', Timothy Fulfoit, prosecuting, told the court.

Prolific stalker, Craig Newton, 38, of Newham, has been sentenced to a year behind bars after launching a 'devious and despicable' campaign of harrassment against his ex, Danielle Dowles and the father of her child, Alex LeGrand

On July 15, 2025, Mr LeGrand described his car as being 'blown up', the court was told. He said an arson attack was carried out on his car by Newton.

The 38-year-old, who has been convicted 13 times for 30 offences since April 2007, installed listening devices in their home by four-way cables (pictured)

Mr Fulfoit added that Ms Dowles was 'fearful for [her] life' during the two-and-a-half year ordeal, with her son becoming 'scared' to speak at home out of fear of listening devices.

'I don't know how this is going to end [Newton] is ruining my life, and I don't know how far he is going to go,' she said in a statement read out in court.

'I have no life anymore because of what he has put us through,' she said. 'I am terrified of what he is capable of.'

Newton's 'multi-faceted' stalking campaign of Ms Dowles began on June 18, 2023, when he called her 99 times in three hours from prison, the court heard.

He continued to phone both her and her mother from behind bars and threatened them if they called the police.

Newton and Ms Dowles began their relationship in May 2022 but it 'fell apart pretty quickly' before he was jailed the following December in relation to eight counts of breaching a restraining order against another ex-girlfriend.

Newton was sentenced to 32 months behind bars for the charges as well as another unrelated matter.

The 38-year-old began his 'pattern of harassment and stalking' in 2014, when he breached a restraining order, Mr Fulfoit said.

He was convicted of harassment, damaging property, as well as repeated restraining order breaches between February 2015 and July 2019.

It was also heard that, after a relationship ended with a previous partner in January 2018, Newton 'embarked on mass calls on any one day without answer' from her.

After their relationship ended, Ms Dowles had 'some contact' with the defendant until February 2023; she then wished to no longer speak with him.

But despite being behind bars, Newton continued to contact her through third parties until his release, the court heard. He would also make 'derogatory' posts about her online.

In December 2023, the first of many tracking devices was found on Ms Dowles' car, the court heard.

In August 2024, another tracking device was discovered amid a probe after her vehicle was found to have been 'smashed into repeatedly by another car', Mr Fulfoit said. A third was discovered almost a year later in March 2025.

Newton was 'lying in wait' at Ms Dowles' home after she attended a friend's birthday party in April 2025, Mr Fulfoit said.

Pictured: Craig Newton and another individual outside Mr LeGrand's offices. One individual can be seen climbing up a ladder. A camera was found outside of LeGrand's workplace, which he was informed about by a colleague on September 9, 2025

Mr LeGrand also found the word 'GRASS' sprayed on the outside of the door and wall of his apartment on August, 20, 2025

Newton installed cameras outside the victims' residences as well as their offices (Pictured: One found in a pest box among shrubbery)

Several cameras were then found outside her address monitoring her and Mr LeGrand's movement to and from the house, the court was told.

When Newton was freed in 2024, he said he intended to 'ruin the relationship between her and Mr LeGrand,' the prosecution told the court.

He then began monitoring Mr LeGrand's movements and asked Ms Dowles why his car had been outside her home overnight and threatened to blow it up.

Two tracking devices were found on Mr LeGrand's car on separate occasions, one in July 2024 and another in May 2025.

In July 2024, Mr LeGrand also received messages from different Instagram accounts, Mr Fulfoit added. A month later, a vehicle 'rammed into his car'.

The following December, a site manager told LeGrand camera devices had been found outside his block of flats.

In July 2025, Mr LeGrand described his car as being 'blown up' or 'damaged extremely'. That same month, he found cameras hidden in pest control boxes outside of his flat, the court heard.

On September 7, 2025, while both Ms Dowles and Mr LeGrand were at Burger and Lobster, Newton hurled 'abusive language' at the pair.

Two days later, cameras were found to have been installed outside of Mr LeGrand's office, with CCTV later showing Newton alongside another individual installing the camera.

Harry Martin, mitigating, asked for both counts to be served as concurrent sentences as they were 'a series of offences of the same type and period'.

'I did not disagree with any other facts, did not wish to add any further about the defendant,' he said.

After striking a plea deal, Newton pleaded guilty to two counts of Section 2A of the Protection from Harassment Act 1997, and was sentenced to a year behind bars.

Judge Oscar Del Fabbro, at sentencing, told Newton: 'This all arose when you were in a relationship which lasted a couple of months with the complainants, and that fell apart pretty quickly'.

He added Newton maintained contact with the victim while in prison, 'no doubt utilising means you were not permitted'.

'You continued your campaign of harassment against the complainant; it was multifaceted, and it was not only against your former partner but indeed against a new partner who formed a new relationship with her,' he added.

'Your ingenuity in stalking these two individuals knew no bounds. It was a catalogue of despicable behaviour on your part.

'You won't understand it; you never will.

'Your ingenuity in stalking these two individuals knew no bounds. It was a catalogue of despicable behaviour on your part,' Judge Oscar Del Fabbro told Newton

'The personal implications of this behaviour must have been obvious to you.

'You designed it that way even though she was no way interested in continuing that relationship.'

The judge said Newton's devious methods of seeking to harass the victims were just 'the tip of the iceberg' of the 'considerable anxiety' caused to both victims.

He added that 'No person should have to endure that behaviour.'

A restraining order was also put in place preventing Newton from contacting either victim for the next decade.

The judge warned Newton: 'Breach of such an order carries a sentence of imprisonment for five years.

'You will be well advised to stay clear of the two individuals named in that restraining order.'

#497. Raging Crufts competitor who drove van into show ring before hurling racist insults at judge after her dogs were barred from contest is fined £4,000

Published: 19:09 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 20:38 BST, 22 October 2026

A raging Crufts competitor who drove a van into a show ring and hurled racist insults at a judge after her dogs were barred from a competition has been fined £4,000.

Marianne Hunter, 63, 'lost her temper' and racially abused a judge for blocking her beloved lurchers from entering the 'Snooty Fox' dog show in Wales, a court heard.

The mother-of-two travelled 270 miles from Kent to the countryside event held in Narberth, West Wales, before she was told her prized pooches could not compete in the same category.

After being denied entry, Hunter, who was described as a business manager for Public Health England, burst into a rage and called dog show judge Tracey Hodges a 'Welsh c***'.

She then drove her white Ford Transit van into the show ring and knocked a participant over while children played nearby, Haverfordwest Magistrates' Court heard.

Hunter's outburst took place at the annual dog show named after Narberth town's local pub The Snooty Fox in June last year.

Prizes at the family dog show held in Pembrokeshire included £100 for each show champion featuring whippets, terriers and lurchers as well as Kennel Club classes.

But refusing one of Hunter's dog entrance into the show caused her to launch a racist and violent tirade.

Marianne Hunter, 63, flew into a racist and violent tirade after her dogs were denied entry into a countryside dog show in Wales

#503. Average salary breaks through £40,000 for the first time - but stealth tax is eating your pay rise

The typical pre-tax salary for those working full-time has smashed the £40,000-a-year barrier for the first time, official findings show.

Average annual earnings for full-time employees were £40,911 in the year to April 2026, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) reveal.

But as pay increases and income tax thresholds stay the same, many more people face higher taxes on their pay.

Average full-time weekly earnings were £811.20 by the end of the period, up 5.8 per cent in a year, while average part-time weekly earnings were up 2.9 per cent to £288.10 in April 2026, the figures show.

The median full-time annual pre-tax salary in Britain increased by 4.5 per cent, a slight fall from 4.6 per cent in the previous period – and also the most sluggish rate since 2021.

Full-time weekly earnings rose fastest for managers, up 6.7 per cent, and slowest for factory workers, up 4.1 per cent.

For women the average full-time pre-tax pay was £37,471, while for men it was £43,934, the ONS said.

The gender pay gap for full-time workers, which does not account for differences in occupation, experience or qualifications, narrowed to 6.8 per cent from 7.2 per cent.

In April 2026, the highest proportion of low-paid employees was found in the hospitality industry and among employees aged 16 to 21 years, according to the ONS.

Staff earning high pay were concentrated in managerial and professional occupations, information and communication, finance and insurance, and among employees aged 45 to 49 years.

The ONS said early estimates for September 2026 indicated that median monthly pay was £2,660, an increase of 4.4 per cent compared with the same period a year ago.

Back in September 2014, the figure was £1,404 a month.

The ONS added: 'A series of lower median pay growth figures were observed in late 2025, likely influenced by the timing of public sector pay settlements having differed from the previous year.'

Bank of England policymakers typically view pay growth markedly above 3 per cent as a sign they face a tougher time getting inflation back to their 2 per cent target.

The national minimum wage is the lowest amount employees can legally be paid, and it normally rises every year.

In April 2026, Labour increased the minimum wage for people aged 21 and over to £12.71 an hour, up 50p from £12.21.

For those aged between 18 and 21, minimum wage rates increased to £10.85 an hour – up 85p from £10.

Chancellor John Healey is expected to announce the next minimum wage increase in his Budget on October 28.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to act on frozen income tax thresholds

Data about pay rises may appear to spell good news, but an ever-growing number of people are being dragged into higher income tax rates as tax thresholds remain frozen.

Tax thresholds have not kept up with the cost of living, since former Chancellor Rishi Sunak froze them at 2021 levels at the tail end of the pandemic – and were then frozen for even longer by Rachel Reeves.

Before, most thresholds used to rise in line with consumer price index inflation.

Crucially, as people's nominal earnings increase relative to tax thresholds, more of their income is taxed.

The resulting 'fiscal drag' is set to raise significant sums for the Treasury's coffers as the average effective tax rate, or the total tax paid as a share of total income, increases more quickly over time.

The current personal allowance most people have is £12,570. This is how much money most people can earn before income tax kicks in.

Recent analysis by Standard Life found the personal allowance would stand at £16,072 in 2026/27 had it kept pace with inflation, which would be £3,502 higher than it is now.

And the higher-rate threshold would be £64,274, rather than £50,270.

In August, Standard Life said the frozen personal allowance added £700.36 to the annual income tax bill of a basic-rate taxpayer who uses the allowance in full.

For someone earning above the inflation-adjusted higher-rate threshold, the combined impact of both frozen thresholds is £3,501.22, it added.

One in six people have hesitated or refused a pay rise, bonus or promotion because they were concerned that higher taxes or lost allowances could reduce the financial benefit, Standard Life claims.

More than a fifth of people said they would consider turning down a pay rise if it meant they would have to pay a higher rate of income tax, Standard Life's findings showed.

Sarah Coles, of AJ Bell, said: 'The average full-time wage has broken through £40,000 for the first time, after weekly pay rose 5.8 per cent in a year.

'This isn't the full picture though, because after inflation, full-time pay was up just 2.7 per cent.

'It means millions of people are getting pay rises which do little more than keep up with rising prices. However, this doesn't stop them from being clobbered by higher taxes.'

She added: 'The real kick in the teeth is that income tax thresholds have remained frozen for the entire period.

'The number of people paying income tax has risen from 33million in the 2021/22 tax year to an estimated 39.8million by 2025/26 – up 6.8million in that time.

'At a more granular level, the number of basic rate taxpayers increased by 3.5million, the number of higher rate taxpayers is up by around 2.9million, and the number of additional rate taxpayers is up 700,000.'

#506. Record numbers of Britons diagnosed with dementia, NHS figures show

Published: 16:05 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 19:19 BST, 22 October 2026

More Britons are being diagnosed with dementia than ever before, new figures show.

A record 523,081 people in England have been told they have the deadly disease by doctors, compared to 512,466 at the end of last year – a rise of 10,615 patients.

This is the first time in six years that the NHS has met its target to ensure two-thirds of over-65-year-olds suffering symptoms have a formal diagnosis.

The last time the health service hit the goal, in March 2020, the number of diagnoses was 470,292 - 11 per cent lower than the most recent figure.

It's estimated that over a million people are living with dementia in the UK, but many are suffering without the oversight of medics.

Experts say that receiving an early diagnosis is key to accessing vital care and treatment that could slow the progression of symptoms.

The rise in diagnoses is thought to be due to better detection of warning signs as well as a genuine increase in prevalence.

More than a million people in the UK are thought to be suffering with dementia, but only a proportion of these receive a formal diagnosis

The ageing population, increase in obesity and lack of exercise among Britons are all thought to be fuelling dementia cases.

The latest data comes amid the Daily Mail and Alzheimer's Society's partnership in a drive to defeat dementia, which claims 76,000 lives a year as Britain’s biggest killer.

The Defeating Dementia campaign aims to raise awareness of the disease, in an effort to increase early diagnosis, boost research and improve care.

Dr Jeremy Isaacs, national clinical director for dementia, NHS England, said it is 'fantastic' that the NHS has met its target.

'Getting a dementia diagnosis is the first step in ensuring the NHS can offer help whether it be a care plan or medication review,' he said.

'There are lots of reasons why people might appear forgetful or absent-minded, but it could be a sign that something is wrong.'

Survey data collected by the Alzheimer's Society shows striking public support for government policies on dementia care.

More than half of Britons (56 per cent) rate dementia among the top three health conditions government should prioritise over the next five years, while almost three quarters (72 per cent) support an 18-week national maximum waiting time for a dementia diagnosis.

Meanwhile, more than four in ten (44 per cent) said more dementia funding would make them more likely to vote for a political party.

Michelle Dyson CB, Chief Executive of Alzheimer's Society, said: 'A target of two thirds is too modest, and we must demand better for dementia.

'Too many people spend months on end waiting for answers, unable to access the support, advice and care that a diagnosis can unlock.

'With new treatments emerging that are most effective in the early stages of disease, the consequences of delayed diagnosis are becoming even more significant.

'We need a more ambitious goal. The UK Government must introduce a maximum 18-week wait for a dementia diagnosis, including starting a care plan and treatment, and invest in the people and services needed to deliver on this goal.'

Minister of State for Mental Health and Social Care Alison McGovern agreed that 'there is still a lot more to do'.

'As we diagnose more people with dementia, we need better treatments and social care so they can live well for longer.'

Asked if he meant that Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: ‘That's on the manager and staff to say, not me.

‘Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable. As you saw with Como, the centre back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.

‘A team that plays through the middle with small connections, if you give them too much time and space then they can hurt you out wide.’

Having conceded to Atletico after 50 seconds last week, United were behind within two minutes as Como star Nico Paz struck the first of his two goals.

‘It's not the first time, we started on the wrong foot, and they scored very early,’ said Fernandes. ‘Not much pressure on the ball, not many good movements with the ball, not many things going our way.

‘Conceding early makes us go into game with a mood of defeat, it's difficult to get out of that, trying to be brave, to have the ball and make something happen. If we are not able to do that, it is going to be very difficult to get out of this situation.’

Fernandes is under contract until next summer with an option to extend until 2028. His form has dipped from last season, when he was named PFA and FWA Player of the Year and broke the Premier League record for assists in a season.

He is expected to keep the captaincy despite his outspoken comments on TNT Sports on Wednesday night.

The Princess of Wales admitted she was missing her eldest son, Prince George - and is looking forward to all three of her children coming home for half term tomorrow, on a surprise engagement today.

Chatting to shocked shoppers inside a joint charity shop and cafe in a small village in Norfolk, Kate, 44, was asked how her children were getting on.

While chatting to locals who had gathered outside the shop after word quickly spread of the royal visit, the princess asked children if they were on half term.

One youngster told her that it’s his last day today, and she replied: 'My children break up tomorrow and I can’t wait to have them all home.'

The princess’ visit to Café 98 in Hoveton, East Anglia’s Children’s Hospices' first and only café located within one of the charity’s retail stores, was kept under wraps due to the café's small size.

Her outfit included Posh Spice's £850 Katherine jacket, matching trousers worth £475 and a black lambswool polo neck that retails for £520. She finished the look with a £290 burgundy belt with a gold buckle.

She later popped into Café 98 in Hoveton, East Anglia's Children's Hospices' first and only café located within one of the charity's retail stores.

And when she walked in, customers enjoying a cup of tea and browsing the rails couldn't believe the future Queen had stopped by.

The Princess of Wales waved to well-wishers after visiting Cafe 98, the East Anglia's Children's Hospices (EACH) cafe, located within their Hoveton retail store in Norfolk

While her visit was initially kept under wraps due to the cafe's small size, word quickly spread, and locals gathered outside to meet Kate

The Princess of Wales was shown how to value donated clothes before they go on sale

Kate in conversation with Cafe 98's shop manager Fran

'Oh yes please,' Kate said, darting over to them. 'Do you come in here quite a bit?'

Looking at the boxes, Prince William's wife said: 'You never know what you're going to find [in a charity shop]. That's what's so nice. It feels a bit more like a treasure hunt.'

Interrupting with a tone of surprise, Ms Landsborough said: 'Do you go to charity shops?'

'Yes, I do,' the princess said. 'I love going round a charity shop. When I was at university in St Andrew's, there were a lot of charity shops.'

Catherine heard more about how the cafe operates when she sat down with Ian Nicholson, EACH’s Director of Retail, and Ms Neary, who started as a volunteer before becoming a paid member of the team, in the cafe.

With an oat milk cappuccino and a plate of sweet treats, including carrot cake, biscoff millionaire’s shortbread and a bakewell blondie, in front of her, the princess asked questions about the number of volunteers, where they get their donations from and how many shops they have.

The princess was then introduced to Christine Rich, who showed her how items were prepared for sale before they sorted items together

The princess was then introduced to Christine Rich, who showed her how items were prepared for sale before they sorted items together, deciding which ones could be sold and which poorer-quality items would be sold as scrap fabric.

Catherine held several of the items up against her as she was sorting through them, and when Ms Rich noticed the label was still on a pink chiffon blouse, she exclaimed: 'Who would pay £105 for a blouse?' Before realising she was in the company of a princess, she quickly moved onto the next item.

When Catherine spotted a moth hole in an otherwise immaculate coat, she asked if it could still be sold in the shop.

The Princess of Wales has yet again proved herself as the authority in autumn fashion donning a coolly elegant Victoria Beckham ensemble.

#509. Homeless man, 61, is charged with murder of housing officer, 47, found stabbed in crashed car as she tried to drive to hospital

Published: 17:00 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 03:16 BST, 23 October 2026

A homeless man has been charged with the murder of a housing officer who was stabbed at a retirement village before crashing her car as she fled the scene for hospital.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, was severely injured after being attacked at work when she got into her car in Bridgend, South Wales, on Monday.

Clifford Foster, 61, was on Thursday charged with murder following the incident at the Ger-Y-Nant sheltered accommodation, run by Valleys to Coast housing association.

It is alleged the out-of-work plasterer was inside a flat at the complex when Ms Barnfield told him he shouldn't have been at the property - and was subsequently stabbed.

After being attacked, Ms Barnfield only managed to drive a short distance before collapsing at the wheel and crashing into a wall.

Police were alerted to a road traffic collision at 12.43pm and two ambulances and an air ambulance rushed to the scene.

It was there that emergency services discovered 'puncture' wounds which were not associated with the crash.

Ms Barnfield, a mother of two, was taken to hospital but was later confirmed to have died.

Clifford Foster, 61, of no fixed address, has been charged with the murder of Eleanor Barnfield

Ms Barnfield, 47, was severely injured after being attacked at work when she got into her car in Bridgend, South Wales, on Monday - she later died in hospital

Emergency services are pictured at the scene of the crash in South Wales. The incident reportedly left locals 'shaken'

Her alleged attacker barricaded himself in a room at the complex, prompting an armed police response and all residents to be evacuated.

A man was later seen being taken away from the scene in the back of a police van after being escorted to the vehicle by at least four uniformed officers.

Other residents have since been able to return to the retirement village, which has 13 social housing flats for people over the age of 60.

Father-of-one Foster is said to have been staying at a nearby 'halfway house' run by homeless charity The Wallich.

Paying tribute this week, Ms Barnfield's family described the mother and grandmother last night as the 'kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world'.

They added: 'She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock.'

South Wales Police said: 'A man has been charged in connection with a murder investigation in Bridgend.

'Clifford Foster, aged 61, of Bridgend, has been charged with murder in connection with the death of 47-year-old Eleanor Barnfield, of Bridgend.

'He is due to appear at Newport Magistrates Court tomorrow.'

Senior Investigating Officer Claire Lamerton said: 'My thoughts remain with Eleanor's loved ones at such a devastating time, and they continue to be supported by specialist officers.

'This is not being investigated as a domestic incident, and I encourage the public to not speculate about the circumstances as court proceedings are now active.'

This afternoon, the Welsh Ambulance Service responded to claims Ms Barnfield had been trying to drive herself to hospital after phoning 999 herself.

The scene outside the Ger-y-Nant retirement home where Ms Barnfield was badly injured at work

Locals said there was a large police presence, including armed officers and a SWAT team. Police described the incident as 'deeply distressing'

A police van believed to contain the suspect left the scene of the alleged stabbing after midnight on Tuesday

The trust said it had no record of any contact from a number belonging to her.

'Following preliminary investigations by the Welsh Ambulance Service, the Trust has been unable to identify any calls from Eleanor Barnfield's phone numbers,' a spokesman said.

'Enquiries are ongoing to establish if any calls were received by other means.'

It previously said: 'The Welsh Ambulance Service were called on Monday at approximately 12.44pm, to reports of a road traffic collision on Coity Road, Bridgend.

'A Cymru High Acuity Response Unit arrived on scene seven minutes after the initial call at 12.51pm, with two emergency ambulances arriving to provide additional support at 13.07pm and 13.13pm.

'Advanced critical care support was delivered by the Emergency Medical Retrieval and Transfer Service who arrived in a Wales Air Ambulance charity helicopter.

'The patient was conveyed by road to hospital.

'We are aware that contradictory and misleading rumours regarding a delayed ambulance response have been circulating on social media.

'These are factually untrue and we would encourage members of the public not to speculate.'

Valleys to Coast said: 'We are deeply saddened by the tragic incident in Bridgend on October 19 and can confirm that a member of our team was involved.

'Eleanor was a much-valued member of the Valleys to Coast team, and her loss has been deeply felt by everyone who knew and worked alongside her.

'She made an important contribution to our organisation and to the communities we serve, and she will be remembered with great warmth and affection by her colleagues.

'Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Eleanor's family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time. We are doing everything we can to support those affected by her loss.'

Floral tributes were left alongside the crumbled brick wall on Coity Road that was covered in an orange plastic meshing.

One tribute read: 'My beautiful friend there are no words to describe how broken I am. You were my rock. You have kept me going through life. I will be forever grateful.

'I will miss you forever. My life will never be the same without you, my heart breaks for your friends and family, your memory will always be kept alive.'

Another read: 'Deeply saddened of your loss. Our thoughts are with you and your family.'

Neighbour Sue Thomas, who lives opposite the residential home, said: 'The residents are back but people going in have to sign in and out.

'You don't expect to go to work and not come home. I feel for her family.'

Gavin Owen, who lives near the scene, watched as SWAT teams swooped outside his house.

He said: 'There was police, everything was cordoned off. So I got scared and worried, and didn't know what was going on.

'When I got home, at the bottom of my street, by the garage, it was cordoned off.

'I had to tell them where I lived and they had to escort me to my front door. They said we're going to have to sign in and out if we want to come in or leave.

'We had people coming to interview us, asking us for ring doorcam footage. And gradually it then expanded, we had standard police officers, then we had men in suits, we had the riot team come and then we had a SWAT team.

'They had ladders up, cable tyres going on the roof, it was just insane.'

Published: 13:04 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 19:02 BST, 22 October 2026

John Goodman said that transferring his addictive behavior from drinking to eating led him to hit nearly 400lbs at one point.

Goodman, 74, explained to The New Yorker about how his weight would rise and fall after he got sober in 2007, when he was 55.

'I'd lose 60 pounds in a summer, gain it all back - 70 pounds, 80 pounds - and that got tiring,' the veteran actor told the outlet. 'I took steps so I wouldn't have to do that anymore.

'I was almost 400 pounds. I was eating alcoholically after I stopped drinking.'

Goodman said his decision to quit drinking came when he 'got sick and tired of being sick and tired.'

Said the actor: 'The thing about instant gratification is you don't really care what's going to happen right after it - which always led to bigger hangovers or me getting the shakes, and having to drink to get rid of the shakes, and that vicious cycle.'

The Daily Mail has reached out to representatives for Goodman for further comment on this story.

John Goodman said that transferring his addictive ways from drinking to eating led him to hit nearly 400 pounds at one point. Pictured in NYC October 5

#511. Spooked Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California to avoid potential billionaire's tax that would claim slice of his fortune

Mark Zuckerberg threatened to flee California over a proposed billionaire tax, but now he's found a creative way to protect his multibillion-dollar fortune.

The Meta boss, worth an estimated $246 billion, has struck a deal that would let him sell a chunk of his shares while retaining his iron hold over the company, provided he commits to staying in California for eight years.

The arrangement comes as the Golden State prepares to vote on a controversial proposal that could see its wealthiest residents hit with a one-time levy on their fortunes.

The measure, known as Proposition 40, would impose a five percent tax on the assets of California residents worth more than $1 billion if voters approve it on November 3.

For Zuckerberg, 42, the potential bill could run into billions of dollars, prompting him to tell Meta's board that he was considering moving his primary residence out of the state.

But rather than risk losing its founder from the California headquarters, Meta has come up with a financial arrangement designed to keep him firmly in place.

Under the deal, the Facebook and Instagram owner will receive a new class of non-voting shares that he can gradually sell without sacrificing his voting power.

Zuckerberg will be able to sell a fifth of those new shares once they are issued, giving him a way to raise cash to cover a potential tax bill if the proposal passes.

Mark Zuckerberg has has struck a deal that would let him sell a chunk of his Meta shares while retaining his iron hold over the company

The deal is conditional on Zuckerberg remaining a company leader and living in California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for the next eight years

The structure will effectively allow him to cash out up to half of his economic stake over time while maintaining control of the company through his existing super-voting shares.

Those shares currently give him approximately 61 percent of Meta's voting power, meaning he can retain the final say over major corporate decisions even if he sells a significant portion of his financial interest.

The deal is conditional on Zuckerberg remaining a company leader and living in California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for the next eight years.

According to a regulatory filing, negotiations between Zuckerberg and a special committee of Meta's board were lengthy and, at times, contentious.

Directors ultimately concluded that keeping him at the helm was critical as the company pours enormous sums into artificial intelligence and battles rivals for dominance.

The new share structure is expected to be introduced through a two-for-one stock split, with the additional class of shares due to begin trading in January 2027.

Meta says the arrangement could also help it raise money for future acquisitions, infrastructure and AI development without diluting Zuckerberg's control.

The company's ambitions are hardly cheap, with internal forecasts indicating it may need to raise hundreds of billions of dollars over several years to finance its plans.

The proposed California tax has become a flashpoint in Silicon Valley, where some of the world's richest people are concerned about the prospect of paying a levy on wealth that can include company shares and other assets

Meta has already forecast capital spending of up to $145 billion for the full year as Zuckerberg pursues his vision of turning the social media giant into an AI powerhouse.

The spending spree comes with risks, however, after the company reported negative $2.1 billion in free cash flow during the third quarter, marking its first quarterly cash burn in at least a decade.

Its latest results nevertheless offered investors some encouragement, with revenue climbing 26 percent year over year to $64.6 billion.

Meta shares rose as much as 6.5 percent in after-hours trading following the earnings announcement before giving back some of those gains.

The proposed California tax has become a flashpoint in Silicon Valley, where some of the world's richest people are concerned about the prospect of paying a levy on wealth that can include company shares and other assets.

Supporters argue the measure could raise substantial funds, while critics warn that wealthy residents could relocate, potentially depriving the state of investment, jobs and future tax revenue.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin, DoorDash chief executive Tony Xu, investor Ron Conway and cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen are among those reported to have spent millions opposing the proposal. Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, by contrast, has said he would not object to paying the tax.

California Governor Gavin Newsom has also opposed the measure, warning that a state-level wealth tax could encourage affluent residents to leave.

California Governor Gavin Newsom has voiced his opposition of the measure, warning that a state-level wealth tax could encourage affluent residents to leave

Zuckerberg's proposed arrangement is not the first time Meta has explored a share structure that would allow its founder to sell stock while retaining control.

The company abandoned a similar plan in 2017 after minority shareholders challenged it, arguing that it would widen the gap between Zuckerberg's voting power and his financial stake.

The latest proposal could also face scrutiny from investors concerned about corporate governance and the ability of founders to maintain control while selling their shares.

For now, Zuckerberg's deal highlights the extraordinary lengths Meta is prepared to go to keep its founder in charge as it enters an expensive new phase of competition.

And with California's billionaire tax heading towards a crucial vote, the outcome could have consequences extending well beyond one of Silicon Valley's most powerful residents.

#512. Terrifying truth about Britain's multiple sclerosis 'surge': Fears that 1 in 5 patients actually DON'T have it... as experts reveal the three conditions often missed by doctors

Published: 12:14 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 18:47 BST, 22 October 2026

For Christina Applegate, being told she didn't have multiple sclerosis (MS) felt like being 'back at square one'.

The actress, 54, had already spent five years battling debilitating symptoms that left her needing to use a wheelchair and cane.

'[My doctor] came into my room and said, "congratulations, you don't have MS,"' she recalled on a podcast this week.

'I was, like, not happy at all… you don't get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden, I'm better. I haven't gotten better. If anything, I've gotten worse.'

As startling as it is, her experience is far from unusual. Data suggests many patients are diagnosed with MS, a condition in which the immune system attacks the protective coating around nerves, only to later be told it was a misdiagnosis.

In fact, studies show that nearly one in five MS patients are later told they don't actually have the condition – in some cases, after receiving treatment for MS for more than a decade.

Speaking to the Daily Mail, neurologists who've been treating the condition for several years have described this type of misdiagnosis as a 'common problem'.

'This week alone, I undiagnosed two patients,' said Dr Dinesh Sivakolundu, a neurologist who works with MS patients. 'It is incredibly common, so I'm glad it is gaining traction now.'

Christina Applegate, pictured in 2023, has revealed her doctor told her she does not have multiple sclerosis despite battling debilitating symptoms for more than five years

The big question is, how and why does it happen? First, it's important to understand what MS is – and why it's so tricky to diagnose.

The condition occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks the protective sheath that covers nerve fibres, known as myelin. As this is destroyed, it interrupts communication between these nerve cells, disrupting signals sent from the brain to the rest of the body.

There are four types of MS, with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS), featuring symptoms that return after periods of remission or recovery, being the most common. It is behind 85 per cent of initial diagnoses.

But because symptoms vary depending on where the nerves are being attacked, not all patients have the same warning signs, which can include struggling to walk or move and numbness.

Multiple sclerosis affects around 150,000 Britons and is the most common disabling neurological disease among younger adults, typically striking between the ages of 20 and 40.

The number of diagnoses in the UK have risen sharply in recent decades. A recent analysis published in the journal JAMA Neurology found prevalence of the condition doubled between 2000 and 2020.

The MS Society – the UK's biggest charity for the disorder – has also reported a significant rise in patients.

Experts have mostly attributed this to improvements in detecting MS, rather than a genuine increase in cases. However some argue that the rise is real, pointing to risk factors like obesity and smoking that could fuel the condition.

Women are about three times more likely to be diagnosed than men. It's not clear why, but scientists have suggested it is linked to hormones and stress.

Crucially, there is no single definitive test for MS. Instead, diagnosing MS involves several steps.

Doctors typically begin by taking a detailed medical history, examining the patient and carrying out tests, including blood tests, to rule out other conditions that can cause similar symptoms.

They then use internationally recognised guidelines, known as the McDonald criteria, to assess whether there is sufficient evidence of MS.

This involves looking for evidence of damage to nerves in different parts of the central nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves.

Much of this damage can be seen on MRI scans as bright spots, known as lesions, which indicate areas where the protective coating around nerves has been damaged.

Doctors examine the number, location and pattern of these lesions, alongside other test results and symptoms, to determine whether MS is the likely cause.

But Dr Sivakolundu warned that mistakes can occur when doctors misinterpret these scans or mistake abnormalities caused by other conditions for signs of MS.

For example, he said it was normal for everyone over 40 to have at least one white spot on their brain, but in some cases, doctors interpret this as a potential sign of MS, potentially leading to a misdiagnosis.

'When the neurologist sees the report, if it is a young patient, they're more likely to get the diagnosis of MS, because now a young patient is having these white spots,' he added.

In a study from 2019, scientists found that of 241 patients referred for an MS diagnosis to two major medical centers in California, 17 to 19 percent were later told they had been misdiagnosed. On average, patients had spent four years being treated before receiving the news that they had been misdiagnosed.

In a 2024 review of six studies, including 1,621 patients, scientists found 16 percent of people diagnosed with multiple sclerosis were later found to not have the condition. In one case, a patient spent 16 years thinking they had the disease before being told it was a mistaken diagnosis.

In the 2019 study, scientists said that the most frequent condition misdiagnosed as MS was migraines, behind about 16 percent of cases.

Severe migraines can trigger symptoms that closely resemble MS, including vision changes, numbness, tingling, dizziness and weakness.

Selma Blair, who revealed her MS diagnosis in 2018, is pictured at The Beverly Hills Hotel

Dr Andrew Solomon, a top MS expert at the University of Vermont, said: 'So far, the literature suggests that many common disorders are mistaken for MS, like migraines, or the consequences of high blood pressure on the brain that causes white matter lesions.

'These are disorders that are frequently referred to neurologists.'

The second-most likely misdiagnosis is radiologically isolated syndrome, behind an estimated nine percent of cases, when anomalies characteristic of MS appear in the brain and spinal cord. These are widely seen as being pre-symptomatic of MS.

Fibromyalgia can also mimic the condition, causing fatigue, pain, tingling and numbness, while psychiatric disorders may present with cognitive difficulties, dizziness and other symptoms that overlap with MS. It can also cause movement problems.

It was not clear what condition Applegate now has. She said she is receiving further tests to determine her diagnosis.

For patients who have been misdiagnosed, doctors say the effect is 'beyond imaginable'.

'The medications for MS are not the most benign. These are medications that suppress your immune system, so it puts you at a higher risk for certain infections, and sometimes, can also increase your malignancy and cancer risks,' Sivakolundu said.

Dr Solomon also noted: 'Patients have side effects from these medications that didn't help them and that they didn't need.

'Some of them participated in clinical trials for MS therapies, so experimental therapies for MS that they were exposed to, had an enormous amount of unnecessary risk.

'They also were not treated for the condition that was correct. So in many cases, they were suffering persistently because the correct condition might not have been recognised and treated appropriately.

'There are many things that could mimic MS in its clinical presentation, the symptoms it presents with, as well as the MRI findings and spinal fluid findings.

'With testing for the disease, there are different pathways to go down, including spinal fluid testing and optic nerve testing. The results from these can affect the diagnoses.'

Doctors say that if you think you have been misdiagnosed with MS, you should speak to your specialist.

'I think anybody with MS should get a second opinion, because it is a diagnosis that's life-changing,' Dr Sivakolundu said.

'If they've seen an MS specialist from the beginning, then I don't think they have to, but if a general neurologist, or a GP is suspecting MS or giving one a diagnosis of MS, I would highly encourage them to see someone who's MS-trained, so they can at least get a second opinion.'

#515. 'It felt like someone was squeezing my jaw tightly and I was sweating profusely': The everyday symptoms that could be signs of middle-aged heart disease

Published: 12:15 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 18:39 BST, 22 October 2026

Hayley Martin has never drunk alcohol or smoked cigarettes, eats healthily and leads a fit and active lifestyle – enjoying yoga, cycling, horse-riding and running marathons.

Yet two years ago, during a routine check, she discovered she had sky-high cholesterol levels, putting her at risk of heart disease.

Specifically she had raised levels of harmful LDL cholesterol, the ‘bad’ type that furs up arteries and can impede blood flow to the heart.

‘I’ve never eaten junk food so doctors said it must just be genetic,’ says Hayley, 56, a full-time carer for her elderly parents, who is married to Peter, 61, a retired truck driver.

It was also found she had developed atrial flutter – intermittent episodes of erratic heartbeats, which can raise the risk of a stroke.

‘Normally, my heart rate is very low, at about 37 beats per minute,’ says Hayley, from Congleton in Cheshire.

‘But suddenly it shot up to 300. It was terrifying.’

It’s a story that chimes with that of TV presenter Davina McCall, 59, who revealed earlier this week that she too has high cholesterol and has been diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. This is despite a healthy lifestyle that revolves around intermittent fasting, a 3km daily morning run and a largely sugar-free diet.

Hayley Martin discovered she had sky-high cholesterol levels during a routine check, despite having a healthy lifestyle

The mother of three, who has already endured breast cancer and a benign brain tumour, has previously revealed she was warned to watch her cholesterol levels when she first got pregnant 20 years ago – describing it as ‘a hidden danger – you can’t see it and you don’t know it’s there’.

If nothing else, Davina’s story is being seen as a huge wake-up call to millions of women across the UK – that heart disease isn’t something affecting mainly men.

In fact, it kills twice as many women in the UK each year as breast cancer – around 23,000.

And while more men develop heart problems, some studies suggest women are more likely to die from them – partly because their symptoms are often blamed on other things.

Yet the British Cardiovascular Society warns women are being underdiagnosed, undertreated and under-represented in clinical trials for heart disease.

‘There’s a real gender gap,’ says Professor Raj Thakkar, past president of the Primary Care Cardiovascular Society.

Hayley’s cholesterol has since been lowered with a daily statin, while her atrial flutter episodes (there have been two) are being monitored but do not currently need treatment.

But she is adamant women everywhere must be more aware of their heart risks.

‘It’s not thought of as a female condition – plus women tend to put themselves last when there are others who need looking after. We’ve got to take heart disease in women more seriously.’

So why is heart disease such a big danger – even in outwardly healthy women – and what can you do to reduce your chances of developing it?

Like Davina, many seemingly healthy women are shocked to find they have one or more heart disease risks – such as high cholesterol or blood pressure.

Davina McCall, 59, revealed earlier this week that she has high cholesterol and has been diagnosed with cardiovascular disease

Having raised cholesterol can block arteries while high blood pressure means constant strain damages the inside of artery walls – causing inflammation which can narrow the vessel and restrict blood flow to the heart.

‘You cannot simply look at someone who is slim and assume their risk factors are low,’ says Dr Laura Corr, a consultant cardiologist in London.

‘And the data shows heart disease is recognised much less rapidly in women.’

There is also a huge genetic influence when it comes to heart disease, in both women and men, she adds.

Oestrogen produced by the ovaries has a protective effect on a woman’s heart by controlling cholesterol levels and keeping blood vessels flexible and smooth, according to the British Heart Foundation.

After the menopause, when oestrogen supply shuts down, heart disease is more common as women often gain weight, their cholesterol and blood pressure increase and the body becomes less effective at processing sugar levels – heightening the risk of type 2 diabetes (which contributes to heart disease by damaging blood vessels).

A US study of more than 10,000 women, published in May in the Journal Of The American College Of Cardiology, found those going through an early menopause (before 45) are 40 per cent more likely to develop heart disease than those who go through it later.

But giving hormone replacement therapy (HRT) specifically for heart disease is not the answer, experts warn, as it can raise the risk of blood clots. (Although this is more likely to happen with pills rather than the patches or gels which bypass the liver by being absorbed through the skin.)

‘There may be some protection from pre-menopausal hormone exposure,’ says Dr Corr. ‘But we don’t prescribe HRT for heart disease in women.’

We all know there is good (HDL) cholesterol and bad (LDL) cholesterol.

HDL can protect against heart disease in both sexes by scooping up excess cholesterol particles in the blood and escorting them back to the liver, where they are broken down and removed as waste.

LDL, meanwhile, sticks to the inside of our arteries and causes the formation of deposits (plaques) that can break away and form blockages that shut off the blood supply to the heart or brain, resulting in a heart attack or stroke.

As a result, the NHS says men and women should keep LDL below 4mmol/L (a measure of how much is in a litre of blood) to reduce damage to the arteries.

But when it comes to HDL, the recommendations are different for women.

The NHS says they need a minimum of 1.2mmol/L – compared to just 1mmol for men.

That’s because women naturally have higher levels of HDL than men due to the effects of oestrogen, which blocks the activity of an enzyme (hepatic lipase) that breaks down and clears good HDL from the blood.

Studies suggest the risks start to escalate in women once their HDL dips below the 1.2mmol/L threshold.

There are steps you can take to increase your HDL, such as losing weight if you’re overweight, regular vigorous exercise (where you’re not able to hold a conversation during it), cut down on foods containing trans fats (such as cakes, biscuits and pies) – and swap white carbs for wholegrain versions.

Experts say as long as women have no other cardiovascular risk factors – such as a strong family history of heart disease at a young age, high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes – raised LDL alone is unlikely to radically alter their chances of a heart attack or stroke.

‘You cannot simply look at someone who is slim and assume their risk factors are low,’ says Dr Laura Corr

‘If a woman is a healthy weight, a non-smoker, eats a balanced diet and takes regular exercise, we probably would not even treat a raised LDL level,’ says Naveed Sattar, a professor of cardiometabolic medicine at the University of Glasgow.

‘The fact is, they may be less at risk [of a heart attack or stroke] than someone else who has a healthy LDL but numerous other cardiac risk factors. Looking at LDL in isolation is not that useful.’

There are other harmful blood fats besides LDL.

Triglycerides (which are measured when you have a cholesterol test), for example, are fats which can also damage blood vessels and raise the risk of heart disease.

The British Heart Foundation says a healthy triglyceride level is below 1.7mmol/L for a fasting test (where you haven’t had anything to eat or drink for at least ten hours) or below 2.3mmol/L for a non-fasting test.

Blood tests can accurately measure cholesterol but there are sometimes external clues that a woman has high levels.

Xanthelasma, yellow bumps that appear on or near the eyelid, is one according to findings presented to the American Academy of Ophthalmology conference in 2025. These are thought to be the result of cholesterol leaking out of tiny blood vessels around the eye.

Research involving 17,000 patients found nearly 50 per cent of those with xanthelasma had high cholesterol – versus 39 per cent in the control group.

A healthy blood pressure reading is defined as anything between 120/80 and 90/60, according to the NHS. But some research suggests the thresholds should be lower in women.

A 2021 study in the journal Circulation, which involved 28,000 men and women over a 28-year period, found that women with systolic (the top reading) between 100 and 109 – ie within the ‘healthy’ range – had a cardiovascular disease risk equivalent to men with a systolic reading of 130 to 139, which qualifies as hypertension (high blood pressure).

One reason may be that, since women’s blood vessels are smaller than men’s in diameter, they are less able to withstand the same pressure and problems develop at a lower blood pressure level.

Studies suggest that, when it comes to heart health, stress is more damaging for women than men

Researchers at the Cedars-Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles said their findings suggested the ideal upper limit for women should be 110, not 120.

In a second study, in 2023, the same team found women’s risk of dying from heart disease spiked at a systolic blood pressure reading that was 12 points lower than in men.

However, major bodies such as the American Heart Association say there is insufficient evidence to support sex-specific blood pressure guidelines.

A spokesman for the British Heart Foundation told the Daily Mail: ‘There is not yet enough evidence to support a change to the recommended blood pressure guidelines for men and women in the UK.’

For either sex, ditching fatty foods in favour of a Mediterranean-style diet rich in olive oil, fish, fruit and veg can reduce levels of ‘bad’ cholesterol.

But in most cases, there is a limit to how much this can achieve – usually no more than about 10 per cent, says Professor Sattar.

Further reductions almost always require taking cholesterol-lowering drugs – often statins.

‘You can make a dent in your cardiovascular risk by eating a more fibre-rich diet and less sugar and fat,’ says Professor Sattar.

Porridge oats contain a soluble fibre, called beta-glucan, which forms a gel in the gut that reduces the amount of cholesterol absorbed into the blood.

But studies show you need 3g a day of beta-glucan to get the right effect on the heart – and a standard 40g serving of porridge contains around 1.4 to 2g, roughly half what’s needed.

Other good sources include shiitake mushrooms, oat milk or beta-glucan supplements.

Chronic stress – such as worrying about work or finances – is bad for everybody’s wellbeing.

But studies suggest that, when it comes to heart health, it’s more damaging for women.

A 2014 study at Duke University in the US studied 310 adults with heart disease in stressful situations and, according to results published in the Journal Of The American College Of Cardiology, the women were more likely to suffer reduced blood flow to the heart and an increase in platelet aggregation – or clotting of the blood.

Both of these are risk factors for a potentially fatal heart attack.

Stress can also trigger an often fatal heart condition called spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) – where heart muscle ruptures as a result of a sudden tear or trauma (there are around four cases every day in the UK).

Intense physical or emotional stress – such as lifting weights or losing a loved one – triggers a sudden surge in stress hormones that can put huge pressure on fragile artery walls.

Women, often young or middle-aged, account for up to 90 per cent of SCAD cases, as blood vessels in and around the heart can be smaller and more delicate than in men.

Hayley suffered spontaneous coronary artery dissection, known as a SCAD, when she was just 39

It’s the biggest cause of heart attacks in women who have no other major risk factors, such as high blood pressure, raised cholesterol or type 2 diabetes.

The symptoms are very similar to a normal heart attack – a crushing, sharp or burning pain in the chest and arms.

Hayley suffered a SCAD when she was just 39.

‘I didn’t have any chest pain – instead, it was like someone was squeezing my jaw tightly and I was sweating profusely, with what I can only describe as a sense of impending doom.

‘I called 999 and when the paramedics arrived to find a 39-year-old woman on the floor, I think they assumed I was just having a panic attack – they told me to stand up.’

But once they attached her to their ECG machine – which measures the electrical activity of the heart – their priorities changed.

‘It was suddenly obvious that this was a total emergency,’ says Hayley. ‘I was blue-lighted straight to A&E.’

The British Heart Foundation recommends that all women over the age of 40 ask their GP or practice nurse for an NHS Health Check. This is a 20 to 30-minute screening appointment (currently only in England) that includes checking blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar readings to assess the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

It will also record whether you have a strong family history of heart disease as this can influence any calculation of your future risk. This may be higher if you have a mother or sister diagnosed with heart disease before 65, or a father/brother diagnosed under 55.

The results are then fed into an algorithm which calculates your risk of having a heart attack, stroke, type 2 diabetes or kidney disease within the next ten years.

Every five years after this, you will be invited for a follow-up check.

‘Chest pain which may feel like crushing or squeezing on your chest’ is how the NHS website describes the main symptom of a heart attack. But some studies suggest more than 40 per cent of women don’t get this sensation.

Instead, many get discomfort – pain, aches or tightness – in the jaw, neck, shoulders, upper back. Even tummy pain can mean a heart attack is happening, as the brain misinterprets where the pain signals are coming from (as sensory nerves for the heart and stomach are very close together). This is one of the ‘silent’ heart attack symptoms more often seen in women than men – though it’s not clear why.

And while the classic profile of a heart attack in a man is the sudden onset of severe pain, studies show that for some women, the first symptoms can appear several weeks before it becomes an emergency.

A 2003 study of 500 women by the University of Arkansas, reported in the journal Circulation, found 80 per cent of them had at least one symptom four weeks or more before being treated for a heart attack.

‘Men get more pain in the chest and the arm but in women it’s often in the back and shoulders,’ says Professor Sattar.

The college student shared a photo on Facebook four days after the deadly crash of her and her mother at the party. 'So happy I got to spend my 21st with you,' she captioned the image.

Leslie leaves behind a 21-year-old daughter, Emarea, whom she loved 'deeply, fiercely, and completely,' her obituary said

A family friend, commenting on Emarea's tribute, revealed that Leslie had been planning the special celebration since at least August.

'You were her world and every milestone she was celebrating YOU!' the friend wrote.

Leslie's best friend, Christel Meinhold, penned a heartbreaking tribute earlier this week in which she praised the businesswoman's dedication to motherhood.

'We were two strong, independent single moms who could handle anything, except, occasionally, our own lives,' Meinhold said.

'Our friendship was built on love, laughter, honesty, and reminding each other when we were being ridiculous.'

Leslie had many passions, including softball, baking, photography, cheering on the Kansas City Chiefs and caring for her dogs and hairless cat.

Her family said that her business, Everything But Weddings (EBW) Photography, allowed Leslie to combine two of her favorite things – 'people and capturing the moments that matter.'

'Through her camera, she preserved celebrations, milestones, smiles, and memories for others,' her loved ones wrote.

Leslie was driving through an intersection around 1.15am when a police SUV driven by Officer Arnold Matthew struck her 2022 Audi SQ5 (file photo) on the passenger side

Leslie brought that same passion to her career in retail, which saw her serving as a District Manager with Signet Jewelers.

She was an 'overachiever' and always determined to succeed, the tribute said. She cared deeply about her job and brought 'drive, high expectations, competitive spirit, and determination' to the workplace.

Leslie was also a baptized Christian whose 'faith was strong and personal.' She demonstrated 'God’s love and grace through the way she treated people.'

Despite the heartbreak, Leslie's family says they have found comfort in knowing that her 'last breath here became her first breath in Heaven, a place without pain or sickness and with everlasting peace.'

The entrepreneur's loved ones added that their 'lives are better because Misty was part of them.'

#517. Forever Living's devoted users swear by its aloe vera-based gels to soothe joints, and the life of a 'rep' is sold as the 'WFH for £100,000 a year' dream. But I worked for them and now, and I'm ready to TELL ALL

This time last year, Alison Bryant was plagued by money worries. For five years, she’d been unable to work thanks to arthritis and her career as a carer had come to a grinding halt.

So when a rep from the aloe vera-based beauty brand Forever Living suggested she take up a lucrative role selling products from home, it seemed like a lifeline.

‘She said I could eventually earn £2,000 a month and in five years I could have the seaside cottage that had been my dream for as long as I could remember,’ says Alison, 57.

This August, Alison left Forever Living after having forked out £5,310.50 on the company’s products and the paraphernalia she needed to sell them – and earned just £154.48. ‘It made me feel sick, working out the amount I spent,’ she tells me. ‘I made a mistake. I was gullible, swept away.’

Forever Living is a multi-level marketing (MLM) company, whose sales reps – or Forever Business Owners (FBOs) as they’re known – earn money recruiting others to join the company, as well as from selling products.

The idea of working from home in a booming wellness industry, supported by a ‘family’ of like-minded women, can certainly sound enticing, especially when viewed alongside pictures reps are encouraged to post on social media of their happy successful lives.

This August, Alison left Forever Living after having forked out £5,310.50 on the company’s products and the paraphernalia she needed to sell them – and earned just £154.48

Most MLM reps – usually women needing flexible work – earn very little indeed and some lose money. They often have to buy stock upfront or stockpile products to meet sales targets. Forever Living – an American company that launched in the UK in 1992 and has an estimated ten million reps worldwide – has consistently denied that it’s a pyramid scheme and points at the physical products it sells as evidence that it does not focus solely on recruiting members.

According to its website’s most recent Income Disclosure Statement in 2022, while most people choose to buy the products at a discount rather than join the MLM, 89.8 per cent of reps received no ‘meaningful’ income, and of the 10.2 per cent who did, 58.6 per cent earned less than £375 a year.

The founder, Rex Maughan, amassed an estimated net worth of over $500million (£373million) before he died in 2001, leaving his son, Gregg, as chief executive.

This April, after accusing the company of misleading people as to how much money they could make, America’s Federal Trade Commission prohibited it from making unsubstantiated earnings claims. In May, Forever Living stopped operating as an MLM in the US. American reps can still sell products, but not profit from recruitment.

In the UK, however, bold claims about income are still being made. Training material I’ve seen from this summer claims new starters can earn £75 to £300 a month (when in fact this could put them in the top 1 per cent of Forever Living earners) and earnings of up to £5,000 a month are ‘possible’ within 16 weeks, it says.

For the ‘very ambitious’, one of the UK’s top sellers suggests in a video recorded this March, a salary of £100,000 is possible.

In response to this, a spokesman for the company says: ‘The £75 figure relates to an example of potential retail profit from product sales.

‘Our Income Disclosure Statement reports bonus and incentive payments made by Forever Living and therefore measures a different form of income. The figures are therefore not directly comparable.’

But for Alison, such distinctions are irrelevant. An inherently private grandmother from Warrington, Cheshire, she cuts an unlikely whistleblower, but within minutes of talking to her it’s clear just how furious she is.

‘It’s just so misleading and can potentially ruin you,’ she says. ‘But I want people to know. You can’t make real money selling products. You can only make money by recruiting a team. I believe it absolutely is a pyramid scheme.’

Alison’s interest in Forever Living was piqued when she met Sarah – as we’ll call the woman who recruited her – selling Forever Living products at a market last spring. Its range of deodorants, soaps, supplements and gel drinks often contain aloe vera, which is said to have anti-inflammatory properties that may help lower cholesterol and blood sugar levels and aid digestion.

‘The natural ingredients appealed,’ says Alison, who believes the £27.09 aloe vera drinking gel helped her joint problems caused by arthritis and the nervous system condition fibromyalgia. ‘I didn’t like synthetic ingredients in health and beauty products.’

Sarah, meanwhile, was a mum in her 50s, who had been with Forever Living for 13 years and worked her way up to manager, the fourth level up. (There are five rungs on the rep ladder, and then another six rungs of leadership reps above that, each earning a progressively higher percentage of sales profits from those they recruit.)

‘I hated being on benefits,’ says Alison. ‘I thought this was something I could do from home.’

She had never heard of MLMs. Sarah told her she’d need to build a team for ‘lasting growth’, but that ‘the idea is you sell goods, first and foremost’.

At £6.83 for a soap and £28.79 for a cleanser, few friends could afford repeat purchases from Alison

To join, she paid £172 for a ‘Start Your Journey Pack’ of two sets of ten products, ‘one to use as a trial, one to sell to friends and family’. She was told to write a list of everyone she knew she could sell products to and join a WhatsApp group with 17 other reps in Sarah’s ‘downline’ (what they call the other women she’d recruited). ‘We had Motivation Mondays where we had to tell each other how much money we’d made,’ says Alison – which was nothing, for the rest of the year, as both she and Sarah were ill.

Nonetheless, Sarah persuaded Alison to come to Forever Living’s bi-annual ‘Success Day’ at a theatre, in which senior reps rev up a room of women who’ve paid £25 for the privilege. ‘They chant. They whoop, “One team! One goal!”’ says Alison, who was chivvied on-stage herself and presented with a sash, to her bemusement, ‘because all I’d really done at this point was buy a box’.

‘Looking back, it was almost cult-like, but at the time I was inspired. They all said they’d quit their day jobs and had life-changing incomes. One said she was earning £30,000 a month.’

Reps are told to set up private Facebook groups and then invite friends to join and sell products, using their happy lives to promote the brand on social media. Alison amassed 20 friends in her private Facebook group but struggled with the concept. ‘I’m quite private. Sarah used to tell me off for not doing it.’

Instead, she focused on selling in person, starting with a sales evening for friends at a hair salon in February. ‘I was enthusiastic and people bought from me,’ say Alison. A second sales evening weeks later was similarly successful and that month she sold more than £1,000 of products.

Forever Living uses an internal virtual currency of CCs (case credits) and to stay ‘active’ and receive sales bonuses, reps have to sell four CCs (around £630 of products) each month.

Alison had made over seven CCs. Granted, that only earned her £70 – 5 per cent of her sales – and a significant proportion included products she’d bought for herself for people to test. ‘But I could see how it would work as a business,’ she says. ‘I just needed to grow.’

But at £6.83 for a soap and £28.79 for a cleanser, few friends could afford repeat purchases.

She tried to drum up custom by contacting local businesses and residents ‘but not one person contacted me out of hundreds of flyers dropped’. In March she earned two CCs. Short of the required four, all her commission went straight to Sarah.

‘She said I needed to build my network, but I’d already approached all my friends and didn’t want to alienate them by asking again.’

In April, she hosted her first of ten market stalls selling Forever Living products. Each time it cost around £35 to hire the stall, and hundreds more in merchandise and equipment. ‘You need a 6ft table, a gazebo, chairs, a tablecloth with the Forever Living logo on it,’ she says. ‘You need flyers, brochures and enough products to put out on your table, open, so people can sample them.’

Even that wasn’t enough to guarantee a table, with so many reps fighting for one coveted spot. ‘The market was saturated. Some days nobody bought anything. Some I just about made back the stall money. Every single penny I earned, I put straight back into products.’

Alison was told by Sarah to hold prize draws at her market stalls so she could use the contact details women gave when they entered ‘to cultivate a relationship’. She says: ‘If they don’t respond, three or four days later you send them a WhatsApp, and then a voice message. You’re supposed to go back to them three times to persuade them to join the business.’

Many of Forever Living's wellness products contain aloe vera, which is said to have anti-inflammatory properties that help lower cholesterol and blood sugar levels and aid digestion

Alison refused. ‘If someone’s given their information for the sole purpose of entering a prize draw, that doesn’t give you the green light to keep the information in your phone and keep contacting them.’

Perhaps unsurprisingly, given her misgivings, she didn’t recruit a single person, which would have earned her the equivalent of two CCs and helped push her up the sales ladder.

To buy the products, Alison took money out of the pension she’d been drawing since she was 55. ‘I’ve never been good with money,’ she admits. ‘You’re not encouraged to look at the finances. Anything you spend is seen as an investment. You’re told you need to buy the products to try them – or how can you sell them?’

When she did voice concerns to Sarah, ‘she said I wasn’t giving it a chance’. ‘If I hadn’t bought anything for a while, she’d text, “I’ve noticed you haven’t put in an order yet.” She needed me to place an order to make her CCs.’

On social media, Sarah posted pictures of herself with her new fancy car, raving about the freedom her role allowed. With Alison, she was more candid.

‘She couldn’t afford to get the radiator on her car fixed and as we got to know each other said she still worked as a carer – another red flag, when you’re trying to sell a luxury lifestyle.’

Every week, reps were encouraged to watch a Transformation Tuesday training video from a senior rep, sent via YouTube link. On Thursdays another training session was released. ‘They were always about recruiting,’ says Alison. ‘I didn’t see one session where they were talking about the products.’

In fact, nobody seemed interested in the products at all. In one training session a senior rep says she used to memorise the ingredients to tell potential customers but gave up because ‘nobody cares’.

‘That was a trigger for me,’ says Alison. ‘I thought “I care.”’

In July, Forever Living told reps it was launching a new moisturiser free from parabens – preservatives in many beauty products that can potentially interfere with the body’s hormone system. ‘I thought our products already were paraben-free,’ says Alison. ‘When I tried to talk about it to Sarah she laughed and said, “you and your parabens”.’

Something inside Alison snapped. ‘When you’re standing under the health and wellness banner and you don’t know what you’re selling, that’s disgraceful.’ Instinct told her to check the company’s finances. She Googled ‘is Forever Living financially stable?’ And suddenly, the penny dropped.

For the first time, she learned Forever Living was an MLM – and what an MLM was. She found Forever Living’s Income Disclosure Statement, and the FTC complaint that alleged Forever Living in the US ‘deceived prospective workers with false and unsubstantiated earnings claims’ using social media posts and videos, images of luxury cars and giant cheques to tout potential earnings.

‘I hadn’t realised the scale of the deception,’ she says. Alison sat on the information for a month, worried about upsetting Sarah.

‘I kept thinking, she needs to know 90 per cent of people don’t earn a living. If you’re recruiting people into a business, you need to have some idea of what you’re getting them into.’ In September, she texted Sarah her findings.

‘I thought she’d be as shocked as I was. I was concerned about her.’

In one training session a senior rep says she used to memorise the ingredients to tell potential customers but gave up because ‘nobody cares’

But within three minutes, she says Sarah removed her from the Forever Living WhatsApp group. When Alison asked why, Sarah accused her of sending ‘false claims’ and texted: ‘I will not allow you to share the same information in there that you sent to myself.’

Astonished, Alison emailed Sarah evidence of every allegation. Sarah didn’t reply, but that evening a picture was posted of her on Facebook attending a recruitment drive promoting Forever Living as an ‘income replacing business’.

‘That made my blood boil,’ says Alison, who texted Sarah, asking: “Have you no shame?”’ Sarah, in turn, posted ‘I absolutely hate bullies’ on social media. When she was asked by her followers who she was referring to, she posted a picture of Alison and wrote: ‘vile’.

Alison assumes Sarah reported her to head office because the same day she received an email from Forever Living’s compliance team asking that ‘abusive comments’ towards other reps were avoided. Any concerns she had about the company, they wrote, could be raised ‘directly’ to the company.

‘They were trying to silence me,’ says Alison. ’But I thought, no, I haven’t bullied anyone. I’m going to defend myself.’ Not least because when she combed through her bank statements to add up everything she’d spent on Forever Living, from products to fuel to travel and merchandise, she found out the £1,000 she feared she’d squandered was actually over £5,000. All but £200 of her pension is now gone.

Her anger isn’t directed at Sarah, whose mind she believes is ‘controlled’ by a company she compares to a cult. ‘She’s not capable of critical thinking. She’s a victim as well.’

But she urges other women promised a better life by Forever Living reps to steer clear. ‘It is an illusion. It has to stop.’

When we put Alison’s allegations to Forever Living, it said: ‘Forever Living has been operating in the UK for almost four decades and takes compliance, product quality and ethical business practices seriously. As a member of the Direct Selling Association, we are committed to maintaining high standards and complying with applicable legal and regulatory requirements. We maintain policies and procedures designed to support compliance by our Forever Business Owners, including in relation to product and income claims, data protection and distributor conduct.

‘Our products are manufactured in accordance with applicable safety and regulatory requirements, and we remain committed to maintaining high standards across our products and business opportunity.’
