#518. 'Keep your eyes on the road': Diogo Jota's new wife's text message to husband revealed in her heartbreaking account of how tragic Liverpool star's Lamborghini crash death unfolded

Published: 11:59 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 18:25 BST, 22 October 2026

Diogo Jota's widow Rute Cardoso has revealed she told him 'keep your eyes on the road' in her final message to the Liverpool star, as she gave a heartbreaking account of the night of his death in a new book.

In a biography about the late Liverpool forward, Cardoso explained she had exchanged messages with Jota shortly after he had left for the Spanish city Santander with his brother Andre Silva.

Jota had planned to travel to the city to drop off a Lamborghini he had rented shortly after the couple's wedding, before taking a ferry back to the UK for pre-season.

Cardoso revealed she had told Jota 'keep your eyes on the road' after he had responded to her message following his departure.

'It was a surprise,' Cardoso said in an extract of the book Diogo Jota: Forever In Our Hearts, shared by the Liverpool Echo, regarding his decision to rent a Ferrari then a Lamborghini in the summer of 2025.

'Unlike most players, who like fancy cars, jewellery and watches, Diogo was never into that sort of thing. He was happy with the cars we had.

Rute Cardoso has given a heartbreaking account of the night of her husband Diogo Jota's death in a new biography

Cardoso explains in the book that she grew increasing concerned after Jota and his brother Andre Silva, left, failed to respond to WhatsApp messages and had not arrived at their hotel

'So perhaps because he'd never been particularly into cars, he took that chance to try driving a Ferrari before our wedding. After that, he would also rent a Lamborghini, which he had to drop off in Santander.

'A few minutes after they'd left, I sent Diogo a message saying, "Safe journey". He replied with an emoji, and I told him to keep his eyes on the road.'

Jota and his younger brother died when the Lamborghini Huracan he was driving careered off a motorway in northern Spain.

Jota, 28, a father-of-three, was travelling back to Liverpool by road after he was advised by doctors not to fly following surgery, and crashed close to Spain's north-west border with Portugal.

He married his childhood sweetheart Cardoso at a church in Porto, Portugal, just 11 days before the devastating collision.

Cardoso explained how she had grown increasingly worried after several WhatsApp messages to Jota were left undelivered.

The first of which was Cardoso informing Jota she had a video to show him, having just received footage from their wedding day.

A subsequent message was also undelivered when she attempted to contact Andre.

Cardoso revealed she had requested to visit the location of the crash which killed Jota and his brother as she made her way to collect his belongings

She then rang the hotel the brothers had been due to stay at in Benavente to break up their journey. After being informed they had not arrived, Cardoso said she then phoned a hospital and the local police without success.

Cardoso then contacted her uncle Vitor, a lorry driver with good contacts in the Spanish transport police.

'Suddenly, my uncle asked me to put Nuno, my brother-in-law, on the line. At that time of night, in the silence, I could make out every word they were saying. I heard my uncle tell him: "The bodies are being taken away". I think he added "to the mortuary", but that's when my mind went blank,' Cardoso said in the book extract.

'Bodies? My brother-in-law froze. My sister took the phone from him and asked my uncle to speak to her. My main concern was to ring Diogo's father and tell him: "You must come here immediately". I rang André's girlfriend and said the same thing: "Paula, come over now".'

Cardoso revealed in the biography, written by former footballer Jose Manuel Delgado, that the family was visited by two psychologists to offer support.

Her uncle called again and passed Cardoso onto a Spanish police officer, who officially informed her of Jota's death.

Cardoso added in the family-authorised biography, which will support the LFC Foundation, that she requested to visit the scene of the accident when en route to mortuary to collect Jota and his brother’s belongings.

'I told the driver I wanted us to take the same route that they had taken,' Cardoso said. 'I imagined that, so many hours on, there would be no traces left, but I wanted to know where it had happened. But when we reached that cursed Kilometre 64, what was left of the car was still there.'

Cardoso had attempted to move closer to the scene of the accident but was stopped by a police officer.

Former Liverpool bosses Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot are among those to have contributed to the biography about Jota

A funeral was held for both Jota and Silva two days after their devastating deaths in a chapel in Gondomar, a city that overlooks Porto, where both brothers played during their academy careers.

Following an investigation, a Spanish court ruled earlier this year that the crash was due to the Lamborghini suffering a blown-out tyre while overtaking a car, before bursting into flames upon hitting a barrier in the middle of the carriageway.

The High Court of Justice in the province of Zamora, north-west Spain, has concluded that no criminal action was necessary regarding the deaths of both Jota and Andre, following the review of the entire evidence.

Jota turned out 123 times for Liverpool, scoring 47 goals, and played a significant role in their 2024-25 Premier League title-winning season.

Former Liverpool bosses Arne Slot and Jurgen Klopp are among those to have contributed to the biography, along with former team-mates.

'This book began as an opportunity to help preserve Diogo’s memory at a moment of profound sadness. My commitment throughout was to tell his story with care, honesty and respect for Diogo, André, and the family and friends who loved them,' said author Delgado.

'What moved me most was the generosity of those closest to them. Family members, teammates, coaches and friends shared their memories to help future generations understand the person Diogo was, and their love for both brothers can be felt on every page.

'While researching the book, I came to understand the unique bond between Diogo and Liverpool FC. Everywhere I went, people spoke not only of his talent, but also his humility, commitment and character.

'My hope is that Forever in our Hearts serves as a fitting tribute to Diogo’s life and legacy, and ensures his story continues to inspire others for years to come.'

The Anfield faithful continuously paid their respects to Jota last season, singing his name in the 20th minute of every match, while the club also retired his No20 shirt.

A permanent memorial to Jota and Andre was installed at Anfield in July.

#519. Judge brands Katie Price a 'dangerous witness' as Kieran Hayler is cleared of rape - as her ex vows to 'rebuild his life after years of absolute hell'

By TOM LAWRENCE, NEWS REPORTER and BARRY KEEVINS

Published: 12:19 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 18:18 BST, 22 October 2026

Katie Price was described by a judge as a 'dangerous witness' after her ex-husband was cleared of raping a 13-year-old girl.

Kieran Hayler, 39, was accused of sexually assaulting and raping the child in West Sussex in 2016.

The ten jury members returned majority decisions on Thursday morning after deliberating for nearly 15 hours.

Judge Mark van der Zwart said former glamour-model Ms Price's personal agenda against her ex-husband nearly collapsed the trial.

He said the time she spent in the witness box should have been limited to prevent her from making allegations.

An 'overwhelming tsunami of prejudice' by Ms Price led to Mr Hayler's defence calling for the jury to be discharged after one day of evidence.

Hayler, of Northchapel, West Sussex, wept as he was released from the dock at Lewes Crown Court.

On the steps of the court, Hayler vowed to 'rebuild his life' after years of 'absolute hell'.

His mother Wendy Hayler and former partner Michelle Pentecost were crying as the verdicts were delivered.

Hayler was cleared of three counts of rape, sexual assault and four alternative charges of sexual activity with a child.

The former couple Kieran Hayler and Katie Price at the UK premiere for the film Fifty Shades Darker in London in 2017

Kieran Hayler with his mother Wendy outside Lewes Crown Court following the verdict

Katie was described by a judge as a 'dangerous witness' after her ex-husband was cleared

Kieran Hayler with his former partner Michelle Pentecost, who gave evidence for the defence

The former stripper met Ms Price in 2012 and proposed on Christmas Day.

They married at a luxury Caribbean resort in January 2013 but separated in 2018 and divorced three years later.

His turbulent relationship with Ms Price was laid bare during proceedings as he accused his ex-wife of setting him up with 'fabricated' allegations and said it was a 'smear campaign against me'.

But the celebrity witness denied being 'angry and vengeful' towards her ex-husband.

Standing next to his mother on the court steps, Mr Hayler said: 'I'd like to thank my friends and family, who've stuck by me for five years and absolute hell.

'I'm grateful to the jury for their careful consideration of this difficult case.

'I'd like to be left in peace now to rebuild my life and spend time with my family.'

It can now be reported that Ms Price's first day of evidence during the trial led to Mr Hayler's defence team calling for the jury to be discharged, accusing her of a 'premeditated attempt to bring down this trial'.

In a legal application to the judge, barrister Arlette Piercy argued that evidence given by Ms Price resulted in an 'overwhelming tsunami of prejudice to us which we are simply unable to deal with'.

Ms Piercy said her evidence was'like lobbing hand grenades into the court'.

Of Ms Price's evidence, the lawyer said: 'She then went on a deliberate, malicious and, in my submission, premeditated attempt to bring down this trial.'

She added that 'the significance of it was written all over the jury's faces'.

Prosecutor Ryan Richter disputed the argument and instead suggested it was from the celebrity witness 'having lost control'.

His Honour Judge Van der Zwart was forced to warn the jury that what she said was 'not correct and you must disregard it'.

'It was submitted that so much prejudice was caused that no judicial direction to the jury could remedy it.

'It was submitted a high degree of necessity had arisen to justify discharging the jury.

In his ruling, the judge described Ms Price as 'what barristers of a previous generation would have called a 'dangerous witness' with a personal agenda in proceedings and who was 'liable to say something prejudicial given half a chance'.

'Discharging this jury was unlikely to prevent the same situation arising again at a re-trial,' he said.

Kieran Hayler outside Lewes Crown Court in East Sussex today, where he was cleared of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault against a 13-year-old girl

The judge said: 'In emotive cases like these, my experience is that it is common for a witness to be supportive of one side or the other, to volunteer unprompted, their belief or opinion of where the truth lies and of whether the defendant is guilty or innocent.

'That rarely results in a jury being discharged and a re-trial being ordered because members of the public serving on juries know perfectly well no one else's opinion about a defendant's guilt or innocence matters.'

The judge said it was not the first time Katie Price had failed to comply with court orders.

He said he felt Katie Price was likely to make further outbursts if she was called as a witness again which did not benefit either the Crown or defence.

He said it was likely the same situation would arise again.

When she returned to court, the judge told Ms Price: 'It is important you listen to and answer the questions and do not provide any more information unless you're asked to do so.'

Despite his warning, Katie Price went on to make a series of unprompted allegations of the defendant having behaved inappropriately with other women and girls.

'It's plain to me that every additional minute she remains in the witness box provides another opportunity for her to volunteer something irrelevant and prejudicial,' the judge said.

Hayler was emotional and bent over as he was told by the judge he could leave the dock and was discharged.

Katie Price is pictured arriving at Lewes Crown Court, East Sussex, on October 14

During the trial, Price was accused by her ex-husband of 'coaching' the alleged victim after discovering messages in which his then-wife suggested he fancied the girl and promised to make her 'a little star'.

Hayler told the court: 'I am attracted to older women,' adding that all his significant relationships had been with older women.

He admitted having affairs with three other women during his marriage to Ms Price but claimed she had also been unfaithful.

The court heard that the couple's relationship had broken down by mid-2013, with Hayler telling jurors that 'trust had gone on both sides'.

Hayler said he discovered messages between his wife and the alleged victim in 2017 while searching Ms Price's phone for evidence that she was having an affair.

The court heard that Ms Price had messaged the teenager, claiming she had heard Hayler and the girl had kissed and that he had 'tried it on' with her.

In another message, the former glamour model told the girl: 'I will make you a little star.'

Hayler said he found the exchange suspicious and took photographs of the messages on his own phone.

Asked by his defence barrister Ms Piercy why he had photographed them, he replied: 'Because she made out that I fancied (the complainant)... I thought, "This is a bit weird".'

During the trial, prosecutor Ryan Richter had put to Mr Hayler: 'Your feud with Katie Price is not what this case is about, is it?'

Mr Richter went on: 'This case is about you having raped a girl, isn’t it?'

Judge Van der Zwart sent the jury, made up of six women and five men, to begin their deliberations on Tuesday afternoon.

In closing speeches on Monday, prosecutor Ryan Richter said: 'You've seen the big personalities, the big egos in this case and you'll judge it, you'll cut through it.

'You'll decide whether those big voices drown out the voice of [the complainant] or whether that voice has made you sure on the counts of this indictment.'

Defence barrister Ms Piercy said in her closing speech that Hayler has been consistent and clear throughout his defence, in what has been a 'roller coaster ride for everybody in this court'.

Hayler and Katie Price at a London film premiere in November 2015

Hayler said the allegations started after he split from his ex-wife and after she checked out of a The Priory rehab clinic following her conviction for rolling her car while under the influence of drink and drugs.

He said: 'The timing is almost identical. Every time something was going bad for her, a bad news story or something to do with me, there would be a threat to do with me and this.'

He said despite being checked into the Priory after her conviction, Katie Price was 'out and about', adding: 'This was three years after our relationship ended.

'She had her phone in the Priory. She was out and about for hairdresser, shopping.

'Then all of a sudden this allegation is made. Miss Price, I think, is behind the allegation.'

Hayler also described finding the aftermath of a drink and drugs binge at Ms Price's home dubbed 'Mucky Mansion' after they split.

The jury heard he found cocaine and empty bottles around the house in Sussex before he moved out in 2018.

#521. Meghan and Harry's 'warm' welcome in Nottingham proves they still have plenty of support in Britain, duchess' US ally Sunny Hostin claims

Meghan and Harry's 'warm' welcome in Nottingham shows the couple still have plenty of support in Britain, an ally of the Duchess of Sussex in the US has claimed.

Published: 18:01 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 18:01 BST, 22 October 2026

A gang of Romanian fraudsters have used a cruel cash machine trick to steal more than £40,000 from unsuspecting pensioners.

CCTV footage shows the brazen crooks distracting elderly victims by dropping banknotes on the floor before secretly swapping their bank cards for fake ones.

The three men travelled across Britain targeting vulnerable customers at Halifax and Lloyds Bank branches, with one victim losing a staggering £11,100 before realising they had been scammed.

Ionut Matei, 40, Vasile Ciubotaru, 45, and Ramonel Mandache, 51, have now been jailed for a combined total of more than 13 years following a nationwide crime spree lasting almost two years.

The gang's calculated trick involved one member watching a victim enter their PIN at a cash machine while another prepared to distract them.

As the unsuspecting customer finished their transaction, one of the fraudsters would deliberately drop a banknote on the floor behind them.

He would then tap the victim on the shoulder and ask whether they had dropped the money.

While the pensioner was distracted, an accomplice would swiftly swap their bank card for a similar-looking one.

The victim would then leave the bank believing they had retrieved their own card, completely unaware that their account was now at the mercy of the criminals.

Ionut Matei, 40, was jailed for five years and six months

CCTV footage shows the brazen crooks distracting elderly victims by dropping banknotes on the floor before secretly swapping their bank cards for fake ones

The three men travelled across Britain targeting vulnerable customers at Halifax and Lloyds Bank branches, with one victim losing a staggering £11,100 before realising they had been scammed

Armed with the stolen cards and PINs, the gang would make cash withdrawals and purchases, sometimes running into thousands of pounds.

Their victims, many of whom were in their 70s and 80s, were left devastated after discovering money had vanished from their accounts.

One pensioner lost £11,100 over almost two weeks before finally discovering they had fallen victim to the scam.

The fraudsters struck across Cheshire, Staffordshire, Nottinghamshire, Greater Manchester, South Yorkshire and Kent between October 2024 and August 2026.

Their activities were eventually uncovered during Operation Rages, a major Cheshire Police investigation into a nationwide theft and fraud operation.

Detectives established that the Romanian nationals had travelled extensively around the country, deliberately seeking out elderly and vulnerable customers using cash machines inside bank branches.

The investigation, which included offences in Warrington and Widnes, also uncovered how the gang had fraudulently obtained cars using fake driving licences in an attempt to conceal their identities and movements.

After extensive CCTV enquiries, officers finally tracked the three men down to Portsmouth, where they were arrested on August 18 this year.

All three refused to answer questions when interviewed by police.

They later pleaded guilty to conspiracy to steal and conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation.

Appearing at Liverpool Crown Court on Monday Matei was jailed for five years and six months.

His sentence also covered an offence of knowingly entering the UK in breach of a deportation order.

Ciubotaru, from Ilford, east London, was handed four years and eight months behind bars.

Vasile Ciubotaru, 45, from Ilford, east London, was handed four years and eight months behind bars

Ramonel Mandache, 51, from East Ham, east London, was sentenced to three years in prison

Mandache from East Ham, east London, was sentenced to three years in prison.

Detective Sergeant Stephanie Bland, the senior investigating officer for Operation Rages, said the gang had caused not only 'significant financial losses' but also a 'lasting impact' on victims' 'confidence and wellbeing'.

She said: 'This was a highly organised criminal enterprise that deliberately targeted elderly and vulnerable members of the public for financial gain.

'Operation Rages was a complex investigation spanning multiple force areas but in policing there are no borders.

'And even though a majority of these offences occurred outside of Cheshire, our officers were determined to identify those responsible for these crimes, bring them before the courts, and provide reassurance to victims and the wider public.

#526. Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition as BBC defamation lawsuit backfires

Published: 16:33 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 17:33 BST, 22 October 2026

A federal judge has ordered Donald Trump to sit for questioning in his $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC by December 11 or risk having the case thrown out.

US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett issued the order at a hearing in Miami on Thursday after the BBC's lawyers complained that Trump had repeatedly stalled appearing for a deposition.

BBC attorney Charles Tobin told the court that with two months left in the discovery period, 'we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff.'

The two sides had agreed on an October 16 sit-down, but the president canceled over a 'matter of national importance.'

Tobin told the court Trump was in fact campaigning in Georgia.

'He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,' Tobin said.

Lett warned that Trump faces sanctions up to and including the dismissal of his lawsuit if he misses the deadline, unless the discovery period is extended beyond December 18.

Trump filed the lawsuit in Florida last December over a BBC Panorama documentary that spliced together parts of his January 6, 2021, speech to make it appear he urged violence at the US Capitol.

Trump speaks at a campaign rally in Pendleton, South Carolina, on Wednesday

The broadcaster apologized for the edit but denies defaming him. Director-general Tim Davie and news chief Deborah Turness resigned over the scandal.

The BBC has asked the court to throw out the case, arguing the documentary never aired in Florida or anywhere in the US and that Trump's claims fall 'well short of the high bar of actual malice' a public figure must clear.

Its lawyers also argued he 'cannot plausibly claim that the documentary harmed his reputation' because he won the 2024 election a week after it aired and carried Florida by a wide margin.

'Indeed, the documentary was prescient in accurately describing the loyalty plaintiff enjoys among his supporters, and that led to his return to the White House,' the BBC's motion added.

BBC lawyers said in an October 13 filing that they first asked for deposition dates in July and chased them repeatedly before both sides settled on October 16.

They said they heard nothing for weeks until Trump's lawyer wrote on September 28 that 'the President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance.'

The lawyer promised to 'endeavor to provide you with a replacement date by the end of this week,' according to the filing. 'He did not,' the BBC's lawyers wrote.

Trump's team then told the broadcaster he 'has no availability whatsoever for a deposition' before discovery closes on December 18 and offered the second or third week of January instead.

'Two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself,' Tobin wrote.

The BBC is also chasing testimony from Ivanka Trump, her husband Jared Kushner and Donald Trump Jr, telling the court the president's two eldest children were with him as he revised his January 6 speech and when he delivered it.

Kushner drafted a statement condemning the Capitol violence that the White House never issued, the BBC says. Trump's lawyers accused the broadcaster of seeking 'politically-driven leverage' over the president through his family.

Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner at Joint Base Andrews on January 20, 2021. The BBC has subpoenaed the pair in the defamation suit

Trump speaks to his supporters outside the White House on January 6, 2021

Police turned away the BBC's process servers at Ivanka and Kushner's Miami home in May, and a Secret Service lawyer later said the agency was not authorized to accept subpoenas for them. A bid to serve Don Jr at Trump Tower also failed.

Lett cleared the way on October 9, allowing the BBC to serve the trio by certified mail to their home and business addresses and by email to Trump's lawyers. The ruling does not settle any objections to the scope of the subpoenas.

Lawyers for both sides tussled on Thursday over the BBC's separate bid to depose Jack Smith, the former special counsel who brought the federal January 6 case against Trump. The president strongly opposes the move.

Smith charged Trump in August 2023 with four felony counts over his bid to overturn the 2020 election, but the case was dropped after his 2024 victory under a Justice Department policy barring the prosecution of a sitting president.

The broadcaster subpoenaed Smith earlier this month, but Trump's lawyers argued in a joint filing that there was no reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear.

'Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter,' they wrote. 'He was not present when President Trump's January 6, 2021, speech... was made, nor did he participate in its preparation.'

Trump's team also argued that 'Smith's testimony would be duplicative,' pointing out that he published a lengthy report on January 6 and testified for hours. 'The entirety of his testimony is publicly available,' the filing said.

'It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him,' the BBC's lawyers countered.

'No one forced Plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol,' they added.

Smith never charged Trump with incitement and wrote in his final report released in January 2025 that prosecutors did not develop direct evidence of 'Trump's subjective intent to cause the full scope of the violence that occurred on Jan. 6.'

#531. BRYONY GORDON: I'm happy to let my 13-year-old wear make-up to school. It doesn't make me a bad mother. At her age I was drinking and smoking - so if blusher is her only vice, I'm thrilled!

When it comes to the Beckhams, it’s so easy to sneer, isn’t it?

Whether it’s Brooklyn teaching us how to cook a spaghetti bolognese, or rumours of Victoria hijacking the first dance at her son’s wedding by ‘dancing inappropriately’ instead of letting his new wife, Nicola Peltz, take centre stage, there truly is something for everyone to scoff at here.

The sarongs, the thrones, the frustrated emails about knighthoods … God bless Brand Beckham and all the hard work they do to remain the subject of so much ridicule.

The latest reason to collectively roll our eyes comes courtesy of Harper, 15, who is apparently poised to launch a skincare range for teens just as soon as she’s got her GCSEs out of the way next summer.

Never one to miss an opportunity to promote Brand Beckham, her mum, Victoria, went on the Today Show in America this week to talk about her daughter’s frustration at not being able to wear make-up to school.

Explaining that Harper was ‘really good at applying natural make-up’, she told the host that her daughter had recently been banned from wearing any in the classroom. ‘[Harper] said: “Why don’t they want me to look my best?” She’s like: “Mummy can’t you call the school?” I’m like, “I can’t, Harper”.’

Predictably, this has sparked uproar among parents who can barely believe Harper felt entitled to ask such a question in the first place. But try as I might to be incensed, I’m struggling. In fact, I’m actually with Harper on this one, because, unlike Victoria, I let my 13-year-old daughter wear make-up to school.

Victoria Beckham went on the Today Show in America this week to talk about her daughter’s frustration at not being able to wear make-up to school

Explaining that Harper was ‘really good at applying natural make-up’, Lady Beckham told the host that she had recently been banned from wearing any in the classroom

Now let me make this clear: I don’t let her wear a lot of make-up. My daughter is not rocking up to Geography with a set of false eyelashes, a smoky eye and bright red lipstick.

It is, as Lady Beckham says, ‘natural make-up’ – some clear mascara on curled eyelashes, a tinted moisturiser, a dab of concealer on the odd spot, powder, blusher, lip gloss.

And obviously, I’d far rather she didn’t feel the need to wear it at all, because she’s 13 and I love her with a ferociousness that doesn’t require blusher.

But if there’s one thing I’ve learnt about parenting, it’s that you’ve got to pick your battles. And the battle against a teenage girl and her make-up bag is not, I’ve realised, one that can be won.

And look, I’m not a pushover. While many of my daughter’s friends are scrolling through TikTok and Instagram, I have steadfastly refused to allow her anywhere near social media – and I won’t do until she’s 16.

Her phone is essentially a walkie-talkie and it will remain that way until she’s old enough to be able to afford to buy one herself.

But if I’d hoped that keeping her away from social media might also remove her from the rampant forces of cosmetic capitalism, I was very much mistaken. Like most Generation Alpha girls, she’s been fascinated with skincare since she was about ten. Don’t take my word for it – head to your nearest branch of Sephora over the weekend, and marvel at the sheer number of children queuing up to get their hands on some Rhode Glazing Milk. Don’t ask me what that is – when I was my daughter’s age, the most we had was bath pearls from The Body Shop and if we were (un)lucky, Sun In hair lightener.

The bit of parenting I was most dreading was the chat about the birds and the bees. I’d no idea that I’d also have to explain to my daughter the difference between AHAs and BHAs and niacinamide – skincare ingredients I barely understand myself at the grand old age of 46.

But this is the world we now live in, and as much as I’d like my daughter and Harper to be spending their time reading a book, or taking in nature, it’s our duty as parents to be realistic. So recently I said: fine. Wear a bit of make-up, if you want, but if I ever catch you with a vape or a Snapchat account, you’re grounded.

I find it fascinating, the amount of time my daughter spends of a morning, blowdrying her hair and curling her eyelashes (a full half an hour most days), because I’ve never been bothered with make-up. I only wear it when someone forcibly applies it to my face – for television or for doing interviews on stage.

For me not wearing make-up is in itself an act of rebellion. I grew up with a mum who told me from the age of 12 that a lady should never leave the house without mascara on.

‘Stuff that!’, I thought, and refused to apply so much as a slick of lip gloss.

Indeed, I remind myself that this is what being a teenager is all about: not the make-up itself, but the desire to be your own person, to escape the strictures of your parents and the notion that you will forever be their baby.

When I was 13, I also did this by sneaking cigarettes and cider. I was feral. And so, I let my daughter have the mascara. I buy her the glazing milk, whatever the hell it might be.

If a bit of blusher is the worst thing that the likes of her and Harper Beckham indulge in as teenagers, then I’ll be absolutely delighted.

#532. I loved to have sex, then cancer stole my love life: Like millions of women, I was put into a medically induced menopause, bringing hot flushes and vaginal atrophy. But as months ticked by, I realised there is hope

As a sex coach, you might imagine my love life has always been adventurous and highly fulfilling.

But although I used to be sensual, playful and brimming with sexual confidence, a few years ago things changed.

Suddenly, I felt entirely lost. It wasn’t that my sex life had completely disappeared, but that the sensual part of me that once felt so alive was out of reach.

I felt protective, hesitant and undeserving of pleasure. I struggled to feel totally present in my body. My sexual connection to myself felt numb and flat.

While my partner was supportive, I started to feel shut down and stuck.

I tried to follow the advice I give clients: that feeling sexually alive isn’t just about sex, but about connecting with your own body, sensuality and pleasure. I tried rekindling that with candle-lit baths and other mindful activities, but I found myself dissociating. When it came to sex, my spark was dimmed.

Sex coach Georgia Rose struggled with sexual difficulties for years after going into remission

The reason? In May 2022, aged 31, I was diagnosed with the blood cancer Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

I knew that chemotherapy would temporarily kill my libido. What I hadn’t anticipated was that for years after I went into remission, my sexual identity would remain shattered.

And I’m not alone. Research shows that over 85 per cent of cancer patients struggle with sexual difficulties, yet embarrassment means the issue is rarely discussed.

I kept thinking that if I, as an expert in this field, was struggling, how on earth were others feeling?

It’s why I speak out about my experience, recording eight sessions with other sex experts – who helped me understand the traumatic effects of cancer on my sexuality, and how to heal – for my podcast Come Undone: A Sex Coach Goes There.

My interest in women’s sexual pleasure was sparked studying social history at Edinburgh University, where I specialised in the history of sex and gender.

It became a passion after a dinner with female friends in my mid-20s, when, after a few glasses of wine, everyone started admitting to faking orgasms.

Although I enjoyed sex, I too had prioritised partners’ needs over my own. We were all self-proclaimed feminists, yet side-lining our pleasure to make our boyfriends feel great. The contradiction jarred – and I couldn’t let it go.

So in 2017 I launched an online survey of 500 women, finding a global epidemic of them faking orgasms, experiencing shame and disconnection from their bodies and desires.

In 2021 I left my full-time job as a TV producer and retrained as a sex coach and clinical sexologist. The more I learned, the more aligned I became with neotantric approaches, which can view sex not simply as a physical act but a spiritual practice that engages the whole body and mind.

My interest in women’s sexual pleasure became a passion after a dinner with female friends in my mid-20s, when everyone started admitting to faking orgasms, writes Georgia

In February 2022, I started feeling breathlessness, with night sweats and chest pain, and large bruises appeared all over my body. An MRI revealed an 11cm tumour next to my heart and I was diagnosed with Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

In hospital, my body was constantly prodded by strangers and punctured with needles for tests, cannulations, and painful biopsies. I had six rounds of chemotherapy, leaving me with nausea, fatigue, mouth sores and no feeling in my fingers and toes.

I didn’t want to feel upset at losing all my hair – I’d always told my clients they were worth more than their appearance – but I was. I didn’t have the energy to exercise and went up a dress size.

I was put into a medically induced menopause, bringing terrible hot flushes and vaginal atrophy. Needless to say, it wasn’t a sexy time.

My partner, whom I married in 2024, understood. We kept our intimacy intact with shared baths, showers and massages and went out for dates when I felt strong enough. He told me I was beautiful and supported me at my worst. We were in the trenches together, and you could argue that’s more intimate than having perfunctory sex. Besides, I told myself, when I was in remission, sex would return to what it was.

During chemotherapy, however, my dad was diagnosed with an aggressive skin cancer. He died aged 75, a few days after I went into remission in January 2023.

While relieved to be free of the disease myself, I was floored by grief. I looked in the mirror and no longer recognised myself. I felt so disconnected from my body. It was like my whole sexual identity had gone.

No doctor had warned me about this. For them, cancer treatment is about survival, not quality of life afterwards, and some are too embarrassed to talk about sex with their patients.

As the months passed, none of the tools I had always relied on to feel sensual – meditation, movement, long baths and self-touch – worked. In fact, I started avoiding them.

And I felt ashamed that as a sex coach I couldn’t find my way back to the woman I used to be.

By early last year, I knew I needed an outside perspective, which is where my idea to put myself through sex coaching and therapy came from. I hoped that speaking candidly would encourage other cancer survivors to do the same.

Key to my recovery was to understand how trauma impacts our body and sexuality. Releasing pent-up anger about my diagnosis was a turning point. One sexual empowerment coach sent me to a rage room, where you pay to smash household objects. Breaking crockery with a crowbar proved unexpectedly cathartic – I ended up sobbing.

Another expert helped me realise how betrayed I felt by my body for developing cancer, and taught me ways to rebuild trust in it. I now believe my body deserves pleasure again.

My goal when I began the sessions was to get back to how I was. But the old me doesn’t exist – and I’ve realised that’s OK, and freed myself of that pressure.

Today, I feel more connected to my body and I’m more confident, light-hearted and vibrant in the bedroom. We are expecting our first baby at the end of the year.

Come Undone is available on YouTube, Apple and Spotify. Find out more at gs-spot.co.uk

Andy Burnham's suggestion of axeing gas standing charges could mean simply adding them to the unit costs, a Cabinet minister said today.

Miatta Fahnbulleh spoke out after the PM's surprise announcement that he has instructed her and Chancellor John Healey to look at removing the fee to cut bills.

The Net Zero Secretary said she was examining 'all the options' and argued that the public 'absolutely hates' not having control over the fixed fee added to energy bills and that 'even shifting it into the unit rate gives people that agency'.

But speaking to reporters in Westminster today she admitted that low-income consumers who use large amounts of energy could be left worse off if the costs simply moved to the unit rate part of the gas bill.

She also raised the prospect of these people receiving taxpayers money to help them cope after the change, saying: 'You need to think about mitigations.'

Miatta Fahnbulleh spoke out after the PM's surprise announcement that he has instructed her and Chancellor John Healey to look at removing the fee to cut bills

Mr Burnham used Prime Minister's Questions yesterday to reveal he wanted the two ministers to investigate and report back to MPs as soon as possible

Standing charges are a fixed daily fee added to energy bills, regardless of how much gas or electricity a customer uses.

The standing charge does not pay for the energy itself but covers the cost of delivering gas and electricity to homes and businesses – including the cost of essential maintenance and infrastructure upgrades.

Campaigners have urged the Government to make plans to support all households with energy costs this winter, with forecasters warning household bills could soar by almost another £300 from January.

Ms Fahnbulleh, who was appointed to head the energy brief by Mr Burnham in July, said making energy more affordable for households and businesses was her top priority.

“Candidly, we will win or lose the next election on our ability to make progress on the cost of living,” she said.

On removing gas bill standing charges, Ms Fahnbulleh told reporters: 'We are looking at the options. The thing I do know is that the public absolutely hate standing charge.

'It is a control question, that thing that before I even use it as energy you are charging x amounts, people just find that really egregious and their ability to manage their energy bills by deciding how much they want to use on their terms is essentially taken away from them.

'Even shifting to the unit rate gives people back agency. What the modelling suggests is that actually for a big stack of low income to middle income households it does mean a reduction in their bills.

'There are some people that will be impacted negatively because they are essentially low income, high users, so you need to think about the mitigations.

'But ... the thing he is very clear on is that we can't faff around we have to get on with it, so watch this space.'

#538. Britain to be battered by TWO storms in 24 hours: Met Office issues warnings for Storm Austen and Storm Boelo with 80mph gales and heavy rain hitting from tonight

Britain will be battered by two named storms in just 24 hours as the country faces damaging winds and travel disruption caused by Storm Austen and Storm Boelo.

Forecasters issued an amber wind warning for the far South West ahead of Austen's arrival around midnight, as well as yellow warnings for much of the rest of England.

The amber warning is in place from 1am to 10am tomorrow for Devon and Cornwall, where gusts of 60 to 70mph will develop with some exposed areas expecting 80mph.

Power cuts may affect homes, while some buildings may be damaged and a 'danger to life' is likely from large waves and beach material being thrown onto coastal roads.

A yellow warning for wind is in place for a wider region of the South West as well as South Wales and along England's South Coast between midnight and 5pm tomorrow.

Strong winds are expected to spread across southern England tonight and tomorrow, with gusts of 50 to 60mph likely and some exposed areas seeing 70mph or above.

Another yellow wind warning has been issued for the South East including London, as well as the Midlands and parts of the North West, from 10am to 9pm tomorrow.

A yellow warning for rain was also imposed in central and eastern Scotland from 6am tomorrow until midnight, where accumulations of 20-40mm are expected widely.

Storm Austen will hit the UK from midnight tonight, with warnings in place until 9pm tomorrow

Met Office warnings for Storm Boelo begin at 6pm tomorrow and will run until 9pm on Sunday

Satellite imagery shows Storm Austen today as it approaches the UK ahead of impact tonight

Up to 60-80mm is also possible in some locations, bringing flooding and travel disruption – with a chance some communities 'will become cut off by flooded roads'.

Yellow warnings for wind were also issued for Boelo – with northern England and Scotland facing gusts of up to 80mph from 6pm on Saturday until 9pm on Sunday.

A separate yellow wind warning was issued for Northern Ireland from 6pm on Saturday until 3pm on Sunday, with 50 to 60mph gusts widely and up to 75mph.

Meteorologists tracking Austen and Boelo in the Atlantic confirmed both low pressure systems are undergoing explosive cyclogenesis, known as a 'weather bomb'.

A weather bomb is officially declared when the central atmospheric pressure of a low pressure system rapidly falls by at least 24 millibars within a 24-hour period.

Met Office senior operational meteorologist Marco Petagna said Austen's pressure will fall by 24mb in just 18 hours, from 1,004 mb to 980mb – and therefore within the threshold. Boelo will deepen from 999mb to 948mb in 24 hours – a drop of 51mb.

The Met Office said the deep area of low pressure for Boelo will be 'invigorated by an active jet stream' as it crosses the Atlantic before reaching Northern Ireland.

Heavy rain will move in from the west through Saturday, spreading widely across the UK through the day – while wind strength will also continue to build through the day.

Boelo [pronounced Boo-loh] is a separate low pressure system to Austen which will bring severe weather tonight. Austen will clear into the North Sea by Friday evening.

The amber warning for wind is in place from 1am to 10am tomorrow for Devon and Cornwall

A yellow warning for wind is in place for a wider region between midnight and 5pm tomorrow

Another yellow wind warning has been issued for the South East from 10am to 9pm tomorrow

A yellow rain warning has been issued in Scotland from 6am tomorrow until 3am on Saturday

Met Office deputy chief forecaster Chris Bulmer said: 'Storm Austen is expected to bring a spell of impactful weather to parts of the UK from Thursday night and through Friday.

'While there remains some uncertainty in the exact track of the storm, there is increasing confidence in the potential for disruptive winds across parts of southwest England, which is why an amber warning has been issued.

'Winds gusts could potentially reach 60 to 70 mph for a time, and these strong winds will be combined with spells of heavy rain. While these winds will not be as strong as those further south and west, a spell of inland gales is possible with gusts around 45 to 55mph during the day tomorrow.

'People in affected areas should keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings as the event develops.'

The strong winds from Austen will lead to large waves and dangerous conditions around the coast of Wales and south-west England.

Speaking about Boelo, Mr Bulmer added: 'Storm Boelo will bring strong winds and heavy rain to Northern Ireland, Scotland and parts of northern England over the weekend, impacting the opposite end of the country to Storm Austen.

'Gusts of 70 to 80mph in exposed coastal areas and high ground are possible, with 50-60mph gusts more widely.

'The strong winds will be accompanied by heavy rain, making for an impactful weekend of weather. Severe weather warnings and forecast detail will continue to develop, so people should keep up to date with the forecast over the next few days.'

A yellow warning for Boelo's 80mph gusts runs from 6pm on Saturday until 9pm on Sunday

A yellow wind warning for Northern Ireland runs from 6pm on Saturday until 3pm on Sunday

People were advised by the Met Office to stay away from cliff edges and well back from stormy seas that could 'sweep you off your feet'.

Homeowners were told to take steps to protect their property from damage and other people from injury, such as checking for loose items outside and planning how to secure them in high winds.

These items include bins, plant pots, garden furniture, trampolines and sheds.

Met Office chief forecaster Neil Armstrong said: 'We've updated amber and yellow severe weather warnings for Storm Austen.

'This is the first stormy weather in the South of the UK this season and we expect some disruption as it moves through.

'With trees in leaf, it is likely fallen branches and trees could obstruct roads and railways so take extra care on the Friday morning commute.'

Network Rail Scotland said that trains tomorrow will be slowed down to keep people safe in the areas expected to see the heaviest rain.

Speed restrictions will be in place on parts of the West Coast Main Line and East Coast Main Line, as well as routes across southern and eastern Scotland.

It said some journeys will take longer as a result, but that the restrictions mean trains can continue running through areas where the weather is at its worst.

Network Rail Scotland said that during Boelo, which is forecast to hit the country on Saturday and Sunday, speed restrictions are likely in the worst-affected areas.

Craig Gorman, head of operational weather strategy at Network Rail Scotland, said: 'We can't control the weather, but we can make sure we're as ready as possible for whatever it brings.

'A big part of our job is staying one step ahead. We're constantly looking at how the forecast is developing and what that could mean for different parts of the railway, allowing us to make the right decisions at the right time.

'We know any disruption from these storms will be frustrating, particularly as it's the weekend, but we'll do everything we can to keep people moving wherever it's safe to do so.'

Before the arrival of the storms, today will be a broadly dry and bright day across the UK – although there will be some blustery conditions in eastern Scotland.

The Met Office has said Austen, Boelo and Chloe will be the first named storms of the season

Ross Macleod, the RNLI's water safety manager, has asked people not to take 'unnecessary risks' when visiting the coast.

He said: 'If you plan to visit the coast or a waterside location, we urge you stay a safe distance from the water as conditions could knock you off your feet or wash you into the sea.'

The forecast comes a week after severe drought was declared in parts of England, amid concerns over dwindling reservoirs because of extremely dry conditions.

The South East and South West have experienced their driest April to September for more than a century - affecting reservoirs in those areas, according to officials.

As a result, 'severe drought' – in which a lack of water affects daily life and the environment in major ways, and can have extensive effects – has been declared in parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex.

But supercharged El Nino conditions in the Pacific which affect weather across the world will put the UK at greater risk of a wet stormy autumn overall, forecasters say.

Garth Smith, head of resilience at the British Red Cross, said: 'With weather warnings being put in place for large parts of the UK this weekend, we're reminding people to take simple but effective steps now to protect themselves, their families, and their homes.

'Hopefully these will only be precautionary, but we know from our experience that many people are not prepared or aware of guidance that will help them better withstand extreme weather events in advance.

'We have practical advice that can make a real difference – from checking in with people who may be more vulnerable, securing loose items in your garden to checking windows and doors, and making an evacuation plan for your household, including pets.

'We also urge people to keep an eye on local weather reports and guidance from local authorities.'

The Met Office storm year runs from September to August, with each 12-month period having its own alphabetical list of names that are used to label successive storms.

This year's list begins with Austen and continues with Boelo, Chloe, Dano and Evelyn, ending at W with Wende.

Storm naming is a partnership between the Met Office, Ireland's Met Éireann and the Dutch service KNMI.

Met Éireann selected the name for the first storm in honour of Austen Nagle, the Irish Meteorological Service's first director.

KNMI picked names from more than 3,000 suggestions submitted by the public, including Boelo – a nearly extinct name from the east Groningen region that has been passed down through the nominator's family for generations.

#539. Scientists pinpoint the exact sky that inspired Van Gogh's The Starry Night

By WILIAM HUNTER, SENIOR SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY REPORTER

Published: 16:00 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 16:51 BST, 22 October 2026

Its swirls have long left art experts suffering for their sanity, as they try to work out whether The Starry Night was indeed real.

But now we understand, it seems, exactly which evening Vincent Van Gogh painted in his iconic work.

For, according to calculations by researchers, the piece depicts the sky as it was just before dawn on July 22, 1889.

The artwork is believed to show the view from the Dutch artist's window in Saint-Remy-de-Provence, France.

It had left critics bitterly divided over whether the scene had been real or was instead merely a figment of his imagination.

Yet it seems all that was needed to crack the decades-old mystery was a spot of star gazing.

The researchers found that in the piece, the waning crescent moon, the planet Venus and the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus were shown as close together.

And that scene exactly matched what would have taken place on that summer night, explained the team from Korea, which published its discovery in the Scientific Reports journal.

A team of Korean researchers have finally settled the debate by pinpointing the precise night sky that inspired Vincent Van Gogh's The Starry Night through the constellation he painted

The Starry Night is the most celebrated painting from Van Gogh's stay at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole mental asylum and inspired Don McLean's hit song Vincent.

The artist found himself there after a serious mental breakdown that May, which famously involved cutting off part of his left ear.

These unusual circumstances have led the painting to be the centre of fervent speculation over its possible hidden meanings or symbolic content.

But the biggest puzzles have been what the painting really shows and when it was painted.

Traditionally, the painting has been dated by a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother, Theo, around June 18, 1889.

But if The Starry Night does resemble the sky as Van Gogh really saw it, then this could not be the case.

That is because in early June, the Moon would have been waning gibbous - when only half of it is visible - which doesn't at all match the slim crescent depicted.

Art historians have also identified the bright cluster of stars in the painting as Aries, but astronomers say this doesn't make sense.

Scientists started by looking at the night sky in Van Gogh's paintings, which have been accurately dated, including Café Terrace at Night (pictured)

Scientists discovered that the paintings did, in fact, accurately depict the night sky, with Café Terrace at Night showing a constellation called the summer triangle and Starry Night over the Rhône capturing the Big Dipper

Lead author Elijah Jeong–hyun Kim, PhD candidate at Kyung Hee University and CEO of SLLAB, says: 'To an observational astronomer, the cluster of stars in The Starry Night is the Hyades in Taurus.'

First, the researchers looked at two of Van Gogh's night sky paintings that are dated very accurately thanks to an abundance of historical sources – Café Terrace at Night and Starry Night over the Rhône.

Using an astronomical model, the researchers were able to reconstruct the night sky as it would have been on the day those paintings were made, and compared it to Van Gogh's field of view.

They discovered that the paintings did, in fact, accurately depict the night sky, with Café Terrace at Night showing a constellation called the summer triangle and Starry Night over the Rhône capturing the Big Dipper.

Using these techniques, the researchers then turned to the question of when The Starry Night itself was painted.

During two trips to France in 2019, the researchers retraced Van Gogh's location to work out his exact view down over the town of Saint-Rémy.

Reconstructing the night sky for that period, they found that the stars would have been arranged just as they are in The Starry Night on July 22 – a month later than had previously been estimated.

Scientists travelled to Saint–Rémy–de–Provence, France, to work out the exact view Van Gogh would have had from the window of his room in the Saint–Paul–de–Mausole mental asylum (pictured)

Researchers found that The Starry Night matches the exact night sky that Van Gogh would have seen from his room in the early hours of July 22, 1889

Statistical analysis then confirmed the correspondence between the five central stars of The Starry Night and the Hyades, with an even closer match in the pen drawing Van Gogh made after the painting.

Checking the historical weather records, the researchers found that the sky that night would have been clear enough for Van Gogh to see such an arrangement.

Additionally, frequent mentions of cicadas in Van Gogh's letters suggest a period of hot weather, which better matches the temperature records for July.

This suggests that Van Gogh likely sketched the night sky as he saw it in the early hours of July 22, and then finished the final painting over the following days.

Mr Kim says: 'I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-Rémy paintings, and at Van Gogh's movements that summer.

'Our conversation with Van Gogh's other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one.'

#540. Recorded crime rockets past 7m incidents a year for first time, amid huge surge in fraud and robbery

Published: 11:20 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 16:43 BST, 22 October 2026

The number of crimes recorded by the police has soared past seven million a year for the first time.

Official figures showed an 8 per cent jump in recorded crime in the year to June, hitting 7,084,375 incidents in England and Wales.

It was the first time the total surpassed seven million since modern crime recording practices began at the turn of the century, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed.

The surge was largely down to a massive 41 per cent leap in reported fraud, to 1.8million offences.

The increase corresponded with the launch of a new service, Report Fraud, in December last year which allows the public to log cyber crime or fraud with City of London Police, which has national responsibilities in relation to financial crime.

The total included a 79 per cent increase to 1.02million in the number of frauds reported to the new service by the banking and financial services body UK Finance.

The surge indicates just how poorly fraud was being recorded under the previous system, Action Fraud, which was repeatedly criticised as ‘not fit for purpose’ by MPs leading it to be dubbed ‘Inaction Fraud’.

A separate measure of crime – the Crime Survey of England and Wales – also showed a surge in fraud.

The survey, which aims to estimate total crime levels including offences which are not reported to police, said there were 4.5million fraud incidents in the year, up 11 per cent.

It said the increase was due to a 13 per cent jump in bank and credit account fraud to 2.8million.

The ONS data shows how the number of ‘real-world’ crimes is continuing to fall as criminals go online.

Police recorded 5.2million crimes in the year excluding fraud and ‘computer misuse’ offences, down 1 per cent in a year.

However, robbery was one category of crime to witness a surge, with a 10 per cent increase year-on-year to its highest level since before the pandemic.

Police forces in England and Wales recorded 88,282 robberies in the year to June, up from 80,469 in the previous 12 months.

The surge was down to a sharp rise in robberies of businesses, which jumped 67 per cent year-on-year to just over 31,000 – the highest on record.

Robbery of personal property, however, dipped 7 per cent to just over 57,000 incidents.

The Association of Convenience Stores (ACS) said the rise in robbery may reflect increasing violence used by shoplifters, which is leading to a shift in the way the crime is recorded by forces.

Recorded shoplifting fell 2 per cent to 519,516 from a near-peak the previous year.

An ACS spokesman said: 'The reason for the marked increase in robberies is likely due to a change in the way that some offences are now recorded as robberies that previously would have been counted as shoplifting offences.'

Should police make tackling fraud a bigger priority?

ACS chief executive Ed Woodall said: 'We are extremely concerned about the changing nature of theft against retailers.

'Offenders are becoming more confident, more brazen, and ultimately more violent in their crimes, threatening retailers and shopworkers to get away with stolen goods.'

He added: 'The Crime and Policing Act marked a big step forward in ensuring that the police treat shop theft more seriously, but many of the key measures from the Act such as the scrapping of the £200 threshold for investigating thefts, and the separate offence for attacking a shopworker are still not in place.

'The Government must act as soon as possible to show that it backs the hardworking people running and working in our nation’s local shops.'

Meanwhile, sexual offences logged by police hit the highest level on record with just under 219,000 in the year – or an average of 600 every day.

It included 74,484 rapes recorded in the year, about 200 lower than the peak seen two years earlier, while other categories of sex crime increased by 5 per cent.

Separately, possession of weapons offences recorded by forces hit a record 63,700, up more than 10 per cent on the previous year.

It included 30,216 offences of possessing an article with a blade or point, up 8.8 per cent in a year and the highest figure since the statistical series began in 2008-09.

Separate data published by the Home Office showed the proportion of crimes which lead to a suspect being taken to court remains stubbornly low.

The year to March saw 8.5 per cent of recorded crimes leading to suspects being charged or summoned, up to 447,514. The previous year's figure was 7.3 per cent.

But the proportion of criminals facing justice is still far below the 15.5 per cent seen in 2015.

The latest figures showed there were 1.9million crimes where investigations were closed without a suspect being identified, making up 37.8 per cent of the total.

It represented a slight improvement on the previous year when the proportion was 39 per cent.

Further figures published by the Ministry of Justice showed a rising number of criminals who are let off with a 'slap on the wrist'.

So-called 'community resolutions' – which allow offenders to dodge prosecution if they agree to apologise to their victim, for example – increased by 9 per cent to an all-time high of 189,000 in the year.

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: ‘Crime is spiralling out of control under Labour.

‘Record numbers of sexual offences, knife crime and shop theft show what happens when criminals know they can get away with it.

‘This is a direct consequence of Labour cutting police numbers by 2,000 and letting thousands of prisoners out of jail early.

‘Victims are being failed at every turn, with 92 per cent of crimes not being solved.

‘Labour needs to stop making excuses and back the police to ensure criminals face consequences.’

He added: ‘The Conservatives have a plan to take back our streets with 10,000 extra police officers, hotspot policing and tripling the stop and search to restore law and order and make sure crime has consequences.’

Crime and policing minister Sarah Jones said: 'This Government is bringing down the crimes that make people’s lives a misery.

'Since the election, knife crime is down 11 per cent, knife-point robberies have fallen by 18 per cent and overall homicides are down 7 per cent.

'Fatal knife attacks are also at their lowest level in 35 years, while thefts such as phone-snatching and pickpocketing have fallen by 20 per cent in just the last year.

'That means fewer victims and safer streets.

'These are huge steps forward, but there is always more to do.

'With more than 3,800 additional neighbourhood officers, our Plan to Halve Knife Crime and stronger powers to recover stolen goods, we will keep pursuing offenders, protecting the public and restoring confidence in policing.'

On spiralling fraud, a Home Office spokesman said: 'This Government is alive to the challenge posed by fraud and is investing £250million to combat it over the next three years.

'This includes a £31million investment for a new Online Crime Centre, combining the data, expertise and capabilities of the police, GCHQ, banks, telecommunications and tech firms.'

'Our Fraud Strategy will tackle the UK’s most commonly experienced crime by strengthening partnerships across sectors, disrupting criminal operations and delivering better support for victims.'

#541. Would YOU take the SELFIE test that could reveal clues about how long you'll live? Scientists develop AI tool that can tell if you're ageing 'too fast' from a picture of your face... and here's how to try it yourself

Published: 12:16 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 16:36 BST, 22 October 2026

Forget how many candles you blew out on your last birthday cake. Scientists increasingly believe there may be a more revealing measure of how well you're ageing – and even how long you might live.

Known as biological age, it reflects the toll that time, lifestyle and health take on the body, rather than simply how many years you've been alive.

It’s not just about vanity: research has linked ageing faster than your years to a greater risk of serious illnesses, including cancer, heart disease and dementia, as well as premature death.

And now, scientists have developed an AI tool that claims to estimate your biological age from nothing more than a selfie.

Developed by researchers at Mass General Brigham in Boston, the AI has been trained on millions of facial images to spot subtle signs of ageing around the eyes, nose and mouth.

And this week, scientists revealed that a related system could even predict cancer patients' chances of survival.

The biological age test available to the public doesn't diagnose illness or predict how long someone has left to live. But it does offer an intriguing glimpse of whether our faces are ageing faster or slower than the years suggest.

So we decided to put it to the test – with some surprising results.

Stacey, 42, from the US, was estimated to be nearly a decade younger by the tool

There was certainly some nervousness among the Daily Mail staff who volunteered to have their faces analysed.

After all, nobody particularly wants to be told they are ageing faster than they should be – especially when the results come with a number attached.

But for most of our volunteers, the news was reassuring. The AI judged almost everyone to be younger than their actual age, in some cases by almost a decade.

Among the biggest winners was Daily Mail US Science and Technology Editor Stacey Liberatore, 42, who was given a biological age of just 32.6 – almost ten years younger than her actual age.

Biological age reflects your body's physiological condition and how well you're aging rather than your actual, chronological age.

Research shows that people who look older than their actual age may have higher health risks - and understanding this can help you make more informed decisions about your health and lifestyle, the researchers say.

To find out your biological age, click this link and follow these three simple steps.

1. Review and complete the research consent form

2. Answer a few demographic and health questions

3. Upload a selfie and wait for your biological age

Stacey doesn't smoke or drink alcohol, two habits known to have a significant impact on long-term health.

Meanwhile, Cameron Roy, 29, was told his biological age was 25.5. He also doesn't smoke and has given up drinking, something he believes may have helped keep his score down.

My fellow Daily Mail health reporter Ciaran Foreman, 24, had similarly encouraging news, receiving a score of just 20.1.

Trainee reporter Tara Russell, 24, was estimated to be 19.3, while The Mail on Sunday's Health Editor Ethan Ennals, 31, was judged to be 28.2.

Elsewhere, the differences were less dramatic.

My mother, Jude, 65, was estimated to be 64, despite the fact she suffers from bone-thinning disease osteoporosis, while I was judged to be 25, which is my actual age.

But not everyone had reason to celebrate.

Mail on Sunday designer Lee Herniman, who recently turned 50, was told his biological age was 56 – making him one of the few participants whose score was significantly older than his actual age.

Lee was 'surprised' by the result, saying he exercises regularly – running and cycling – and has no known long-term health conditions. However, the father-of-two admits to enjoying sun holidays and, as a former amateur footballer, underwent surgery on both knees following injuries in his 30s.

His love of sunshine may offer one possible explanation. Research has shown that prolonged sun exposure can accelerate visible facial ageing, causing wrinkles and changes in skin texture that can make people appear older than their years.

Indeed, a review of seven studies involving more than 3,300 people found that those with the greatest exposure to sunlight consistently looked older than people of the same age who spent less time in the sun.

However, this doesn't necessarily mean Lee's body is ageing faster, or that he is at greater risk of ill health.

Of course, being told you look younger than you are is flattering – particularly when the verdict comes from a supposedly impartial computer rather than a well-meaning friend.

Lee, 50, scored one of the highest biological ages of the group

Does a biological age ten years younger than your real age suggest you're healthier than other people your age? And, more importantly, does it mean you're likely to live longer?

There is growing evidence that how quickly our bodies age may be an important indicator of our future health.

Studies involving tens of thousands of people have found that those whose biological age is older than their actual age face a greater risk of developing serious illnesses, including heart disease and cancer, as well as dying prematurely.

One major analysis, involving more than 40,000 people, found that every five years of accelerated biological ageing was associated with an eight to 15 per cent higher risk of death.

Other research has linked faster biological ageing with dementia and type 2 diabetes, suggesting the process may offer clues about our vulnerability to a range of diseases.

Most of this research has relied on sophisticated tests that analyse changes in our blood, cells and DNA to estimate how quickly our bodies are ageing.

The new AI tool takes a very different approach, using nothing more than the appearance of our faces.

So can something as simple as a selfie really reveal what's happening inside our bodies?

According to Dr Raymond Mak, one of the researchers behind the technology, it does.

Scientists have long known that people of the same age can look remarkably different, and that some of those differences may reflect their underlying health.

The researchers believe their AI can detect subtle facial changes associated with ageing that might otherwise go unnoticed.

And their findings suggest these changes could have real medical significance.

One of the most promising applications is in cancer care, where doctors must decide how aggressively to treat patients who may be physically frail.

'You could have two 70-year-olds come in with a diagnosis of lung cancer,' Dr Mak explained.

Cameron Roy, 29, was told his biological age was 25.5. He doesn't smoke and has given up drinking, something he believes may have helped keep his score down

'One may have smoked their entire life, be wheelchair-bound and look five or even ten years older than they actually are.

'The other may still be working, exercising regularly and resemble a fit and healthy 50-year-old.'

Although both patients are the same age, their bodies may be very different in terms of how well they can cope with treatment.

The younger-looking patient might be able to tolerate aggressive chemotherapy, for example, while the older-looking patient could be at greater risk of serious side effects.

Doctors already make these judgements using their clinical experience, but researchers hope AI could provide a more objective assessment.

In one study of cancer patients, a companion AI system trained to predict survival from facial photographs identified a group at particularly high risk of dying.

More than half of these patients died within 90 days, compared with just two per cent of those judged to be at lowest risk.

The technology is still experimental and cannot replace conventional medical assessments. Nor does it mean that a healthy person whose face looks older is necessarily at greater risk of dying.

But the findings suggest our faces may contain important clues about our underlying health that even experienced doctors struggle to detect.

Intriguingly, the researchers also discovered that the technology is surprisingly difficult to fool.

When they tested it on people who had undergone cosmetic procedures, including facelifts and Botox, they found that these treatments made little difference to their estimated biological age.

Even though patients looked younger to the naked eye, the AI was still picking up signs of ageing.

But if cosmetic surgery can't turn back our biological clocks, is there anything that can?

It's a question that has fuelled a booming longevity industry, with enthusiasts spending thousands on supplements, specialist diets and tests promising to reveal – and even reverse – the ageing process.

Yet according to Dr Francesco Lo Monaco, a cardiologist and founder of the National Heart Clinic, the most effective ways to protect our health as we age are considerably less glamorous.

Zoe Hardy was judged by the tool to be 25, which is how old she actually is.  Her mother Jude, 65, scored a biological age of 64 despite suffering from osteoporosis

'The biggest gains still come from the basics,' he said.

Regular exercise is particularly important, with a combination of cardiovascular activity and strength training helping to protect the heart, maintain muscle mass and preserve bone strength.

Diet matters too. Research suggests that following a Mediterranean-style diet, rich in vegetables, fibre and healthy fats, is associated with a lower risk of several age-related diseases.

And getting enough sleep may be just as important.

Studies have linked regularly sleeping fewer than six hours a night with a greater risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.

Crucially, Dr Lo Monaco says it is never too late to make changes.

'From what I see in clinic, there is no age at which it becomes meaningless to make positive changes,' he said.

'Even in your sixties, those improvements can make a meaningful difference.'

However, while healthier habits can reduce the risk of disease, that doesn't necessarily mean they will produce a younger biological age score – or that lowering such a score will guarantee a longer life.

But experts warn against becoming too fixated on a single biological age score – particularly one calculated from a photograph.

'Appearance can be misleading,' said Dr Lo Monaco.

'People can look ten years younger than they really are, and AI is very good at identifying clues linked to smoking, alcohol use and sun exposure.

'But looking young and being biologically healthy are not necessarily the same thing.'

Indeed, someone could receive a reassuringly youthful score while unknowingly living with high cholesterol, raised blood pressure or another condition that increases their risk of serious illness.

And a person whose face appears older than their years may be perfectly healthy.

For this reason, the AI cannot replace blood tests, scans or other medical checks, and there is no evidence that an individual selfie score can reliably predict how long a healthy person will live.

For now, scientists caution that a biological age score is not a reliable prediction of how long an individual will live. And there is still no proof that lowering that score will, in itself, extend your life.

But Dr Mak believes the technology could eventually offer something more useful than a one-off assessment.

Because the AI can analyse old photographs as easily as new ones, it may be possible to track how quickly someone's face is ageing over several years – and identify changes that warrant further investigation.

'One of the unique things about this test is that people already have years, sometimes decades, of photos stored on their phones,' he said.

'A sudden acceleration in ageing may be a warning sign.'
