#542. How to make the perfect cup of coffee... according to PETER HITCHENS

Published: 11:24 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 16:35 BST, 22 October 2026

I did not know what coffee really was until I was 14 years old. My first taste of it was a great revelation, and I have never got over it.

Now I can hardly find the real thing anywhere outside my own kitchen.

Just as proper music has been driven out of our lives by guitars and drums, proper coffee has been displaced by a bitter ocean of headache-inducing espresso on one side, and a great lake of instant brown liquid on the other.

I drink these things because they are better than nothing.

Drown the espresso in a bucket of milk and it can be bearable, under the right conditions. Instant coffee is all right if you don’t think of it as coffee, but as a different drink, something warm, wet and inoffensive to punctuate the livelong day.

Until 1965, I used to drink a lot of the tinned powdered instant version of the time, disgustingly sugared. My brother and I, in our provincial, suburban ignorance, thought it faintly sophisticated. Those were also the last days of ‘frothy coffee’, served in glass cups and saucers in pretentious fake-Italian cafes, and tasting roughly as you might imagine a donkey would taste.

Powdered instant was certainly better than the bottled substance, also known as coffee, which my grandfather mixed with boiled milk as his mid-morning refreshment. Amazingly, you can still get Camp Coffee. And I noticed some years ago that its once-imperialist label had been radically altered to suit the multicultural times.

They might perhaps have been better occupied reforming the contents. I don’t think I would drink it now.

And then came the great discovery. I had won a scholarship to school and my parents generously asked me what I would like to do to celebrate it. I knew immediately.

We must go, I insisted, on the Golden Arrow, from Calais to Paris. The Golden Arrow, long before Eurostar and the Chunnel, was a beautiful way to go to Paris by super-comfortable train. The best bit came after you had picked your way across the tracks at Calais, and been through the freezing French customs shed (it was December). There we were given a compartment to ourselves, in a beautiful old-pre-war blue and gold Pullman car (not the ludicrously perfect type you get on the Orient Express now).

As the train steamed (it did steam then) towards Paris, we were served a feast of beautifully cooked food. And after the apple tart came the coffee, each cup with its own battered metal filter. And at that moment I was seduced by France. I had never tasted anything like it before and I have spent quite a lot of time and effort since, trying to reproduce that first delight.

The rest of the meal had been superb, as expected. But this coffee altered my entire view of the world. If I could get hold of it again, and keep doing so, my life would be transformed for the better.

I knew for the first time what coffee actually was, or at least what it was supposed to be.

The word had altered its meaning in the internal dictionary of my mind. How can I explain it? It tasted the way freshly ground coffee smells. It was not bitter, or weak. I could have drunk it black, but preferred it with hot milk.

There were many good things about that first visit to Paris – a thing nobody ever gets over. We were there smack in the middle of Charles de Gaulle’s first proper election since he had seized power in 1958, and his mischievous visage, with its enormous nose, hung over everything. So I should mention here the great man’s own view on English coffee.

Brought a cup of it at the Foreign Office after he had arrived in London for the first time in 1940, he is supposed to have asked: ‘Ah, is this perhaps the famous English tea?’

It is wholly believable. Whether he was joking or not, there simply was no relation between proper French coffee, as it was then, and the fluid served under that name in England. Like all brief visions of wonderful things, this one has spoiled me.

When we returned to Oxford, my home town, it was back to the Rule of Nescafe.

One tiny outpost among the spires was the now-vanished Elizabeth Restaurant, much favoured by rich Leftists. Its staff were able to conjure superb coffee out of an amazing apparatus like an alchemist’s retort, all gurgling tubes and glass spheres.

But there was no room in my house for such a machine even if I could have found or afforded it.

As the years went by, I found proper coffee roasters, learned to grind the beans myself, experimented with complex devices, and occasionally hit the target. On repeated visits to France, I noticed a severe falling-off in quality. Then came the Starbucks revolution, and there is now almost nothing, anywhere, but espresso coffee.

Why has this happened? For those who like that sort of thing, that is the sort of thing they like. But most of the time it is just too strong, and if it is not strong, it does not taste of much.

Even Americans can make good coffee if they grasp that it is no good making it feeble and thin (as they often do) as the great Lou Mitchell’s in Chicago, home of the world’s best breakfast, demonstrates.

There are long queues outside in winter, presumably made up of Americans sick of the scratchy brown fluid they call coffee over there. Turkish coffee is good.

Even Soviet coffee could be superb, but there was usually no milk, so I learned to marry it with the excellent local ice cream. It was never hot, but it was always delicious.

But eventually I found out a simple thing. All you need for good coffee is good beans, properly ground (preferably by hand) and a good solid jug.

Pour water that has just boiled on to the grounds, stir them, leave until the grounds have risen to form a sort of crust on top. Then, after a minute or two, pass a cold spoon through that crust, wait till the grounds have sunk to the bottom, and pour.

Do not then put cold milk in it. It will ruin the taste. Heat your milk gently, and it will be far better. Or, if you are not an obsessive hater of fat, as so many deluded people are these days, try actual cream.

You will not need sugar to soften it. It will not blast your skull or make your brain buzz or jangle. You do not have to swamp it with great vats of steamed, skimmed milk.

It has no pretentious Italian name for you to mispronounce. It is just coffee, and when I drink it I am back on the great soft cushions of the Golden Arrow again, bound for Paris for the very first time.

Adrian McAnarney (pictured), a 57-year-old father of two from Katesbridge, County Down, died after falling around 100ft from a mountain path in Snowdonia while preparing to trek to Mount Everest base camp

A post-mortem found he died from multiple crush injuries. Assistant coroner Sarah Riley concluded his death was accidental. McAnarney is pictured

The Llanberis mountain rescue team rushed to the scene along with a rescue helicopter but Adrian was pronounced dead at the rescue base.

Wife Monica McAnarney said her husband had had a passion for hiking and was planning to climb to Mount Everest base camp this November.

Adrian's hiking mission was set to take place in aid of the Northern Ireland Hospice charity.

The inquest in Caernarfon heard a post-mortem examination found he died from multiple crush injuries.

Assistant coroner Sarah Riley said Adrian, of Katesbridge, County Down, had fallen from height on Crib Goch resulting in fatal injuries.

#545. Fresh agony for family of nine-year-old girl after Attorney General refuses appeal over boy, 16, who was cleared of killing her despite fatally stabbing her in the chest

Published: 15:54 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 15:56 BST, 22 October 2026

There is fresh agony today for the family of a nine-year-old girl who died after being fatally stabbed by a teenage boy, after the Attorney General refused to refer the case to the Court of Appeal despite acknowledging a 'misdirection' of the jury.

Aria Thorpe died after being stabbed in her chest at her home in Weston-super-Mare, North Somerset, on December 15 last year.

A 15-year-old boy, now 16, admitted to holding the knife when Aria sustained her fatal injuries but claimed in court it had been an accident.

After stabbing the nine-year-old, he fled the scene without calling for help and travelled to a nearby railway station where he told a group of children he had 'accidentally stabbed' her.

He then told one of the group, who he knew: 'I'm a murderer. I accidentally killed someone.'

Yet at court, the teenager was acquitted of both murder and manslaughter, and walked free.

Since the verdict Aria's father Tom Thorpe and her wider family have been campaigning after suffering a 'robbery of justice' over the 'incomprehensible' loss of the youngster.

They vowed to fight the verdict and have claimed the trial judge erred by telling the jury they must be sure that the teenager intended to 'kill or cause really serious harm' to Aria with his actions, rather than allowing a manslaughter conviction on the basis of recklessness.

Aria Thorpe died after being stabbed in her chest at her home in Weston-super-Mare, North Somerset, on December 15 last year

Aria, pictured with father Tom Thorpe and his partner Sophie, was stabbed once in the chest

The family say that if they cannot overturn the boy's acquittal, they want to ensure that points of law are clarified to prevent other families being faced with a similar situation.

This will culminate in a campaign for Aria's Law, which will seek to clarify the definition of manslaughter for future cases.

But there was a fresh setback this week after Attorney General Ellie Reeves said she was unable to refer Aria's case to the Court of Appeal over what she described as a 'jury misdirection' by the presiding judge.

'After careful consideration, I have concluded that this case does not raise a point of law that is unclear or otherwise in need of further clarification to prevent a similar jury misdirection in future cases,' she told the Daily Mail.

'The grounds for referral to the Court of Appeal were not met in this case.'

In response, her family told the Daily Mail they will 'not accept' the decision.

'Sadly, another set back but we stay hopeful that something can be done and/or lessons are learnt from this massive injustice,' they said.

'How can the justice system acknowledge things went wrong but yet we can't do anything about it?'

They continued: 'We certainly aren't going to accept the notification from the Attorney General that the law was clear but it was just not followed correctly.

'We are not going to accept that there is no other means of remediation.

'Aria's killer walked out of court before we even did and now lives a free life.'

The Attorney General has now declined to refer her case to the Court of Appeal over the 'jury misdirection'

It came after they appealed to their local MP, Suella Braverman, who wrote to Ms Reeves and asked for the case to be sent under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1972.

This allows the Attorney General to refer a point of law to the Court of Appeal for clarification after a defendant has been acquitted.

The letter read: 'Aria's family, and I wish to see the Court of Appeal asked to clarify whether the judge was right to direct the jury as she did: specifically, whether recklessness as to death or really serious harm was properly excluded from the jury's consideration, and whether the directions given adequately reflected the established bases of manslaughter, including gross negligence manslaughter and unlawful act manslaughter, as well as any residual role for recklessness in homicide directions.

'We are concerned that, if the direction given in this case was wrong in law, juries in future cases may be denied a route to a manslaughter conviction that Parliament and the common law intend them to have, with serious implications for victims' families and for public confidence in the justice system.'

However, after reviewing the case, Ms Reeves said she was not able to send it to the Court of Appeal on this basis.

There is also currently no option for the verdicts to be reviewed: under UK law, serious offences including murder and manslaughter can be retried only if 'new and compelling' evidence has emerged.

Aria's family say their 'immediate primary goal' is to 'understand how and why the justice system failed Aria'.

They plan to continue sharing news of their campaign on social media pages on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook.

Attorney General Ellie Reeves KC MP said: 'This case was shocking and it is clear the tragic loss of Aria Thorpe has left an immeasurable gap in her family's lives.

'I was asked to refer this case to the Court of Appeal and seek its opinion on a point of law. This power is reserved for instances where clarification is necessary to prevent a potential error of law from influencing future decisions in similar cases.'

'After careful consideration, I have concluded that this case does not raise a point of law that is unclear or otherwise in need of further clarification to prevent a similar jury misdirection in future cases. The grounds for referral to the Court of Appeal were not met in this case.

'I appreciate that this outcome will be deeply disappointing for Aria's family. I have given this request the most careful consideration, and my role is limited to making references on a point of law, meaning even if this request had met the grounds for referral, this could not overturn the acquittal.'

#548. Meet one of the deadliest men in Britain...that you've never heard of: The Turkish gangster who unleashed hell on the streets of London and cheated death three times

Published: 09:59 BST, 14 October 2026 | Updated: 15:18 BST, 22 October 2026

It is, by all accounts, a miracle that Beytullah Gunduz has survived long enough to face justice in Britain.

The Turkish mafia boss, known to his gangland associates as 'Beyto', cheated death three times in five years during his ascent to becoming a feared and ruthless 'Mr Big' in London's underworld.

For over a decade, Gunduz, 40, has been a 'high-ranking' leader of the Hackney Turks, one of the most feared organised crime groups in Britain.

His gang, also known as the Bombacilar, Turkish for 'Bombers', have been synonymous with drugs and violence since the 1980s. By 2003, they controlled around 90 per cent of the heroin arriving in Britain.

'The ruthlessness of those Turkish gangs was legendary,' says Dal Babu, a retired police officer who survived a botched execution by a Turkish gang member in the 1980s when a bullet got stuck in the barrel of a hitman's gun.

'They were able to have a real hold on communities. The police were just overwhelmed.'

Fast forward to today and the Bombacilar's notorious feud with their rivals the Tottenham Turks, is still raging in north London, claiming at least 20 lives in tit-for-tat violence over the last two decades.

Gunduz himself became a central figure when he was accused of hiring a hitman to kill Zafer Eren, the godfather of the Tottenham Turks, in 2013. He was cleared in the courts, but sources insist 'everyone knew it was him'.

In the following years, he was said to have had a £200,000 bounty put on his head by his enemies but the cash was never collected. The mob boss continued to stay one step ahead of his enemies – often by sheer luck.

He was served an 'Osman warning', which alerts potential targets of a threat to their life, by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, escaped death when a gunman's firearm jammed the following year, and was the intended target of the infamous shooting that left a nine-year-old girl with a bullet lodged in her brain in 2024.

Despite being either responsible for or the target of brutal violence on the streets of the capital, Gunduz's 80 previous convictions have until now been for relatively minor offences, only ever spending time in jail for three months for dangerous driving and threatening behaviour in 2019.

But last month, he was jailed for life with a minimum of 20 years after being convicted of ordering the shooting of Onur Guzel, 38, outside his father's Umut 2000 restaurant, in Dalston, east London. His gunman, Dogan Over, fled to Istanbul and is still at large.

Guzel survived the shooting outside the Turkish restaurant – which has been recommended by top chefs and featured in a New York Times list of the top 25 dishes to eat in London – but suffered serious injuries.

Gunduz – described in the Old Bailey as a 'high-ranking member' of his gang 'at the heart of extorting the local community' – had wrongly accused the Guzel family of paying £100,000 to the Tottenham Turks for protection, and demanded the same amount.

The gang leader – who refused to leave Thameside Prison to attend the hearing out of fear he would be attacked – has now finally been taken off the streets.

Born in Turkey in 1986, Gunduz migrated to Britain when he was just a 10-year-old boy.

He was enrolled into a secondary school in Hackney, which – like Tottenham – has a large Turkish and Kurdish community.

By all accounts, Gunduz got on well with other children in the multi-cultural neighbourhood. But he was not academically gifted and was drawn in by the powerful gangs who controlled the communities.

Dal Babu, who pounded the beat as a police constable in Tottenham, told The Crime Desk: 'What really struck me was how sophisticated the Turkish mafia was in that area.

Beytullah Gunduz, 40, a high-ranking member of the Hackney Turks organised crime group, was found guilty of conspiring to murder Onur Guzel

The gunman's arm captured on CCTV in Umut 2000 shooting last year where Mr Guzel was shot in the torso

'There was significant criminality going on and it was all under the radar. They had an incredible level of loyalty.

'There were instances where drugs had gone missing and people would just be shot and killed.'

Gunduz became wrapped up in a world of criminality, working his way up to the top of the Hackney Turks.

A source in the Turkish community, who gave the name 'Yilmaz' to protect his identity, admits there were two sides to Gunduz, who was 'very charming towards women, very popular in the community and among his gang'.

'But when he needed to be scary and intimidating he was,' the source adds.

He reportedly has at least one child with a woman who lives in north London. But Yilmaz says his long-term girlfriend, Eylem Kahraman, 'went to prison because of him'.

In January 2018, Kahraman, a 31-year-old solicitor, was jailed for three years after she tried to dissuade a witness in a kidnap trial from coming to court and testifying.

Unsurprisingly, Gunduz has long denied any affiliation to a gang.

During his trial earlier this year, he was asked by his barrister Graham Trembath KC what he did for a living.

'I bought and sold cars, and received benefits from the DWP,' Gunduz said, adding that he made a lot of money betting on football.

'That is obviously a lie,' says a man named Hakan, who is familiar with the Turkish underworld in London and wished only to give his first name in fear of reprisals.

'He's not making a living from football bets, he's just a gambling addict', he told us.

'His money was coming from drugs - cocaine, weed, heroin, they have drug cafes in Hackney which you can walk in and get drugs just like going into a coffee shop and getting breakfast.'

Police found the Kia Nero used in the attack minutes later in a nearby street, where it had been set on fire

Just weeks before, Gunduz had been demanding £100,000 from Mr Guzel, whose father owns the popular Umut 2000 restaurant in Dalston, east London (pictured). He accused the family of supporting the Tottenham Turks

Gunduz was also cross-examined in the witness box by prosecutor Jane Bickerstaff KC.

She said: 'Onur Guzel told us you were a member of the Hackney Turks.'

Ms Bickerstaff asked: 'What had you been doing that might make him think that?'

'I don't know, I'm not part of any gang or criminal activity,' Gunduz said, before feigning ignorance of the activities of the Hackney Turks or the Tottenham Turks.

She asked: 'Are you aware that they extort money from local businesses?'

Gunduz is listed as a director of a company called BG Cars, which sources say was a front for a cash-producing business which he could hide behind while doing what he really does – drug dealing and extortion.

Hakan says Gunduz's gang made large sums from extortion, which is known in Turkish as haraç, a word which dates back to the Ottoman Empire when it was a form of tax.

'BG Cars was just a cover-up, to wash the money,' he adds.

Indeed, it was a botched extortion attempt that led to Gunduz's downfall.

Gunduz organised the shooting of Onur Guzel outside Umut 2000 on June 20 last year – after two failed attempts.

Shots were previously fired at a house in Enfield, north London, which was close to the home of a member of the Guzel family on April 5.

Two days later, a gunman fired shots at Umut 2000 after it had closed for the night.

When it came to the trial, the terrified victim gave evidence from behind a green curtain.

Onur Guzel said a man he knew as 'Beyto' who was part of a local gang known as 'the Bombs' approached him on April 12, 2025.

He said the pair asked him who had been responsible for shooting up the restaurant before suggesting the Tottenham Turks might have been to blame.

Eylem Kahraman (pictured), said to be the long-term girlfriend of Gunduz who 'went to prison for him'

On another occasion, Beyto and an associate called 'Mus' met with Mr Guzel's father. They falsely accused him of paying protection money to their 'enemies' and demanded £100,000 to even the score.

The Guzel family did not have that sort of money and refused, sparking a devastating response from Beytullah Gunduz.

On June 20 last year, a stolen white Kia Niro drove past Umut 2000 and at 10.51pm, the gunman leaned across and fired through the passenger window, hitting Onur Guzel, who was standing outside.

Seven minutes later, CCTV caught Gunduz and his friend getting out of a Mercedes and looking towards the scene.

Detectives later arrested Gunduz, but the suspected gunman had already fled to Turkey.

While Gunduz may be spending the next two decades behind bars, he can think himself lucky to be alive. He should have been dead. Three times.

First, we should explain why he was a marked man.

Although the Baybasin family, led by 'Europe's Pablo Escobar' Huseyin Baybasin and his brother Mehmet, built the foundations of the Hackney Turks' heroin trade in the 1980s, the gang's feud with their Tottenham rivals has been dominated by two families that have their roots in central Anatolia.

The Armagans, who are a leading family in the Bombacilar gang, hail from the impoverished village of Kirkisrak, while the Erens – the bosses of the Tottenham Turks – are from the Maraş district of the nearby town of Elbistan.

The war escalated when gang member Kemal Armagan swore revenge after he was beaten up at the Manor Club snooker hall in Haringey, north London, in January 2009. The Erens were among those involved in the fight.

It is claimed that Armagan told police: 'I'm old school, I'll sort it out myself.'

And so it was that years of brutal violence followed, with gangsters and members of the public murdered and maimed on the streets of London and across Europe.

In February 2012, Kemal Armagan's brother Ali was shot dead outside Turnpike Lane Underground Station in north London.

Then, in the early hours of 22 April 2013, Zafer Eren, one of the leaders of the Tottenham gang, and cousin of one Kemal Eren, was shot dead in north London.

The gunman was 23-year-old Jamie Marsh-Smith, a ruthless contract killer who was nicknamed 'Freddy' after the notorious character from the Nightmare on Elm Street films.

Beytullah Gunduz, the gang boss who has just been jailed for life, went on trial accused of hiring Marsh-Smith to kill Zafer Eren, but a jury acquitted him in November 2014.

Forensics at the scene of Evin, where a nine-year-old girl was caught in the crossfire of a Turkish gangland shooting in Dalston

Our source, Yilmaz, told us: 'Zafer Eren's killing was a revenge attack for Ali Armagan's murder.

'Beytullah Gunduz was the one who hired the hitman but was found not guilty by a jury, but everyone outside knew it was him.'

From then on, he was the Tottenham Turks' top target and they reportedly put out a £200,000 contract on his life.

In the autumn of 2019 one of the leaders of the Tottenham Turks, Kemal Eren – known as 'Parmaksiz', which translates to 'No Fingers', after they were blasted off in a shooting – tried to have Gunduz killed.

From the sanctuary of Turkey, Eren used an encrypted phone to orchestrate the attack on Gunduz and two other lieutenants, using middleman Leon Smith.

Scotland Yard intercepted the plans and the Osman warning was issued.

Detectives also put covert surveillance devices in Smith's house and uncovered the details of the plot before the assassination attempt could go ahead. Strike one.

Then on 21 August 2020 Gunduz was shot in the neck in Clissold Park, Stoke Newington, but the firearm jammed, stopping the gunman from delivering a fatal second bullet. Strike two.

The third attempt on Beytullah Gunduz's life made headlines across the country in May 2024.

At 8pm Gunduz arrived outside the Evin restaurant in Dalston, east London, and shook hands with his friends, Erdal Ozmen, Mustafa Kiziltan, Kenan Aydogdu and Nasser Ali.

They sat at a table and chatted while eating, drinking and smoking.

But just after 9pm, Gunduz left. Strike three.

Ali Armagan and Izzet Eren were two godfathers of the Hackney Turks and Tottenham Turks respectively

Seventeen minutes later a gunman – hired by the Tottenham Turks – arrived on a high-powered Ducati motorbike and fired six shots at his table.

One bullet missed and went through a window, hitting a nine-year-old girl, who was eating an ice cream during a family trip to London. She was seriously injured but miraculously survived.

Mr Kiziltan, Mr Aydogdu and Mr Ali were all wounded too. The fourth man at the table – Erdal Ozmen – was unharmed, but would be gunned down in Stoke Newington a year later.

Tottenham Turks associate Javon Riley, 33, was jailed for life with a minimum of 34 years for ordering the Evin shooting, but the gunman is still at large.

The fact he is willing to do 34 years in prison rather than reveal who the gunman was shows the reach the Turkish gangs still have, former police officer Dal Babu says.

The retired Met Officer told the Mail: 'You've got somebody who's prepared to do 34 years rather than name people and negotiate.

'There are still significant holds that these groups have. That is somebody who is very concerned about what could happen to him inside prison or indeed his family.'

Six weeks after the attack outside Evin restaurant, the Hackney Turks hit back. But this time, their target was not in this country.

On July 10 2024 a key leader of the Tottenham Turks, 41-year-old Izzet Eren, was assassinated while sitting at a pavement café in Chișinău, Moldova.

Two men – one of whom, Kemal Armagan, is allegedly the boss of the Hackney gang – face trial in Moldova.

As for Beytullah Gunduz, will he retain his power behind bars?

'Don't be surprised if Gunduz is sent back to Turkey in a few years,' Hakan says, pointing out that Izzet Eren, a dual Turkish-British citizen, was deported.

'Gunduz is finished,' our source Yilmaz adds. 'All his friends turned against him and there isn't really anyone left here in the UK that will be able to control them.

'I give it a maximum of three or four years and both the Bombers and the Tottenham Turks will properly die down.'

Mr Babu also believes the once hugely powerful Turkish gangs could be losing their hold over the capital.

'They've lost the power that they once had because it was very much around the heroin trade.

'In the 80s, you had a high level of violence between the Turkish gangs, and there was always somebody to step up because it was incredibly lucrative.

'But we've seen key people either being arrested or deported.

'You've now got extensive CCTV, you've got a police force that has lots of Turkish officers, greater community confidence and people are prepared to talk.'

Beytullah Gunduz once ruled the streets of north London with an iron fist, driving around in flash cars, bullying locals and styling himself as a 'charming' ladies man, while underlings were sent down for his crimes.

But now the once-feared 'Bombers' boss faces years inside without a network of lieutenants to help and protect him from enemies with a lust for revenge.

After years at the top his luck on the streets of Hackney finally ran out, but whether the same will happen in the cells and on the landings of Britain's highest security jails remains to be seen.

#551. Worldwide website emergency explained: How a critical PHP weakness sparked a global cybersecurity alert - and exactly what it means for you

By WILIAM HUNTER, SENIOR SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY REPORTER

Published: 11:12 BST, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 15:00 BST, 22 October 2026

A critical weakness in the internet's foundations has gone unnoticed for decades.

But with the use of AI, it has finally been brought to light - triggering a global cybersecurity alert.

Researchers this week revealed fatal vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language - a critical open-source system built into millions of websites, from Wikipedia to government agencies.

Wiz, one of the companies that discovered the flaw, estimates '70 per cent of the internet' is affected as a result.

It has left security agencies scrambling to contain the damage since PHP released an update to patch the vulnerability on Wednesday.

Now cybersecurity experts are warning of a wave of hacking attempts in the coming weeks as more details about the vulnerability are made public - putting your private data at risk.

Thai Duong, chief of Calif, one of the companies that found the vulnerability, told the Daily Mail: 'The reality is that there's very little the average internet user can do.

'Should they be concerned? Yes, but there's no need to panic. The responsibility lies with website operators, hosting providers and the broader security community.'

Here, we explain what the vulnerability is and how it could affect you.

Cybersecurity researchers using AI tools sparked a worldwide website emergency this week by revealing fatal vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language. Pictured: Researchers using the PHP website to hack a dummy website

PHP, which stands for Hypertext Preprocessor, is a core piece of internet technology that has been used around the world since the early 2000s.

It was one of the very first pieces of 'server-side' web code, and has since become embedded in a vast swath of the modern internet.

Whenever you visit a website, PHP is the piece of software that gathers the information you need and presents it in a way you can actually read online.

Mr Duong says: 'PHP was one of the first successful dynamic languages designed for the web.

'As an early mover, it just happens that a lot of popular software in the internet ecosystem was written in PHP. Some of the biggest internet websites are written in PHP.'

Since it is free and open–source, meaning it is not operated by a private company or provided by a single supplier, it's particularly popular with governments and universities.

Experts compare finding a flaw in PHP to discovering that a certain type of brick has a safety recall. As such, a lot of infrastructure will be affected and it's up to the owners themselves to find out where the weakness lies.

Websites have been cautioned to update to the latest version of PHP or go offline to avoid hackers. Wikipedia temporarily took several systems offline on Wednesday as a result

PHP, which stands for Hypertext Preprocessor, is an open–source programming language used in lots of websites.

It is what experts call a 'server–side' web language, which lets webpages 'talk' to databases on servers.

That makes it vital for things like shopping or filling in forms online.

PHP started being used in the early 2000s and is now a 'building brick of the internet', making up millions of websites.

Even websites that don't directly rely on PHP might use third–party tools, extensions, or plugins that do.

This means up to 70 per cent of all websites online are reliant on the security of PHP.

The vulnerability in PHP is absolutely fatal for any unpatched website, since it allows hackers to remotely execute code inside PHP itself.

In simple terms, that means hackers can essentially seize control of any website without needing to guess or steal the passwords.

Mr Duong says: 'Once compromised, attackers could steal sensitive data, modify website content, or disrupt operations.

'They could also use the compromised websites as a foothold to penetrate deeper into an organization's internal network.'

Likewise, experts warn that criminals can spy on and steal data from affected servers, impersonate and control legitimate websites, infect visitors with malware, edit content on websites, shut down entire sites or lock the owners out and steal huge amounts of private data.

Shockingly, these weaknesses have been hidden inside the architecture of the internet for years.

Professor Richard Buckland, of the University of New South Wales, says: 'The PHP developers have known about this vulnerability for a long time.

'Two years ago they started to worry about it seriously. Apparently, they initially didn't think it was urgent as they couldn't see how an attacker could make use of the weakness.'

However, the current crisis has come to a head thanks to the work of cybersecurity researchers employing AI tools.

Wiz and Calif worked with ChatGPT maker OpenAI as part of the 'Patch the Planet' project, which is hunting for these exact types of core weaknesses.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, whose firm discovered the significant flaws with a tool it created

OpenAI says Calif used its cutting-edge AI model, GPT-5.6 Sol, to find two fatal weaknesses in PHP, with Wiz independently discovering and verifying the same bugs.

In a blog post, OpenAI said it considers this to be 'one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory'.

Wiz added: 'With 70 per cent of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated.

'It marks an AI inflexion point. The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade – what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit.'

On Wednesday, developers behind the PHP platform released a new version of the software that includes a fix for the two vulnerabilities.

The responsibility will now fall on individual companies and website operators to ensure their sites are updated to the latest version of PHP.

National bodies and cybersecurity agencies have been urging websites to be sure they are protected or go offline.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said: 'Organisations using any version of PHP are affected, and all organisations are highly encouraged to update to the latest fixed version.'

Meanwhile, the American National Security Agency wrote on X: 'Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities.

The National Security Agency cautioned that websites should update their systems or go 'offline until it can be fully mitigated'

'If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommend that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.'

Even the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, took to social media to urge people to check their website's security.

She wrote on X: 'We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight.

'If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk.'

The true scope of the changes will likely become apparent in the coming days, but multiple major sites have already gone down for short periods in preparation.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia, took down 'a number of other systems' as a precaution, leaving people unable to access some parts of the site.

The BBC took down sites hosting programmes such as Doctor Who and The Traitors.

Multiple Scottish public organisations have taken their websites down, including councils and health boards across the country.

Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi urged people to check their website's security or go offline

If you operate a website, you need to make sure that it is updated to the latest version of PHP.

Anyone who runs their own company should also speak to their IT admin and make sure everything is secure.

For the average person, there are no active steps you can take to avoid the issue.

Make sure you have two–factor authentication set up and avoid handing over too much personal information to websites.

Use guest checkouts on online stores to limit how much information you leave behind.

Avoid any suspicious websites where possible and pay attention to updates from government cybersecurity agencies.

Meanwhile, major national organisations have also taken the drastic step of taking their sites down, with the Finnish, Australian and Dutch governments all going offline.

In the Netherlands, the Dutch Parliament, the Dutch cybersecurity agency and the public-facing website for the Port of Rotterdam were taken offline.

It is not clear currently whether any sites have actually been hacked.

But internet service operators are already reporting an increase in hacking attempts, as well as worrying signs that the vulnerability was being used prior to the patch's release.

Matthew Prince, CEO of cybersecurity firm Cloudflare, wrote on X: 'In the 10 hours before it was publicly ​announced, across the network we saw ‌thousands of attempts to exploit it.

'That jumped to tens of ​thousands in the 45 minutes post–announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions ​now.'

Dr Junade Ali, cybersecurity expert at the Institution of Engineering and Technology, says: 'These new security vulnerabilities are significant, and there is evidence they are already being exploited. A number of firewall companies have already implemented protections.'

Likewise, Amazon says that the weakness is being 'broadly exploited in the wild' and reported that it had faced attacks using the vulnerability as early as October 17 – four days before the public reveal.

Details of the flaw were then leaked to social media on Tuesday, leading to another attack on Amazon's systems on October 21.

We don't currently know if anyone has been hacked, but cybersecurity company Cloudflare has reported 'millions' of attempts since the patch was made public

CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in a blog post that the attack appeared to have been 'conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure'.

No one is certain how details of the vulnerability appeared to have become public prior to the announcement, but experts speculate that criminals might have employed AI tools of their own.

Dr Shaanan Cohney, of the University of Melbourne, says: 'AI now makes it far too easy for attackers to find a flaw even when only its existence has been announced and not the details.

'Previously, the window between the announcement of a potential vulnerability and the time it took for a security researcher or hacker to find the specific vulnerability was long enough that one could responsibly put out an announcement.

'AI has changed things, and this means that now the world has to rethink how we handle the disclosure process of vulnerabilities.'

If you operate your own website, it is absolutely critical that you make sure the PHP patch has been applied.

However, even the average internet user needs to be cautious in the coming weeks.

With so many websites affected, experts are anticipating an increase in cybercrime and hacking attempts that could affect your private information.

Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at ESET, told the Daily Mail: 'For people who run their own websites, it is advised to make sure the fix has been applied to any vulnerable sites and to speak to their IT admins to make sure all is secure.

'But for the average internet user, they should use this situation as a reminder that data on websites can very quickly be stolen and that it is important to reduce the amount of sensitive data we hand over.'

Cybersecurity experts advise using multi–factor authentication services like Microsoft Authenticator and avoiding giving details to suspicious websites while the issue is resolved

Mr Moore recommends using multi–factor authentication, passkeys, and digital pay services rather than handing over card details to websites that might have been compromised.

He also recommends using a guest account when making online purchases to 'reduce the amount of information left on a website that could one day become vulnerable.'

Even if websites do implement the patch, the PHP vulnerability is so deep in the internet architecture that sites may still be vulnerable.

Most websites include multiple software components, plugins, and third–party services which they have very little control over.

If just one of these doesn't patch the PHP weakness, it could lead to the entire network becoming compromised.

Likewise, since PHP is such old software, some website operators may not even know that they have it in their systems.

Professor Buckland says: 'Don't believe everything you read on websites over the next few days or longer. It may be possible for malicious attackers to change wording on sites you trust.

'Wait for government announcements, but in the meantime, you can probably trust that cyber–mature organisations such as banks and telcos have done their patching already. For other websites, perhaps avoid logging into or visiting them for a few days.'
